required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach only with a staged, fail-closed rollout: deploy and verify RLP-capable router builds on all eight servers before any client sets the bit, and gate client activation on a router-version/health check. Document the new wire semantics, remove Power Peg only after the compatibility window, and add integration tests covering old/new router combinations plus monitoring and a rapid kill switch.
Every gateway, client, replay path, and alternate producer that can emit orders is included in the compatibility inventory.
No old router will receive an RLP-flagged order during the manual, non-atomic deployment window.
The bit is unused outside the observed month of production traffic, including stored, delayed, replayed, and non-production messages.
All router components and operators can verify the exact deployed build before client activation.
RLP handling can be made fail-closed and operationally reversible if a server is missed or a rollout partially fails.
A new client sending the bit to an old router could make the supposedly unreachable Power Peg path reachable, causing incorrect routing or other order damage.
Manual deployment without build verification can leave servers running incompatible binaries, with no immediate detection.
The month-long traffic observation may miss infrequent clients, batch/replay jobs, dormant code paths, or future producers.
Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a fallback and increases blast radius if RLP handling has defects.
Semantic reuse can create confusion in logs, support procedures, stored messages, and mixed-version incident response.

Run an integration test against one currently deployed or representative pre-release router, send a valid order with the header bit set, and observe whether the router enters Power Peg handling rather than rejecting or safely ignoring the order.
If the old router activates Power Peg, the proposed rollout is unsafe without a compatibility mechanism; it confirms that client activation must not precede verified router replacement.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator automated recovery, but make promotion region-aware and explicitly fence the failed primary before allowing writes; normally promote an East replica, reserving West promotion for an East-region failure. Define and test an RPO, replication-lag thresholds, application routing behavior, and recovery-time budget, and do not enable unattended recovery across all clusters until these checks pass. Raft protects the Orchestrator decision, not MySQL data durability or split-brain safety.
An East replica will normally be available and sufficiently caught up to serve the East application during a primary-host failure.
The failed primary can be reliably fenced or terminated before the replacement is made writable.
Consul integration and application retry/write behavior will route new connections to the promoted primary without unacceptable connection or DNS caching delays.
The acceptable RPO permits any asynchronous replication lag, including cross-region lag.
Orchestrator's recovery actions, topology updates, and promotion are safe for every cluster under the proposed automation.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged writes and create an unacceptable RPO; Raft does not make replication synchronous.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and divergence when connectivity returns.
Promoting a West replica may add roughly 60 ms or more to every write and may not satisfy the application's latency or availability requirements.
Unattended recovery for all clusters can amplify a topology error, bad promotion choice, or Consul integration failure into a broad outage.
The stated under-one-minute objective is not demonstrated: detection, promotion, fencing, Consul propagation, client reconnection, and application retries may exceed that budget.

During a controlled East-primary host failure, continuously issue uniquely identified committed writes, then promote the configured candidate and verify every acknowledged write ID is present before declaring recovery successful; also measure detection-to-write-readiness time.
Any missing acknowledged write falsifies safe automated promotion under the current asynchronous design; a recovery time over 60 seconds falsifies the stated objective.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-repurposing approach, but deploy gateway/router support disabled with strict validation, a centralized allowlist and kill switch, and compatible binaries before launch. Prove legacy-bit non-emission across all supported clients rather than inferring it from one month of production traffic, then canary and incrementally enable RLP while verifying actual build IDs, effective configuration, routing results, errors, and latency.
No current or supported client can emit the Power Peg bit under any supported configuration or order path.
Gateway and router versions handling the repurposed bit can be fully deployed before clients begin setting it.
The router can centrally disable RLP and reject invalid flag combinations without affecting legacy traffic.
The bit is exposed and routable consistently through every relevant gateway and router version.
Client rollout can be coordinated so the bit is not set before server compatibility is confirmed.
A stale, archival, or rarely exercised client sets the bit and unintentionally activates RLP.
Partial gateway/router deployment produces inconsistent interpretation, dropped orders, or failed routing.
Immediate client activation skips canarying and removes any safe period for detecting compatibility defects.
Compatibility checks accept unknown flag combinations or fail open.
Operators cannot verify the binary and effective RLP configuration actually running on each host.

Inventory every supported client release, its source/configuration paths, and retained traffic captures, then test representative order submissions for any nonzero Power Peg value.
Any supported client or configuration found capable of setting the bit falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires explicit sender identification, migration blocking, or rollout segmentation before repurposing it.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but initially restrict it to the main East-primary cluster and prefer an East-local replica for host failures; reserve West promotion for confirmed East-region failure. Add reliable fencing so an isolated old primary cannot accept writes, and define the acceptable asynchronous RPO before enabling promotion regardless of region. Validate the complete detection-to-reconnect-and-write path, including ambiguous commits, under one minute; pseudo-GTID simplifies topology but does not establish freshness or prevent data loss.
Orchestrator can complete detection, candidate selection, promotion, and topology publication within the remaining 25 seconds after its 30-second trigger.
A Raft quorum will remain available throughout East database failures.
Orchestrator can reliably distinguish the freshest candidate, or the business explicitly accepts asynchronous replication loss.
The old primary can be fenced automatically at the host, network, or MySQL-access layer.
East application instances can reconnect to a West primary and tolerate roughly 60 ms database RTT.
A network partition can produce dual writable primaries because Orchestrator consensus does not itself fence the old database.
Asynchronous promotion can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft and pseudo-GTID do not prevent this.
Selecting a West replica for an East host failure shifts every write across regions and may exceed latency or throughput limits.
Enabling recovery for all clusters simultaneously creates a correlated automation blast radius.
Consul updates or Rails connection recovery may finish after promotion, or retries may duplicate non-idempotent writes.

In staging, partition the primary from Orchestrator while keeping a database client connected; after 35 seconds, attempt writes through both the old primary and the advertised replacement, while timing when a new write succeeds.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts a conflicting write after replacement promotion, or if end-to-end writable recovery takes longer than 60 seconds. Success requires automatic fencing or refusal of old-primary writes, exactly one authoritative writer, and timely service rediscovery.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for jobs: AFS/AOF persistence does not persist Pub/Sub messages for disconnected subscribers, and an in-worker retry wrapper cannot recover a message that was never delivered. Instead, simplify and harden RabbitMQ with a minimal topology, quorum queues for critical work, standardized idempotent handlers, graceful worker draining, and automated upgrades; consider Redis Streams only through a separately tested migration pilot.
That AOF makes Pub/Sub messages durable while subscribers are unavailable.
That job delivery is optional or can be reconstructed reliably from another source.
That every subscriber is continuously connected and processing each message exactly once.
That running RabbitMQ and Redis paths simultaneously will not cause duplicate side effects.
That sub-millisecond latency and high throughput imply the needed delivery semantics.
Payment, fulfillment, email, or indexing events can be silently lost during worker restarts, deployment, network partitions, or Redis failover.
A transiently healthy subscriber may acknowledge or attempt processing immediately before crashing, with no broker-side redelivery guarantee.
Dual-running paths can send the same job to both systems unless deduplication is proven, risking duplicate payment or fulfillment effects.
Treating Redis cache and rate-limit pressure as isolated becomes unsafe once job loss or restart pressure is coupled to those services.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ after a week would remove the only tested replay path for poison jobs, delayed retries, and DLQ investigation.
Reduce operational burden in place: standardize a small RabbitMQ queue/exchange topology, use quorum queues for critical durable jobs, implement explicit retry/DLQ streams or queues, require idempotency for all side effects, add graceful draining for frequent deployments, and automate node replacement and upgrades. This directly targets the reported toil without replacing at-least-once delivery with fire-and-forget messaging.
In a non-production Redis instance, subscribe to a test channel, publish 1,000 uniquely numbered payloads, terminate the subscriber before it can process them, restart it, and compare received IDs; also inspect Redis persistence and restart behavior.
The restarted subscriber receives zero or only a small number of the previously published messages, proving that AOF does not provide queued recovery and falsifying the durability assumption. Delivery while continuously subscribed would validate only transport performance, not failure safety.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse direction, but do not enable clients based solely on one month of observed traffic. First audit every client and gateway path that writes or interprets the bit, deploy the new router build to all eight servers with artifact verification, and stage activation with shadow metrics, a kill switch, and explicit mixed-version testing before clients set the bit.
No current, archived, dormant, external, failover, replay, or recovery component sets or interprets the header bit.
All router nodes and relevant recovery processes will run the RLP-capable build before any client sets the bit.
Older routers preserve unknown header bits, so mixed-version operation is safe during staged deployment.
RLP eligibility and all required routing data already exist; a new message field is genuinely unnecessary.
RLP failure can be contained without exposing orders to divergent routing, duplicate execution, or loss of service.
A dormant or external client can set the retired bit and unintentionally activate RLP or incompatible semantics.
Manual deployment can leave servers on different builds, producing inconsistent routing with no prompt detection.
Early client activation can send RLP requests to unprepared routers, causing rejects, latency spikes, or incorrect order handling.
Removing the Power Peg code may eliminate latent behavior relied on by diagnostics, replay, or recovery tooling if the bit is not actually unreachable.
A new RLP failure path without tested fallback, rate limits, or a kill switch can harm order execution under adverse liquidity or latency conditions.

Perform a repository, binary-interface, configuration, and client inventory search for the exact header bit mask and legacy Power Peg flag across all client, gateway, replay, recovery, and external integration sources.
Any current or dormant component that sets, clears, or branches on the bit falsifies the 'provably unused' premise and blocks direct reuse without a compatibility plan; a complete audit finding no such use confirms that specific premise.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver path and global log-only phase, but require deterministic PCRE safety/latency tests, mandatory peer approval, per-rule automatic abort thresholds, and a rehearsed kill switch before activation. After logging, block on a small traffic slice for 5-10 minutes and check errors, p99 latency, CPU, and rule match volume before global blocking; emergency execution time should be capped and measured end to end.
The rule engine bounds regex execution, or CI can reliably detect catastrophic backtracking using adversarial inputs.
Quicksilver can activate log mode and later blocking globally within minutes, with consistent version state at every PoP.
Log evaluation adds acceptable CPU and latency even when a request produces many matches.
Match-volume telemetry is available within minutes and has useful PoP-, customer-, and traffic-normalized baselines.
A single rule can be disabled immediately without disrupting the rest of the WAF configuration.
A vulnerable or pathological PCRE consumes enough CPU in log mode to degrade customer traffic before any match threshold is evaluated.
A broad signature produces many benign matches; the ten-minute observation either misses rare events or causes an extended global denial when switched to block.
A bad configuration is partially activated across PoPs, yielding inconsistent protection and difficult incident diagnosis.
Telemetry is delayed, aggregated too coarsely, or unavailable during the disclosure, leaving the team to block without production evidence.
The process is rushed, omitting security review or rollback verification precisely when operational pressure is highest.
Use the proposed path as the standard, but define it as a gated incident release: static and adversarial regex validation, peak-load replay, global log mode for 10 minutes, a 5-10 minute blocking canary, then global block. This is a modification rather than a separate architecture because it preserves the proposal's low operational complexity while adding protections for false positives and rollout failure.
Replay the candidate regex plus worst-case encodings and match-heavy inputs through the actual PCRE engine in log mode under representative peak-load concurrency, while measuring proxy CPU, p99 latency, and per-rule match throughput.
The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation can breach the defined CPU or latency budget, cannot terminate within the rule-execution timeout, or produces enough matches/events that telemetry or rollback cannot process within minutes.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain the expedited Quicksilver path, but add worst-case CPU/latency limits, verify atomic and authenticated version activation, and provide an independently tested kill switch before blocking globally. Use representative canaries and centralized attack/false-positive telemetry, and deploy a minimal containment rule immediately while the complete signature is validated.
CI payload-corpus coverage is sufficient to detect harmful rules and known attack variants.
Quicksilver can activate one version atomically and consistently across every PoP within the response window.
The candidate rule has bounded worst-case CPU and regex-backtracking behavior under peak load.
Ten minutes of global log-mode telemetry is sufficient to expose false positives and attack misses.
A tested rollback or kill switch can remove the rule globally within minutes without proxy restart.
A catastrophically expensive regex could exhaust CPU across all proxies before log mode detects it.
A false positive could then block legitimate traffic globally when the rule changes to block mode.
A partial or delayed rollout could leave inconsistent protection despite a nominally immediate publish.
Encoding, parser, or protocol variants may pass the corpus and remain unblocked.
Compilation, cache invalidation, or activation performed on the request path could itself cause an outage.
Publish a minimal, narrowly scoped containment rule immediately, then validate and activate the full signature through corpus, performance, representative canary, atomic-version, and automated rollback gates within the hour.
Benchmark the exact candidate rule against worst-case and representative payloads at peak concurrency, including any CI-corpus edge cases, while measuring proxy CPU and request latency.
The proposal is falsified if the rule can exceed the predefined CPU or latency budget, show superlinear backtracking, or miss disclosed exploit variants; safe bounded behavior supports proceeding with the additional rollout controls.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep decimal strings as the canonical representation, but do not change all v1 responses without establishing backward compatibility. Prefer a new API version, or prove that every v1 consumer accepts strings and update web/mobile/SDK decoders before release. Explicitly handle ID fields in requests, URLs, pagination, errors, and all serializers, and add cross-client tests.
All v1 consumers can tolerate a JSON string in the id field within the release window.
The change is applied consistently to every response and request representation of an order ID.
Clients and generated SDKs will not coerce decimal strings through JavaScript Number.
Clients send IDs back as strings and URL-safe values without passing through an unsafe numeric representation.
No legacy numeric-ID endpoint or compatibility path is required during migration.
Older mobile or partner clients may reject string IDs, causing outages or failed orders.
An unupdated endpoint, error payload, or pagination payload may still emit numeric IDs and reintroduce precision loss.
SDK regeneration may produce JavaScript clients that parse or coerce IDs as Number despite the OpenAPI string type.
Clients may continue sending corrupted numeric IDs in requests or URLs after receiving string IDs.
An in-place v1 contract change can break consumers immediately, with no version boundary for rollback or migration.
Introduce a new API version that makes decimal strings canonical while retaining the existing numeric-ID version temporarily, then migrate first-party clients, SDK templates, and high-traffic partners with a documented deprecation plan.
Run a contract inventory and compatibility test: enumerate every v1 response/request field carrying an order ID, then execute representative requests against the web app, iOS/Android decoders, generated partner SDKs, and at least one legacy consumer.
If any field remains numeric, any client rejects or coerces strings, or any legacy consumer cannot be updated during the two-week window, the proposed in-place v1 change is unsafe; those results falsify its compatibility assumptions.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Retain Orchestrator automated recovery, but require reliable primary fencing, explicitly define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, and verify atomic Consul endpoint replacement with client reconnection. Do not enable this blindly for all clusters or claim Raft makes failover safe: Raft protects topology decisions, not MySQL writes or replication consistency.
A failed old primary is made read-only or reliably fenced before another replica is promoted, including during network partitions.
Applications resolve the writable endpoint through Consul and reconnect after its value changes without retaining independent connections to the old primary.
Orchestrator selects a candidate with acceptable replication lag, and detection, promotion, discovery propagation, and reconnection consistently complete within the remaining time after the 30-second threshold.
Some acknowledged writes may be lost under asynchronous replication, or the deployment will add a replication mechanism that provides the required durability.
The promoted replica and its dependent systems can handle production write traffic from East, including approximately 60 ms cross-region latency.
A network partition can leave the old primary accepting writes while Orchestrator promotes another node, causing split brain and irreversible divergence.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft quorum does not establish that the candidate contains the latest committed write.
The 30-second detection threshold leaves only about 30 seconds for promotion, Consul propagation, connection draining, and application reconnection, making the under-one-minute objective fragile.
Selecting a West replica 'regardless of region' may unnecessarily move writes across 60 ms even when a sufficiently current East replica is available.
Blind enablement across clusters can promote unsafe candidates or update unsupported discovery integrations, and pseudo-GTID does not remove the need to validate binlog-position and replication semantics.
Use Orchestrator as the recovery coordinator, but add an explicit fencing mechanism for every possible primary, configure and test region-aware candidate eligibility against measured replica lag, and route clients through a Consul-managed logical primary endpoint that switches atomically and supports fast connection refresh. Validate an explicit RPO and use native MySQL 5.7 GTID where applicable rather than treating pseudo-GTID as a durability mechanism.
In staging, continuously write committed, uniquely numbered rows through the current primary; isolate that primary from Orchestrator and replicas while leaving it reachable by the application, trigger automated recovery, then continue writing to the old endpoint.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary still accepts committed writes after another node is promoted, or if recovery plus Consul/client convergence exceeds 60 seconds. It is supported only if fencing prevents old-primary writes and the measured convergence meets the objective.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator and Raft as the failover mechanism, but do not enable unqualified promotion of any replica across regions. Configure explicit candidate eligibility, split-brain/fencing protections, and Consul/application health-routing integration; define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, including writes during detection and promotion. Validate that East application hosts can reliably use a West primary and that recovery completes within the one-minute objective.
East application hosts have production-grade network connectivity and acceptable latency to a West MySQL primary.
Orchestrator is correctly integrated with the application's Consul-based primary discovery and can atomically publish the new endpoint.
The deployment has fencing or equivalent protection against an isolated old primary continuing to accept writes.
Promoting a cross-region asynchronous replica will lose no writes that the product requires to retain.
All clusters use compatible MySQL 5.7 binary logging, Pseudo-GTID, credentials, and replication settings for Orchestrator recovery.
A 30-second reachability threshold can trigger failover during a transient partition while the East primary continues accepting writes, creating divergent primaries and irreversible data loss.
Asynchronous cross-region replication permits committed East writes to be absent from the West replica at promotion time; selecting the most advanced replica does not eliminate this RPO.
Promoting a West replica without verified East-to-West database routing or adequate client/network behavior can cause an extended application outage rather than sub-minute recovery.
Orchestrator's topology update alone does not guarantee that every Rails connection pool, Consul consumer, and connection-establishment path will follow the new primary.
Enabling automated recovery for all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can cause simultaneous or unsafe failovers during a regional event.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, uniquely identifiable writes, kill the East primary, and measure from failure detection through successful application writes while checking the old primary, selected replica, Consul endpoint, and write continuity.
The proposal is falsified if writes accepted by the old primary are missing after promotion, the old primary remains writable, East clients cannot write to the promoted replica within the required interval, or Consul/application traffic does not converge to the new primary.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach only with a staged, fail-closed rollout: deploy and verify RLP-capable router builds on all eight servers before any client sets the bit, and gate client activation on a router-version/health check. Document the new wire semantics, remove Power Peg only after the compatibility window, and add integration tests covering old/new router combinations plus monitoring and a rapid kill switch.
Every gateway, client, replay path, and alternate producer that can emit orders is included in the compatibility inventory.
No old router will receive an RLP-flagged order during the manual, non-atomic deployment window.
The bit is unused outside the observed month of production traffic, including stored, delayed, replayed, and non-production messages.
All router components and operators can verify the exact deployed build before client activation.
RLP handling can be made fail-closed and operationally reversible if a server is missed or a rollout partially fails.
A new client sending the bit to an old router could make the supposedly unreachable Power Peg path reachable, causing incorrect routing or other order damage.
Manual deployment without build verification can leave servers running incompatible binaries, with no immediate detection.
The month-long traffic observation may miss infrequent clients, batch/replay jobs, dormant code paths, or future producers.
Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a fallback and increases blast radius if RLP handling has defects.
Semantic reuse can create confusion in logs, support procedures, stored messages, and mixed-version incident response.

Run an integration test against one currently deployed or representative pre-release router, send a valid order with the header bit set, and observe whether the router enters Power Peg handling rather than rejecting or safely ignoring the order.
If the old router activates Power Peg, the proposed rollout is unsafe without a compatibility mechanism; it confirms that client activation must not precede verified router replacement.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table receiving 25k inserts/s and bulk deletes. Keep it enabled for anti-wraparound protection, but raise its per-table trigger threshold and throttle its I/O cost; explicitly vacuum only during a bounded low-traffic window after confirming that the required work completes within that window. Monitor dead-tuple growth, vacuum duration, bloat, transaction age, and business-hour I/O before and after rollout.
A weekly VACUUM can scan and compact all pages made dead by the bulk deletes within the Sunday window.
The bulk-delete volume is small enough to maintain a bounded dead-tuple population.
Cron execution is monitored and will not be silently skipped, overlap, or terminate a vacuum on every run.
The table's transaction ID age will remain far from wraparound thresholds.
Most visible latency is caused by vacuum-generated I/O rather than delete WAL, checkpoint, or filesystem behavior.
Disabling table autovacuum also disables its anti-wraparound safety, creating a path to an emergency, prolonged vacuum and severe database impact.
A weekly vacuum may not complete on a 1.8 TB table, causing dead tuples and bloat to grow continuously between runs.
A failed cron invocation can leave the table without autovacuum indefinitely.
Overlapping manual VACUUM jobs can multiply storage-engine and WAL I/O.
Regular VACUUM reclaims dead space for reuse but does not return space to the operating system, so filesystem-level bloat may remain or worsen.
Use per-table autovacuum settings: keep `autovacuum_enabled=true`, increase `vacuum_threshold` and `vacuum_scale_factor` so routine vacuuming is not triggered too frequently, and use table-specific `vacuum_cost_delay`/`vacuum_cost_limit` values to reduce I/O bursts. Run a separately scheduled off-peak `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` only if measurements show one is needed, with a single-job lock, a strict completion deadline, alerting, and escalation that restarts autovacuum if the schedule fails.
Sample hourly during one week: `SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, age(datmin) FROM pg_stat_user_tables s JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=s.relid WHERE s.relname='events';`, and correlate the result with vacuum logs and disk I/O.
If dead tuples or transaction age continue rising throughout the week, a vacuum cannot complete within the low-traffic window, or vacuum-related I/O still overlaps business hours, the weekly-off-peak assumption is disproven.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Keep the billing-core/clean-model direction, but reject the three-month single cut-over. First build a representative historical invoice corpus and characterize existing behavior, then introduce immutable inputs and service-specific adapters with incremental migrations and dual-run comparisons. Preserve the old implementation until equivalence and rollback criteria are demonstrated for all 37 plans and cross-service effects.
Historical invoice inputs and provider responses are sufficient to deterministically reproduce current outputs.
The five services can be migrated independently without changing business semantics during the transition.
The new model can represent all grandfathering, proration, tax, rounding, and billing-cycle variations without lossy mappings.
Other teams can tolerate or be isolated from a long-lived billing-v2 branch and eventual integration conflict.
Unit tests for billing-core can establish real invoice equivalence rather than merely validate the new model.
A single cut-over can change invoices for grandfathered plans, rounding, proration, tax, or payment sequencing, causing financial and contractual damage.
Deleting the old implementation removes the reference oracle needed to detect semantic regressions.
A shared mutable BillingContext may have service-specific mutation and interpretation behavior that a clean model silently normalizes.
A long branch will conflict with approximately 40 weekly PRs and force risky late integration.
A nominally unified core may still be interpreted differently by each service, preserving duplication while creating migration complexity.
Create billing-core as a versioned, pure domain boundary, but migrate rule families incrementally. Add characterization/golden tests from historical invoices, adapt legacy context into immutable typed inputs, migrate one service or rule family at a time, and use shadow or dual-run comparisons before switching behavior. Retain the old path behind a controlled flag until all 37 plans pass production-like equivalence tests.
Build a small replay harness over a representative set of stored historical invoices and provider responses, running the current production path and billing-core candidates and comparing normalized invoice line items, totals, tax, and proration outputs.
If the current path cannot be replayed deterministically, or if any representative historical case lacks enough information to reproduce the invoice, the proposed single cut-over and its claimed equivalence cannot be validated; the missing behavior must be characterized before migration.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Retain the wave migration, but add shadow-mode validation and explicitly freeze automatic reduction for user-ID during migration and until its reports and enforcement behavior are proven across regions. Before deregistration, compare both systems’ usage and decisions at peak load, and retain a tested rollback path until the new system meets availability and write-rejection targets.
The new system can disable automatic reduction for user-ID without affecting other services.
Usage reports are complete, sufficiently current, and consistent across regions.
Legacy and new systems use equivalent allocation, accounting, grace-period, and enforcement semantics.
Registration changes can be coordinated so the service is never simultaneously unenrolled or subject to conflicting enforcement.
The new manager can meet user-ID’s latency, availability, and multi-region consistency requirements.
A delayed or understated usage report can cause the new system to reject valid user-ID database writes across regions.
Automatic reduction can lower user-ID allocation below demand before the grace-period buffer accounts for actual reporting lag.
A mismatch in quota semantics can unexpectedly enforce a lower effective limit than the legacy manager.
Deregistering from legacy before validating the new path removes the ability to roll back safely.
Inconsistent or missing regional data can produce different enforcement outcomes, causing partial or intermittent login-account write failures.
Migrate noncritical services first in shadow mode, then migrate user-ID with automatic reductions disabled and a deliberately padded, fixed allocation. Dual-report and compare usage and decisions under peak multi-region load, retain legacy fallback for a defined observation period, and only then deregister legacy; enable automatic reductions later once operational evidence supports it.
Run user-ID in dual-reporting shadow mode for a representative peak-load period, including all regions, and compare the legacy and new systems’ usage totals, allocation values, and would-reject decisions; also measure report age and cross-region convergence.
The proposal would be falsified if reports are materially stale or region-inconsistent, semantics differ, or the new system would reject writes that the legacy system accepts under the copied allocation.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse direction only as a time-boxed compatibility measure, but make rollout two-phase: deploy the backward-compatible RLP-capable router to all eight servers, verify exact build identity and RLP readiness, then permit clients to set the bit through a centrally controlled admission gate. Do not remove Power Peg in the same release; retain it behind an explicit server-side deny/default-off control until the RLP path is proven and rollback safety is established.
No legitimate producer outside the inspected production traffic—including replay, recovery, administrative, test, archived, or failover clients—can set the bit.
No order can reach a stale or old router after clients begin setting the bit.
The gateway can centrally withhold RLP-bit traffic until every production server is verified RLP-capable.
RLP eligibility is implemented consistently by all clients, gateways, and routers.
The old router's Power Peg behavior cannot be activated by the new RLP traffic if mixed versions occur.
A stale router may receive the RLP bit and execute the retired Power Peg algorithm, misrouting orders across the entire 3M-order/day workload.
Rollback to a pre-RLP router while clients still set the bit may immediately create mixed-version behavior.
A month of traffic does not establish that archived, replayed, test, administrative, or failover producers never set the bit.
Manual deployment provides no reliable evidence that all eight servers run the intended build.
Simultaneously removing Power Peg and introducing RLP makes rollback and incident diagnosis substantially harder.
If the date cannot accommodate a versioned message change, isolate RLP traffic on a separate listener or transport with an RLP-capable router fleet, so legacy routers can never receive the RLP signal. If isolation is infeasible, retain a coordinated protocol-version change and seek a staged exchange launch rather than relying on bit semantics.
In a production-like staging test, run an unmodified pre-RLP router and send otherwise valid orders with the reused header bit set through the actual gateway-to-router path; also search every producer and replay/recovery code path for writes to the bit.
Any old-router path that accepts and acts on the set bit, or any non-RLP producer capable of setting it, falsifies the proposal's safety premise and requires a separate admission boundary or replacement approach.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Add an explicit reconciliation and cutover protocol: pre-populate historical usage, disable automatic reductions until each service has established complete reporting with the new manager, and require warm-up plus health verification before deregistration. For user-ID, use conservative fixed allocations, cross-region enforcement testing, and an independently controlled rollback/kill switch; do not rely on the generic grace period as the sole safeguard.
Copying the current allocation also initializes enough historical usage data to prevent immediate automatic reduction.
Registration and deregistration cannot create an interval in which inconsistent quota decisions are enforced.
Usage-reporting completeness and freshness are comparable between the legacy and new systems.
The new manager's reduced allocation propagates consistently across all user-ID database regions.
Weeks of unchanged reported usage reliably predict future peak demand.
An automatic reduction below the user-ID database's real retained-data footprint could reject writes globally across regions, including account creation and login flows.
During migration, the service might report to one manager while enforcement or stale usage data is obtained from the other, producing inconsistent accept/reject decisions.
The claimed grace period may begin before sufficient observations are collected, allowing an unproven allocation reduction.
Allocation copies may omit reserved, archival, replication, compaction, or growth requirements that the legacy manager included.
Deregistering the legacy manager without a tested rollback path could leave the service with no effective quota enforcement or make rollback unsafe.
Migrate noncritical services through a shadow period with dual reporting and decision comparison, followed by atomic enforcement cutover. Keep automatic reductions disabled until parity and forecasting thresholds are proven, then enable them first for low-risk services and only later for user-ID under fixed safety floors and regional write-failure tests.
In staging, run user-ID with identical storage and replicated writes while the new manager is set just below current observed usage but above the proposed operational floor; then toggle manager registration during a write and inspect all regional write outcomes.
The proposal is unsafe if any region rejects a normal write, decisions differ between managers or regions, or registration transition changes enforcement before reporting is reconciled.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not fully disable autovacuum or rely on a fixed weekly schedule for a 1.8 TB table with bulk deletes. Keep it enabled as a safety net, tune autovacuum thresholds and cost limits for `events`, and explicitly trigger or schedule a strongly throttled vacuum after bulk deletes; retain a bounded off-peak manual vacuum if weekly maintenance is still needed.
Dead-tuple production and vacuum throughput are stable enough for Sunday's window to be predictable.
The bulk deletes are small and are not themselves a major source of write-latency spikes.
A low-traffic window exists that is long enough for a throttled vacuum to finish.
Disabling normal autovacuum cannot cause PostgreSQL's anti-wraparound autovacuum to run later.
Weekly ANALYZE is frequent enough to prevent materially stale statistics.
Autovacuum already runs for many hours; a weekly cron vacuum could overlap business hours and reproduce or prolong the latency problem.
Large delete batches may create enough dead tuples to exceed safe thresholds before Sunday.
Without autovacuum, vacuum backlog or transaction-age emergencies receive no normal cleanup and may trigger disruptive anti-wraparound work.
Default vacuum cost settings may still generate unacceptable I/O even during the cron window.
Statistics can become stale between weekly runs, causing poor query plans.
Use continuous, throttled targeted autovacuum with appropriately low scale-factor/threshold values and conservative cost limits, then trigger a throttled vacuum soon after each bulk delete. This adapts to actual churn while spreading I/O; monitor dead tuples, vacuum backlog, database age, and latency before considering additional off-peak runs.
Compare existing autovacuum log start/finish timestamps and dead-tuple counts around one bulk-delete cycle; calculate the observed vacuum rate and extrapolate cleanup duration for the week's accumulated dead tuples.
If projected cleanup time exceeds the available 02:00-to-business-hours window, or bulk deletes can generate more dead tuples than that window can process, the weekly-only proposal is falsified.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach, but do not ship it as described without a compatibility check across every client/gateway/parser, an explicit rollback control, and a per-server build/version verification after the manual deployment. Preserve the old Power Peg code until rollout is proven safe rather than deleting it in the same release; a month of zero observed bits does not prove that all readers treat it identically.
The bit is unused by every current and planned client, gateway, parser, diagnostic tool, and counterparty, not merely absent in observed traffic.
All relevant components can agree on the new meaning without a wire-format change and will not reject or ignore it.
The new RLP path is functionally, operationally, and performance-tested for eligible and ineligible orders.
The router can distinguish RLP eligibility consistently, including orders that lack the bit.
A documented kill switch can disable RLP without requiring a synchronized client and router redeployment.
A legacy or divergent implementation interprets the bit as Power Peg, causing unintended routing or inconsistent behavior.
Removing the old code eliminates the safest fallback and makes rollback dependent on a new build or another control.
Manual deployment leaves servers on mixed builds, producing nondeterministic participation and making incidents hard to attribute.
Launch-day client flag changes expose untested interactions at full volume, including latency, matching, liquidity, and risk-limit failures.
A configuration or eligibility mismatch causes some RLP-eligible orders to bypass RLP or some ineligible orders to enter it.

Perform a repository/protocol inventory and staging end-to-end test: search all parsers and routing branches for the bit, then send representative orders with it set and unset through each client/gateway version and verify identical non-RLP behavior except for the intended RLP selection.
Any additional semantic use, a component that ignores or rejects the bit, or changed behavior for ineligible/non-RLP orders falsifies the claimed compatibility and blocks the proposed release.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-repurposing approach, but deploy gateway/router support disabled with strict validation, a centralized allowlist and kill switch, and compatible binaries before launch. Prove legacy-bit non-emission across all supported clients rather than inferring it from one month of production traffic, then canary and incrementally enable RLP while verifying actual build IDs, effective configuration, routing results, errors, and latency.
No current or supported client can emit the Power Peg bit under any supported configuration or order path.
Gateway and router versions handling the repurposed bit can be fully deployed before clients begin setting it.
The router can centrally disable RLP and reject invalid flag combinations without affecting legacy traffic.
The bit is exposed and routable consistently through every relevant gateway and router version.
Client rollout can be coordinated so the bit is not set before server compatibility is confirmed.
A stale, archival, or rarely exercised client sets the bit and unintentionally activates RLP.
Partial gateway/router deployment produces inconsistent interpretation, dropped orders, or failed routing.
Immediate client activation skips canarying and removes any safe period for detecting compatibility defects.
Compatibility checks accept unknown flag combinations or fail open.
Operators cannot verify the binary and effective RLP configuration actually running on each host.

Inventory every supported client release, its source/configuration paths, and retained traffic captures, then test representative order submissions for any nonzero Power Peg value.
Any supported client or configuration found capable of setting the bit falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires explicit sender identification, migration blocking, or rollout segmentation before repurposing it.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Change recovery to East-first promotion and explicitly fence or irreversibly demote the old primary before exposing the new writable endpoint; Orchestrator Raft quorum alone does not provide database fencing. Specify the Consul/proxy update mechanism, validate replica currency and application reconnection, and measure end-to-end first successful write within 60 seconds. Verify application-tier HA separately if East application availability is in scope.
Orchestrator can identify the most up-to-date eligible replica without promoting a stale West replica during an East-only failure.
The old primary can be reliably fenced or forced into super_read_only with stale sessions terminated before promotion.
Consul or a database proxy will atomically expose only the promoted primary to applications.
Replicas contain every required binlog transaction and have compatible MySQL 5.7 replication configuration.
Applications reconnect, retry safely, and remain available when an East application host fails.
The old primary may remain writable during a network partition, causing split brain and irreversible divergence.
Selecting by region without a reliable replication-position comparison could promote a substantially stale West replica.
Pseudo-GTID operation does not guarantee zero acknowledged-write loss or prove that the chosen replica is current.
Detection, promotion, service-discovery propagation, and connection-pool recovery may exceed the one-minute target.
Unspecified endpoint updates or unsafe write retries can leave clients targeting the failed primary or duplicate transactions.
Use Orchestrator-driven East-first recovery with pre-promotion fencing, an explicitly validated replica-health check, and a Consul/proxy-controlled writable endpoint; retain West as a separate disaster-recovery path rather than a normal host-failure fallback.
Run one isolated-primary game-day test while continuously attempting writes through the application's resolved database endpoint, and record the last acknowledged East write, promotion time, endpoint-change time, and first successful write.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts any write after promotion, the promoted node lacks the last acknowledged transaction, or the first successful application write occurs more than 60 seconds after failure.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach, but add an RLP runtime feature flag that defaults off, deploy and verify the new router build on all eight servers before clients set the bit, and canary enablement after mixed-version testing. Remove or hard-disable Power Peg, document the bit's new meaning, and prohibit binary rollback once clients emit it unless old binaries can be guaranteed incapable of interpreting it.
All supported client and gateway versions—and future configuration paths—leave the bit zero today and can reliably set it only for RLP-eligible orders.
The bit has one defined meaning at every gateway-to-router hop and is not transformed, masked, or reserved by protocol handling.
Router configuration can disable RLP immediately without a restart or redeployment.
The new router correctly rejects or safely handles RLP-marked orders before rollout completes.
Power Peg has no dormant side effects outside its supposedly unreachable routing branch.
A legacy, niche, or future client that sets the bit could unintentionally invoke RLP or an incompatible router behavior.
An old router receiving the newly used bit may activate the retained Power Peg path, especially during rollback or incomplete deployment.
A month of captures proves only historical non-use, not that every producer and deployment configuration is safe.
The manual process may leave servers on different builds, producing node-dependent behavior at roughly 3M orders per day.
Enabling RLP globally without a kill switch could amplify incorrect routing, rejects, or latency until operators intervene.

Perform an exhaustive bit-level producer audit: inspect all supported gateway, SDK, and client versions plus configuration and protocol-decoding code, then sample raw messages from each active producer path.
The proposal is falsified if any legitimate producer can set the bit, any intermediate hop can preserve or alter it unexpectedly, or any deployed client version can interpret it as Power Peg rather than only zero-or-RLP routing.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Retain the streaming approach, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. First verify the exact Consul 1.10 client/server compatibility and upgrade order, then canary it on a bounded production segment with explicit rollback criteria before staged expansion; benchmark a production-representative workload because 200 nodes may not predict behavior across thousands of services.
The stated `use_streaming_backend` setting is supported by the exact Consul 1.10 build and has the required server-side support.
Agents, servers, and clients can be upgraded in a compatibility-preserving order, including during rollback.
Streaming preserves the consistency, freshness, and failure semantics required for every health subscription.
The observed CPU and network reduction at 200 nodes generalizes to the production service and node cardinality.
The cluster and client fleet have enough temporary capacity for rolling upgrades and canary monitoring.
A simultaneous fleet-wide switch could remove or degrade the sole discovery path for all services without a fallback.
An unsupported setting or incorrect mixed-version deployment could make streaming ineffective or cause client failures.
A 200-node test may miss scale-dependent CPU, memory, bandwidth, Raft, or connection effects.
Incorrect rollout or rollback sequencing could create incompatible server-agent combinations.
Streaming could return stale or incomplete health data unless consistency and reconnect behavior are explicitly tested.

Run a production-representative streaming canary or isolated load test spanning thousands of services and the expected concurrent client count, while measuring health-update correctness, server CPU, network bytes, and reconnect behavior.
The approach is supported if it materially reduces CPU and network while preserving timely and consistent health results; the proposal is falsified if reduction disappears at scale, resource use regresses, or correctness or failover behavior degrades.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but add a shadow period and require near-zero enforcement-decision equivalence before each service is deregistered from the legacy manager. Treat user-ID as a separately approved cutover with cross-region failure testing, conservative temporary headroom, and an immediate rollback switch; do not assume the grace period alone makes automatic allocation reduction safe.
Copying an allocation preserves the exact units, effective time, grace-period state, and regional consistency used for enforcement.
Both managers make identical enforcement decisions for the same usage history.
Allocation and usage timestamps and telemetry are accurate and comparable, including during replica failover.
Deregistering the legacy registration does not bypass required reporting or audit integrations.
Automatic quota reduction is paused or guarded during migration anomalies and has sufficient service-specific headroom.
An unobserved semantic or configuration mismatch can reject legitimate writes immediately when a service moves.
For user-ID, inconsistent enforcement across replicas can turn a quota decision into failed logins, account updates, or region-dependent behavior.
Weeks-long grace periods may still be unsafe for bursty services, delayed telemetry, or allocation changes near the reduction threshold.
Direct deregistration removes the legacy fallback before migration behavior is validated, making rollback and incident comparison harder.
Dashboards provide visibility but do not prove enforcement equivalence, completeness of reporting, or cross-region consistency.
Use a staged migration per wave: dual-report to the new manager in shadow mode, replay recent histories and compare decisions, add bounded headroom while monitoring, then switch enforcement behind a reversible flag. Validate user-ID with fault-injection and cross-region write tests before its cutover, and shut down the legacy system only after a bounded observation period and audit confirmation.
Replay each service's recent usage and allocation history through both managers in a non-enforcing environment, then run a cross-region write test at the quota boundary for user-ID; compare the resulting allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision divergence, stale or incomplete usage signal, or region-dependent allow/reject result falsifies the safety of direct registration and deregistration; consistent results support proceeding with gated cutovers.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach only with a staged, fail-closed rollout: deploy and verify RLP-capable router builds on all eight servers before any client sets the bit, and gate client activation on a router-version/health check. Document the new wire semantics, remove Power Peg only after the compatibility window, and add integration tests covering old/new router combinations plus monitoring and a rapid kill switch.
Every gateway, client, replay path, and alternate producer that can emit orders is included in the compatibility inventory.
No old router will receive an RLP-flagged order during the manual, non-atomic deployment window.
The bit is unused outside the observed month of production traffic, including stored, delayed, replayed, and non-production messages.
All router components and operators can verify the exact deployed build before client activation.
RLP handling can be made fail-closed and operationally reversible if a server is missed or a rollout partially fails.
A new client sending the bit to an old router could make the supposedly unreachable Power Peg path reachable, causing incorrect routing or other order damage.
Manual deployment without build verification can leave servers running incompatible binaries, with no immediate detection.
The month-long traffic observation may miss infrequent clients, batch/replay jobs, dormant code paths, or future producers.
Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a fallback and increases blast radius if RLP handling has defects.
Semantic reuse can create confusion in logs, support procedures, stored messages, and mixed-version incident response.

Run an integration test against one currently deployed or representative pre-release router, send a valid order with the header bit set, and observe whether the router enters Power Peg handling rather than rejecting or safely ignoring the order.
If the old router activates Power Peg, the proposed rollout is unsafe without a compatibility mechanism; it confirms that client activation must not precede verified router replacement.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Retain streaming, but replace the single all-services rollout with a staged production canary followed by measured expansion. Upgrade servers sequentially while preserving Raft quorum, then enable streaming on a bounded client cohort and monitor CPU, network, update latency, stale results, errors, and lock/KV behavior before proceeding; retain and test a documented rollback path throughout the six-week window.
Consul agents and servers can be upgraded to 1.10 in a supported order without breaking the five-server Raft quorum.
Clients at the selected canary scope support streaming and can revert cleanly to blocking queries.
The 200-node staging result remains representative of production subscription volume and update rates.
Streaming preserves health-update freshness and correctness under network interruption and server failure.
The cluster has enough six-week capacity for canarying, observation, rollback rehearsal, and final rollout.
A simultaneous fleet-wide upgrade or setting change could disrupt the sole discovery cluster and leave no fallback.
Streaming regressions could serve stale or missing health updates, causing incorrect routing at service scale.
Insufficient production canary capacity could allow CPU or network growth to overwhelm the cluster during the holiday peak.
A mixed or unsupported server/agent upgrade sequence could threaten quorum or client compatibility.
Failure to validate rollback could leave operators without a safe recovery mechanism when streaming behavior fails.

Run a controlled staging A/B soak at representative subscription cardinality, with identical update churn and streaming enabled versus disabled, while injecting one server failure and a client network interruption.
Streaming is supported if server CPU and network load materially decrease without increased errors, stale-query duration, unhealthy routing decisions, or loss of recovery after interruption; falsified if gains disappear at representative load or correctness/fallback behavior degrades.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Replace the three-month big-bang rewrite with incremental modularization followed by a strangler migration. Add characterization and differential tests first, extract immutable calculation modules, then migrate plan cohorts or workflows with shadow comparisons and bounded rollback before deleting legacy code.
The 37 plans can be represented comprehensively by the proposed Plan, ProrationPolicy, TaxRule, and related model.
Historical or expected invoice outputs are available to prove behavioral equivalence.
The five services can consume a new core incrementally without requiring a synchronized cut-over.
Three engineers can sustain three months of dedicated work despite 40 weekly incoming PRs and associated integration work.
Billing differences can be diagnosed and replayed independently from payment, notification, and other side effects.
Missing legacy rounding, proration, timezone, sequencing, or grandfathering behavior could change many customer invoices.
The large final PR would combine model, data, and five-service integration changes, making defects and merge conflicts difficult to isolate.
There is no shadow comparison, cohort rollout, or rollback mechanism before destructive cut-over.
Frequent upstream changes can invalidate mappings and force repeated rework throughout the three-month branch.
Deleting legacy code immediately may remove undocumented recovery behavior needed when compatibility gaps are discovered.
Retain the clean billing-core goal, but establish it in production incrementally. Begin with characterization tests and immutable interfaces, migrate pure calculation paths one at a time, run old and new logic against captured historical invoices, and switch plan cohorts or service workflows gradually. Remove each legacy path only after its equivalence and rollback criteria are met.
Run a short spike migrating one regular and one grandfathered plan, including their proration, tax, rounding, and retry-related inputs, into billing-core and compare its invoices with the current implementation across historical fixtures and edge cases.
If either plan exposes cross-service side effects, undocumented exceptions, or repeated invoice differences requiring redesign rather than mechanical mapping, the proposed clean model and single cut-over are not credible within the stated scope.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Replace Redis Pub/Sub with Redis Streams using per-job-type or sharded streams, consumer groups, explicit acknowledgements, pending-entry recovery, and bounded retry/DLQ handling. Validate stream throughput, AOF recovery, and pod-restart redelivery under realistic payload sizes before migration, and add idempotency because dual-running and at-least-once processing will otherwise duplicate payments, fulfillment, email, or indexing.
The workload can tolerate loss of in-flight jobs when a subscriber disconnects.
Jobs do not require acknowledgement, durable backlog, or redelivery.
Running RabbitMQ and Redis dispatch simultaneously can be made idempotent.
Redis Streams throughput and persistence meet the 300 jobs/s peak with production payload sizes and replication overhead.
AOF recovery time and data loss during Redis failures are operationally acceptable.
Pub/Sub does not persist messages; AOF provides no recovery for published jobs, so pod redeployments and disconnects can silently lose webhooks, payments, emails, or indexing work.
Redis Pub/Sub broadcasts each message to every subscriber rather than reliably load-balancing a consumer group, potentially multiplying work across replicas.
A worker-side retry wrapper cannot recover jobs lost before receipt, while process crashes after receipt can cause unretried loss.
Dual-running dispatches both systems and can trigger duplicate business side effects unless every handler is strongly idempotent.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ removes backlog and DLQ visibility unless equivalent operational tooling and recovery semantics are implemented first.
Use Redis Streams as the managed-by-the-team replacement: organize job types into bounded streams, consume through consumer groups, acknowledge only after successful processing, recover pending entries with visibility timeouts, and send poison jobs to a durable retry/DLQ stream.
Subscribe with redis-cli, terminate the subscriber, PUBLISH one uniquely identifiable job, restart the subscriber, and inspect whether it receives the job; repeat after the publisher or Redis process restarts.
The restarted subscriber receives no job, confirming that Pub/Sub cannot provide durable acknowledgement or redelivery despite Redis AOF.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Change recovery to East-first promotion and explicitly fence or irreversibly demote the old primary before exposing the new writable endpoint; Orchestrator Raft quorum alone does not provide database fencing. Specify the Consul/proxy update mechanism, validate replica currency and application reconnection, and measure end-to-end first successful write within 60 seconds. Verify application-tier HA separately if East application availability is in scope.
Orchestrator can identify the most up-to-date eligible replica without promoting a stale West replica during an East-only failure.
The old primary can be reliably fenced or forced into super_read_only with stale sessions terminated before promotion.
Consul or a database proxy will atomically expose only the promoted primary to applications.
Replicas contain every required binlog transaction and have compatible MySQL 5.7 replication configuration.
Applications reconnect, retry safely, and remain available when an East application host fails.
The old primary may remain writable during a network partition, causing split brain and irreversible divergence.
Selecting by region without a reliable replication-position comparison could promote a substantially stale West replica.
Pseudo-GTID operation does not guarantee zero acknowledged-write loss or prove that the chosen replica is current.
Detection, promotion, service-discovery propagation, and connection-pool recovery may exceed the one-minute target.
Unspecified endpoint updates or unsafe write retries can leave clients targeting the failed primary or duplicate transactions.
Use Orchestrator-driven East-first recovery with pre-promotion fencing, an explicitly validated replica-health check, and a Consul/proxy-controlled writable endpoint; retain West as a separate disaster-recovery path rather than a normal host-failure fallback.
Run one isolated-primary game-day test while continuously attempting writes through the application's resolved database endpoint, and record the last acknowledged East write, promotion time, endpoint-change time, and first successful write.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts any write after promotion, the promoted node lacks the last acknowledged transaction, or the first successful application write occurs more than 60 seconds after failure.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Deploy and verify the new router build on all eight production servers before any client sets the reused bit. Treat any server still running the old binary as incompatible, because setting the bit could activate the retired Power Peg path. Add automated post-deploy verification of build identity and an explicit launch gate that prevents client enablement until every server passes the RLP routing smoke test.
No currently deployed or future client, gateway, replay, or administrative tool can set the reused header bit.
The old Power Peg implementation is genuinely harmless if accidentally reached, rather than capable of misrouting, rejecting, or corrupting orders.
All eight production servers can be upgraded and positively verified before launch-day client changes.
The new router behavior is backward-compatible for clients that do not set the bit.
The reused bit cannot be set accidentally by malformed input, retries, or protocol translation.
A stale router binary would interpret an RLP-enabled order as Power Peg traffic, potentially causing severe misrouting or order failure.
The one-month traffic observation may miss infrequent clients, legacy binaries, replayed messages, administrative tools, or future producers.
Manual deployment without build verification can leave servers mixed-version despite appearing operationally healthy.
Removing the old code path in the same release increases the consequences of any partial or failed deployment.
Client enablement occurring before router verification creates an immediate launch-day compatibility failure.

Run a controlled compatibility smoke test against the exact binary intended for each of the eight servers, using a non-production valid order with the bit set and a destination that distinguishes RLP from Power Peg.
Every server must demonstrably use the new RLP path; any server selecting Power Peg, rejecting the message, or lacking the new build falsifies the rollout plan and must block client enablement.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave structure and placing user-ID later, but do not deregister any service until the new system has shadow-evaluated real usage and demonstrated parity with the legacy decision for an agreed observation period. Start automatic reductions in non-enforcing or conservatively bounded mode, and add explicit completeness, cross-region, rollback, and emergency-bypass gates; dashboards alone are insufficient.
Copying the current allocation preserves the legacy system's units, scope, grace-period semantics, and enforcement behavior.
New-system usage reports are complete, timely, deduplicated, and consistent across regions before legacy enforcement is removed.
Automatic allocation reductions cannot produce a harmful false reduction or reduce resilience below required peaks during the grace period.
Each wave can be rolled back or temporarily bypassed without losing authoritative quota enforcement, especially for replicated user-ID writes.
A wave's services and policies are fully inventoried, with no legacy-only exceptions or split registrations.
A semantic mismatch or incorrect allocation translation could reject valid user-ID writes and impair login globally.
Stale, missing, duplicated, or regionally inconsistent reports could trigger enforcement or reduction against incorrect usage.
The proposal has no pre-enforcement comparison, so discrepancies are discovered while users are exposed rather than during shadow operation.
The observation that a grace period is long does not protect against a sharp usage increase, report outage, replication event, or misconfigured reduction policy.
Wave rollback may restore legacy registration only after data or policy diverges, leaving no safe immediate enforcement path.
Use shadow-first wave migration: register a cohort without making the new system authoritative, compare historical and live usage, effective allocations, grace-period transitions, and would-be write decisions against the legacy manager, and require predefined parity thresholds. Then enforce on a small cohort, retain tested rollback or bypass controls through the observation period, and enable automatic reduction only after telemetry completeness and reduction behavior are validated; migrate user-ID with conservative limits and cross-region failure testing.
Run the new quota engine in non-enforcing mode for one representative cohort, replay available historical reports, and compare its effective allocation, reduction schedule, and enforcement decisions with the legacy manager over a period covering grace-period transitions.
Any unexplained decision mismatch, missing/late report, cross-region discrepancy, or materially different reduction schedule falsifies copy-and-deregister as a safe default; exact agreement across representative cases supports proceeding with the modified gates.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain global log mode as an expedited detection lane, but require preflight regex-complexity and worst-case CPU benchmarks plus benign-regression testing before promotion. Promote to block through automated 1%, 10%, 50%, and 100% cohorts with latency, error, CPU, match-rate, and false-positive gates, and preserve an atomic, tested global rollback to the last known-good ruleset.
Candidate regexes cannot cause pathological CPU usage on production proxy hardware.
The CI payload and benign-request corpora represent production attacks and legitimate traffic.
Quicksilver can atomically roll back the ruleset on every machine within the required window.
A ten-minute global log interval provides enough traffic and representative PoP coverage for reliable promotion decisions.
The rule-management system supports automated cohort control and managed-rule rollback.
A catastrophic regex can overload proxies even in log mode because evaluation remains in the inline request path.
A false-positive rule can block legitimate customers globally before cohort-level safeguards detect it.
Ten minutes may omit low-volume PoPs, customers, payload variants, and benign edge cases.
Promotion or rollback performed manually may miss the one-hour objective.
An unsafe rule could become fleet-wide before aggregate match and error signals reveal the problem.
Use a narrowly scoped emergency mitigation immediately, deploy the production rule globally in log mode, and then promote it through minute-scale cohorts with automated safety gates. Require a known-good signed configuration, regex complexity limits, representative benign testing, and a tested one-click global rollback.
Benchmark each candidate regex on production proxy hardware using generated worst-case inputs plus the CI payload and benign corpora, while measuring request latency and CPU.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes material CPU saturation, latency inflation, or unacceptable error rates; otherwise the benchmark clears the most immediate catastrophic-regression risk, though production cohort gates are still required.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Retain the Redis read-through cache, but do not deploy the current 15-minute TTL-only design. First prove production-like p95; an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests are misses, so the p95 request is likely still paying the roughly 180 ms permissions-service call, making the claimed 40 ms p95 implausible. Add event-driven invalidation with bounded lag, and require a demonstrated hit rate and end-to-end p95 below 120 ms before broad rollout.
The 85% hit rate from log replay applies to production traffic and to identical key and action distributions.
A cache hit is sufficiently cheap that the overall p95—not merely average latency—falls below 120 ms.
Permission events identify all affected user/document/action entries, including HR account and group-membership changes.
Revoked access may remain cached for up to 15 minutes without violating security requirements.
Redis failure is handled fail-closed and does not silently bypass authorization.
With 15% misses, p95 remains a cache miss and can exceed the 120 ms budget, especially under peak load.
Stale grants, shared-document permissions, and HR-driven revocations can remain valid for 15 minutes.
A malformed or incomplete event-to-cache mapping can leave security-sensitive entries uncleared.
Per-user/document keys may create high Redis memory cardinality and eviction pressure at 2,500 rps.
The log-replay estimate may be biased by replay timing, request coalescing, or a different production workload.
Use the same cache only as one layer, but add Kafka-based invalidation and, if replay confirms that the attainable hit rate is below roughly 95%, build an asynchronously maintained authorization projection with synchronous fail-closed fallback. Local singleflight can reduce duplicate misses, but it cannot remove the tail caused by independent misses.
Replay a production-representative 24-hour trace through the exact cache-key and cache-miss implementation, preserving request timing and measuring the full GET /documents/:id latency distribution with Redis enabled.
If p95 remains above 120 ms, or if the measured hit rate is materially below the replayed 85%, the proposal's latency claim is falsified. Separately, replay a grant followed by a revoke and verify cache visibility; any grant remaining usable for 15 minutes confirms the invalidation risk.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with a durable, atomic Postgres reservation using a conditional status update and a unique coupon redemption constraint. Reserve using a stable order/idempotency key before charging, then finalize or reconcile by order ID; do not hold a database lock during payment I/O.
All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process instance.
No competing application instance, pod, or horizontally scaled replica exists.
Processes cannot restart or crash between reading and updating the coupon.
Coupon lookup and redemption are handled exclusively by this mutex-owning service.
The existing check-and-update cannot interleave with any other database writer.
Concurrent requests handled by different replicas can both observe an available coupon and attempt redemption, causing duplicate orders or charges.
A process crash can permanently lose the mutex state while leaving partially completed work.
Cleanup after lock release can create lifecycle and race bugs under high concurrency.
The solution does not define safe behavior for payment timeouts, retries, failures, or abandoned reservations.
The test only validates one process and therefore provides no evidence of cross-replica correctness.
