Use an atomic Postgres state transition to reserve the coupon with an idempotency token and order ID, enforce one redemption per coupon_id with a unique constraint, and perform the charge outside the database transaction through an idempotent interface. Finalize or reconcile reservations by stable order ID.
Start two independent application instances against the same database and issue simultaneous redemption requests for the same coupon code, one to each instance.
If both instances can pass the availability check and create separate orders or charges, the proposal is falsified; a single-process concurrency test cannot rule this out.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on the table and rely on a weekly manual vacuum. Keep autovacuum enabled with table-specific cost settings to smooth I/O, use rate-limited retention deletes, and investigate partitioning if routine vacuum still scans the full table. Validate the schedule against actual vacuum duration, dead-tuple growth, transaction horizons, and peak-load latency.
The table can accumulate dead tuples for an entire week without exceeding acceptable bloat or query-performance limits.
A weekly VACUUM can complete before the next traffic peak and without being blocked by old transactions or locks.
Traffic is consistently lowest at 02:00 Sunday and the workload tolerates a concentrated vacuum then.
The bulk deletion job does not create unacceptable WAL, lock, or index-I/O spikes.
Monitoring can detect missed cron runs, vacuum cancellation, dead-tuple growth, and bloat before damage occurs.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe bloat to develop, producing longer and more damaging cleanup runs and degraded queries.
A weekly vacuum may overlap peak traffic or fail to finish, leaving dead tuples and index bloat accumulating.
Concentrating cleanup on Sunday can recreate write-latency and I/O spikes rather than spread maintenance across the day.
Long-running transactions or conflicting locks can prevent vacuum from reclaiming rows, regardless of the cron schedule.
A failed or delayed cron job has no automatic fallback cleanup, while a Grafana bloat alert may arrive after operational damage.
Use measured, table-specific autovacuum tuning, such as an appropriate vacuum cost limit and delay, combined with smaller rate-limited retention deletes and index validation. If vacuum must regularly scan the full 1.8 TB table or cannot complete safely, migrate to time-based partitions and drop expired partitions.
Over one complete retention cycle, record n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, vacuum duration, and p99 latency in pg_stat_user_tables and system I/O metrics.
If n_dead_tup grows substantially between scheduled runs, vacuum duration approaches or exceeds seven days, vacuum is canceled or blocked, or p99 latency rises during the weekly run, the weekly-manual-vacuum proposal is falsified.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not run this type-altering migration against the 900M-row table for Tuesday’s release; PostgreSQL will rewrite the table and rebuild dependent indexes while holding a strong lock, and transactional DDL does not make that operation brief or nonblocking. Add a nullable BIGINT amount_thousandths column, dual-write exact thousandths for new orders, update readers with an explicit legacy fallback, and defer historical backfill/consolidation to a later release.
No active query or transaction can hold or repeatedly reacquire locks on orders during the potentially hours-long rewrite.
All indexed and dependent structures can tolerate a full table and index rebuild within the release window.
Every old and new application instance tolerates the renamed column before and after the migration.
Downstream systems preserve NUMERIC values exactly rather than converting them through floating point.
The order currency is available to decide whether existing values are cents or another established minor unit.
Changing INTEGER to NUMERIC requires a full-table rewrite in PostgreSQL 15; ALTER COLUMN RENAME does not avoid it.
The AccessExclusive lock blocks reads and writes, creating checkout downtime and violating the 99.95% SLO.
Because migrations run while old pods are still serving, the initial lock wait can itself become an outage.
Heavy WAL and I/O can create replica lag or overload the primary despite lower overnight write traffic.
NUMERIC(19,4) permits four fractional digits but does not encode which currencies require three; inconsistent scaling could produce financial corruption.
Use an additive migration: add amount_thousandths BIGINT NULL, write both amount_minor and amount_thousandths transactionally for new orders, and define reporting as amount_thousandths when present, otherwise amount_minor * 100. This is metadata-only on PostgreSQL 15 and can be deployed next Tuesday; backfill old rows in later, throttled batches only after consumers are compatible.
On a production-sized restore, run the proposed ALTER under a short lock_timeout while normal traffic or representative sessions are active, then roll it back; separately time the same statement on an isolated copy.
A lock timeout while any query is active falsifies the assumption of a safe short deployment window; a rewrite duration materially exceeding the release or recovery budget independently falsifies readiness for Tuesday.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Retain streaming, but verify and configure `use_streaming_backend` in the scope required by Consul 1.10—particularly whether it is a server-side setting rather than only a client setting—and perform a production canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Progressively expand only after validating client compatibility, streaming-session errors, CPU, network, latency, and Raft health across servers and representative failure scenarios.
The installed client versions and service integrations support Consul 1.10 streaming correctly.
`use_streaming_backend` is being enabled in the configuration scope that actually activates the feature.
A mixed-version rolling upgrade and selective enablement are supported during deployment.
Streaming reduces load at 18,000-node production scale, not only in the 200-node staging environment.
Consul can safely recreate streaming sessions after server failure or leader election.
Enabling the option only on clients may leave the server blocking-query backend active, wasting the rollout while creating unnecessary risk.
A global rollout could expose unresolved protocol, load, or failure-recovery defects across every service with no discovery fallback.
Insufficient client-version compatibility could cause stale or missing dependency data.
Streaming-session leaks or poor reconnect behavior could offset CPU savings and increase network load.
A failed server or leader change could disrupt subscriptions more severely than ordinary blocking queries.

Check the exact Consul 1.10 configuration documentation and schema for `use_streaming_backend`, then enable it in the documented scope in staging and verify active streaming sessions through server metrics or logs.
If the option is server-scoped, the client-only proposal is incorrect; if the documented scope is client-side, no streaming sessions appear, or staging CPU/network do not improve materially, the proposed rollout is falsified.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable per-table autovacuum based only on the assumption that append-mostly data bloats slowly. Keep it enabled with a measured per-table cost throttle, retain automatic analyze, and ensure low-IO cleanup can continue across the weekend without spilling into Monday; use a monitored fallback only if manual maintenance is demonstrably safer. Reassess time-based partitioning or retention if this cannot meet the latency objective.
A full vacuum completed within the low-traffic window or early weekend.
The dead-tuple creation rate is low enough that seven days cannot produce material bloat or excessive index cleanup.
No long-running transaction or replication issue prevents timely dead-row removal.
Storage latency remains acceptable when other low-traffic workloads run during Sunday vacuum.
Cron failures, cancellation, or lock waits will be detected and retried automatically.
Disabling autovacuum also disables that table's automatic analyze unless a separate mechanism is established.
Vacuum currently runs for many hours; with only a short 02:00 window and 20% traffic, the manual run may still overlap Monday business traffic.
Several missed or canceled runs can allow dead tuples and index bloat to accumulate rapidly after bulk deletes.
Weekly snapshots of bloat may detect degradation too late and may not show vacuum progress, index-cleanup work, or transaction horizons.
A weekly VACUUM ANALYZE workload can create another IO spike even though it starts at night.
Tune autovacuum for events with per-table vacuum_cost_delay and vacuum_cost_limit, keeping autovacuum and autoanalyze enabled; validate the settings using vacuum progress, dead tuples, bloat, and foreground p99 latency over multiple delete cycles. If vacuum cannot finish with acceptable daytime IO, implement time-based retention so old data is detached rather than repeatedly mass-deleted and vacuumed from the 1.8 TB table.
Run SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events'; immediately before and after a representative off-peak vacuum cycle.
A substantial or rapidly growing dead-tuple share, no recent completed analyze, or a vacuum that cannot finish before peak traffic would falsify the assumptions behind a weekly schedule and require continuous throttled maintenance or structural partitioning.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Keep automatic maintenance enabled and retune it per table: lower the vacuum trigger threshold/scale factor and increase the autovacuum cost delay to spread reads and writes over time. Schedule controlled off-peak vacuum capacity if necessary, continuously monitor dead-tuple growth and vacuum progress, and retain frequent autoanalyze; do not rely on a fixed weekly full-table vacuum for a 1.8 TB table.
The observed autovacuum IO can be smoothed by throttling without falling behind the deletion rate.
A full vacuum of events can complete within one low-traffic window and before the next deletion cycle.
Dead-tuple creation remains low enough that frequent maintenance can keep pace.
Weekly ANALYZE produces sufficiently fresh planner statistics for this workload.
The cron job will not remain running, be canceled, or overlap a subsequent run.
Disabling table autovacuum also disables autoanalyze, potentially causing stale statistics and poor query plans.
Dead tuples and table/index bloat may exceed safe bounds before the weekly vacuum, degrading scans and increasing write amplification.
At 25k inserts/s, even the default 20% scale-factor threshold can be reached in roughly 4.2 days, contradicting the claim of slow accumulation.
A vacuum lasting many hours may still create unacceptable IO or overlap the next scheduled run.
Maintenance delays can eventually force urgent anti-wraparound or manual vacuum activity with larger latency and duration spikes.
Retain autovacuum on events, lower `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` and `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`, and tune per-table autovacuum cost delay/limit to smooth IO while verifying that vacuum throughput exceeds dead-tuple production. Use a longer off-peak maintenance window and alerts based on dead tuples, bloat, and vacuum duration; keep autoanalyze independent and frequent.
Using existing logs and `pg_stat_all_tables` for `events`, measure a representative deletion cycle's dead-tuple growth, vacuum duration, and completion time relative to the proposed seven-day interval.
If vacuum cannot finish before the next cycle or dead tuples/bloat remain above the pre-agreed bound, the weekly schedule is falsified; stable low bloat and reliable completion would support the schedule's feasibility, though not its safety under autovacuum being disabled.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Retain the wave migration, but add shadow-mode validation and explicitly freeze automatic reduction for user-ID during migration and until its reports and enforcement behavior are proven across regions. Before deregistration, compare both systems’ usage and decisions at peak load, and retain a tested rollback path until the new system meets availability and write-rejection targets.
The new system can disable automatic reduction for user-ID without affecting other services.
Usage reports are complete, sufficiently current, and consistent across regions.
Legacy and new systems use equivalent allocation, accounting, grace-period, and enforcement semantics.
Registration changes can be coordinated so the service is never simultaneously unenrolled or subject to conflicting enforcement.
The new manager can meet user-ID’s latency, availability, and multi-region consistency requirements.
A delayed or understated usage report can cause the new system to reject valid user-ID database writes across regions.
Automatic reduction can lower user-ID allocation below demand before the grace-period buffer accounts for actual reporting lag.
A mismatch in quota semantics can unexpectedly enforce a lower effective limit than the legacy manager.
Deregistering from legacy before validating the new path removes the ability to roll back safely.
Inconsistent or missing regional data can produce different enforcement outcomes, causing partial or intermittent login-account write failures.
Migrate noncritical services first in shadow mode, then migrate user-ID with automatic reductions disabled and a deliberately padded, fixed allocation. Dual-report and compare usage and decisions under peak multi-region load, retain legacy fallback for a defined observation period, and only then deregister legacy; enable automatic reductions later once operational evidence supports it.
Run user-ID in dual-reporting shadow mode for a representative peak-load period, including all regions, and compare the legacy and new systems’ usage totals, allocation values, and would-reject decisions; also measure report age and cross-region convergence.
The proposal would be falsified if reports are materially stale or region-inconsistent, semantics differ, or the new system would reject writes that the legacy system accepts under the copied allocation.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on `events` without measuring whether vacuum is actually the dominant source of business-hour latency. Keep it enabled, apply conservative table-specific autovacuum cost/threshold tuning, and monitor dead tuples, vacuum progress, bloat, WAL, checkpoint activity, and foreground latency. If a predictable schedule is necessary, run a throttled maintenance vacuum more frequently or with explicit time limits rather than relying exclusively on a weekly job; the proposed approach otherwise risks trading latency spikes for severe bloat and vacuum catch-up work.
Dead-tuple creation remains low enough for a weekly vacuum to complete before another backlog forms.
The Sunday 02:00 window is long enough for VACUUM to finish under realistic production IO load.
Disabling table autovacuum will not interfere with other required maintenance behavior or emergency vacuum needs.
Grafana bloat metrics are available, sufficiently accurate, and will alert on vacuum lag or rapidly growing dead tuples.
The vacuum job can be monitored and retried or throttled if traffic, duration, or IO deviates from expectations.
A failed, delayed, or overrun cron job lets dead tuples and index bloat accumulate, increasing scan and index costs.
A weekly VACUUM may itself create a large IO spike, merely moving the problem into a lower-traffic period.
The assumption that append-mostly inserts imply slow dead-tuple growth ignores the stated periodic bulk deletes.
Disabling autovacuum removes the safety net needed when delete volume or query access patterns change.
Bloat monitoring alone may miss WAL, checkpoint, or storage-latency saturation caused by the manual vacuum.
Retain autovacuum on `events` and first tune its per-table cost delay/limit and thresholds so maintenance is spread predictably across the week. Coordinate batch deletes with vacuum and schedule a monitored, throttled catch-up vacuum only if measurements show autovacuum cannot keep up; evaluate time-based inheritance partitioning as a separate longer-term migration.
During one representative business cycle, record `pg_stat_all_tables` dead tuples, `last_autovacuum`, and `last_autoanalyze` for `events`, plus filesystem IO and write p99; then compare them with a controlled, throttled maintenance vacuum while autovacuum remains enabled.
If vacuum is disabled and the scheduled job cannot keep the dead-tuple backlog bounded—or if its IO still produces unacceptable latency—the proposal is falsified. If autovacuum is confirmed to dominate the spikes and tuned autovacuum is insufficient, that supports the operational scheduling direction but not an unmonitored weekly-only design.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. First run a representative production-like benchmark comparing streaming with the current blocking-query path, including index churn, result sizes, client resource usage, reconnect behavior, and correctness/freshness checks; then deploy to a small observable canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Expand by cohort only after stable operation through normal traffic, leader changes, partitions, and reconnects, while testing cheap blocking-query tunings as a control.
All client versions and discovery endpoints support Consul 1.10 streaming with unchanged required semantics.
The 200-node staging environment and observed 60% CPU reduction predict production server, network, and client savings.
Streaming preserves consistency, indexing, freshness, and blocking-read behavior for callers.
Clients and the network can handle the resulting long-lived connection and push-fanout load without reconnect or resync storms.
A deterministic rollback to the existing blocking-query path remains available.
A fleet-wide rollout could break incompatible clients or alter discovery freshness and consistency behavior.
Synchronized reconnects or resyncs could increase CPU, network traffic, and latency rather than reduce them.
Client-side CPU, memory, or connection exhaustion could damage availability even if server CPU improves.
A staging benchmark may not represent production service counts, index churn, result sizes, or failure conditions.
Without cohort thresholds and rollback criteria, a regression could affect all services before it is detected.
Use a benchmark-gated canary rollout: establish baseline metrics, enable streaming for a deterministic small cohort, compare against the existing path and blocking-query tuning, and expand only after correctness, freshness, resource, and failure-scenario thresholds pass.
Run a representative staging load test with current clients versus streaming clients, using production-like service counts, index churn, result sizes, and forced reconnects, while validating discovery outputs and recording server/client CPU, network, memory, connection count, latency, and freshness.
Streaming is supported and materially reduces total CPU and network use without increased client resource usage, reconnect amplification, errors, latency, or differences in required discovery results; otherwise the proposal is not validated.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform the type change and rename in the pre-deploy migration. Use an expand/backfill/contract rollout: add a nullable NUMERIC column without rewriting the table, backfill in small batches, deploy code that dual-writes and reads compatibly, validate counts and totals, then retire the old column in a later release after rollback and replication checks. Separately confirm the intended scale and representation for three-decimal currencies before selecting NUMERIC(19,4).
The pre-deploy migration completes while old application pods and reporting jobs continue serving reads and writes.
The table rewrite and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock duration are compatible with the 99.95% checkout SLO and Tuesday release deadline.
A NUMERIC(19,4) value has the intended business representation for currencies with three-decimal minor units.
No external consumers depend on the orders.amount column name beyond the three known reporting jobs.
The deployment can tolerate a schema transition in which both amount and amount_minor exist.
On a roughly 900M-row, 410-GB indexed table, changing INTEGER to NUMERIC will require a full table rewrite and prolonged ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locking, blocking checkout traffic and likely causing an SLO violation.
Because migrations run before old pods are replaced, renaming amount to amount_minor immediately breaks the currently running application and any unupdated reporting queries.
A failed or rolled-back rewrite may consume substantial database resources and create replication lag, while statement_timeout does not protect the migration because the migration role has none.
The migration is unlikely to fit the next-Tuesday release window without an extended outage or emergency operational intervention.
Using scale 4 without a documented currency and API contract can produce incorrect arithmetic or silently incompatible serializer/reporting behavior.
Add a nullable NUMERIC column, backfill in bounded batches with operational throttling, deploy backward-compatible code that writes both representations and reads the new one with a fallback, validate row counts and financial totals, and only then remove or rename the legacy column in a later contract migration.
Run the proposed ALTER against a production-sized restore or an equivalent PostgreSQL 15 dataset while measuring lock acquisition, rewrite duration, transaction termination, and old application queries.
If the ALTER holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for materially longer than the deployment/maintenance window, blocks checkout writes, or causes old amount queries to fail after the rename, the proposed rollout is unsafe and must be replaced.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Do not enable unrestricted promotion of the West replica under asynchronous replication. Restrict automatic recovery to a fenced, recently verified East replica, enable semi-synchronous replication where supported, and explicitly integrate Orchestrator recovery with Consul plus stale-primary fencing. Permit West promotion only as an operator-approved, acknowledged-data-loss procedure; Raft consensus protects Orchestrator decisions but does not make asynchronous MySQL replication current or prevent a database split brain.
An East replica normally remains available when the East primary host fails, which is not stated.
Orchestrator is configured with a safe promotion candidate, fencing, recovery timeouts, and Consul hooks for every relevant cluster.
The application can route writes to a West-promoted primary over the existing network and tolerate approximately 60 ms plus additional connection latency.
Promoting an asynchronously replicated West node without losing acknowledged writes is acceptable, despite replication lag.
Consul updates and application client behavior will reliably converge within the one-minute objective.
West promotion can lose committed writes because asynchronous replication may not have received them; choosing the apparently most advanced replica does not eliminate this.
A network partition or stalled primary can leave the old primary accepting writes after promotion unless storage/network fencing is enforced; Orchestrator Raft quorum does not fence MySQL.
Promoting a West node while application servers remain in East may create connectivity, latency, DNS/Consul propagation, and write-availability failures.
Applying automated recovery to all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can trigger simultaneous or incorrect promotions.
A 30-second detection threshold does not guarantee recovery under one minute after detection, topology repair, Consul propagation, and application reconnection.
Use Orchestrator automation only for a pre-approved East-local replica, configure semi-synchronous replication for East replicas, fence the failed primary before promotion, and have Consul publish a versioned primary endpoint. Keep West as an explicitly operator-invoked disaster-recovery path with documented possible data loss.
During sustained writes to the East primary, record `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` on the West replica and execute a controlled primary failure followed by West promotion; compare acknowledged write IDs with rows present on the promoted replica.
If any acknowledged write is absent on the promoted West replica, or if East applications cannot route and commit writes to it within one minute, the proposed cross-region automated promotion fails the stated safety/availability objective.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a high-churn table without measuring vacuum throughput against dead-tuple creation. Keep autovacuum enabled, use table-specific cost and concurrency limits to spread its I/O, and convert bulk deletes into bounded, rate-limited batches; schedule supplemental vacuum during low traffic only if measurements show it is needed. Verify the result using write p99, dead-tuple growth, and vacuum completion time.
Dead-tuple production remains low enough for one weekly vacuum to finish and for the table not to accumulate severe bloat between runs.
The weekly vacuum's read and write I/O will not create a larger spike even at 20% of peak traffic.
Autovacuum is not needed for transaction visibility or other operational behavior beyond the explicitly scheduled vacuum.
The bulk deletes are already bounded or otherwise do not create lock, WAL, or index-maintenance bursts.
Grafana bloat metrics are sufficiently fresh and accurate to detect a developing vacuum backlog.
Disabling autovacuum can let dead tuples and index bloat accumulate faster than the weekly job can remove them, eventually increasing scans, index size, storage use, and write amplification.
A manual weekly VACUUM can itself become a multi-hour I/O event, simply moving the latency spike to Sunday rather than eliminating it.
If the job fails, is canceled, or runs behind schedule, there is no automatic cleanup safety net.
A single VACUUM does not return disk space to the operating system; severe bloat may require VACUUM FULL or another disruptive rewrite.
The proposal does not address delete batching, so retention jobs may still cause foreground WAL, lock, and index I/O spikes.
Use table-specific autovacuum cost limits and concurrency, plus bounded rate-limited deletes. Add a monitored, low-traffic vacuum or reindex procedure only when measurements show that normal autovacuum cannot keep up.
Before changing settings, record `n_dead_tup`, `n_live_tup`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`, and total table/index size from `pg_stat_user_tables` and `pg_class` at several intervals, then run a controlled `VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events` while measuring duration, I/O, and write p99.
If dead-tuple growth is substantial and the vacuum requires many hours or materially raises p99 even at low traffic, weekly manual vacuum is unsafe. If vacuum completes well within the low-traffic window and dead-tuple growth remains bounded, the proposal's core schedule is plausible, but autovacuum smoothing and delete batching are still safer.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the big-bang rewrite with a versioned billing kernel and strangler migration. First capture immutable production-derived inputs and expected outputs as replay fixtures, then migrate one end-to-end rule class at a time behind a compatibility adapter, with declarative plan definitions where feasible.
All behavior across the five services can be reproduced from a bounded set of stored inputs.
The new model can express every historical and grandfathered plan behavior before cutover.
All five services can change atomically despite high upstream merge rates.
Three months is sufficient to achieve full invoice parity and coordinate a single release.
Deleting the old implementation cannot invalidate pending, retried, credited, or partially paid invoice workflows.
Uncaptured legacy edge cases involving historical plans, proration, tax, payment ordering, retries, credits, time zones, currencies, or rounding could produce incorrect invoices.
A single cutover creates a repository-wide release dependency and sharply increases rollback and coordination risk.
Five services may temporarily use incompatible billing contracts during the three-month migration.
Unit tests of a newly designed model can validate its intended behavior without proving parity with production behavior.
Deleting the old path eliminates the fallback needed when late parity defects are discovered.
Build the same versioned billing-core boundary, but preserve the existing path and introduce a compatibility adapter that reproduces current outputs. Establish replay-based characterization fixtures, classify the 37 plans, and migrate complete billing flows incrementally with observable parity metrics and reversible cutovers.
Run the current production implementation against a curated corpus of sanitized historical invoices containing grandfathered plans, retries, credits, taxes, proration, and payment allocations, comparing every stored input with every expected output.
If the existing implementation cannot deterministically reproduce the corpus from snapshotted inputs, or if the proposed new model cannot match a significant number of cases without special-case code, the single-cutover timeline and parity claim are disproven.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Keep scheduled off-peak maintenance, but do not disable autovacuum until vacuum duration, dead-tuple production, and low-traffic I/O headroom are measured. Retain autovacuum as a safety net with events-specific cost and worker settings, bound bulk deletes into smaller transactions, and monitor vacuum runtime, bloat, dead tuples, WAL, and write latency.
A full VACUUM ANALYZE of events can complete during the Sunday window without materially affecting foreground writes.
Dead-tuple production is slow and predictable enough that weekly cleanup will prevent unbounded bloat.
Sunday 02:00 has sufficient I/O and write headroom despite traffic being only about 20% of peak.
The current bulk-delete volume is not bursty or concentrated enough to require more frequent maintenance.
Cron failures and missed runs would be detected before the table becomes unsafe.
Disabling autovacuum can allow dead tuples, stale statistics, and bloat to accumulate continuously if cron fails, is delayed, or cannot finish.
A weekly full-table vacuum may exceed its maintenance window and still create substantial I/O, WAL, and checkpoint pressure.
Moving vacuum to a lower-traffic period can degrade the remaining ingestion workload if disk bandwidth is already constrained.
Batching is not addressed, so a single bulk delete can leave the table needing long vacuum cycles regardless of schedule.
Monitoring bloat alone may miss unsafe free-space consumption, index growth, WAL amplification, or vacuum overlap.
First retune per-table autovacuum parameters and make expiration deletes incremental and index-efficient. Use measured results to determine whether an off-peak VACUUM ANALYZE is still needed; this preserves a safety net and bounds maintenance work without assuming a weekly cadence is sufficient.
Enable detailed autovacuum logging for one complete expiration cycle, then compare events vacuum duration, trigger dead-tuple count, and I/O with foreground p99 write latency. Use existing logs or statistics if they already contain this history.
The proposal is falsified if vacuum cannot reliably complete in the intended low-traffic window, dead tuples continue growing after completed runs, or foreground write latency rises materially whenever vacuum runs; confirmation would show bounded vacuum duration, stable bloat afterward, and no meaningful latency penalty during the chosen window.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but limit it initially to the main East-primary cluster and prefer a healthy East replica rather than any replica regardless of region. Before production, require verified stale-primary fencing, atomic service-discovery redirection, connection draining/retry, and measured end-to-end recovery below one minute. Define the 30-second threshold as detection time, not total recovery time, and document that asynchronous failover can lose acknowledged writes.
Orchestrator detects a failed primary within approximately 30 seconds even when it is hung, isolated, or only partially partitioned.
A healthy, sufficiently current East replica will exist and be eligible when recovery triggers.
The failed primary is fenced at the host, network, or database layer before the replacement becomes writable.
Orchestrator can reconfigure remaining replicas and update Consul, while all application instances promptly refresh and drain old connections.
The three-site Raft quorum is available, healthy, and fast enough to complete detection and recovery within the remaining time budget.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, causing split brain and divergent committed transactions.
A region-blind selector may promote the West replica, increasing write latency and potentially selecting a staller copy.
Service discovery may update centrally while application connection pools continue using the old endpoint, delaying or extending an outage.
Pseudo-GTID simplifies topology verification but does not make asynchronous acknowledged writes durable or prove replica ordering under every failure.
Applying recovery to all clusters creates correlated automation risk; one misconfiguration could cause simultaneous, uncoordinated promotions.

Run one isolated-network game day in which clients can still reach the old primary while the new primary can reach its replicas and Consul; trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write on the old primary immediately before and throughout promotion.
The design is confirmed only if the old primary is reliably fenced from accepting writes before promotion, no conflicting writable nodes exist, and the application reaches the new primary within 60 seconds; any successful old-primary write or missed deadline falsifies it.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but initially restrict it to the main East-primary cluster and prefer an East-local replica for host failures; reserve West promotion for confirmed East-region failure. Add reliable fencing so an isolated old primary cannot accept writes, and define the acceptable asynchronous RPO before enabling promotion regardless of region. Validate the complete detection-to-reconnect-and-write path, including ambiguous commits, under one minute; pseudo-GTID simplifies topology but does not establish freshness or prevent data loss.
Orchestrator can complete detection, candidate selection, promotion, and topology publication within the remaining 25 seconds after its 30-second trigger.
A Raft quorum will remain available throughout East database failures.
Orchestrator can reliably distinguish the freshest candidate, or the business explicitly accepts asynchronous replication loss.
The old primary can be fenced automatically at the host, network, or MySQL-access layer.
East application instances can reconnect to a West primary and tolerate roughly 60 ms database RTT.
A network partition can produce dual writable primaries because Orchestrator consensus does not itself fence the old database.
Asynchronous promotion can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft and pseudo-GTID do not prevent this.
Selecting a West replica for an East host failure shifts every write across regions and may exceed latency or throughput limits.
Enabling recovery for all clusters simultaneously creates a correlated automation blast radius.
Consul updates or Rails connection recovery may finish after promotion, or retries may duplicate non-idempotent writes.

In staging, partition the primary from Orchestrator while keeping a database client connected; after 35 seconds, attempt writes through both the old primary and the advertised replacement, while timing when a new write succeeds.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts a conflicting write after replacement promotion, or if end-to-end writable recovery takes longer than 60 seconds. Success requires automatic fencing or refusal of old-primary writes, exactly one authoritative writer, and timely service rediscovery.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Retain streaming, but verify and configure `use_streaming_backend` in the scope required by Consul 1.10—particularly whether it is a server-side setting rather than only a client setting—and perform a production canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Progressively expand only after validating client compatibility, streaming-session errors, CPU, network, latency, and Raft health across servers and representative failure scenarios.
The installed client versions and service integrations support Consul 1.10 streaming correctly.
`use_streaming_backend` is being enabled in the configuration scope that actually activates the feature.
A mixed-version rolling upgrade and selective enablement are supported during deployment.
Streaming reduces load at 18,000-node production scale, not only in the 200-node staging environment.
Consul can safely recreate streaming sessions after server failure or leader election.
Enabling the option only on clients may leave the server blocking-query backend active, wasting the rollout while creating unnecessary risk.
A global rollout could expose unresolved protocol, load, or failure-recovery defects across every service with no discovery fallback.
Insufficient client-version compatibility could cause stale or missing dependency data.
Streaming-session leaks or poor reconnect behavior could offset CPU savings and increase network load.
A failed server or leader change could disrupt subscriptions more severely than ordinary blocking queries.

Check the exact Consul 1.10 configuration documentation and schema for `use_streaming_backend`, then enable it in the documented scope in staging and verify active streaming sessions through server metrics or logs.
If the option is server-scoped, the client-only proposal is incorrect; if the documented scope is client-side, no streaming sessions appear, or staging CPU/network do not improve materially, the proposed rollout is falsified.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Do not enable unrestricted promotion of the West replica under asynchronous replication. Restrict automatic recovery to a fenced, recently verified East replica, enable semi-synchronous replication where supported, and explicitly integrate Orchestrator recovery with Consul plus stale-primary fencing. Permit West promotion only as an operator-approved, acknowledged-data-loss procedure; Raft consensus protects Orchestrator decisions but does not make asynchronous MySQL replication current or prevent a database split brain.
An East replica normally remains available when the East primary host fails, which is not stated.
Orchestrator is configured with a safe promotion candidate, fencing, recovery timeouts, and Consul hooks for every relevant cluster.
The application can route writes to a West-promoted primary over the existing network and tolerate approximately 60 ms plus additional connection latency.
Promoting an asynchronously replicated West node without losing acknowledged writes is acceptable, despite replication lag.
Consul updates and application client behavior will reliably converge within the one-minute objective.
West promotion can lose committed writes because asynchronous replication may not have received them; choosing the apparently most advanced replica does not eliminate this.
A network partition or stalled primary can leave the old primary accepting writes after promotion unless storage/network fencing is enforced; Orchestrator Raft quorum does not fence MySQL.
Promoting a West node while application servers remain in East may create connectivity, latency, DNS/Consul propagation, and write-availability failures.
Applying automated recovery to all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can trigger simultaneous or incorrect promotions.
A 30-second detection threshold does not guarantee recovery under one minute after detection, topology repair, Consul propagation, and application reconnection.
Use Orchestrator automation only for a pre-approved East-local replica, configure semi-synchronous replication for East replicas, fence the failed primary before promotion, and have Consul publish a versioned primary endpoint. Keep West as an explicitly operator-invoked disaster-recovery path with documented possible data loss.
During sustained writes to the East primary, record `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` on the West replica and execute a controlled primary failure followed by West promotion; compare acknowledged write IDs with rows present on the promoted replica.
If any acknowledged write is absent on the promoted West replica, or if East applications cannot route and commit writes to it within one minute, the proposed cross-region automated promotion fails the stated safety/availability objective.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Do not use an in-process mutex as the correctness boundary. Implement a database-backed atomic claim using a conditional update such as `UPDATE coupons SET redemption_state='pending', order_id=... WHERE code=... AND redeemed_at IS NULL AND redemption_state='pending'`, requiring exactly one affected row; use a unique constraint on `orderId` and an idempotency key for retries, then finalize or compensate the claim around charging.
Each coupon is redeemed through only one Node.js process at a time, which is false with 4-12 replicas.
Concurrent requests for a code reach the same process, which a round-robin Service does not guarantee.
The charge provider offers idempotency keyed by coupon or order.
Coupon and order records can be committed independently from the external charge.
The existing Prisma schema permits an atomic conditional update or can be changed this week.
Requests routed to different pods hold different mutexes and can both pass the redeemedAt check.
Both requests can charge customers before either process persists redeemedAt.
A process crash after charging can leave a coupon pending and permanently prevent later redemption unless recovery exists.
Retries after a client timeout can duplicate the external charge unless the provider receives a stable idempotency key.
A process-local Map can grow or retain mutexes incorrectly if cleanup is not exception-safe.
Use Postgres as the serialization authority. Atomically transition an available coupon to a pending claim with a conditional update and verify `count === 1`; persist a stable idempotency/claim identifier, charge using that identifier, and then mark it redeemed. Add explicit handling for pending-claim recovery and unique constraints preventing one order from claiming multiple coupons. The proposed unit test should be supplemented with a multi-process integration test against one database.
Run two redeem requests for the same coupon concurrently against two independently started application instances sharing the same Postgres database, with a controllable charge mock, then assert that at most one charge occurs.
The current proposal is falsified if both instances succeed and invoke charge twice; the replacement is supported if exactly one atomic claim and one charge occur.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but place the user-ID service in a dedicated early canary with dual reporting and shadow enforcement, and do not deregister the legacy manager until multi-region validation and rollback are proven. Initially disable automatic reductions or set an explicit allocation floor for the user-ID service, then enable reductions only after monitoring shows accurate usage, expected headroom, and safe behavior under replication and failover. Keep the legacy manager available through the quarter until each service has completed an observation period and an independently tested rollback.
The new quota manager can accurately receive and attribute user-ID usage from every region without a reporting gap during handoff.
Allocation values and quota semantics are identical between the legacy and new managers, or any differences have been reconciled.
The user-ID database has enough write and authentication headroom for delayed, stale, or inconsistent usage data.
Automatic quota reduction can be delayed, overridden, or given a safe minimum allocation for at least the user-ID service.
A tested rollback can restore legacy enforcement without losing writes or creating divergent quota state.
Automatic reduction during the weeks-long grace period could still reject legitimate account writes when usage reporting is delayed or inaccurate, causing login or account-access failures.
Because the database replicates writes across regions, one region's stale or excessive usage report could trigger quota rejection in another region and produce global user-visible impact.
Registering the user-ID service in the new manager before shadow validation could make it subject to enforcement based on incomplete or differently interpreted telemetry.
Deregistering the legacy manager before proving rollback would remove the only known safe enforcement path and make recovery dependent on the new system's state.
A copied allocation may not account for migration traffic, failover, backlog, or growth, leaving insufficient capacity despite apparently matching configuration.
Migrate the user-ID service first under dual reporting and shadow evaluation, with reductions disabled and both managers receiving data. Compare decisions across regions, test quota rejection and recovery under simulated failover and stale telemetry, then perform a canary handoff with immediate rollback; migrate the remaining services in waves and enable reductions gradually only after verified headroom and stable telemetry.
In a staging replica of the user-ID database, verify whether the new manager supports a per-service hold on automatic allocation reduction; if it does, lower the simulated allocation below current usage and exercise writes and logins in each region.
If there is no reliable hold, override, or rollback mechanism, or if any reduced allocation causes legitimate writes or logins to be rejected in any region, the proposed unrestricted-reduction migration is unsafe.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but require explicit old-primary fencing, an approved promotion policy, pre-promotion topology/lag checks, and cluster-by-cluster canarying. Do not automatically select the most up-to-date replica regardless of region; use a designated preference and account for East application latency, replication lag, and a declared RPO.
A West promotion remains reachable from East application servers with acceptable latency and connection stability.
The old East primary can be conclusively fenced before the promoted replica accepts writes.
Orchestrator detection plus Raft election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and discovery convergence consistently complete within 60 seconds.
The chosen replica's replication lag and connection state provide a tolerable committed-write RPO.
Orchestrator 3.x, MySQL 5.7, and pseudo-GTID behave correctly through these failure and recovery transitions.
A network partition can trigger promotion without fencing the old primary, causing split brain and divergent writes.
Promoting a lagging West replica can lose committed transactions despite pseudo-GTID.
Automated reconfiguration can stall or partially complete, extending write unavailability or leaving inconsistent topology.
An unreachable West primary can make East applications fail or suffer unacceptable latency because service discovery alone does not ensure connectivity.
Applying automation to all clusters at once can create simultaneous elections, discovery churn, and an operator overload during the failure.

In a production-like staging environment, run one isolated end-to-end game day: continuously commit marked writes, hard-kill the East primary, record write errors and failure timing, and verify fencing, selected replica, data present, topology repair, and application recovery.
The proposal is supported only if there is a single authoritative primary, no unexplained lost acknowledged writes, all application writes recover within 60 seconds, replicas converge, and service discovery settles consistently; a split brain, unacceptable loss, or recovery beyond 60 seconds falsifies it.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not execute permanent deletion against an unvalidated generic ID list: first resolve every ID through a typed inventory/detail API and require that it identifies the intended legacy add-on installation, not a site or product. Stage the operation using the reversible `mark` mode where feasible, add preflight, authorization, checkpointing, bounded retries, and an explicit stop/rollback procedure, then permanently delete only the verified set before the deadline. Log object identity and response status without exposing customer data, and reconcile the final result against the source inventory.
The product team's list contains only add-on installation IDs and has not been accidentally combined with site or product IDs.
The platform exposes a reliable way to inspect each ID's object type and associated site before deletion.
`mode=mark` is reversible for these installations and does not affect other objects on the site.
The deletion API is idempotent and batch failures can be safely retried without duplicate or cascading effects.
Permanent deletion is required by the data-minimisation policy before backend shutdown, rather than merely soft-deleting or disabling the add-on.
A single site ID in the list could permanently delete the entire site, including unrelated products and data, with recovery requiring per-site backup restoration.
A stale, malformed, or incorrectly scoped ID list could delete a valid customer object that is not the retired add-on.
Partial batch failure or unsafe retry behavior could leave installations behind or produce an unclear completion state before shutdown.
The proposal's claim that permanent mode satisfies data-minimisation policy is not established by the supplied facts and may unnecessarily destroy recoverable data.
Logging raw responses could expose customer or site data if responses contain sensitive fields.
Run a typed, preflighted migration: reconcile the supplied IDs against the legacy add-on installation inventory, soft-delete the verified installations, verify the resulting state, and permanently delete only after an explicit completion check. Use a dry-run or test-site execution first, with a manifest of expected object IDs and a kill switch that halts on type, count, or site mismatches.
Resolve a representative sample of the product team's IDs through the platform's site/object inventory or detail API and inspect each object's type, installation identity, and parent site.
Every sampled ID is confirmed as the intended `Insight Legacy` add-on installation and maps to the expected site; any site, product, unknown, or mismatched object falsifies the proposal as written.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not perform a direct type change or rename on the 900M-row table. Add a nullable major-unit NUMERIC(19,3) column with expand/backfill/switch/contract, dual-write it, and gate reporting cutover on complete reconciliation. Preserve the existing integer column during rollout rather than changing its representation in place.
The existing amount values are integer minor units whose scale varies by currency, not major-unit numbers that can safely be stored as NUMERIC(19,4).
PostgreSQL can complete the ALTER with acceptable lock duration, replica lag, storage use, and rollback behavior on a 900M-row table.
All application versions and every reporting/export consumer can tolerate the renamed column and new numeric representation during deployment.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the intended wire and reporting format despite currencies using zero, two, or three minor-unit digits.
Historical three-decimal values' lost precision can be ignored or recovered from another source.
A table rewrite or long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock can breach the 99.95% availability SLO.
Renaming the column breaks mixed-version deployments and any consumer not included in the three query updates.
Leaving existing values numerically unchanged (for example, 1234 cents) while presenting them as major units produces orders that are 100 times too large.
Changing all integer values into a fixed four-decimal representation corrupts currency semantics and can misstate historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values.
The migration may exhaust disk or delay replication, causing checkout and reporting outages.
Use the additive NUMERIC(19,3) major-unit migration described in the independent position, with currency-aware backfill, rate limiting, dual-write compatibility, reconciliation, and a separately gated reporting cutover.
Run a read-only semantic check joining a representative sample of orders to currency metadata: compare the stored integer amount with the expected major-unit value (for example, integer 1234 cents for a two-decimal currency should become 12.34, not 1234).
If the proposed ALTER leaves existing values numerically unchanged, as its stated approach does, it confirms that the column is not a correct major-unit representation; additionally, a production-like migration dry run showing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock or rewrite exceeding the deployment/SLO window independently falsifies the deployment plan.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Retain autovacuum on `events` and tune its per-table thresholds and I/O cost limits so vacuum work is gradual rather than bursty. Measure vacuum duration, dead-tuple growth, bloat, and wraparound distance before and after tuning, and batch the bulk deletes to limit dead-tuple production.
A complete `VACUUM ANALYZE` of the 1.8 TB table reliably finishes before the next weekly run and during low-impact hours.
Weekly vacuum keeps dead-tuple and bloat growth within safe operational limits at peak ingestion.
Plain `VACUUM` provides enough reusable space without increasing file size.
The bulk-delete schedule and volume are compatible with a fixed weekly maintenance window.
Autovacuum can safely be disabled without creating transaction-ID wraparound or visibility-map maintenance risk.
A fixed weekly job may overlap with the prior run, leaving only partial coverage and causing unbounded bloat.
Disabling autovacuum can allow transaction-ID wraparound emergencies and stale statistics or visibility maps.
Plain `VACUUM` does not return most ended-file space to the operating system, so filesystem-level bloat may remain.
Reading and rewriting a 1.8 TB table can create sustained I/O contention and degrade ingestion throughout the maintenance window.
The single maintenance job provides no adaptive response when delete volume, vacuum duration, or bloat changes.
Use per-table autovacuum tuning for `events`: raise the vacuum scale factor and thresholds, and set suitable per-table vacuum cost delay/cost-limit values to smooth I/O while preserving emergency vacuum capability. Validate the settings with production-like timing, monitor `pg_stat_all_tables`, `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` where applicable, relation size, dead tuples, and transaction-ID age, and reduce delete-bloat production through smaller delete batches.
On a production-sized copy, run `VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events` while sampling elapsed time, physical read/write rates, ingestion latency, relation size, and dead-tuple counts.
If the vacuum cannot complete within the proposed low-traffic window, materially increases relation size, or pushes write p99 above 500 ms, the weekly plain-vacuum design is falsified.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month cut-over with incremental modularization: first build an invoice characterization harness from historical production invoices, including grandfathered plans and mid-cycle proration, discounts, taxes, payments, retries, and notifications. Introduce billing-core behind compatibility adapters with immutable inputs and parity gates, migrate services or billing dimensions incrementally behind flags, and remove legacy paths only after equivalence is demonstrated.
All 37 plans and undocumented legacy exceptions can be accurately inferred from historical invoices before migration.
The five services can be changed and deployed compatibly despite frequent merges from other teams.
A new domain model can reproduce legacy behavior without preserving legacy billing constraints.
Invoice-level outputs are sufficient to detect all relevant behavioral differences.
The team can complete and validate a cross-service replacement within three months without a rollback path.
A big-bang cut-over can systematically change invoice totals, proration, taxes, discounts, or payment handling for grandfathered customers.
Deleting the old implementation eliminates comparison and rollback paths before parity is proven.
Porting 37 plans into a clean model is likely to encode undocumented exceptions incorrectly or omit cross-service state transitions.
Frequent external merges make a large cross-repository change difficult to integrate and isolate.
Without realistic characterization fixtures, unit tests may validate the new model rather than actual production-equivalent behavior.
Use the proposed billing-core extraction, but deliver it incrementally. Establish a cross-service historical invoice fixture corpus and replay comparison first; then wrap existing behavior, add immutable inputs and a plan-definition registry, migrate one capability or service at a time behind feature flags, and require line-item and total-level parity before each legacy-path removal.
Replay a representative sample of historical invoices covering all 37 plans and key grandfathered mid-cycle transitions through the proposed billing-core model, comparing every line item and total with stored production outputs.
Any material mismatch, missing fixture scenario, or inability to reproduce a legacy transition would falsify the claim that a single cut-over can safely replace the existing implementation.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table whose cleanup is demonstrably hours long. Instead, retain autovacuum, tune per-table trigger and cost-delay settings to smooth maintenance I/O, and investigate batching bulk deletes and reducing unnecessary index maintenance. Instrument and trial these changes before considering partitioning for longer-term retention redesign.
Dead-tuple production is low enough for one Sunday vacuum to keep pace with both inserts and expired-row deletes.
That vacuum can scan the entire table, clean indexes, and update statistics before Sunday traffic resumes.
No long-running transactions, prepared transactions, or other blockers will delay dead-row cleanup.
A full-table vacuum at 02:00 will not overlap bulk deletes or cause WAL, checkpoint, or storage-I/O saturation.
Bloat and transaction-age metrics remain safe despite monitoring only through Grafana graphs.
Dead tuples may accumulate rapidly enough for visibility, index, planner, or XID-wraparound problems to develop before or during weekly maintenance.
If vacuum exceeds the low-traffic window, its I/O will move into business hours and produce the same or larger latency spikes.
Long-running transactions can make the weekly vacuum ineffective and prevent vacuum-only data from being removable.
Bulk deletes may run concurrently with the scheduled vacuum, invalidating the assumption that 02:00 is consistently available.
A missed or failed cron invocation leaves the table without autovacuum fallback, creating an operational single point of failure.
Tune events-specific autovacuum thresholds and vacuum_cost_delay so cleanup is distributed predictably rather than eliminating it. Verify that the autovacuum worker can keep up with dead-tuple production; also reduce delete and index-maintenance work before evaluating partitioning as a structural solution.
During one representative business cycle, record pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze, autovacuum log start/finish times, XID age, and disk I/O; also time a manual VACUUM ANALYZE outside the proposed low-traffic window.
The probe falsifies the proposal if manual vacuum requires materially more than the available low-traffic window or leaves n_dead_tup and XID age trending upward between runs. It supports the premise only if ordinary autovacuum is consistently falling behind, the full vacuum reliably finishes in the window, and it is the dominant source of write-latency spikes.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum for the entire high-churn table. Keep it enabled with a per-table autovacuum threshold and cost configuration, or schedule bounded off-peak maintenance while continuously measuring dead tuples, bloat, vacuum duration, and wraparound distance. Validate that maintenance can complete between bulk-delete cycles before choosing any manual schedule.
Dead-tuple creation and transaction-ID consumption remain low enough for weekly maintenance to keep up.
A VACUUM of the 1.8 TB table can complete within the low-traffic window and does not itself create unacceptable IO spikes.
Bulk deletes do not leave long-running transactions that prevent vacuum from reclaiming dead tuples.
The measured bloat and dead-tuple growth can be detected before operational impact.
Storage has sufficient free space and maintenance IO does not interfere with peak ingestion.
Dead tuples may accumulate faster than the weekly vacuum removes them, causing severe bloat, degraded scans, and worsening write latency.
The scheduled VACUUM may run for many hours and recreate the same IO spikes, merely moving them to Sunday.
Disabling regular autovacuum can allow transaction-ID wraparound pressure; anti-wraparound behavior in PostgreSQL 9.4 must be explicitly verified rather than assumed.
A single large VACUUM may generate sustained IO and WAL/checkpoint pressure even when traffic is only 20% of peak.
Autovacuum configuration or monitoring may miss tables and thresholds needed to prevent unbounded bloat.
Retain autovacuum and tune the table with a suitably lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor or explicit vacuum threshold, then use pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_activity, and a bloat measurement tool to verify that workers complete. If a manual vacuum is still needed, use short, observable, off-peak runs with cost throttling rather than disabling maintenance for a week.
Measure events dead tuples, autovacuum/vacuum timestamps and duration, and vacuum progress over one full delete cycle; compare the dead-tuple growth rate with the number of tuples a completed vacuum can remove.
If dead tuples or estimated bloat grow substantially between maintenance runs, or a vacuum cannot complete before the next cycle, the weekly-manifestation proposal is falsified.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep the string-based wire-format change, but expand the rollout plan before implementation: update every ID-bearing response and OpenAPI-generated SDK, explicitly change Swift/Kotlin/Moshi decoding, fix web parsing and non-display paths, and test representative old and regenerated partner clients. Ship an expedited compatibility notice and a short migration window; do not assume regenerating SDKs is sufficient for deployed clients or partner integrations.
All relevant v1 response fields, including list and nested responses, can be changed consistently to string IDs.
The web, iOS, Android, and partner clients can accept string IDs or receive compatible generated types within the available release cycle.
Existing numeric IDs and internal storage/query logic can remain unchanged while only the JSON representation changes.
The API can publish a breaking contract change and support communication to approximately 40 partner integrations within two weeks.
No downstream code relies on JSON numeric typing for validation, sorting, analytics, routing, or serialization.
Existing clients that decode IDs as numeric JSON will fail, reject responses, or silently mishandle the changed type after rollout.
A partial implementation could fix the web app while leaving list, nested, or newly added ID fields numeric and still corrupting JavaScript values.
Regenerated SDKs may declare strings while handwritten or older partner clients still require numbers, causing outages or truncation.
Changing the OpenAPI type alone may not change runtime serializers, examples, mocks, or generated model code consistently.
Mobile and partner clients with slow update cycles may experience an extended incompatible transition despite the API release.

Run a representative legacy Swift Codable, Kotlin/Moshi, and JavaScript client against a response containing the string ID "1234567890123456789", and inspect the generated OpenAPI model plus one list and one nested response.
If any supported client rejects the string, silently changes the value, or any authoritative response still emits a JSON number, the proposal as currently stated is not rollout-ready; this confirms the need for explicit compatibility handling and endpoint-wide tests.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not send the untyped list directly to permanent deletion. Resolve every ID against an authoritative inventory, require it to be an active "Insight Legacy" add-on installation, reject site IDs and unknown or ambiguous records, and obtain a reviewed deletion manifest before execution. Then canary the process, use checkpoints and fail-closed stopping rules, and permanently delete only the validated manifest while recording request and response evidence.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies the intended add-on installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The product team's list is complete, current, and free of stale, duplicated, malformed, or incorrectly scoped IDs.
Permanent deletion removes the installation and its legacy data without cascading into unrelated products or site content.
The API returns enough metadata or errors to verify object type and successful deletion.
Completing validation and a controlled canary is possible before the backend shutdown.
A single site ID in the list could permanently destroy an entire customer site and all products on it.
IDs from the same 24-character format may be misclassified because no type validation is performed.
A stale or incorrect product-team manifest could irreversibly delete valid customer objects.
Unexpected API behavior or cascading deletion could affect unrelated product data.
Batching and weekend scheduling do not mitigate irreversible damage; on-call monitoring detects failures only after they occur.
Generate a canonical manifest by joining the product-team list to authoritative object metadata, including object type, site ID, add-on name/version, and status. Require 100% type and scope matches, explicitly assert that no site IDs or ambiguous records remain, and produce a signed count and hash for approval. Test a small representative sample, verify deletion and unaffected site data, then execute idempotently with per-ID results, checkpoints, an exact allowlist, and immediate halt on any mismatch.
Run a read-only preflight that resolves every supplied ID through the canonical inventory or object metadata API and asserts object_type = add-on installation, add-on = Insight Legacy, expected site association, and uniqueness; explicitly search for any resolved site object.
The direct permanent-delete approach is falsified if even one ID is missing, ambiguous, duplicated across object types, identifies a site, or identifies a different add-on. It is safe to proceed only if all records match the expected type and scope and the manifest count reconciles exactly.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Keep the expedited global log-to-block model, but require a versioned atomic bundle, explicit benign-regression and PCRE complexity budgets, and automated promotion based on block volume, 5xx rate, latency, and CPU—not match volume alone. Preserve the previous bundle for immediate rollback, and define who can terminate or reverse the release; add a brief 1% block canary only if it still meets the one-hour objective.
A globally activated log-mode rule is propagated atomically and consistently within minutes.
Ten minutes of telemetry is timely and representative enough to expose false positives and operational regressions.
The CI suite includes benign requests in addition to attack payloads and runs before expedited activation.
Rule compilation and matching have enforced CPU, memory, and worst-case backtracking limits.
Block-mode changes can be rolled back globally within minutes without waiting for another configuration deployment.
A high-cost PCRE consumes substantial proxy CPU in log mode before match-count monitoring detects degradation.
A benign traffic pattern absent from CI causes a global false-positive outage when block mode begins.
Match volume alone can remain normal while latency, 5xx responses, or regional traffic distributions deteriorate.
A non-atomic Quicksilver update can produce mixed rule versions or activate block mode before every proxy has validated the bundle.
Telemetry delay or concurrent updates can cause unsafe promotion or rollback to an unintended bundle.
Use the proposed global log window as the emergency safety gate, but combine it with deterministic pre-activation limits and automated multi-signal promotion: global log for 5–10 minutes, immediate rollback on any safety threshold breach, then block at 1% and 100% if latency and traffic permit. This is safer than relying on a fixed ten-minute timer while remaining within the disclosure-hour target.
Replay a representative benign and adversarial request corpus through the candidate rule in log mode on a production-like proxy at measured peak request rate, comparing CPU and p99 latency with the rule disabled.
The design is viable only if worst-case evaluation stays within an agreed CPU and latency budget and no unbounded backtracking occurs; materially higher p99 latency, CPU saturation, or pathological evaluation time falsifies the claim that log mode is a safe universal first stage.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Keep scheduled off-peak maintenance, but do not disable autovacuum until vacuum duration, dead-tuple production, and low-traffic I/O headroom are measured. Retain autovacuum as a safety net with events-specific cost and worker settings, bound bulk deletes into smaller transactions, and monitor vacuum runtime, bloat, dead tuples, WAL, and write latency.
A full VACUUM ANALYZE of events can complete during the Sunday window without materially affecting foreground writes.
Dead-tuple production is slow and predictable enough that weekly cleanup will prevent unbounded bloat.
Sunday 02:00 has sufficient I/O and write headroom despite traffic being only about 20% of peak.
The current bulk-delete volume is not bursty or concentrated enough to require more frequent maintenance.
Cron failures and missed runs would be detected before the table becomes unsafe.
Disabling autovacuum can allow dead tuples, stale statistics, and bloat to accumulate continuously if cron fails, is delayed, or cannot finish.
A weekly full-table vacuum may exceed its maintenance window and still create substantial I/O, WAL, and checkpoint pressure.
Moving vacuum to a lower-traffic period can degrade the remaining ingestion workload if disk bandwidth is already constrained.
Batching is not addressed, so a single bulk delete can leave the table needing long vacuum cycles regardless of schedule.
Monitoring bloat alone may miss unsafe free-space consumption, index growth, WAL amplification, or vacuum overlap.
First retune per-table autovacuum parameters and make expiration deletes incremental and index-efficient. Use measured results to determine whether an off-peak VACUUM ANALYZE is still needed; this preserves a safety net and bounds maintenance work without assuming a weekly cadence is sufficient.
Enable detailed autovacuum logging for one complete expiration cycle, then compare events vacuum duration, trigger dead-tuple count, and I/O with foreground p99 write latency. Use existing logs or statistics if they already contain this history.
The proposal is falsified if vacuum cannot reliably complete in the intended low-traffic window, dead tuples continue growing after completed runs, or foreground write latency rises materially whenever vacuum runs; confirmation would show bounded vacuum duration, stable bloat afterward, and no meaningful latency penalty during the chosen window.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Retain Consul 1.10 streaming, but verify that `use_streaming_backend = true` is configured on servers rather than only on clients, then deploy through mixed-version server and client canaries with explicit health, freshness, error-rate, CPU, and network thresholds. Do not enable it fleet-wide based on a 200-node test; validate rollback, Raft backup, and behavior during leader changes and partitions, and complete production qualification within the six-week window.
The staging 200-node workload and 60% CPU result remain representative of 18,000 nodes and thousands of services.
The Consul 1.10 feature supports every blocking-query health endpoint and query parameter used in production.
Mixed 1.9/1.10 server and agent versions are supported throughout the rollout and rollback period.
Clients can interoperate with streaming servers without explicit client-side enablement or code changes.
Consistent, current results and ACL behavior are preserved during server push and reconnect scenarios.
If this is a server-side backend option, configuring only clients will leave production CPU unchanged while creating a false sense of completion.
A simultaneous fleet-wide cutover could make an untested stream correctness or availability regression affect every dependency lookup with no fallback cluster.
Streaming may not cover all health query forms currently used, so uncovered workloads could retain the original high load.
Leader changes, disconnects, or slow consumers could expose stale dependency results, connection growth, or new server load patterns.
Upgrading a critical Consul cluster without tested rollback, configuration backups, and a recent Raft snapshot increases outage and data-recovery risk.

Check the exact Consul 1.10 documentation/source for `use_streaming_backend` configuration scope and run `consul validate` against a minimal client-only and server configuration.
The proposal is falsified if the option is server-only, is rejected as a client option, or is not supported by the deployed 1.10 build; if it is server-side, a small server canary should then show streaming headers/connections and materially lower server CPU without increased stale or failed responses.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the namespaced Redis read-through cache, but replace the 15-minute TTL with a short bounded TTL with jitter and consume permission-events to invalidate all affected user/document/action keys, including share, unshare, account-removal, and group-membership changes. Add request coalescing and upstream-load monitoring, and define an explicit stale-grant SLO; cached grants must not remain valid beyond that SLO when invalidation is delayed.
A 15-minute stale-grant window is acceptable to authorization owners despite the stricter correctness requirement for unauthorized access.
Access-log replay accurately predicts production hit rates, including action and group-membership fan-out.
Redis can sustain cache traffic and existing session traffic at 2,500 requests per second with acceptable tail latency.
The permissions service can handle cold-cache, expiry, and coordinated miss load without becoming overloaded.
The boolean decision is safely reusable for the exact userId, docId, and action key without omitted policy or tenant context.
Revoked access can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes because the proposal has no event-driven invalidation.
Coordinated expiry, deployment, or restart can cause a cache stampede and overload permissions-service.
Access-log replay may overstate hit rates or omit low-frequency, high-risk permission changes, invalidating the latency estimate.
Redis eviction, contention, or failure can sharply reduce hit rates and drive authorization load upstream.
