Incomplete key or policy context could return a cached decision for the wrong action, document, tenant, or scope.
Use Redis cache-aside with permission-events-driven deletion, short jittered TTLs, request coalescing, and measured rollback criteria. If event propagation cannot meet the required revocation SLO, adopt an event-fed projection with permissions-service reconciliation rather than relying on long TTL expiry.
Cache an allow decision for a test user/document/action, revoke that permission through the production authorization path, and immediately repeat the read while event processing is disabled or delayed.
The read continues returning allow until the 15-minute TTL expires, demonstrating an unacceptable stale-grant window and disproving reliance on access-log hit-rate evidence for authorization correctness.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Retain global log mode as an expedited detection lane, but require preflight regex-complexity and worst-case CPU benchmarks plus benign-regression testing before promotion. Promote to block through automated 1%, 10%, 50%, and 100% cohorts with latency, error, CPU, match-rate, and false-positive gates, and preserve an atomic, tested global rollback to the last known-good ruleset.
Candidate regexes cannot cause pathological CPU usage on production proxy hardware.
The CI payload and benign-request corpora represent production attacks and legitimate traffic.
Quicksilver can atomically roll back the ruleset on every machine within the required window.
A ten-minute global log interval provides enough traffic and representative PoP coverage for reliable promotion decisions.
The rule-management system supports automated cohort control and managed-rule rollback.
A catastrophic regex can overload proxies even in log mode because evaluation remains in the inline request path.
A false-positive rule can block legitimate customers globally before cohort-level safeguards detect it.
Ten minutes may omit low-volume PoPs, customers, payload variants, and benign edge cases.
Promotion or rollback performed manually may miss the one-hour objective.
An unsafe rule could become fleet-wide before aggregate match and error signals reveal the problem.
Use a narrowly scoped emergency mitigation immediately, deploy the production rule globally in log mode, and then promote it through minute-scale cohorts with automated safety gates. Require a known-good signed configuration, regex complexity limits, representative benign testing, and a tested one-click global rollback.
Benchmark each candidate regex on production proxy hardware using generated worst-case inputs plus the CI payload and benign corpora, while measuring request latency and CPU.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes material CPU saturation, latency inflation, or unacceptable error rates; otherwise the benchmark clears the most immediate catastrophic-regression risk, though production cohort gates are still required.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but initially disable automatic quota reductions or add a per-service reduction freeze while validating parity and rollback behavior. Migrate the user-ID service only after testing replicated writes, reporting lag, and enforcement at the allocation boundary; retain legacy registration and a tested rollback path until each wave is proven stable.
The new manager can copy allocations without changing quota semantics or effective capacity.
Both managers can remain registered during migration, or equivalent shadow enforcement and rollback are available.
Reported usage is sufficiently complete, timely, and comparable across regions and services.
Automatic reductions cannot cause a service's legitimate burst usage to exceed its allocation.
Deregistering from the legacy manager does not remove an independent enforcement path or monitoring dependency.
Automatic reductions may reject writes for the user-ID service, including login/account operations, violating the no-user-visible-impact requirement.
Usage-reporting lag or regional replication inconsistency could make the new manager undercount usage and permit writes beyond the intended quota, or overcount and reject valid writes.
Migrating the user-ID database's enforcement path without a tested rollback could interrupt authentication globally.
A copied allocation may not represent current effective limits, causing an immediate quota breach during cutover.
Deregistration before parity is established could eliminate the only known-good enforcement or usage signal.
Use a staged shadow migration: dual-register services, mirror and compare usage and enforcement decisions while preserving legacy behavior, keep allocations frozen and reductions disabled, then canary enforcement and rollback before making the new manager authoritative. Handle user-ID separately with multi-region write-failure and authentication tests.
Inspect the new quota system's configuration/API and run a non-production simulation for one canary service whose reported usage stays below allocation, followed by a burst that reaches the current allocation.
If the allocation is reduced during the grace period or the burst is rejected because of the reduction, the proposed 'no user-visible impact' assumption is falsified; if reductions can be disabled and enforcement is unchanged, the mitigation is viable.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable per-table autovacuum based only on the assumption that append-mostly data bloats slowly. Keep it enabled with a measured per-table cost throttle, retain automatic analyze, and ensure low-IO cleanup can continue across the weekend without spilling into Monday; use a monitored fallback only if manual maintenance is demonstrably safer. Reassess time-based partitioning or retention if this cannot meet the latency objective.
A full vacuum completed within the low-traffic window or early weekend.
The dead-tuple creation rate is low enough that seven days cannot produce material bloat or excessive index cleanup.
No long-running transaction or replication issue prevents timely dead-row removal.
Storage latency remains acceptable when other low-traffic workloads run during Sunday vacuum.
Cron failures, cancellation, or lock waits will be detected and retried automatically.
Disabling autovacuum also disables that table's automatic analyze unless a separate mechanism is established.
Vacuum currently runs for many hours; with only a short 02:00 window and 20% traffic, the manual run may still overlap Monday business traffic.
Several missed or canceled runs can allow dead tuples and index bloat to accumulate rapidly after bulk deletes.
Weekly snapshots of bloat may detect degradation too late and may not show vacuum progress, index-cleanup work, or transaction horizons.
A weekly VACUUM ANALYZE workload can create another IO spike even though it starts at night.
Tune autovacuum for events with per-table vacuum_cost_delay and vacuum_cost_limit, keeping autovacuum and autoanalyze enabled; validate the settings using vacuum progress, dead tuples, bloat, and foreground p99 latency over multiple delete cycles. If vacuum cannot finish with acceptable daytime IO, implement time-based retention so old data is detached rather than repeatedly mass-deleted and vacuumed from the 1.8 TB table.
Run SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events'; immediately before and after a representative off-peak vacuum cycle.
A substantial or rapidly growing dead-tuple share, no recent completed analyze, or a vacuum that cannot finish before peak traffic would falsify the assumptions behind a weekly schedule and require continuous throttled maintenance or structural partitioning.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not alter and rename the existing column in the 900M-row table. Use an expand migration adding a BIGINT minor-unit column plus an explicit per-order scale, deploy backward-compatible dual writes, backfill in throttled batches, validate, and only then cut over reads and reporting.
The existing INTEGER values and their units are suitable for direct conversion to NUMERIC(19,4), despite the required 2- or 3-decimal scale.
The application and all writers can tolerate the ALTER's lock and rewrite duration.
Old application versions, queued jobs, and reporting consumers will all use the renamed representation immediately.
The NUMERIC(19,4) precision and scale match every currency and future write without rounding or overflow.
No indexes, constraints, foreign keys, or deployment mechanisms make the type alteration substantially more disruptive.
PostgreSQL will generally rewrite the table for an INTEGER-to-NUMERIC type alteration, causing prolonged locks, bloat, replica lag, statement timeouts, and likely deployment failure at 900M rows.
NUMERIC(19,4) does not document whether values are cents, three-decimal minor units, or another scale, so existing orders can be silently misinterpreted.
The rename plus same-PR application changes can break old pods, queued writes, external integrations, or reports that still reference orders.amount.
Converting or rounding monetary values during the rewrite can corrupt financial totals if the legacy column is not already the intended exact unit.
Transactional DDL only provides atomicity; it does not make the rewrite online, bounded in duration, or safe for concurrent traffic.
Add a nullable BIGINT amount_minor column and an explicit immutable scale (for example, 2 or 3) with an online schema migration. Release dual-write code compatible with both schemas, backfill indexed rows in small throttled batches while monitoring lag, validate counts/totals/samples, then switch reads and reports before a later release considers retiring the legacy column.
On a production-sized disposable PostgreSQL clone, record pg_class.relfilenode for orders, run BEGIN; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; COMMIT;, and compare the relation file and elapsed lock/rewrite metrics.
A changed relation file and materially long ALTER duration confirm that the migration rewrites the large table rather than being a metadata-only online change, falsifying the proposal's safety premise.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain Quicksilver-based acceleration, but classify rules by confidence and deploy high-confidence signatures directly to block while broad rules use log mode and selected-PoP canaries. Before rollout, enforce regex complexity limits and per-rule CPU/latency budgets; automatically revert on proxy health, customer error-rate, or match-distribution thresholds, with a pretested global kill switch.
Passing the fixed CI corpus is strong enough to bound catastrophic false positives across production traffic.
All proxies have enough spare CPU to evaluate new log-mode rules during peak traffic without degrading TLS or HTTP processing.
Quicksilver provides sufficiently fast, atomic, version-consistent mode changes and global rollback.
Central match-volume telemetry is timely and complete enough to detect harmful rules within the ten-minute window.
A safe precompiled PCRE pattern or equivalent timeout mechanism can prevent catastrophic backtracking.
A globally blocked false positive could immediately disrupt traffic for many customers before the log-mode signal is detected.
A complex regex could cause pathological backtracking, raising request latency and exhausting CPU across edge proxies.
Delayed or partial Quicksilver propagation could leave some PoPs exposed or produce inconsistent enforcement.
Ten minutes of log mode leaves the newly disclosed attack unblocked during the observation period.
Aggregate match volume may conceal a severe false positive affecting a small customer or a concentrated real attack.
Use a risk-tiered expedited rollout: immediately block narrowly scoped, high-confidence exploit signatures, while logging broad rules and selectively canary-blocking them by PoP. Promote broad rules using production health and false-positive thresholds, rather than making a single global decision based only on aggregate match volume.
Run the exact candidate regexes through the production PCRE engine against a representative peak-traffic trace containing sampled benign requests and all CI attack payloads, comparing shadow evaluation with the rules disabled.
The proposal is falsified if even a small candidate set causes backtracking or exceeds the proxy's allocated CPU/p99 latency budget, or if observed benign matches indicate a plausible customer-wide false positive; acceptable overhead and expected-only attack matches support the rollout.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Retain the clean billing-core direction, but replace the three-month big-bang rewrite with incremental adoption behind compatibility-tested interfaces. First freeze current invoice behavior with characterization tests and production-derived fixtures, then migrate one bounded billing capability at a time while continuously comparing legacy and new results before deleting legacy code.
The team can obtain representative historical billing inputs and expected invoice outputs for all 37 plans.
Existing behavior can be characterized sufficiently despite low happy-path coverage and six years of implicit proration rules.
The five services can adopt a new package interface without coordinated release or compatibility hazards.
Invoice output equality is sufficient to detect behavioral regressions, including tax, payment, and notification side effects.
The team can maintain a dedicated integration branch and reconcile frequent upstream merges throughout the migration.
A single cut-over could change invoices for grandfathered plans or uncommon proration, tax, timing, and lifecycle combinations.
Deleting the old implementation after only unit tests would remove the effective behavioral oracle and rollback path.
A three-month branch exposed to roughly 40 merged PRs per week will encounter substantial integration conflicts and stale assumptions.
Shared mutable context may encode undocumented cross-service behavior that a clean domain model does not capture.
Coordinated changes across five services create deployment, ordering, data-migration, and partial-outage risks.
Use a strangler migration: establish golden-master characterization tests and an immutable billing-core API, introduce an adapter around the existing implementation, migrate calculations capability by capability, and shadow-compare proposed and legacy results on real or anonymized cases. Keep legacy code as a temporary fallback until production comparison and invoice-level reconciliation pass, then remove it incrementally.
Create the smallest representative golden corpus that covers all 37 plans, all 11 grandfathered plans, and known proration edge cases, then run the existing implementation and proposed billing-core model against identical inputs and compare complete invoice outputs and side-effect commands.
Any unexplained difference, inability to express a historical case without behavior-breaking special cases, or missing relevant case data would show that the proposed clean model and single-cut-over strategy are not safe as written.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator-based recovery, but restrict promotion to a verified, sufficiently caught-up East replica and require explicit fencing of the old primary before any new primary becomes writable. Define measurable detection, fencing, promotion, discovery-propagation, and Rails-reconnect deadlines; validate replica capacity and connection-retry safety under load. Use East-local semi-synchronous replication only if the agreed RPO requires stronger acknowledged-write durability, while retaining asynchronous West replication.
At least one East replica is reachable, sufficiently caught up, and has adequate CPU, memory, IOPS, and write capacity.
The old primary can be fenced reliably before the replacement is promoted or exposed for writes.
The three-site Raft deployment can reach quorum within the failover deadline; a three-site quorum does not guarantee availability if two sites fail.
Applications use a stable Consul-managed writable endpoint and safely reconnect or retry after topology changes.
The agreed RPO permits the replication lag and any acknowledged-write loss from asynchronous replication.
Promoting a West or otherwise stale replica can silently lose recently acknowledged writes.
Raft consensus does not fence the old primary, allowing split brain and divergent writes if it remains reachable.
Updating service discovery before promotion completes can direct applications to an unavailable or unsafe endpoint.
A 30-second detection threshold does not establish completion within the required 60-second end-to-end objective.
Non-idempotent retries during connection resets can duplicate application side effects, while insufficient replica capacity can cause write failures after promotion.
Use the proposed Orchestrator promotion, but make it an explicitly fenced East-local failover with a stable writable service, tested end-to-end recovery timing, and optional validated MySQL 5.7 semi-synchronous replication for stronger RPO.
Run one controlled East-primary failure and, from the old primary host, attempt a write while monitoring Orchestrator promotion and Consul endpoint changes.
If the old primary accepts writes before fencing, promotion is unsafe and the proposal is falsified; if the complete sequence exceeds the agreed 60-second deadline, the stated objective is also falsified.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Retain the wave migration, but add shadow-mode validation and explicitly freeze automatic reduction for user-ID during migration and until its reports and enforcement behavior are proven across regions. Before deregistration, compare both systems’ usage and decisions at peak load, and retain a tested rollback path until the new system meets availability and write-rejection targets.
The new system can disable automatic reduction for user-ID without affecting other services.
Usage reports are complete, sufficiently current, and consistent across regions.
Legacy and new systems use equivalent allocation, accounting, grace-period, and enforcement semantics.
Registration changes can be coordinated so the service is never simultaneously unenrolled or subject to conflicting enforcement.
The new manager can meet user-ID’s latency, availability, and multi-region consistency requirements.
A delayed or understated usage report can cause the new system to reject valid user-ID database writes across regions.
Automatic reduction can lower user-ID allocation below demand before the grace-period buffer accounts for actual reporting lag.
A mismatch in quota semantics can unexpectedly enforce a lower effective limit than the legacy manager.
Deregistering from legacy before validating the new path removes the ability to roll back safely.
Inconsistent or missing regional data can produce different enforcement outcomes, causing partial or intermittent login-account write failures.
Migrate noncritical services first in shadow mode, then migrate user-ID with automatic reductions disabled and a deliberately padded, fixed allocation. Dual-report and compare usage and decisions under peak multi-region load, retain legacy fallback for a defined observation period, and only then deregister legacy; enable automatic reductions later once operational evidence supports it.
Run user-ID in dual-reporting shadow mode for a representative peak-load period, including all regions, and compare the legacy and new systems’ usage totals, allocation values, and would-reject decisions; also measure report age and cross-region convergence.
The proposal would be falsified if reports are materially stale or region-inconsistent, semantics differ, or the new system would reject writes that the legacy system accepts under the copied allocation.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month big-bang rewrite with characterization-first incremental extraction. Capture golden invoice results for all 37 plans, introduce immutable billing inputs and policy interfaces behind an adapter for the existing mutable context, then migrate one bounded behavior or service at a time with shadow comparisons and rollback switches. Only after parity is demonstrated should the legacy implementation be removed; separately build a configuration-driven plan onboarding path that reduces adding a plan to data, policy references, and tests rather than code changes.
The proposed domain model can represent every grandfathering, proration, tax, payment, and notification behavior, including interactions that are currently implicit.
Historical inputs are available to reproduce existing invoices exactly for all 37 plans and relevant edge cases.
Billing dependencies can be isolated sufficiently to replace BillingContext without coordinated production cutovers.
The five services and plan behavior will remain stable enough for a three-month branch and a final integration without losing concurrent changes.
A single atomic cut-over is operationally possible and reversible if any generated invoice differs.
Low test coverage and six years of implicit proration rules make silent invoice regressions likely across taxes, credits, renewals, cancellations, and payment timing.
A long-lived branch will conflict with roughly 40 weekly PRs, especially changes touching the same services, and may omit fixes merged into main.
Incremental deletion within three months provides little room to distinguish intentional legacy quirks from defects, making rollback and defect isolation difficult.
Shared mutable context may encode undocumented cross-service side effects that cannot be reproduced from the proposed domain objects alone.
An atomic cut-over can stop invoicing or payments broadly, while post-cut-over recovery from a rewrite with limited production history is substantially harder.
First inventory every plan-specific rule and create golden-file characterization tests from current production invoices and targeted edge-case scenarios. Extract pricing, proration, tax, and invoice calculation behind typed, immutable interfaces while retaining the old implementation as a reference; migrate consumers incrementally, compare old and new outputs in shadow mode, and remove each legacy path only after parity. Once behavior is safely modularized, add a versioned plan-definition schema with validation, effective dates, migration tooling, and a standard test template so new plans require configuration and tests rather than edits spread across five services.
Before implementing billing-core, select representative invoice fixtures covering all 37 plans, including at least one grandfathered plan, and have the team attempt to express their inputs and expected outputs solely as Plan, Subscription, Invoice, ProrationPolicy, and TaxRule objects.
The approach is falsified if any real scenario requires behavior that cannot be represented or deterministically reproduced by the proposed model; if all scenarios map cleanly, that would support the model and make a more incremental migration safer.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Keep the batched deletion objective, but add authoritative ID/type and parent-site validation, deduplication, inventory reconciliation, and an independently verified completion report. Test a small canary cohort and rollback/backup restoration before expanding to permanent deletion; use idempotent retries and explicit handling of partial failures and rate limits.
The product-team list is complete, current, and contains only add-on installation IDs.
The deletion API exposes or can be joined to authoritative object type and site ownership data.
Permanent deletion is isolated to the retired add-on and does not cascade into other products or the site.
The API handles duplicate or repeated deletion requests safely and reports failures reliably enough for reconciliation.
A tested site-by-site backup restore can recover a wrongly deleted site before the backend shutdown.
A 24-character site ID or another object ID is permanently purged because the batch has no type verification.
The supplied list is stale or incomplete, leaving installations behind or causing unrelated deletions.
Undisclosed dependencies cause removal of shared data belonging to other products.
Timeouts, partial failures, pagination, or rate limits cause the job to report incomplete success.
Weekend execution delays detection until after business impact, with no tested recovery path.
Use a preflight-and-cohort process: resolve and type-check IDs, reconcile them against an authoritative installation inventory, test backup restoration and deletion scope, permanently delete a small canary cohort, verify affected sites and remaining objects, then expand with monitoring and reconciliation.
Run a non-destructive or isolated test that submits a known site ID and a known add-on installation ID to the deletion workflow, with a type-validation check before any permanent call; inspect the recorded object type, parent site, and deletion scope.
If the workflow cannot reliably distinguish the two IDs or shows that deleting an installation also removes the site or other-product data, the proposed permanent batch process is unsafe and must not run.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not use a single blocking type-alter/rename migration. Add an exact BIGINT minor-unit column (or a numeric representation with an explicit currency exponent), update writers and readers compatibly, and backfill in small, throttled, restartable batches. Keep the legacy column and application contract available until the rolling deployment and reporting queries are fully migrated; validate conversion semantics before writing three-decimal amounts.
The migration must complete while old application pods remain online and before the 25-minute rolling deploy finishes.
Existing integer values represent two-decimal minor units, and their conversion to three-decimal amounts can be determined unambiguously from currency metadata.
NUMERIC(19,4) has sufficient range for the intended amount and currency-exponent model, and does not introduce unintended rounding or arithmetic behavior.
A table rewrite, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, WAL generation, and index/storage growth can be tolerated at the chosen time.
All consumers—including old pods, background workers, exports, and ad hoc SQL—can tolerate a compatibility period with old and new amount fields.
ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a 900M-row table can rewrite hundreds of gigabytes, hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, generate substantial WAL, and exceed the 30-second application statement timeout or maintenance-window budget.
Renaming amount before replacing pods makes every old Django query and likely old reporting/client query fail immediately during the deployment; transactionality does not provide rolling-deploy schema compatibility.
NUMERIC(19,4) alone does not encode currency precision: existing values such as 1234 may mean 12.34 in cents, while a three-decimal value may require a different scaling rule. Silent interpretation errors can corrupt financial calculations.
Unchecked numeric scale, precision, constraints, and conversion rules can permit invalid or rounded values.
A large rewrite may cause replica lag or consume temporary/WAL resources, impairing the 99.95% checkout SLO even if the migration eventually succeeds.
Use an expand/contract migration: add a new exact amount representation plus currency/exponent metadata, dual-write it transactionally, and have a feature flag select the new field when available. Backfill existing rows in small batches outside a single long transaction, validate counts and sampled conversions, and retain amount until reporting, all application versions, and downstream consumers are confirmed compatible. Prefer BIGINT minor units with a known maximum and ISO currency exponent; use NUMERIC only if a documented, enforced currency-scale model is required.
In a disposable PostgreSQL transaction, rename orders.amount and run the exact SELECT used by the currently deployed application: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; SELECT amount FROM orders LIMIT 1; ROLLBACK;
The SELECT fails with column "amount" does not exist, proving that the proposed migration breaks currently running pods during the required pre-deploy/rolling-deploy window.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Streaming is the preferred direction, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. Upgrade through normal Raft-compatible rolling procedures, then enable it for a small production canary and expand by controlled cohorts with CPU, network, freshness, error-rate, and reconnect metrics plus explicit rollback thresholds. Retain blocking-query fallback until representative clients have survived a server-loss or rolling-restart test.
All production clients support the relevant 1.10 streaming backend and can be upgraded or configured without incompatible agent versions.
Streaming preserves health-update ordering, completeness, authorization, and freshness semantics for every consumer.
The 200-node staging result is representative of production polling rates, update rates, query diversity, and reconnect behavior.
A tested rollback to blocking queries is possible before the rollout reaches most clients.
Clients will not synchronize reconnection attempts after a server, network, or deployment event.
A fleet-wide configuration change exposes version skew or unsupported-client failures across all 18,000 nodes simultaneously.
A correlated disconnect or deploy triggers a reconnect storm that recreates or exceeds current server load.
Semantic differences silently deliver stale or incomplete health state, causing failed dependency resolution without obvious client errors.
The 200-node benchmark understates production query diversity or update fan-out, so staging gains fail to materialize.
An untested rollback becomes impractical after broad adoption, turning a client defect into a cluster-wide discovery outage.

Enable streaming for one small, representative production cohort, then terminate and restore its connections while comparing server CPU, network traffic, update freshness/completeness, client errors, and reconnect concurrency against a blocking-query control cohort.
The proposal is supported if CPU and network remain materially lower without correctness errors or harmful reconnect amplification; stale or missing updates, sustained CPU/network regression, client failures, or a reconnect storm falsifies the fleet-wide rollout as currently proposed.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month big-bang rewrite with incremental modularization followed by a strangler migration. Add characterization and differential tests first, extract immutable calculation modules, then migrate plan cohorts or workflows with shadow comparisons and bounded rollback before deleting legacy code.
The 37 plans can be represented comprehensively by the proposed Plan, ProrationPolicy, TaxRule, and related model.
Historical or expected invoice outputs are available to prove behavioral equivalence.
The five services can consume a new core incrementally without requiring a synchronized cut-over.
Three engineers can sustain three months of dedicated work despite 40 weekly incoming PRs and associated integration work.
Billing differences can be diagnosed and replayed independently from payment, notification, and other side effects.
Missing legacy rounding, proration, timezone, sequencing, or grandfathering behavior could change many customer invoices.
The large final PR would combine model, data, and five-service integration changes, making defects and merge conflicts difficult to isolate.
There is no shadow comparison, cohort rollout, or rollback mechanism before destructive cut-over.
Frequent upstream changes can invalidate mappings and force repeated rework throughout the three-month branch.
Deleting legacy code immediately may remove undocumented recovery behavior needed when compatibility gaps are discovered.
Retain the clean billing-core goal, but establish it in production incrementally. Begin with characterization tests and immutable interfaces, migrate pure calculation paths one at a time, run old and new logic against captured historical invoices, and switch plan cohorts or service workflows gradually. Remove each legacy path only after its equivalence and rollback criteria are met.
Run a short spike migrating one regular and one grandfathered plan, including their proration, tax, rounding, and retry-related inputs, into billing-core and compare its invoices with the current implementation across historical fixtures and edge cases.
If either plan exposes cross-service side effects, undocumented exceptions, or repeated invoice differences requiring redesign rather than mechanical mapping, the proposed clean model and single cut-over are not credible within the stated scope.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on `events` without measuring whether vacuum is actually the dominant source of business-hour latency. Keep it enabled, apply conservative table-specific autovacuum cost/threshold tuning, and monitor dead tuples, vacuum progress, bloat, WAL, checkpoint activity, and foreground latency. If a predictable schedule is necessary, run a throttled maintenance vacuum more frequently or with explicit time limits rather than relying exclusively on a weekly job; the proposed approach otherwise risks trading latency spikes for severe bloat and vacuum catch-up work.
Dead-tuple creation remains low enough for a weekly vacuum to complete before another backlog forms.
The Sunday 02:00 window is long enough for VACUUM to finish under realistic production IO load.
Disabling table autovacuum will not interfere with other required maintenance behavior or emergency vacuum needs.
Grafana bloat metrics are available, sufficiently accurate, and will alert on vacuum lag or rapidly growing dead tuples.
The vacuum job can be monitored and retried or throttled if traffic, duration, or IO deviates from expectations.
A failed, delayed, or overrun cron job lets dead tuples and index bloat accumulate, increasing scan and index costs.
A weekly VACUUM may itself create a large IO spike, merely moving the problem into a lower-traffic period.
The assumption that append-mostly inserts imply slow dead-tuple growth ignores the stated periodic bulk deletes.
Disabling autovacuum removes the safety net needed when delete volume or query access patterns change.
Bloat monitoring alone may miss WAL, checkpoint, or storage-latency saturation caused by the manual vacuum.
Retain autovacuum on `events` and first tune its per-table cost delay/limit and thresholds so maintenance is spread predictably across the week. Coordinate batch deletes with vacuum and schedule a monitored, throttled catch-up vacuum only if measurements show autovacuum cannot keep up; evaluate time-based inheritance partitioning as a separate longer-term migration.
During one representative business cycle, record `pg_stat_all_tables` dead tuples, `last_autovacuum`, and `last_autoanalyze` for `events`, plus filesystem IO and write p99; then compare them with a controlled, throttled maintenance vacuum while autovacuum remains enabled.
If vacuum is disabled and the scheduled job cannot keep the dead-tuple backlog bounded—or if its IO still produces unacceptable latency—the proposal is falsified. If autovacuum is confirmed to dominate the spikes and tuned autovacuum is insufficient, that supports the operational scheduling direction but not an unmonitored weekly-only design.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain expedited Quicksilver distribution, but add production-shaped CPU/latency and false-positive gates before global log mode, and require automated global rollback on latency, error, CPU, or false-positive thresholds. Make block promotion and rollback per-rule, and validate attack coverage across encodings, methods, paths, headers, and protocol variants rather than relying only on match volume.
Quicksilver can atomically promote the same version from log to block and roll it back worldwide within minutes.
Ten minutes of global match telemetry is representative enough to reveal false positives and performance degradation.
Logging the rule does not materially increase regex CPU cost on the shared request path.
The CI payload corpus covers the attack's relevant protocol variants and benign traffic.
Central telemetry exists with sufficiently low latency to trigger automated rollback.
Catastrophic regex backtracking can degrade all customer traffic during the ten-minute global logging phase.
Low match volume can conceal broad false positives that block authentication, payments, APIs, or encoded requests.
A missed encoding or protocol variant can produce false confidence before global enforcement.
Partial or slow propagation can leave PoPs inconsistent during promotion or rollback.
Manual interpretation of ten minutes of telemetry can delay rollback beyond the mitigation window.
Use a narrowly scoped detector with automated correctness, CPU-cost, and canary gates; publish it through Quicksilver, monitor centrally, and automatically disable the individual rule on defined regressions before promoting it to global blocking.
Replay the candidate against the CI attack corpus and production-shaped benign traffic at peak concurrency while measuring proxy CPU, request latency, errors, and false-positive matches.
The proposal is falsified if any variant is missed or if log/block evaluation causes a material CPU, latency, error, or false-positive regression; otherwise the result supports using the rule in log mode but still does not prove propagation and rollback safety.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Replace the three-month branch and single cut-over with incremental strangler migration: first capture current behavior as characterization and golden-invoice tests, then introduce an immutable billing-core behind an adapter and migrate one plan cohort at a time. Run old and new calculators in shadow mode, establish invoice-level parity across all 37 plans, and retain rollback and legacy grandfathered-plan paths until production evidence is sufficient.
The current implementation's behavior is sufficiently documented or reproducible to serve as the compatibility specification.
All 37 plans can be represented by the proposed domain model without losing historical proration, tax, payment, or notification behavior.
A three-month branch can remain synchronized with roughly 40 weekly main-branch merges without excessive conflict and integration cost.
A comprehensive production invoice corpus can be obtained for replay and comparison.
Services can be migrated incrementally behind a stable adapter rather than requiring an atomic release.
Low happy-path coverage is likely to conceal proration and mutation-order edge cases, causing incorrect customer invoices or charges.
The long-lived branch will diverge from main, making merges unsafe and potentially discarding fixes introduced during the migration.
A single cut-over concentrates unknown failures across all plans and all five services, with limited ability to isolate or roll back individual cases.
Testing only billing-core will not detect integration differences in tax, payments, notifications, persistence, or service orchestration.
Deleting the implementation before parity evidence is available removes the only known behavior oracle and substantially increases incident and recovery risk.
Use a continuously integrated strangler migration. First build a shared adapter around the mutable BillingContext and add characterization tests plus historical invoice golden files. Then implement immutable domain types and dual-run both calculators in shadow mode without changing customer-facing results. Migrate current plans in small cohorts, followed by the 11 grandfathered plans, using feature flags, reconciliation dashboards, and per-cohort rollback; remove legacy code only after sustained invoice parity.
Create one replay test that runs a stratified sample of recent historical invoices covering all 37 plans through the proposed billing-core and compares normalized line items, taxes, totals, credits, and proration components against the persisted production results.
Any non-zero unexplained difference falsifies the claim that the new model can preserve existing invoices and shows that a single cut-over would be unsafe; zero differences across the sample would support, but not prove, migration readiness.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Do not activate the repurposed bit until every production router is verified on the new build; otherwise clients can unintentionally enable the still-compiled Power Peg path on an unupgraded server. Use a two-phase rollout: first deploy the RLP-capable, Power-Peg-disabled build to all eight servers with client activation gated separately, verify each server's build and behavior, then enable the bit no later than launch day.
No current or retained client, saved message, replay process, or internal producer can emit the retired bit.
All eight production routers will be upgraded and verified before any client starts setting the bit.
The new router safely rejects or ignores the bit until RLP activation is explicitly enabled.
Old and new binaries are never mixed in a deployment batch while clients are setting the bit.
The protocol owner has confirmed that semantic reuse of the retired bit is permitted.
During the manual rollout, an old router receiving a flagged order may execute Power Peg and misroute orders.
A deployment or version-reporting mistake on one server could affect RLP orders despite fleet-wide verification.
Unknown legacy or queued producers could unexpectedly activate the bit, making one month of observed traffic insufficient assurance.
A partially deployed fleet could produce inconsistent order behavior across otherwise identical RLP orders.
Stage deployment and activation separately: ship a release that removes Power Peg and supports RLP but keeps the bit gated by an operator-controlled runtime feature flag, upgrade and verify the entire fleet, and only then enable RLP and client-side bit emission.
Run the currently deployed production router build in a test environment with the header bit set to 1 and route-eligible test orders through it.
If the deployed build enters the retired Power Peg path rather than rejecting or safely ignoring the order, the proposed rollout is unsafe until all routers are upgraded and the bit remains disabled.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not migrate durable job dispatch to Redis Pub/Sub; AOF does not persist Pub/Sub messages or subscriber acknowledgements, so disconnects and routine worker redeployments will lose jobs. If eliminating RabbitMQ is required, prototype Redis Streams with consumer groups, explicit acknowledgement, pending-entry recovery, bounded retries, and dead-letter handling; otherwise retain RabbitMQ and automate its operational maintenance.
Losing jobs during subscriber disconnects or worker restarts is acceptable, which conflicts with payments, email, fulfilment, and indexing workflows.
Redis AOF persistence somehow makes Pub/Sub deliveries durable.
Every relevant job type is idempotent and can tolerate duplicate or missing execution.
The existing in-worker retry wrapper can recreate broker-level acknowledgement, redelivery, and dead-letter semantics without durable message state.
Peak-load tests include realistic payload sizes, slow consumers, reconnects, and failover rather than only publish throughput.
Messages published while workers are disconnected, restarting, or briefly unsubscribed are irretrievably dropped.
There is no acknowledgement or atomic completion mechanism, creating uncontrolled at-most-once delivery.
Reconnection storms and slow consumers can cause unbounded memory pressure or overload Redis, affecting caching and rate limiting.
Existing five-retry and DLQ behavior cannot be preserved reliably, causing infinite retries, duplicate side effects, or silent loss.
Moving production jobs onto the same Redis deployment increases the blast radius of Redis failover and corruption for both dispatch and existing services.
Use Redis Streams consumer groups as a durable Redis-based queue, with explicit XACK, XAUTOCLAIM for recovery, stream trimming, visibility-timeout handling, and a dead-letter stream. Validate Redis cluster failover, AOF recovery, backpressure, and recovery behavior before migration, and isolate the workload from the cache deployment where possible.
Start a subscriber that acknowledges receipt, disconnect it, publish a uniquely identified job, reconnect, and run an XINFO-style consumer-group check for any recoverable pending or unconsumed entry.
With Redis Pub/Sub, the job is absent after reconnection and zero messages are recoverable, proving the proposed design cannot provide durable dispatch.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Do not use a process-local mutex when every deployment has multiple replicas; requests for the same coupon can reach different processes and both pass the unlocked check. Enforce the invariant in Postgres with an atomic conditional claim or a unique redemption record, then handle payment idempotency and ambiguous client retries explicitly.
All requests for a coupon necessarily reach the same Node.js process, which is contradicted by the Deployment HPA and round-robin Service.
A new request cannot enter between check and update, including after lock cleanup or process termination.
chargeOrder and the subsequent coupon update are atomic or recoverable as one business operation.
A successful coupon update cannot be lost after money has been charged.
The client retry is the only source of duplicate attempts, rather than concurrent requests already in flight.
Two requests routed to different pods can both observe redeemedAt as null and both redeem the coupon, preserving the reported loss mechanism.
A process crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt leaves a paid order with an apparently reusable coupon.
Map cleanup can create overlapping mutexes if a new request removes or replaces an entry while another request is queued, depending on cleanup timing.
A 2-second client timeout can retry the payment independently of the coupon update and charge twice even if local coupon access is serialized.
A same-process concurrency test can pass while production cross-pod races remain untested.
Perform an atomic Postgres claim such as UPDATE coupons SET redemption_state='CLAIMED', order_id=$order, claim_token=$token, claimed_at=now() WHERE code=$code AND redemption_state='AVAILABLE', accepting only a request that updates one row. Enforce a unique coupon redemption invariant in the database, invoke chargeOrder with an order/payment idempotency key, and finalize the claim only after confirmed success; reconcile timed-out or ambiguous claims against payment state rather than automatically releasing them. This avoids locks across payment latency and does not depend on pod affinity.
Run the redemption request concurrently against two separate service instances, preferably with distinct Node.js processes sharing the same Postgres database, using the same fresh coupon.
If both return success or both reach the charge operation, the process-local mutex is disproven. A correct database-enforced solution should return success exactly once and AlreadyUsed or the same idempotent result to the other request.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not perform a single pre-deploy rename on this table. Use an expand/contract rollout: add the new scaled numeric column, deploy dual-write/backfill-compatible code, backfill in bounded online batches, switch reads, and only later remove or rename the old column. Choose NUMERIC(19,3), or explicitly document a four-unit scale, and verify migration duration, lock behavior, disk capacity, and application compatibility before release.
Existing INTEGER values are exact cent/minor-unit values and no lossy conversion is required.
The release can tolerate a substantial schema backfill and temporary additional storage.
Old application pods and any unupdated SQL consumers can continue accessing the original column during the migration.
PostgreSQL and the Django/database driver behavior for NUMERIC serialization has been tested end to end.
The reporting jobs can be switched atomically or are compatible with the expand/contract transition.
Changing INTEGER to NUMERIC on a roughly 900-million-row table is likely to rewrite the table and hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking night-time writes for far longer than a normal deployment window.
The migration runs before old pods are replaced, but the rename immediately removes the amount column those pods and potentially other consumers use, causing production read failures during the 25-minute rolling deployment.
A 410-GB indexed table plus rewrite/WAL and temporary objects may exhaust disk or overload streaming replicas, despite the migration role having no statement timeout.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes the storage and serialization contract and does not clearly match the required three-decimal minor-unit scale, creating financial and reporting compatibility risks.
Transactional DDL rollback does not make a long-running rewrite safe; lock acquisition, WAL, disk pressure, and replica impact can still block or disrupt checkout.
Use an online expand/contract migration: add a new NUMERIC(19,3) column without removing amount, deploy code that dual-writes and reads it, backfill existing rows in small indexed batches with rate and lock monitoring, validate totals, switch readers, and retire the old column in a later release.
On a production-sized staging clone, run the proposed ALTER under normal monitoring while an unchanged application pod executes a representative SELECT amount FROM orders query.
The ALTER holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock or exceeds the release window, and the unchanged pod fails with an undefined-column error after the rename; this directly falsifies the proposed rollout.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the in-process async mutex with an indexed atomic Postgres claim, such as an UPDATE guarded by redeemedAt IS NULL or an insert into a redemptions table with a unique coupon identifier, and require exactly one successful claimant before charging. Persist CLAIMED/SUCCESS/FAILED state and use a stable payment idempotency key derived from the coupon and order; a same-process concurrency test does not validate correctness across replicas or retries.
All redemption requests are handled by one process, with no multiple Kubernetes replicas, rolling deployments, or horizontal autoscaling.
The mutex is held across the complete check/update/payment sequence and cannot be interrupted by process termination.
Payment timeouts and retries can be safely handled without releasing the coupon before the provider's outcome is known.
The application can durably record and reconcile claim state.
The coupon code uniquely identifies the coupon and can be protected by a database uniqueness constraint.
Two requests routed to different replicas can both observe the coupon as unused and redeem or charge it twice.
A process crash or pod eviction drops the mutex, allowing another request to proceed while the first payment may still complete.
A timeout or crash after payment but before redeemedAt is written can cause duplicate charges on retry.
The proposed concurrent test can pass while production routing exposes none of these races.
Map cleanup and lock release logic can introduce additional races or leak entries under contention.
Use an atomic database state transition to claim the coupon, backed by a unique coupon redemption record, then call chargeOrder with a stable coupon/order idempotency key and reconcile ambiguous or failed claims.
Inspect the production deployment and run two redemption requests through separate service replicas, or reproduce the flow with two application instances sharing the database while using distinct in-process mutex maps.
If two replicas can both reach the redemption path and both observe redeemedAt as null, the mutex-based proposal is falsified; only an atomic database claim should allow one request to proceed.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep strings as the lossless representation, but do not redefine v1 without an explicit compatibility and migration plan. Ship a string-ID v2 immediately, and either announce a time-bounded v1 breaking change or add an opt-in representation for legacy clients; update all internal consumers of the v1 contract and provide partner migration guidance and telemetry.
First-party clients can change their ID types and parsing logic before the response format changes.
Generated SDKs will map the changed OpenAPI type to a lossless type in every supported language.
The API can version or negotiate the two ID representations within two weeks.
Partner consumers can tolerate an announced v1 type change, or the organization accepts their breakage.
The server response schema is the authoritative copy of the OpenAPI contract and all relevant consumers can be regenerated.
Deployed iOS, Android, and partner clients will reject string IDs or deserialize them into numeric types that still lose precision.
JavaScript consumers may coerce string IDs to Number, preserving the existing corruption despite the server change.
Regenerating SDKs will not repair direct REST consumers, cached bundles, or already released applications.
Changing v1 while calling it a weekly release is likely to cause partner outages and a rollback.
A v2 rollout without traffic migration leaves most current consumers on the unsafe v1 endpoint.

Run a representative order response through the current web, iOS, Android, and one generated partner SDK deserialization path after changing the fixture ID to a decimal string.
Any strict numeric deserialization failure, conversion to Number, or loss of precision falsifies immediate safe rollout to all v1 consumers and confirms that compatibility versioning or a staged client rollout is required.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but do not enable it for all health subscriptions in one rollout. First verify the exact 1.10 configuration scope and client compatibility, then canary representative cohorts, measure CPU, network, update correctness, and reconnect behavior under realistic load, and expand only against explicit thresholds. Retain a tested configuration rollback and use query/watch tuning as a complementary control.
The deployed client and server versions support the same streaming protocol and configuration semantics.
`use_streaming_backend` is set at the correct agent/server scope and actually causes production health reads to use streaming rather than merely enabling an unused feature.
The 200-node staging workload is representative of production subscription breadth, result sizes, churn, and holiday concurrency.
Streaming preserves watch ordering, completeness, and freshness during reconnects and leader changes.
The rollout can be stopped or reverted quickly enough to prevent a fleet-wide failure.
A mixed-version or mis-scoped rollout leaves blocking queries active or causes incompatible streaming behavior.
An all-at-once change can create a reconnect or subscription storm, increasing CPU, network, Raft pressure, and latency.
Incorrect streaming freshness or missed-event handling could leave services with stale dependency state or route traffic to unhealthy instances.
The staging CPU reduction may not scale linearly when every service subscribes simultaneously.
Because there is no discovery fallback, a streaming defect or partition could broadly disrupt service resolution.
Use a staged canary: begin with a bounded, diverse set of services and nodes, validate correctness and resource metrics during expected load, then expand by cohorts. Keep the existing blocking-query configuration available for immediate rollback, and add endpoint/watch coalescing or narrower subscriptions if streaming does not deliver the expected fleet-wide reduction.
Run the proposed 200-node staging configuration under a production-representative subscription mix and concurrent holiday-level load, while comparing effective configuration and measuring server CPU, network bytes, streaming versus blocking-query counts, and watch freshness or missed updates.
The proposal is falsified if clients do not actually use streaming, or if streaming causes material missed/stale updates, a reconnect storm, or higher server CPU/network than the current blocking-query baseline at representative load; a reproducible, scalable CPU reduction with correct updates supports expansion.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the namespaced Redis read-through cache, but replace the 15-minute TTL with a short bounded TTL with jitter and consume permission-events to invalidate all affected user/document/action keys, including share, unshare, account-removal, and group-membership changes. Add request coalescing and upstream-load monitoring, and define an explicit stale-grant SLO; cached grants must not remain valid beyond that SLO when invalidation is delayed.
A 15-minute stale-grant window is acceptable to authorization owners despite the stricter correctness requirement for unauthorized access.
Access-log replay accurately predicts production hit rates, including action and group-membership fan-out.
Redis can sustain cache traffic and existing session traffic at 2,500 requests per second with acceptable tail latency.
The permissions service can handle cold-cache, expiry, and coordinated miss load without becoming overloaded.
The boolean decision is safely reusable for the exact userId, docId, and action key without omitted policy or tenant context.
Revoked access can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes because the proposal has no event-driven invalidation.
Coordinated expiry, deployment, or restart can cause a cache stampede and overload permissions-service.
Access-log replay may overstate hit rates or omit low-frequency, high-risk permission changes, invalidating the latency estimate.
Redis eviction, contention, or failure can sharply reduce hit rates and drive authorization load upstream.
Incomplete key or policy context could return a cached decision for the wrong action, document, tenant, or scope.
Use Redis cache-aside with permission-events-driven deletion, short jittered TTLs, request coalescing, and measured rollback criteria. If event propagation cannot meet the required revocation SLO, adopt an event-fed projection with permissions-service reconciliation rather than relying on long TTL expiry.
Cache an allow decision for a test user/document/action, revoke that permission through the production authorization path, and immediately repeat the read while event processing is disabled or delayed.
The read continues returning allow until the 15-minute TTL expires, demonstrating an unacceptable stale-grant window and disproving reliance on access-log hit-rate evidence for authorization correctness.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not run this type-altering migration against the 900M-row table for Tuesday’s release; PostgreSQL will rewrite the table and rebuild dependent indexes while holding a strong lock, and transactional DDL does not make that operation brief or nonblocking. Add a nullable BIGINT amount_thousandths column, dual-write exact thousandths for new orders, update readers with an explicit legacy fallback, and defer historical backfill/consolidation to a later release.
No active query or transaction can hold or repeatedly reacquire locks on orders during the potentially hours-long rewrite.
All indexed and dependent structures can tolerate a full table and index rebuild within the release window.
Every old and new application instance tolerates the renamed column before and after the migration.
Downstream systems preserve NUMERIC values exactly rather than converting them through floating point.
The order currency is available to decide whether existing values are cents or another established minor unit.
Changing INTEGER to NUMERIC requires a full-table rewrite in PostgreSQL 15; ALTER COLUMN RENAME does not avoid it.
The AccessExclusive lock blocks reads and writes, creating checkout downtime and violating the 99.95% SLO.
Because migrations run while old pods are still serving, the initial lock wait can itself become an outage.
Heavy WAL and I/O can create replica lag or overload the primary despite lower overnight write traffic.
NUMERIC(19,4) permits four fractional digits but does not encode which currencies require three; inconsistent scaling could produce financial corruption.
Use an additive migration: add amount_thousandths BIGINT NULL, write both amount_minor and amount_thousandths transactionally for new orders, and define reporting as amount_thousandths when present, otherwise amount_minor * 100. This is metadata-only on PostgreSQL 15 and can be deployed next Tuesday; backfill old rows in later, throttled batches only after consumers are compatible.
On a production-sized restore, run the proposed ALTER under a short lock_timeout while normal traffic or representative sessions are active, then roll it back; separately time the same statement on an isolated copy.
A lock timeout while any query is active falsifies the assumption of a safe short deployment window; a rewrite duration materially exceeding the release or recovery budget independently falsifies readiness for Tuesday.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
The in-process mutex cannot serialize requests across the 4–12 replicas, so concurrent retries routed to different pods can both redeem the coupon. Use a Postgres-backed atomic state transition or distributed lock, ideally with a unique redemption record and idempotent order charging; explicitly define compensation or retry behavior if charging fails after the coupon is claimed.
All redemption requests for a coupon may reach different application replicas.
Postgres is shared by every replica and is the authoritative consistency boundary.
A coupon may have only one successful redemption across the entire service.
Payment charging can be made idempotent or reconciled with the coupon state transition.
Two requests handled by different pods can both pass the check and charge orders.
The concurrency test can pass in one Node process while masking the production multi-replica failure.
Claiming before charging can consume the coupon when charging fails unless compensation or a pending state exists.
Holding a database transaction or lock across payment I/O may violate the checkout p99 target.
Replace the process-local mutex with a database-level compare-and-set or transaction. For example, atomically transition an eligible coupon to a unique pending redemption using `UPDATE ... WHERE redeemed_at IS NULL AND status = 'AVAILABLE'`; persist a unique order/redemption identifier, then make charging idempotent and finalize or compensate pending claims. A unique redemption ledger or constraint provides an additional correctness barrier.
In a test environment, deploy at least two replicas and send simultaneous same-code redemption requests with connections explicitly routed to different pods; repeat enough times to cover the observed 50–300 ms overlap.
If two requests can both reach chargeOrder and succeed, the proposal is disproven; a correct database-backed implementation should allow exactly one claim or redemption and reject the other.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on the table and rely on a weekly manual vacuum. Keep autovacuum enabled with table-specific cost settings to smooth I/O, use rate-limited retention deletes, and investigate partitioning if routine vacuum still scans the full table. Validate the schedule against actual vacuum duration, dead-tuple growth, transaction horizons, and peak-load latency.
The table can accumulate dead tuples for an entire week without exceeding acceptable bloat or query-performance limits.
A weekly VACUUM can complete before the next traffic peak and without being blocked by old transactions or locks.
Traffic is consistently lowest at 02:00 Sunday and the workload tolerates a concentrated vacuum then.
The bulk deletion job does not create unacceptable WAL, lock, or index-I/O spikes.
Monitoring can detect missed cron runs, vacuum cancellation, dead-tuple growth, and bloat before damage occurs.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe bloat to develop, producing longer and more damaging cleanup runs and degraded queries.
A weekly vacuum may overlap peak traffic or fail to finish, leaving dead tuples and index bloat accumulating.
Concentrating cleanup on Sunday can recreate write-latency and I/O spikes rather than spread maintenance across the day.
Long-running transactions or conflicting locks can prevent vacuum from reclaiming rows, regardless of the cron schedule.
A failed or delayed cron job has no automatic fallback cleanup, while a Grafana bloat alert may arrive after operational damage.
Use measured, table-specific autovacuum tuning, such as an appropriate vacuum cost limit and delay, combined with smaller rate-limited retention deletes and index validation. If vacuum must regularly scan the full 1.8 TB table or cannot complete safely, migrate to time-based partitions and drop expired partitions.
Over one complete retention cycle, record n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, vacuum duration, and p99 latency in pg_stat_user_tables and system I/O metrics.
If n_dead_tup grows substantially between scheduled runs, vacuum duration approaches or exceeds seven days, vacuum is canceled or blocked, or p99 latency rises during the weekly run, the weekly-manual-vacuum proposal is falsified.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Replace the three-month big-bang cut-over with characterization tests followed by a strangler migration. Introduce stable billing interfaces and migrate plan cohorts or capabilities incrementally, using shadow calculations and invoice diffs as gates; retain a narrow compatibility layer for grandfathering until coverage is complete.
Historical production invoices and inputs are available for comprehensive golden-master and replay testing.
All 37 plans and grandfathered behavior can be expressed accurately in the proposed model without preserving the mutable BillingContext semantics.
The five services and downstream consumers can adopt a new package without incompatible deployment or release constraints.
The team can continuously integrate billing changes arising from roughly 40 weekly PRs rather than isolating them for three months.
Feature flags, shadow traffic, replay tooling, and immediate rollback can be implemented before migration.
Rare proration, tax, reversal, rounding, and account-specific rules may be discovered only near cut-over, making the clean model incomplete.
The long-lived branch will conflict with ongoing main-branch changes, especially in the same billing services.
One cut-over can corrupt many invoices simultaneously and provide limited rollback granularity.
The absence of shadow execution and diffing makes semantic differences difficult to diagnose before they affect customers.
Deleting the old implementation could remove undocumented behavior relied upon by grandfathered accounts or adjacent services.
Build a characterization harness from historical invoice cases, then define pure, typed policy interfaces behind a compatibility boundary. Migrate one plan cohort or policy capability at a time, compare old and new calculations in shadow mode, route production through the new implementation incrementally, and remove the legacy path only after explicit diff thresholds are met.
Run the current billing implementation and a thin billing-core prototype over a stratified corpus of replayable historical invoices, including every plan and at least one mid-cycle grandfathered change per plan.
The proposal is viable only if outputs match exactly, aside from explicitly approved changes, across high-risk event combinations. Any unmatched legacy behavior that cannot be represented cleanly, or volume/coverage too large to test before cut-over, falsifies the readiness assumptions for a big-bang approach.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum solely on the assumption that append-mostly data makes dead tuples accumulate slowly; retain it as a safety mechanism or use carefully bounded table-specific autovacuum settings. Replace bulk retention deletes with incremental, rate-limited batches that complete before the next cycle, and replay peak ingestion plus deletion in staging while measuring vacuum duration, dead tuples, WAL, checkpoints, and I/O before relying on a weekly manual vacuum.
The weekly vacuum can finish within the low-traffic window without materially affecting ingestion.
Retention deletes are small enough that their resulting dead tuples and index work remain manageable.
Dead tuples and index bloat accumulate slowly enough that waiting seven days is safe.
Grafana already exposes actionable bloat and vacuum-duration metrics with alert thresholds.
Traffic at Sunday 02:00 leaves enough I/O and CPU headroom for maintenance.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe dead-tuple and index-bloat growth if a manual vacuum fails, is canceled, or does not finish.
A multi-hour vacuum of a very large events table can still create a maintenance I/O spike despite running off-peak.
Off-peak bulk deletes still generate WAL, index churn, and subsequent vacuum work; scheduling them off-peak does not remove their cost.
The schedule may not keep up with peak ingestion or recurring retention volume, causing unbounded maintenance lag.
A bloat-only dashboard may not reveal checkpoint pressure, index-write cost, or vacuum cancellation promptly.

In production-like staging, run one peak-insert retention cycle with autovacuum disabled and the Sunday manual-vacuum settings, sampling pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_user_tables, checkpoint/WAL statistics, index sizes, and I/O from before the bulk delete until VACUUM completes.
The proposal is falsified if the vacuum exceeds the available window, dead tuples or index size grow materially between runs, ingestion latency rises during maintenance, or WAL/checkpoint/I/O pressure shows that off-peak execution merely shifts the original spike.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the Redis cache direction, but do not ship a 15-minute TTL without consuming permission-events and invalidating affected entries; use a short TTL as a fallback only. Prove the latency target with a representative load test: an 85% hit rate leaves 15% of requests taking the uncached path, so the current ~340 ms miss latency is approximately the p95 and the claimed ~40 ms p95 is not credible unless misses are also made fast or the hit rate is substantially higher.
permission-events reliably identifies every user/document/action decision affected by a write, membership change, or account removal
Kafka event delivery and processing are fast enough to remove revoked decisions before the next request
The 85% replay hit rate applies to production traffic and to the relevant request/key distribution, not just a historical log window
Cache hits can safely serve authorization decisions for the entire interval between writes
Redis capacity, eviction policy, key cardinality, and hot-key behavior remain acceptable at peak load
A 15-minute stale-positive window can allow users to access documents after sharing, action, group-membership, or account revocation.
Group or HR invalidations may affect many users/documents; without a defined fan-out/indexing strategy, stale entries may persist or invalidation may be prohibitively expensive.
A cache stampede on popular or newly changed documents can send large synchronized bursts to the permissions service at 2,500 rps.
Redis eviction, cluster failures, or memory pressure can silently reduce hit rate and overload the permissions service.
The proposed rollout can meet dashboards showing a high aggregate hit rate while p95 remains above budget because the uncached requests are precisely the slow tail.
Use an event-driven authorization decision cache: consume permission-events, maintain an affected-key index or a user/document decision version, and delete or version-bump matching entries; retain a short TTL and request coalescing as safety nets. Validate the event schema and invalidation completeness for group and HR changes before enabling positive caching, then benchmark p95 using production-shaped key reuse and revocation traffic.
Replay a representative production access trace against a deployment with the proposed Redis read-through cache and a permissions-service stub whose uncached p95 is 180 ms; measure end-to-end p95 at 2,500 rps while logging hit and miss latencies.
With only 85% cache hits, approximately the top 15% of requests are misses, so end-to-end p95 should remain near the uncached path (roughly 300-340 ms), not fall to ~40 ms; this would falsify the stated performance claim.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not perform an in-place type conversion and rename on the 900M-row table. Use an expand-and-contract migration: add a currency-aware numeric column, deploy dual-write/application support, backfill in committed batches with rate limits, validate reconciliation, switch reads, and only then retire the old column. Schedule cutover with an explicit rollback plan and verify it against production-like data volume.
Every order has enough currency information to distinguish two-decimal currencies from three-decimal currencies.
Existing integer values use a known scale and can be converted without changing their business meaning.
The reporting jobs and all other consumers can tolerate a compatibility period with the old column.
The database has sufficient free space, WAL capacity, and I/O headroom for an online backfill.
A 25-minute rolling deployment can safely span a migration that may take substantially longer than 25 minutes.
On PostgreSQL 15, converting INTEGER to NUMERIC generally requires a full table and index rewrite, holding a strong lock and blocking reads and writes for an unbounded period.
Because migrations run before old pods are replaced, the atomic transaction does not provide application compatibility: after commit, old code and reporting SQL referring to amount will fail.
The rewrite can generate enormous WAL, increase replica lag, exhaust disk or I/O capacity, and cause missed checkout writes or prolonged downtime.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes storage and arithmetic semantics but does not define the currency or conversion rules; incorrectly interpreting existing values can cause financial corruption.
A single long backfill or cutover can exceed the release window, leaving the migration partially complete or making rollback unsafe after application changes begin.
Add a nullable numeric representation (preferably with explicit currency and an agreed scale), backfill it in small committed batches while rate-limiting and monitoring replication/WAL, deploy code that dual-writes and reads the new representation after validation, then switch reports and rename or drop the legacy column in a later change. Preserve the old column until reconciliation and rollback criteria pass.
Run the exact ALTER TABLE on a production-sized or representative clone while measuring lock waits, duration, relfilenode changes, WAL volume, and replica lag.
A relfilenode change lasting far beyond the deployment window, or measurable blocking/lag, falsifies the claim that a transactional DDL migration is safe for this table; also verify that pre-deploy pods issue queries for amount after the migration commits.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Replace Redis Pub/Sub with Redis Streams using per-job-type or sharded streams, consumer groups, explicit acknowledgements, pending-entry recovery, and bounded retry/DLQ handling. Validate stream throughput, AOF recovery, and pod-restart redelivery under realistic payload sizes before migration, and add idempotency because dual-running and at-least-once processing will otherwise duplicate payments, fulfillment, email, or indexing.
The workload can tolerate loss of in-flight jobs when a subscriber disconnects.
Jobs do not require acknowledgement, durable backlog, or redelivery.
Running RabbitMQ and Redis dispatch simultaneously can be made idempotent.
Redis Streams throughput and persistence meet the 300 jobs/s peak with production payload sizes and replication overhead.
AOF recovery time and data loss during Redis failures are operationally acceptable.
Pub/Sub does not persist messages; AOF provides no recovery for published jobs, so pod redeployments and disconnects can silently lose webhooks, payments, emails, or indexing work.
Redis Pub/Sub broadcasts each message to every subscriber rather than reliably load-balancing a consumer group, potentially multiplying work across replicas.
A worker-side retry wrapper cannot recover jobs lost before receipt, while process crashes after receipt can cause unretried loss.
