Dual-running dispatches both systems and can trigger duplicate business side effects unless every handler is strongly idempotent.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ removes backlog and DLQ visibility unless equivalent operational tooling and recovery semantics are implemented first.
Use Redis Streams as the managed-by-the-team replacement: organize job types into bounded streams, consume through consumer groups, acknowledge only after successful processing, recover pending entries with visibility timeouts, and send poison jobs to a durable retry/DLQ stream.
Subscribe with redis-cli, terminate the subscriber, PUBLISH one uniquely identifiable job, restart the subscriber, and inspect whether it receives the job; repeat after the publisher or Redis process restarts.
The restarted subscriber receives no job, confirming that Pub/Sub cannot provide durable acknowledgement or redelivery despite Redis AOF.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the header-bit approach, but do not make an unverified global client-side launch the release mechanism. Add explicit compatibility tests, reject or safely quarantine any legacy Power Peg path before RLP enablement, deploy an identical verified artifact with post-deploy build/configuration checks, and use an allowlisted canary with monitoring and rollback before broad client activation.
No current or future non-RLP client, gateway, replay tool, retry path, or intermediary can set the bit.
The RLP specification permits the bit to carry order-level routing intent and does not require distinct semantics from Power Peg.
Every client that will set the bit can be released and coordinated with the router before launch, despite the unchanged wire layout.
Removing the old Power Peg implementation cannot invalidate persisted state, hidden configuration, or downstream assumptions.
The router can distinguish an RLP order from an invalid or unexpected legacy order and fail closed.
A month of zero observed bits is not proof that all traffic sources, historical messages, retries, or future integrations leave it unset.
A client or gateway may set the bit based on stale Power Peg documentation or a copied conditional, unexpectedly activating RLP.
The manual eight-server deployment can leave mixed binaries or configurations, producing inconsistent order behavior.
Deleting Power Peg in the same release creates a hazardous rollback if any legacy producer can still emit the bit.
Enabling all RLP-eligible clients simultaneously could expose router defects at the full ~3M-orders/day load before detection.
For RLP decisions that can be made from client/account identity or router policy, use a server-side allowlist and keep the bit unused until a formally versioned per-order contract is available. If the program explicitly requires per-order signaling, the proposed bit is preferable, but only with the safeguards above.
Run a repository-wide static and binary/protocol audit of every encoder, decoder, configuration default, retry/forwarding path, and client release artifact for assignments to the target header bit, followed by replay tests of legacy Power Peg configurations against the new router.
Any non-RLP path capable of setting the bit, any decoder that treats it as Power Peg, or any legacy configuration that remains effective falsifies safe direct reuse; otherwise it supports proceeding with canary rollout.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain the expedited path, but require versioned, signed configuration with local schema/resource validation, an automated global kill switch, and staged enforcement that still completes within one hour. Do not treat CI corpus success or ten minutes of low log volume as sufficient evidence of safety, because benign traffic may be absent or insufficiently represented and catastrophic PCRE backtracking remains possible.
Quicksilver can atomically distribute versioned WAF configuration to every proxy within the required latency.
Every proxy can reject invalid, incompatible, or computationally unsafe rules before activation.
The CI benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives.
Ten minutes of traffic across all PoPs provides statistically meaningful coverage.
A rule can be disabled and previous configuration restored automatically within minutes.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic at every edge simultaneously.
A PCRE pattern with pathological backtracking could saturate already CPU-bound proxies; log mode still executes the regex.
A malformed or incompatible configuration could cause proxy reload failures or inconsistent enforcement.
Low observed match volume could conceal false positives because attack types and benign traffic vary by customer and PoP.
A partial Quicksilver distribution or failed flip could leave the fleet exposed or produce an unreviewable mixed state.
Publish a signed, versioned rule bundle with a precomputed PCRE complexity/resource limit; validate and benchmark it on proxy builds, enable observation on a small representative canary for several minutes, then automatically progress through 1%, 10%, and 100% block enforcement within the one-hour objective. Continuously compare match rates, latency, CPU, errors, and representative benign traffic, with automatic rollback on any threshold breach.
Replay a production-representative benign request trace plus the CI payload corpus through the exact proxy/WAF build, measuring incremental p99 latency and CPU while enabling the proposed rule in log mode.
The proposal is falsified if any single rule exceeds the defined per-request CPU/latency budget, causes PCRE resource growth with input length, or matches representative benign traffic at a rate that would create material customer impact.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator automated recovery, but make promotion region-aware and explicitly fence the failed primary before allowing writes; normally promote an East replica, reserving West promotion for an East-region failure. Define and test an RPO, replication-lag thresholds, application routing behavior, and recovery-time budget, and do not enable unattended recovery across all clusters until these checks pass. Raft protects the Orchestrator decision, not MySQL data durability or split-brain safety.
An East replica will normally be available and sufficiently caught up to serve the East application during a primary-host failure.
The failed primary can be reliably fenced or terminated before the replacement is made writable.
Consul integration and application retry/write behavior will route new connections to the promoted primary without unacceptable connection or DNS caching delays.
The acceptable RPO permits any asynchronous replication lag, including cross-region lag.
Orchestrator's recovery actions, topology updates, and promotion are safe for every cluster under the proposed automation.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged writes and create an unacceptable RPO; Raft does not make replication synchronous.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and divergence when connectivity returns.
Promoting a West replica may add roughly 60 ms or more to every write and may not satisfy the application's latency or availability requirements.
Unattended recovery for all clusters can amplify a topology error, bad promotion choice, or Consul integration failure into a broad outage.
The stated under-one-minute objective is not demonstrated: detection, promotion, fencing, Consul propagation, client reconnection, and application retries may exceed that budget.

During a controlled East-primary host failure, continuously issue uniquely identified committed writes, then promote the configured candidate and verify every acknowledged write ID is present before declaring recovery successful; also measure detection-to-write-readiness time.
Any missing acknowledged write falsifies safe automated promotion under the current asynchronous design; a recovery time over 60 seconds falsifies the stated objective.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
An in-process mutex cannot serialize the 4-12 Kubernetes replicas, so concurrent requests routed to different pods can still both pass the check and redeem the coupon. Replace it with a Postgres-backed atomic redemption claim or unique redemption record, and make charging/retry handling idempotent so a client retry cannot create a second order charge.
All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process, which is false with multiple replicas.
The service is not horizontally scaled or restarted during the redemption window.
The charge operation can be safely retried or reconciled using an idempotency key.
Postgres uniqueness or conditional-update semantics are available for the coupon redemption operation.
The existing test exercises multiple application instances rather than only two calls in one process.
Two requests handled by different pods can both observe redeemedAt as null and both charge orders.
A process crash after charging but before updating redeemedAt leaves a charged order with an apparently unused coupon.
A timeout-driven retry can repeat the charge unless order/payment idempotency is enforced.
Naively deleting a mutex entry after release can allow a new mutex to be created while an earlier waiter still exists, breaking serialization within a process.
A database claim that occurs before a failed charge can permanently consume a coupon unless failures are explicitly released or reconciled.
Use a durable Postgres operation: atomically claim the coupon with an UPDATE ... WHERE redeemedAt IS NULL and a unique redemption identifier, or insert into a redemptions table with UNIQUE(coupon_id). Persist an order/payment idempotency key and state transitions so retries return the existing result; handle charge failure with an explicit recoverable state and reconciliation. Add a test that sends concurrent requests through separate service instances or directly validates the atomic database operation.
Run two concurrent redeem requests for one coupon while forcing them to different pods, for example by scaling the Deployment to at least two replicas and targeting separate pod IPs through separate test clients.
If both requests succeed or both reach the charge operation, the in-process mutex proposal is falsified; a correct database-backed claim should allow exactly one claim and return AlreadyUsed or the original idempotent result to the other request.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Do not perform a three-month big-bang replacement. Build billing-core incrementally with characterization tests and golden invoice comparisons for all 37 plans, then migrate one bounded workflow at a time behind an adapter while retaining the legacy path for rollback. Use production shadowing and explicit reconciliation before switching invoice generation, tax, payments, and notifications.
The existing 37 plans and their historical edge cases can be faithfully represented by the proposed clean domain model.
Unit tests for billing-core will be sufficient despite proration, tax, payment, and notification behavior currently spanning five services.
All five services can switch atomically to the new package without requiring coordinated changes across the other teams.
Historical plan definitions and representative invoice scenarios are available and cover grandfathered pricing behavior.
A single cut-over can provide an acceptable rollback and reconciliation strategy.
Unknown proration and grandfathering rules will produce silently incorrect invoices when the old code is deleted.
A three-month branch will diverge from roughly 40 weekly main-branch changes, creating integration and deployment failures.
A cut-over affecting invoicing, tax, and payments can cause duplicate charges, missed invoices, or irreversible customer-billing damage.
Deleting the legacy implementation eliminates the fastest rollback path and makes diagnosis difficult when production behavior differs.
The 22% existing coverage leaves critical service-level interactions untested, so a model that passes unit tests may still break end-to-end billing.
Use a strangler migration: first freeze and characterize current behavior with golden invoices and contract tests, then introduce billing-core behind a compatibility adapter and migrate subscriptions and invoice calculation incrementally. Shadow invoices in production, compare outputs and side effects, migrate tax/payments/notifications only after parity, and remove legacy code only after a defined bake period.
Create a representative golden corpus containing current production or captured outputs for all 37 plans, including the 11 grandfathered plans, proration changes, cancellations, renewals, taxes, payment failures, and retries; run both implementations against identical inputs and compare invoice line items, totals, taxes, due dates, and side effects.
Any unexplained difference, missing scenario, or inability to replay historical inputs falsifies the claim that a single cut-over can preserve invoices and supports incremental migration instead.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Retain the string-ID objective, but do not silently change the existing v1 wire type in the same release. Add a safe string field or a parallel versioned response, update the web client and generated SDK guidance, and schedule removal of the numeric field after measuring consumer migration. Provide explicit compatibility tests for JavaScript, Swift, Kotlin, and representative partners before broad rollout.
Existing v1 clients and partner integrations can tolerate a JSON type change, despite independently deployed versions and weekly mobile release cycles.
All order response paths, caches, fixtures, webhooks, and gateway schemas can be changed consistently and atomically.
Generated SDKs will safely deserialize string IDs in every target language after regeneration.
No consumer performs numeric operations, numeric validation, or exact type matching on the ID.
The API and partner ecosystem can absorb an immediate breaking contract change within two weeks.
Current JavaScript clients will continue rounding IDs until they deploy a compatible parser, so the user-facing defect may remain in the field.
Current mobile and partner clients may reject string IDs, lose the field, or deserialize it incorrectly, causing outages or incorrect order actions.
Incomplete coverage could leave list, detail, cached, or mocked responses with numeric IDs and perpetuate silent corruption.
Strict schema validation, database bindings, or business logic expecting a number may fail server-side or in downstream systems.
Regenerating and releasing SDKs does not update already-deployed partner integrations within the stated two-week window.
Use an additive migration: introduce `id_string` (or a new v2 response where `id` is a string), keep v1 numeric `id` temporarily, and update the web client immediately to consume the safe field. Publish a deprecation and removal date only after partner and mobile adoption is measured; then make the string representation canonical in a new major API version.
Run representative current JavaScript, Swift, and Kotlin clients plus the existing generated partner SDK against a v1 response containing `id` as a string, using the proposed regenerated SDKs and current production contracts.
If any supported client rejects the response, loses or changes the ID, requires a numeric type, or fails strict validation, the immediate all-v1 string change is unsafe and the additive/versioned migration is required.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver rollout, but do not make global blocking conditional only on aggregate match volume. Require bounded PCRE evaluation (complexity limits and a per-rule CPU/time budget), production-like load validation, and an automated rollback based on proxy latency, error rate, and false-positive indicators. Use a short 1% blocking canary with monitoring before global blocking, and aggregate or sample log-mode matches rather than performing unbounded per-request logging; this can still complete within the one-hour objective.
The CI corpus and benign-request set provide sufficiently representative coverage for newly disclosed attacks.
Quicksilver propagation and rule activation are atomic and fail-safe across all proxies and regions.
The WAF engine can enforce per-rule evaluation limits and disable a rule without taking down the proxy.
There is sufficient CPU headroom to evaluate the new rule on every request during log mode.
A reliable, low-latency signal exists for distinguishing attack matches from false positives.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, increase request latency, or cause an outage even when it does not block requests.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic globally after only ten minutes of insufficiently targeted monitoring.
Attackers could deliberately generate high match volume, making log mode itself expensive or obscuring benign false positives.
Inconsistent Quicksilver updates could leave some machines blocking while others only log, complicating incident response.
CI payload coverage may miss the disclosed exploit variant, allowing the rule to be published without detecting the actual attack.

Run a production-like peak-load benchmark with the candidate rule enabled in log mode on the proxy, comparing CPU utilization, p95/p99 latency, request errors, and match-processing cost against the same workload without the rule.
The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation materially reduces available CPU or violates the proxy's latency/error SLOs, or if match volume causes unsafe logging overhead; negligible overhead and stable latency support proceeding with the expedited path.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep string serialization as the target representation, but do not make an uncoordinated type change in existing v1 responses. Add a versioned or explicitly negotiated string-ID representation, update the web client and mobile models first, and provide a compatibility/deprecation period for partner SDKs before removing the numeric representation.
Existing deployed clients can tolerate receiving a JSON string where their model expects an integer.
The web frontend is updated in the same deployment and explicitly parses or renders the string form.
Partner integrations will update their deployed SDKs before the server changes.
The API can support a negotiated or versioned response during migration.
Changing the OpenAPI type will not cause generated SDKs to silently break source or runtime compatibility.
The existing Swift Codable Int64 model will typically fail decoding when the JSON value changes from a number to a string.
The existing Kotlin/Moshi Long adapter may reject a string, causing mobile request or response failures.
The roughly 40 partner integrations and their already-deployed SDKs can break immediately when v1 changes.
A regenerated SDK does not update integrations that are already deployed, so weekly SDK publication does not provide migration coverage.
Web components that perform numeric comparisons, sorting, or formatting may produce incorrect behavior even after avoiding JavaScript precision loss.
Introduce a new API version or negotiated representation that returns IDs as strings, migrate consumers incrementally, and retain the existing numeric v1 representation until usage has been audited and a deprecation deadline has passed.
Decode a response containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the currently released Swift model and Kotlin/Moshi model.
If either current model throws a type-mismatch or parsing exception, the proposed v1 cutover is incompatible with the deployed client population and requires a migration or versioned representation.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Retain the Redis read-through cache, but consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected authorization keys; do not rely solely on a 15-minute TTL for revocations or account/group removal. Also validate the latency claim with a production-shaped load test: an 85% hit rate still places the p95 request on the slow miss path, so the cache must exceed roughly 95% hit rate to bring p95 below 120 ms without a faster miss path.
Permission events contain enough identifiers to invalidate every affected `userId/docId/action` key, including indirect group and account changes.
The permissions service's Kafka publication is durable, ordered sufficiently, and has bounded end-to-end delivery latency.
A bounded stale-grant window is acceptable to the security owner; otherwise positive grants cannot safely be cached for 15 minutes.
The permissions decision depends only on the proposed user, document, and action inputs.
Peak key cardinality and Redis request volume fit the existing cluster's capacity.
Unshared documents, removed accounts, or removed group memberships could remain authorized for up to 15 minutes.
At 85% hits, 15% of requests are misses, so p95 is still a permissions-service miss and may remain above the 120 ms budget.
Malformed, incomplete, delayed, or replayed invalidation events could leave revoked grants cached until TTL expiry.
A high-cardinality workload could impose substantial memory and command pressure on the session Redis cluster.
Use Redis caching with event-driven invalidation, a short bounded TTL, and denial on authorization-service errors; require a measured hit rate above 95% before treating the p95 objective as met.
Replay representative production traffic through the proposed Redis cache at the measured 85% hit rate and measure end-to-end p95, including the actual permissions-service miss latency.
If p95 remains near the cache-miss path rather than falling to about 40 ms, the stated latency benefit is falsified; if revoking permissions can remain cached for 15 minutes under the event stream, the safety design is also falsified.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse direction only as a time-boxed compatibility measure, but make rollout two-phase: deploy the backward-compatible RLP-capable router to all eight servers, verify exact build identity and RLP readiness, then permit clients to set the bit through a centrally controlled admission gate. Do not remove Power Peg in the same release; retain it behind an explicit server-side deny/default-off control until the RLP path is proven and rollback safety is established.
No legitimate producer outside the inspected production traffic—including replay, recovery, administrative, test, archived, or failover clients—can set the bit.
No order can reach a stale or old router after clients begin setting the bit.
The gateway can centrally withhold RLP-bit traffic until every production server is verified RLP-capable.
RLP eligibility is implemented consistently by all clients, gateways, and routers.
The old router's Power Peg behavior cannot be activated by the new RLP traffic if mixed versions occur.
A stale router may receive the RLP bit and execute the retired Power Peg algorithm, misrouting orders across the entire 3M-order/day workload.
Rollback to a pre-RLP router while clients still set the bit may immediately create mixed-version behavior.
A month of traffic does not establish that archived, replayed, test, administrative, or failover producers never set the bit.
Manual deployment provides no reliable evidence that all eight servers run the intended build.
Simultaneously removing Power Peg and introducing RLP makes rollback and incident diagnosis substantially harder.
If the date cannot accommodate a versioned message change, isolate RLP traffic on a separate listener or transport with an RLP-capable router fleet, so legacy routers can never receive the RLP signal. If isolation is infeasible, retain a coordinated protocol-version change and seek a staged exchange launch rather than relying on bit semantics.
In a production-like staging test, run an unmodified pre-RLP router and send otherwise valid orders with the reused header bit set through the actual gateway-to-router path; also search every producer and replay/recovery code path for writes to the bit.
Any old-router path that accepts and acts on the set bit, or any non-RLP producer capable of setting it, falsifies the proposal's safety premise and requires a separate admission boundary or replacement approach.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. Start with a small, representative client canary while retaining blocking queries and a centrally managed rollback switch, then expand only after measuring CPU, inbound/outbound traffic, errors, discovery latency, index lag, and freshness against baseline under service churn. Verify the exact server/client compatibility and streaming configuration requirements before production deployment rather than relying only on the vendor recommendation and staging CPU result.
All relevant client versions can be upgraded or configured for streaming within six weeks.
Streaming preserves required discovery freshness, ordering, index behavior, and failure semantics in the production workload.
Client populations and their configuration can be centrally identified, segmented, and rolled back.
Production network capacity can absorb increased or bursty push fan-out without harming other traffic.
The staging benchmark's 60% CPU reduction is representative of production query and churn patterns.
A fleet-wide rollout could expose stale-discovery or failure-propagation defects before they are detected.
Unmeasured push fan-out could increase outbound bandwidth, latency, or packet loss and degrade the cluster.
A staging-only CPU comparison may conceal production differences in query rate, service churn, payload size, or client behavior.
Upgrading agents and servers to 1.10 could introduce compatibility or upgrade-order risks that are not addressed.
No explicit rollback mechanism is provided, so an adverse rollout could affect all services simultaneously.
Use a representative production canary with control and treatment cohorts, explicit expansion/rollback thresholds, and continued availability of existing polling behavior; add polling tuning or server capacity only if canary measurements show they are still needed.
Run the exact proposed client/server versions in a production-like canary with representative services and churn, comparing streaming clients with unchanged blocking-query clients for CPU, inbound/outbound traffic, errors, discovery latency, index lag, and stale-result rate.
The proposal is supported only if streaming materially reduces CPU without exceeding predefined network, error, propagation-lag, or freshness limits; comparable clients that show stale results, excessive fan-out, or degraded failure detection would falsify the rollout as currently proposed.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver path, but do not allow an arbitrary CI-passing PCRE to enter the inline request path or automatically block globally after a fixed 10-minute observation period. Require a strict evaluation-time/CPU budget, reject unsafe regex constructs, preserve an independently controlled kill switch and atomic rollback, and validate benign traffic volume and latency during the log period before enabling blocking.
The WAF engine enforces a hard per-rule evaluation timeout and can safely terminate pathological PCRE execution.
Quicksilver updates are versioned and can be rolled back consistently across all PoPs within minutes.
CI's benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives before global enforcement.
Log-mode evaluation has a bounded CPU and memory cost comparable to block-mode evaluation.
A global configuration update can be gated, audited, and reversed without waiting for the normal staged pipeline.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, degrade or halt all customer traffic because WAF evaluation is inline and proxies are already CPU-bound.
Ten minutes of match-volume observation may miss low-frequency false positives, false negatives, regional traffic differences, or application-specific behavior.
Automatic global blocking could deny legitimate requests across every customer immediately, with no safe mechanism to disable the rule quickly.
Configuration propagation or version skew could produce inconsistent enforcement across PoPs and make rollback unreliable.
The safety check may itself overload the request path if log mode materially increases latency or creates large match/event volumes.

Run each candidate PCRE against the production benign corpus and representative attack payloads using the production WAF engine, with a hard timeout, while measuring p99 evaluation latency and CPU time.
The proposal is falsified if any CI-passing rule exhibits superlinear execution, exceeds the proxy's defined per-request CPU/latency budget, or causes the corpus run to approach the timeout; otherwise this supports retaining the expedited path with the stated safeguards.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not immediately permanently delete IDs from an unvalidated generic list. Reconcile and type-check every installation, test cascade behavior, migrate in reversible site cohorts, verify site and unrelated-product integrity, then permanently delete validated installations with retries, deadline tracking, and alerting.
The product team's list is complete, current, duplicate-free, and contains only add-on installation IDs.
The generic API internally identifies each object by type rather than treating any 24-character value as deletable.
Permanent installation deletion has no destructive side effects on sites or other products.
A successful HTTP response reliably represents deletion of every requested ID.
Batching, pausing, and on-call monitoring can complete the purge before backend shutdown.
A site or product ID in the list could cause irreversible deletion of the entire site or unrelated data.
Undocumented cascading could damage other products even when the listed ID is correctly typed.
Partial failures could be missed, leaving installations active during backend shutdown.
A stale or incorrect list could delete installations that should be retained or fail to remove all required ones.
The irreversible job could begin without a tested rollback path or evidence that other product data remains intact.
Use a phased migration: obtain typed metadata for every supplied ID, reconcile counts per site, and first use mark mode or a typed add-on removal operation on a small cohort. Verify that only the legacy installation is affected, then permanently delete that cohort; expand gradually while monitoring per-ID results, unrelated-product integrity, completion time, and errors. Reserve irreversible deletion for reconciled IDs and establish a final cutoff before month-end.
On a disposable site containing Insight Legacy plus unrelated products, record typed metadata for the site, product, and installation IDs; call DELETE with the installation ID in permanent mode, then query all three objects and their site data.
The probe supports the proposal only if the API confirms the input is an add-on installation, the installation is permanently removed, the site and unrelated product remain unchanged, and the response clearly reports per-ID success. Any site/product deletion, ambiguous typing, or unreliable outcome falsifies the proposed direct permanent-deletion approach.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Retain Consul 1.10 streaming, but verify that `use_streaming_backend = true` is configured on servers rather than only on clients, then deploy through mixed-version server and client canaries with explicit health, freshness, error-rate, CPU, and network thresholds. Do not enable it fleet-wide based on a 200-node test; validate rollback, Raft backup, and behavior during leader changes and partitions, and complete production qualification within the six-week window.
The staging 200-node workload and 60% CPU result remain representative of 18,000 nodes and thousands of services.
The Consul 1.10 feature supports every blocking-query health endpoint and query parameter used in production.
Mixed 1.9/1.10 server and agent versions are supported throughout the rollout and rollback period.
Clients can interoperate with streaming servers without explicit client-side enablement or code changes.
Consistent, current results and ACL behavior are preserved during server push and reconnect scenarios.
If this is a server-side backend option, configuring only clients will leave production CPU unchanged while creating a false sense of completion.
A simultaneous fleet-wide cutover could make an untested stream correctness or availability regression affect every dependency lookup with no fallback cluster.
Streaming may not cover all health query forms currently used, so uncovered workloads could retain the original high load.
Leader changes, disconnects, or slow consumers could expose stale dependency results, connection growth, or new server load patterns.
Upgrading a critical Consul cluster without tested rollback, configuration backups, and a recent Raft snapshot increases outage and data-recovery risk.

Check the exact Consul 1.10 documentation/source for `use_streaming_backend` configuration scope and run `consul validate` against a minimal client-only and server configuration.
The proposal is falsified if the option is server-only, is rejected as a client option, or is not supported by the deployed 1.10 build; if it is server-side, a small server canary should then show streaming headers/connections and materially lower server CPU without increased stale or failed responses.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the reserved-bit approach, but do not enable it on clients until every production router is running the RLP-aware build and the deployed versions have been independently verified. Use a staged rollout with canaries, server-level health checks, explicit rollback criteria, and a client kill switch; retain rollback compatibility until the new router fleet is proven stable. Document the bit's new protocol meaning and test behavior for mixed old/new clients and malformed or retried messages.
The current router's Power Peg path is harmless or can be made harmless when the bit is set; zero observed traffic does not establish how old binaries will behave once clients begin setting it.
All order-message producers, including gateways, simulators, retries, and external clients, can be identified and updated or prevented from setting the bit prematurely.
Every one of the eight routers can be upgraded and its exact build verified before client activation.
The RLP implementation has defined behavior for unsupported, duplicated, delayed, and retried orders, and rollback will not occur while RLP-setting clients remain active.
The exchange permits semantic reuse of a previously defined protocol bit without requiring a separate compatibility or governance review.
Clients setting the bit before all routers are upgraded could cause legacy routers to invoke the retired Power Peg algorithm, producing incorrect routing or order loss.
Manual deployment can leave servers on different builds; a later client rollout could expose some orders to incompatible behavior.
Removing the Power Peg implementation eliminates a straightforward rollback target, and rolling back while clients set the RLP bit could recreate the original danger.
A month of production traffic cannot prove the bit is unused by infrequent clients, archived gateways, maintenance tools, or future integrations.
Bit corruption, stale messages, retries, or an unrecognized bit state could accidentally select RLP or Power Peg behavior without a clear rejection/failsafe policy.
If the exchange permits the approximately one-month coordinated change, add an explicit RLP indicator or protocol/version field rather than redefining historical semantics. Otherwise, use the reserved bit only with a fully gated fleet rollout and a compatibility-preserving router release.
In staging, send one otherwise valid order to the currently deployed pre-RLP router with the header bit set, and compare its routing and resulting audit record with the same order using the bit clear.
If the old router invokes Power Peg, rejects the order, or produces any different routing outcome, client activation before complete fleet upgrade is unsafe and the proposal requires modification.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Add a shadow-and-compare phase before each cohort moves, using historical and live near-threshold traffic to verify usage semantics, allocation/grace behavior, and regional consistency. Keep a time-bounded legacy fallback with explicit rollback criteria, and initially disable automatic reductions or prove their parity before enabling them; dashboards alone are insufficient validation.
Legacy and new usage reports have identical units, scope, deduplication, and timestamp semantics.
Copying current allocations also preserves grace-period and delayed/missing-report behavior.
Services can switch registration and enforcement paths at runtime and safely recover from quota-manager outages.
Regional replication and failover enforce consistent quota decisions.
Automatic reductions cannot reject legitimate writes before the grace period provides safe rollback time.
User-ID writes begin failing in wave 3 because new quota decisions differ near allocation thresholds.
Semantic reporting differences create false quota exceedances or allow excess storage.
Replication lag or regional conflicts cause inconsistent write acceptance and account-data divergence.
An omitted service or lost connectivity leaves usage unmanaged while deregistered from the legacy manager.
Enabling automatic reductions during migration compounds allocation mismatches and removes the rollback safety margin.
Use compatibility-gated shadowing: normalize reports through a compatibility layer, compare decisions and allocations without enforcement, then migrate lower-risk services in cohorts before user-ID. Retain a controlled legacy fallback until parity, resilience, audit, and rollback exit criteria pass.
Replay historical and recent live user-ID usage, including near-threshold, delayed, missing, and out-of-order reports, through both managers in shadow mode and compare every allocation and enforcement decision by region.
Any material unexplained decision mismatch, false rejection, regional divergence, or difference in grace and missing-report behavior would falsify the proposed wave cutover as currently specified.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep strings as the lossless representation, but do not redefine v1 without an explicit compatibility and migration plan. Ship a string-ID v2 immediately, and either announce a time-bounded v1 breaking change or add an opt-in representation for legacy clients; update all internal consumers of the v1 contract and provide partner migration guidance and telemetry.
First-party clients can change their ID types and parsing logic before the response format changes.
Generated SDKs will map the changed OpenAPI type to a lossless type in every supported language.
The API can version or negotiate the two ID representations within two weeks.
Partner consumers can tolerate an announced v1 type change, or the organization accepts their breakage.
The server response schema is the authoritative copy of the OpenAPI contract and all relevant consumers can be regenerated.
Deployed iOS, Android, and partner clients will reject string IDs or deserialize them into numeric types that still lose precision.
JavaScript consumers may coerce string IDs to Number, preserving the existing corruption despite the server change.
Regenerating SDKs will not repair direct REST consumers, cached bundles, or already released applications.
Changing v1 while calling it a weekly release is likely to cause partner outages and a rollback.
A v2 rollout without traffic migration leaves most current consumers on the unsafe v1 endpoint.

Run a representative order response through the current web, iOS, Android, and one generated partner SDK deserialization path after changing the fixture ID to a decimal string.
Any strict numeric deserialization failure, conversion to Number, or loss of precision falsifies immediate safe rollout to all v1 consumers and confirms that compatibility versioning or a staged client rollout is required.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep IDs as strings, but do not change the existing v1 schema in place. Introduce a versioned v2 contract with string IDs and an explicit migration/deprecation window for v1, while immediately updating the web client and testing or updating mobile and partner deserializers. Regenerating SDKs alone does not make a breaking response-schema change safe for already deployed clients or independently upgraded partner integrations.
All existing clients can be upgraded or patched before the API changes.
Swift's default Int64 Codable decoding and Moshi's default Long adapter can be configured to accept JSON strings.
Approximately 40 partner integrations control their SDK upgrade and application deployment schedules.
There is no independently deployed or cached client that must continue consuming v1 indefinitely.
The API gateway, analytics pipeline, and internal consumers will all tolerate the changed JSON field type.
Existing Swift and Kotlin models will generally fail to decode a JSON string into Int64 or Long with their default adapters.
Changing the OpenAPI field from integer/int64 to string is source-breaking for generated SDKs, potentially causing partner compilation failures.
Already deployed mobile and partner clients can break immediately after deployment because they cannot be upgraded atomically with the API.
A partial rollout may leave consumers decoding the same logical field as different types, causing outages, rejected orders, or support incidents.
The two-week deadline is unlikely to cover store review and staggered mobile adoption across the user base.
Add a string-typed field such as `id_string` while retaining the legacy numeric `id` during migration, and make it the sole identifier in a new versioned v2 endpoint. Update the web client to use the string field immediately; deprecate the numeric field only after usage data shows consumers have migrated. This preserves ID generation and gives clients an unambiguous, non-lossy contract without an uncoordinated breaking change.
Feed a response containing `"id": "1234567890123456789"` through the currently shipped Swift Codable model, Moshi Long model, and one representative generated partner SDK.
Any default decoder rejecting the string or returning a compile-time type mismatch falsifies the claim that the in-place v1 change is safe with existing clients; explicit adapters or regenerated string-typed models are required.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum for the entire high-churn table. Keep it enabled with a per-table autovacuum threshold and cost configuration, or schedule bounded off-peak maintenance while continuously measuring dead tuples, bloat, vacuum duration, and wraparound distance. Validate that maintenance can complete between bulk-delete cycles before choosing any manual schedule.
Dead-tuple creation and transaction-ID consumption remain low enough for weekly maintenance to keep up.
A VACUUM of the 1.8 TB table can complete within the low-traffic window and does not itself create unacceptable IO spikes.
Bulk deletes do not leave long-running transactions that prevent vacuum from reclaiming dead tuples.
The measured bloat and dead-tuple growth can be detected before operational impact.
Storage has sufficient free space and maintenance IO does not interfere with peak ingestion.
Dead tuples may accumulate faster than the weekly vacuum removes them, causing severe bloat, degraded scans, and worsening write latency.
The scheduled VACUUM may run for many hours and recreate the same IO spikes, merely moving them to Sunday.
Disabling regular autovacuum can allow transaction-ID wraparound pressure; anti-wraparound behavior in PostgreSQL 9.4 must be explicitly verified rather than assumed.
A single large VACUUM may generate sustained IO and WAL/checkpoint pressure even when traffic is only 20% of peak.
Autovacuum configuration or monitoring may miss tables and thresholds needed to prevent unbounded bloat.
Retain autovacuum and tune the table with a suitably lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor or explicit vacuum threshold, then use pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_activity, and a bloat measurement tool to verify that workers complete. If a manual vacuum is still needed, use short, observable, off-peak runs with cost throttling rather than disabling maintenance for a week.
Measure events dead tuples, autovacuum/vacuum timestamps and duration, and vacuum progress over one full delete cycle; compare the dead-tuple growth rate with the number of tuples a completed vacuum can remove.
If dead tuples or estimated bloat grow substantially between maintenance runs, or a vacuum cannot complete before the next cycle, the weekly-manifestation proposal is falsified.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on `events` without measuring whether vacuum is actually the dominant source of business-hour latency. Keep it enabled, apply conservative table-specific autovacuum cost/threshold tuning, and monitor dead tuples, vacuum progress, bloat, WAL, checkpoint activity, and foreground latency. If a predictable schedule is necessary, run a throttled maintenance vacuum more frequently or with explicit time limits rather than relying exclusively on a weekly job; the proposed approach otherwise risks trading latency spikes for severe bloat and vacuum catch-up work.
Dead-tuple creation remains low enough for a weekly vacuum to complete before another backlog forms.
The Sunday 02:00 window is long enough for VACUUM to finish under realistic production IO load.
Disabling table autovacuum will not interfere with other required maintenance behavior or emergency vacuum needs.
Grafana bloat metrics are available, sufficiently accurate, and will alert on vacuum lag or rapidly growing dead tuples.
The vacuum job can be monitored and retried or throttled if traffic, duration, or IO deviates from expectations.
A failed, delayed, or overrun cron job lets dead tuples and index bloat accumulate, increasing scan and index costs.
A weekly VACUUM may itself create a large IO spike, merely moving the problem into a lower-traffic period.
The assumption that append-mostly inserts imply slow dead-tuple growth ignores the stated periodic bulk deletes.
Disabling autovacuum removes the safety net needed when delete volume or query access patterns change.
Bloat monitoring alone may miss WAL, checkpoint, or storage-latency saturation caused by the manual vacuum.
Retain autovacuum on `events` and first tune its per-table cost delay/limit and thresholds so maintenance is spread predictably across the week. Coordinate batch deletes with vacuum and schedule a monitored, throttled catch-up vacuum only if measurements show autovacuum cannot keep up; evaluate time-based inheritance partitioning as a separate longer-term migration.
During one representative business cycle, record `pg_stat_all_tables` dead tuples, `last_autovacuum`, and `last_autoanalyze` for `events`, plus filesystem IO and write p99; then compare them with a controlled, throttled maintenance vacuum while autovacuum remains enabled.
If vacuum is disabled and the scheduled job cannot keep the dead-tuple backlog bounded—or if its IO still produces unacceptable latency—the proposal is falsified. If autovacuum is confirmed to dominate the spikes and tuned autovacuum is insufficient, that supports the operational scheduling direction but not an unmonitored weekly-only design.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep wave-based migration and user-ID-last, but add shadow-mode decision comparison, explicit exit criteria per wave, and independently reversible cutover controls. Do not enable automatic quota reduction on the first authoritative cutovers: validate reporting completeness and grace-period behavior first, then enable it service by service; dashboards alone are not safety controls.
Copying an allocation preserves its effective value, unit, and reset/grace-period semantics in the new system.
Deregistering a service immediately redirects all usage reports and enforcement checks to only the new manager.
Usage reporting is complete and timely enough that automatic reduction cannot mistake missing telemetry for low usage.
The new manager's decisions are consistent across regions before user-ID begins relying on them.
Service owners can detect and reverse a bad cutover before user-ID writes are affected.
A missing or delayed report may be treated as low usage and trigger an inappropriate allocation reduction.
Deregistration can create an enforcement gap if old and new registrations do not update atomically.
Semantic differences in grace periods or allocation units can cause premature capacity reclamation.
User-ID replication may apply different quota decisions across regions.
A single quota mistake can reject account writes globally, making the wave difficult to reverse.
Usage/allocation dashboards may display apparently valid data while omitting stale, duplicated, or rejected reports.
Use a staged strangler design: run the new manager in shadow mode, compare every prospective accept/reject and allocation-reduction decision with the current authority, and promote one low-risk service at a time behind reversible flags. Keep user-ID shadowed through the final quarter and cut it over only after regional lag, failover, and partition tests; preserve a time-boxed rollback path before shutting down legacy.
Replay historical and synthetic low-usage, missing-report, stale-report, threshold-crossing, and grace-period-boundary events through both managers and compare accept/reject and allocation-reduction decisions.
The proposal is supported only if decisions match for all valid telemetry and the new system demonstrably fails safe—never reducing allocation or rejecting writes—during missing, stale, or divergent telemetry; any silent discrepancy or unsafe fallback falsifies readiness.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach, but add an RLP runtime feature flag that defaults off, deploy and verify the new router build on all eight servers before clients set the bit, and canary enablement after mixed-version testing. Remove or hard-disable Power Peg, document the bit's new meaning, and prohibit binary rollback once clients emit it unless old binaries can be guaranteed incapable of interpreting it.
All supported client and gateway versions—and future configuration paths—leave the bit zero today and can reliably set it only for RLP-eligible orders.
The bit has one defined meaning at every gateway-to-router hop and is not transformed, masked, or reserved by protocol handling.
Router configuration can disable RLP immediately without a restart or redeployment.
The new router correctly rejects or safely handles RLP-marked orders before rollout completes.
Power Peg has no dormant side effects outside its supposedly unreachable routing branch.
A legacy, niche, or future client that sets the bit could unintentionally invoke RLP or an incompatible router behavior.
An old router receiving the newly used bit may activate the retained Power Peg path, especially during rollback or incomplete deployment.
A month of captures proves only historical non-use, not that every producer and deployment configuration is safe.
The manual process may leave servers on different builds, producing node-dependent behavior at roughly 3M orders per day.
Enabling RLP globally without a kill switch could amplify incorrect routing, rejects, or latency until operators intervene.

Perform an exhaustive bit-level producer audit: inspect all supported gateway, SDK, and client versions plus configuration and protocol-decoding code, then sample raw messages from each active producer path.
The proposal is falsified if any legitimate producer can set the bit, any intermediate hop can preserve or alter it unexpectedly, or any deployed client version can interpret it as Power Peg rather than only zero-or-RLP routing.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but do not enable automatic quota reduction for the user-ID service until a global peak-load test demonstrates that its allocation has sufficient headroom for the entire reduction and regional replication delay window. Make manager cutover explicit and reversible to avoid overlapping enforcement or an enforcement gap, and retain a protected allocation and tested rollback path for user-ID throughout migration.
Copied allocations include enough capacity for user-ID growth and traffic spikes.
Usage reports are accurate, timely, and consistent across regions.
Quota decisions propagate to every database replica before writes are evaluated.
Registration and deregistration cannot create dual authority or an enforcement gap.
The stated grace period includes all propagation, scheduling, and regional failover delays.
Automatic reduction could cause user-ID database writes to be rejected during normal or peak login traffic.
A stale or region-specific usage report could trigger an unsafe quota reduction.
Concurrent registration in both managers could produce conflicting enforcement decisions.
A gap during deregistration could leave user-ID writes without quota enforcement.
Insufficient regional consistency could allow the global allocation to be exceeded before enforcement converges.
Migrate noncritical services in waves, but place user-ID in shadow mode first and use a fixed, protected allocation for its initial cutover. Enable automatic reduction only after production-scale testing across regions establishes safe headroom, then increase usage or allocation alerts before each reduction.
Run a production-scale user-ID write test against the new system using current and forecast peak traffic, exercising all regional replicas with realistic propagation delay and one failover.
Any legitimate account create or update is rejected, any replica observes a different enforcement state, or projected usage approaches the copied allocation before the earliest possible reduction confirms the proposal is unsafe as written.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the in-process mutex with a database-enforced available/pending state machine and pass a stable idempotency key to chargeOrder. Atomically claim a coupon with a conditional update; only the request that changes state may charge, and retries must return the existing redemption result rather than charge again. Add a cross-process integration test, not only an in-memory concurrent-call test.
All redemption requests can be coordinated through the same Postgres database.
The in-process mutex would be shared by every request, which is false with four to twelve Deployment replicas.
The existing single-process test is representative of the client retry path.
chargeOrder can be coordinated by serializing execution, despite being an external side effect.
Postgres uniqueness or conditional updates can enforce one successful claimant.
Concurrent requests routed to different pods can both observe an unused coupon and both charge, continuing the financial loss.
A process crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt permanently permits another redemption.
A client retry after an ambiguous two-second timeout can charge twice even if the original process completed.
The Map and cleanup logic can leak mutex entries or leave incorrect state under exceptional concurrency.
The proposed test passes in one process while providing no protection for the actual production topology.
Add redemption status and a stable request/order idempotency key, then claim the coupon using an atomic conditional update such as UPDATE ... SET status='pending', redemption_id=?, order_id=? WHERE code=? AND status='available'. Execute the idempotent charge under that claim, finalize it conditionally, and have retries look up and resume or return the existing result. This coordinates all pods, makes ownership durable, and addresses post-charge timeout retries; rollout should be expedited with the smallest safe schema and service changes this week.
Run two concurrent redemption requests for one fresh coupon through two different pod instances, with the first call delayed between the read and charge, and inspect coupon state plus charge-provider idempotency records.
The proposal is wrong if both instances report successful claims or the provider receives two charge attempts for the same coupon/order; a shared database state machine should produce one claim and at most one provider charge.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Replace the big-bang rewrite with a versioned billing kernel and strangler migration. First capture immutable production-derived inputs and expected outputs as replay fixtures, then migrate one end-to-end rule class at a time behind a compatibility adapter, with declarative plan definitions where feasible.
All behavior across the five services can be reproduced from a bounded set of stored inputs.
The new model can express every historical and grandfathered plan behavior before cutover.
All five services can change atomically despite high upstream merge rates.
Three months is sufficient to achieve full invoice parity and coordinate a single release.
Deleting the old implementation cannot invalidate pending, retried, credited, or partially paid invoice workflows.
Uncaptured legacy edge cases involving historical plans, proration, tax, payment ordering, retries, credits, time zones, currencies, or rounding could produce incorrect invoices.
A single cutover creates a repository-wide release dependency and sharply increases rollback and coordination risk.
Five services may temporarily use incompatible billing contracts during the three-month migration.
Unit tests of a newly designed model can validate its intended behavior without proving parity with production behavior.
Deleting the old path eliminates the fallback needed when late parity defects are discovered.
Build the same versioned billing-core boundary, but preserve the existing path and introduce a compatibility adapter that reproduces current outputs. Establish replay-based characterization fixtures, classify the 37 plans, and migrate complete billing flows incrementally with observable parity metrics and reversible cutovers.
Run the current production implementation against a curated corpus of sanitized historical invoices containing grandfathered plans, retries, credits, taxes, proration, and payment allocations, comparing every stored input with every expected output.
If the existing implementation cannot deterministically reproduce the corpus from snapshotted inputs, or if the proposed new model cannot match a significant number of cases without special-case code, the single-cutover timeline and parity claim are disproven.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform an in-place type conversion and rename on the 900M-row table. Use an expand-and-contract migration: add a currency-aware numeric column, deploy dual-write/application support, backfill in committed batches with rate limits, validate reconciliation, switch reads, and only then retire the old column. Schedule cutover with an explicit rollback plan and verify it against production-like data volume.
Every order has enough currency information to distinguish two-decimal currencies from three-decimal currencies.
Existing integer values use a known scale and can be converted without changing their business meaning.
The reporting jobs and all other consumers can tolerate a compatibility period with the old column.
The database has sufficient free space, WAL capacity, and I/O headroom for an online backfill.
A 25-minute rolling deployment can safely span a migration that may take substantially longer than 25 minutes.
On PostgreSQL 15, converting INTEGER to NUMERIC generally requires a full table and index rewrite, holding a strong lock and blocking reads and writes for an unbounded period.
Because migrations run before old pods are replaced, the atomic transaction does not provide application compatibility: after commit, old code and reporting SQL referring to amount will fail.
The rewrite can generate enormous WAL, increase replica lag, exhaust disk or I/O capacity, and cause missed checkout writes or prolonged downtime.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes storage and arithmetic semantics but does not define the currency or conversion rules; incorrectly interpreting existing values can cause financial corruption.
A single long backfill or cutover can exceed the release window, leaving the migration partially complete or making rollback unsafe after application changes begin.
Add a nullable numeric representation (preferably with explicit currency and an agreed scale), backfill it in small committed batches while rate-limiting and monitoring replication/WAL, deploy code that dual-writes and reads the new representation after validation, then switch reports and rename or drop the legacy column in a later change. Preserve the old column until reconciliation and rollback criteria pass.
Run the exact ALTER TABLE on a production-sized or representative clone while measuring lock waits, duration, relfilenode changes, WAL volume, and replica lag.
A relfilenode change lasting far beyond the deployment window, or measurable blocking/lag, falsifies the claim that a transactional DDL migration is safe for this table; also verify that pre-deploy pods issue queries for amount after the migration commits.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not execute permanent deletion until every supplied ID is independently confirmed to be an Insight Legacy add-on installation associated with the intended site. Add authoritative type and ownership validation, a dry-run inventory, a small canary batch, bounded retries, and post-batch reconciliation before processing the full list.
The product-team list is complete and contains no site IDs or unrelated add-on IDs.
The job can obtain authoritative object type and site ownership before deletion.
Permanent deletion of an installation cannot cascade into other products or site data.
The API provides reliable per-ID results and safely handles retries.
A canary and recovery procedure can be completed before full execution.
A mixed or malformed list could permanently delete customer sites and their other products because both object types share the same ID format.
An incorrect validation or site mapping could cause irreversible cross-tenant deletion.
Transient failures could leave installations undeleted before backend shutdown.
Undetected partial failures could produce an inaccurate completion report.
Permanent deletion cannot use the stated 14-day restore window, so errors require site-by-site backup restoration.
Use a type-constrained workflow: generate and review an inventory, validate every ID as the intended Insight Legacy installation, canary a small batch and verify site integrity, then process the remainder in auditable batches. Prefer a product-specific uninstall or reversible soft deletion where available, reserving permanent deletion for independently verified installations.
In a non-production environment, call the exact endpoint with one known add-on installation ID and one known site ID, inspecting whether object type is validated and whether unrelated data is affected.
If the endpoint cannot distinguish or enforce object type before deletion, or either ID can cause deletion of the other object type, direct permanent batch deletion is unsafe.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform a direct type change or rename on the 900M-row table. Add a nullable major-unit NUMERIC(19,3) column with expand/backfill/switch/contract, dual-write it, and gate reporting cutover on complete reconciliation. Preserve the existing integer column during rollout rather than changing its representation in place.
The existing amount values are integer minor units whose scale varies by currency, not major-unit numbers that can safely be stored as NUMERIC(19,4).
PostgreSQL can complete the ALTER with acceptable lock duration, replica lag, storage use, and rollback behavior on a 900M-row table.
All application versions and every reporting/export consumer can tolerate the renamed column and new numeric representation during deployment.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the intended wire and reporting format despite currencies using zero, two, or three minor-unit digits.
Historical three-decimal values' lost precision can be ignored or recovered from another source.
A table rewrite or long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock can breach the 99.95% availability SLO.
Renaming the column breaks mixed-version deployments and any consumer not included in the three query updates.
Leaving existing values numerically unchanged (for example, 1234 cents) while presenting them as major units produces orders that are 100 times too large.
Changing all integer values into a fixed four-decimal representation corrupts currency semantics and can misstate historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values.
The migration may exhaust disk or delay replication, causing checkout and reporting outages.
Use the additive NUMERIC(19,3) major-unit migration described in the independent position, with currency-aware backfill, rate limiting, dual-write compatibility, reconciliation, and a separately gated reporting cutover.
Run a read-only semantic check joining a representative sample of orders to currency metadata: compare the stored integer amount with the expected major-unit value (for example, integer 1234 cents for a two-decimal currency should become 12.34, not 1234).
If the proposed ALTER leaves existing values numerically unchanged, as its stated approach does, it confirms that the column is not a correct major-unit representation; additionally, a production-like migration dry run showing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock or rewrite exceeding the deployment/SLO window independently falsifies the deployment plan.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the phased migration, but exempt the user-ID service from automatic quota reduction or configure a conservative floor based on measured peak usage, replication lag, and operational growth. Validate this behavior under write load before cutover, and retain legacy reporting or an equivalent rapid rollback path until the new system is proven stable.
The new quota system supports a per-service exemption, fixed floor, or equivalent override for automatic reduction.
Reported user-ID usage includes all distributed writes and is sufficiently current across regions.
Current allocations have enough headroom for normal peaks and cross-region replication lag.
An allocation reduction can be detected and reversed before production writes are rejected.
Automatic reduction below actual user-ID usage could cause login-related database writes to be rejected globally.
Regional reporting lag could make usage appear low, trigger reduction, and then expose the replicated database to quota-exceeded failures.
A single user-ID quota incident could prevent authentication or account updates for all users.
Deregistering from the legacy manager without a tested rollback may remove the recovery path needed during regional instability.
Migrate ordinary services in waves as proposed, but use a protected cutover for user-ID: maintain redundant reporting, disable or constrain reclaim for that service, test quota decisions with production-shaped load, and only then switch enforcement.
In a production-like test, drive user-ID usage to its current peak plus replication lag, allow the new system's grace period to elapse, and verify whether its allocation is reduced below actual usage and whether a subsequent cross-region write is rejected.
Any reduction below the protected usage floor, or any rejected write, falsifies the claim that enabling automatic reduction for user-ID is safe without an override.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not execute the direct type alteration and rename in the pre-deploy job. Replace it with a phased expand/dual-write/backfill/switch/contract rollout, using an explicitly defined three-decimal representation and a compatibility window; enable the new currencies only after reconciliation and replica-lag validation.
The existing integer values can be interpreted using a persisted, reliable currency code.
The required maximum precision is three decimal places, not four.
All old and new code, jobs, and queries can tolerate a staged schema transition.
The release environment can provide enough disk and WAL capacity for a new column and batched backfill.
There is a rollback path and operational monitoring for replication lag, lock waits, and data mismatches.
PostgreSQL may rewrite the 900M-row table and hold a strong lock during ALTER TABLE, blocking the 1,200 writes/s peak and likely violating checkout SLO.
The same-migration rename breaks pods, reporting jobs, exports, ETL, and any raw SQL still referencing orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) creates an undocumented four-decimal contract and does not solve how existing integers map to major or minor units for each currency.
A full historical conversion may misinterpret legacy amounts, corrupt totals, or produce inconsistent values across paths.
Generating substantial WAL and I/O can cause replica lag, storage pressure, and rollback difficulty before the new application is available.
Use an expand-and-contract migration: add a new fixed-scale representation (preferably BIGINT with a documented currency-specific scale, or NUMERIC(19,3) if the API stores major units), deploy dual reads/writes, backfill in rate-limited batches, reconcile totals, switch reports and checkout, then remove the old column after the compatibility window. This avoids an unbounded table rewrite in the release job and makes rollback possible.
On a representative staging clone, run the proposed ALTER with a short lock_timeout and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL generation, and replication lag.
If it cannot acquire the lock promptly or produces prolonged strong-lock blocking, substantial WAL, or unacceptable replica lag, the proposed one-migration approach is disproven for this release; even successful completion would still not remove its mixed-version rename risk.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the wire-format approach, but phase it: deploy RLP-capable routers while retaining the unreachable Power Peg branch, add automated per-server build/capability verification, and centrally gate client activation until all eight routers are confirmed ready. Remove Power Peg only in a later release after an agreed compatibility window and review of retry, replay, and failover behavior.
No current, dormant, archived, internal, or external client can set the retired bit.
RLP eligibility truly fits a single boolean and does not require separate client/router state.
A central activation gate can prevent RLP clients from reaching any unupgraded router.
The proposed bit owner will approve reuse and can change its documented meaning.
Power Peg removal does not affect parsing, persistence, metrics, replay, or rollback behavior when the bit is clear.
A missed client or integration setting the bit could invoke unexpected RLP behavior or an unsafe intermediate Power Peg path.
Client launch before fleet-wide router completion could send RLP orders to incompatible routers.
Manual deployment can leave one server on an unknown build, with no automated detection.
Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a straightforward rollback path and complicates mixed-version troubleshooting.
A month of production traffic may not cover dormant, rare, archived, test, or partner-specific bit-writing paths.

Run an automated bit-write audit across all current client binaries and repositories, including test tools, administrative utilities, archived integrations, and any gateway code capable of writing the header; then compare the result with the protocol owner’s reservation history.
Any discovered writer that may set the bit for Power Peg or any other meaning falsifies immediate semantic reuse; only an authoritative protocol-owner confirmation plus an exhaustive zero-writer inventory supports it.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain the expedited Quicksilver path, but add worst-case CPU/latency limits, verify atomic and authenticated version activation, and provide an independently tested kill switch before blocking globally. Use representative canaries and centralized attack/false-positive telemetry, and deploy a minimal containment rule immediately while the complete signature is validated.
CI payload-corpus coverage is sufficient to detect harmful rules and known attack variants.
Quicksilver can activate one version atomically and consistently across every PoP within the response window.
The candidate rule has bounded worst-case CPU and regex-backtracking behavior under peak load.
Ten minutes of global log-mode telemetry is sufficient to expose false positives and attack misses.
A tested rollback or kill switch can remove the rule globally within minutes without proxy restart.
A catastrophically expensive regex could exhaust CPU across all proxies before log mode detects it.
A false positive could then block legitimate traffic globally when the rule changes to block mode.
A partial or delayed rollout could leave inconsistent protection despite a nominally immediate publish.
Encoding, parser, or protocol variants may pass the corpus and remain unblocked.
Compilation, cache invalidation, or activation performed on the request path could itself cause an outage.
Publish a minimal, narrowly scoped containment rule immediately, then validate and activate the full signature through corpus, performance, representative canary, atomic-version, and automated rollback gates within the hour.
Benchmark the exact candidate rule against worst-case and representative payloads at peak concurrency, including any CI-corpus edge cases, while measuring proxy CPU and request latency.
The proposal is falsified if the rule can exceed the predefined CPU or latency budget, show superlinear backtracking, or miss disclosed exploit variants; safe bounded behavior supports proceeding with the additional rollout controls.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver path and global log-only phase, but require deterministic PCRE safety/latency tests, mandatory peer approval, per-rule automatic abort thresholds, and a rehearsed kill switch before activation. After logging, block on a small traffic slice for 5-10 minutes and check errors, p99 latency, CPU, and rule match volume before global blocking; emergency execution time should be capped and measured end to end.
The rule engine bounds regex execution, or CI can reliably detect catastrophic backtracking using adversarial inputs.
Quicksilver can activate log mode and later blocking globally within minutes, with consistent version state at every PoP.
Log evaluation adds acceptable CPU and latency even when a request produces many matches.
Match-volume telemetry is available within minutes and has useful PoP-, customer-, and traffic-normalized baselines.
A single rule can be disabled immediately without disrupting the rest of the WAF configuration.
A vulnerable or pathological PCRE consumes enough CPU in log mode to degrade customer traffic before any match threshold is evaluated.
A broad signature produces many benign matches; the ten-minute observation either misses rare events or causes an extended global denial when switched to block.
A bad configuration is partially activated across PoPs, yielding inconsistent protection and difficult incident diagnosis.
Telemetry is delayed, aggregated too coarsely, or unavailable during the disclosure, leaving the team to block without production evidence.
The process is rushed, omitting security review or rollback verification precisely when operational pressure is highest.
Use the proposed path as the standard, but define it as a gated incident release: static and adversarial regex validation, peak-load replay, global log mode for 10 minutes, a 5-10 minute blocking canary, then global block. This is a modification rather than a separate architecture because it preserves the proposal's low operational complexity while adding protections for false positives and rollout failure.
Replay the candidate regex plus worst-case encodings and match-heavy inputs through the actual PCRE engine in log mode under representative peak-load concurrency, while measuring proxy CPU, p99 latency, and per-rule match throughput.
The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation can breach the defined CPU or latency budget, cannot terminate within the rule-execution timeout, or produces enough matches/events that telemetry or rollback cannot process within minutes.
