required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but initially restrict it to the main East-primary cluster and prefer an East-local replica for host failures; reserve West promotion for confirmed East-region failure. Add reliable fencing so an isolated old primary cannot accept writes, and define the acceptable asynchronous RPO before enabling promotion regardless of region. Validate the complete detection-to-reconnect-and-write path, including ambiguous commits, under one minute; pseudo-GTID simplifies topology but does not establish freshness or prevent data loss.
Orchestrator can complete detection, candidate selection, promotion, and topology publication within the remaining 25 seconds after its 30-second trigger.
A Raft quorum will remain available throughout East database failures.
Orchestrator can reliably distinguish the freshest candidate, or the business explicitly accepts asynchronous replication loss.
The old primary can be fenced automatically at the host, network, or MySQL-access layer.
East application instances can reconnect to a West primary and tolerate roughly 60 ms database RTT.
A network partition can produce dual writable primaries because Orchestrator consensus does not itself fence the old database.
Asynchronous promotion can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft and pseudo-GTID do not prevent this.
Selecting a West replica for an East host failure shifts every write across regions and may exceed latency or throughput limits.
Enabling recovery for all clusters simultaneously creates a correlated automation blast radius.
Consul updates or Rails connection recovery may finish after promotion, or retries may duplicate non-idempotent writes.

In staging, partition the primary from Orchestrator while keeping a database client connected; after 35 seconds, attempt writes through both the old primary and the advertised replacement, while timing when a new write succeeds.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts a conflicting write after replacement promotion, or if end-to-end writable recovery takes longer than 60 seconds. Success requires automatic fencing or refusal of old-primary writes, exactly one authoritative writer, and timely service rediscovery.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator-based recovery, but restrict promotion to a verified, sufficiently caught-up East replica and require explicit fencing of the old primary before any new primary becomes writable. Define measurable detection, fencing, promotion, discovery-propagation, and Rails-reconnect deadlines; validate replica capacity and connection-retry safety under load. Use East-local semi-synchronous replication only if the agreed RPO requires stronger acknowledged-write durability, while retaining asynchronous West replication.
At least one East replica is reachable, sufficiently caught up, and has adequate CPU, memory, IOPS, and write capacity.
The old primary can be fenced reliably before the replacement is promoted or exposed for writes.
The three-site Raft deployment can reach quorum within the failover deadline; a three-site quorum does not guarantee availability if two sites fail.
Applications use a stable Consul-managed writable endpoint and safely reconnect or retry after topology changes.
The agreed RPO permits the replication lag and any acknowledged-write loss from asynchronous replication.
Promoting a West or otherwise stale replica can silently lose recently acknowledged writes.
Raft consensus does not fence the old primary, allowing split brain and divergent writes if it remains reachable.
Updating service discovery before promotion completes can direct applications to an unavailable or unsafe endpoint.
A 30-second detection threshold does not establish completion within the required 60-second end-to-end objective.
Non-idempotent retries during connection resets can duplicate application side effects, while insufficient replica capacity can cause write failures after promotion.
Use the proposed Orchestrator promotion, but make it an explicitly fenced East-local failover with a stable writable service, tested end-to-end recovery timing, and optional validated MySQL 5.7 semi-synchronous replication for stronger RPO.
Run one controlled East-primary failure and, from the old primary host, attempt a write while monitoring Orchestrator promotion and Consul endpoint changes.
If the old primary accepts writes before fencing, promotion is unsafe and the proposal is falsified; if the complete sequence exceeds the agreed 60-second deadline, the stated objective is also falsified.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Add an explicit migration safety gate for the user-ID service: keep its allocation fixed above observed peak usage plus reporting-lag and growth headroom, with alerts and a tested rollback path before enabling automatic reductions. Verify equivalent quota units and continuous reporting, and perform a staged cutover that cannot create a registration gap or prematurely enforce a reduced allocation.
Legacy and new quota systems use identical allocation and usage units.
Copying the current allocation preserves all existing quota protections.
Service reporting has bounded lag and remains continuous during manager handoff.
Allocation will not be reduced below actual user-ID database usage.
Usage can grow materially during the grace period or reporting delay.
Automatic reduction could lower the user-ID allocation below real distributed-database usage, causing login-related writes to be rejected across regions.
A gap or mismatch during deregistration and registration could leave usage unreported or enforce an incorrect quota.
Different accounting semantics could make the copied allocation smaller in the new system than in the legacy system.
Stale or lagging reports could trigger reductions based on usage that is no longer current.
An untested rollback could restore the legacy manager after writes have been rejected.

In staging, configure the user-ID service exactly as proposed and simulate reporting below allocation through one full grace period while actual usage remains near the pending reduced allocation; then attempt a database write.
If the allocation is reduced below actual usage and the write is rejected, the automatic-reduction design is unsafe as proposed; if the system maintains a safe floor and accepts the write, that specific risk is refuted.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator as the topology manager, but do not enable unconditional promotion of the most up-to-date replica across regions. Restrict automation to proven candidates, add explicit lag and reachability checks, enforce fencing of the old primary, and make East-local promotion the normal path with West promotion reserved for a tested East outage procedure. Validate the complete detection-to-write-recovery duration and data-loss behavior under continuous writes before declaring the one-minute objective met.
A candidate with the highest available replication position contains every acknowledged write required by the application.
Orchestrator can safely classify host failure without allowing the old primary to continue accepting writes after promotion.
East-only Rails clients can reach and tolerate a West primary through the discovery and connection-reconnection path.
Thirty seconds plus promotion, topology propagation, and application reconnection consistently fits inside the one-minute objective.
Pseudo-GTID and Orchestrator topology metadata provide reliable candidate ordering but sufficient promotion safety.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can permanently lose committed transactions, despite Raft consensus protecting the orchestration decision itself.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, creating split brain, divergent transactions, and potential corruption or unrecoverable conflicts.
Promoting a West replica may exceed the objective or degrade write latency and connection behavior for East-only application servers.
Consul updates or cached Rails connections may direct some applications to stale or changing endpoints during failover, causing failed or retried writes.
A Raft quorum outage can prevent automated promotion precisely when the primary is unavailable, leaving the manual runbook necessary.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, recorded writes while killing the East primary, then measure transaction success, whether any acknowledged write is absent from the promoted replica, old-primary writability, and time until all applications are writing to the new primary.
A complete pass requires zero acknowledged-write loss, inability of the old primary to accept writes, and end-to-end write recovery under 60 seconds. Any acknowledged-write loss, split-brain writes, or recovery above one minute falsifies the proposal as written.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Keep the new billing-core direction, but replace the three-month branch and single cut-over with incremental migration: first capture characterization tests and invoice outputs for all 37 plans, then introduce billing-core behind a compatibility boundary and migrate one plan/service slice at a time. Run shadow calculations and reconcile old versus new results in production before switching writes, and use a staged rollout with rollback rather than deleting the legacy path at the end. Merge continuously with main to avoid accumulating incompatible changes.
A representative corpus of existing invoices and proration/tax/payment edge cases can be obtained for parity testing.
The five services can be migrated behind an adapter or feature flag without changing externally observable billing behavior.
Three engineers can maintain continuous integration with the main branch while implementing the migration.
The legacy implementation can remain available temporarily as a rollback and comparison path.
Invoice generation, not just plan definitions, is sufficiently covered to detect behavioral regressions.
A long-lived branch will conflict with roughly 40 weekly main-branch PRs and may become impossible to integrate safely.
A big-bang cut-over can produce incorrect invoices for grandfathered plans or evolved proration, tax, payment, and notification interactions.
Deleting the old implementation eliminates the rollback path and the ability to reconcile production discrepancies.
Low existing test coverage leaves hidden billing behavior undiscovered despite unit tests for the new model.
The shared mutable BillingContext creates coupling that may make a clean package boundary impossible without coordinated service changes.
Use a strangler migration: establish golden-master invoice fixtures, extract billing-core behind an adapter, migrate read-only or low-risk paths first, shadow-compare every invoice without charging customers, then switch cohorts of plans incrementally while retaining the legacy calculator as a temporary fallback. Remove old code only after production parity and rollback criteria are met.
Build a golden-master harness that runs the current production billing path for all 37 plans across representative subscription, upgrade, downgrade, cancellation, tax, payment-failure, and proration scenarios, then compare exact invoice line items, totals, taxes, payment instructions, and notifications with billing-core.
Any unexplained difference in legacy invoices, especially for the 11 grandfathered plans or proration edge cases, falsifies the claim that a single cut-over can safely preserve behavior and requires staged migration or expanded compatibility work.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Representing Snowflake IDs as strings is the correct long-term fix, but changing every existing v1 response in the next release is not safely compatible with already deployed clients. Introduce a versioned or explicitly negotiated string-ID representation, update the web/mobile clients and generated SDKs to accept it, and retain numeric v1 responses only for a bounded migration period with a documented deprecation path.
Existing Swift Codable and Kotlin/Moshi clients reject a JSON string when decoding an Int64/Long field.
Regenerated partner SDKs will not be deployed atomically with the API change.
The API can support a new endpoint version or content-negotiated representation within two weeks.
Clients can be updated to use the new representation before the server stops emitting numeric IDs.
Current iOS and Android versions may fail order retrieval or list decoding rather than merely displaying an incorrect ID.
Older web clients will continue to parse numeric IDs through JavaScript's Number type until they switch representations.
Partner integrations generated from the changed OpenAPI schema may experience source-level or runtime breaking changes.
Changing the v1 contract without a migration window can cause widespread order lookup and reconciliation failures.
Add a new major API version, or a negotiated response mode, in which IDs are strings; update first-party clients and SDKs to consume that mode, then deprecate numeric v1 IDs after usage has migrated. Do not silently change the wire type under the same v1 contract.
Decode a fixture containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the currently released Swift Codable model and an unmodified Moshi Long adapter.
If either client rejects the string or requires a custom adapter, the proposed same-contract rollout is incompatible and must be modified; if both transparently accept it, compatibility risk is lower but partner SDK behavior still needs verification.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Keep the Consul 1.10 and streaming direction, but do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling order, enable streaming for a small production-representative canary, define CPU/network/freshness/error thresholds, and expand only after observing a sustained benefit. Document and test client rollback and ensure mixed-version behavior is understood before broader deployment.
The 200-node staging result predicts production CPU, network, memory, and freshness behavior at fleet scale.
All deployed service-discovery clients and libraries support the Consul 1.10 streaming backend and the proposed configuration.
A supported mixed-version rolling upgrade preserves health, KV, and lock availability.
Streaming maintains required freshness, ordering, and authorization semantics.
The production rollout has enough time and operational capacity for canarying, monitoring, and rollback.
A fleet-wide flag change could create reconnect or watch storms, excessive client load, or stale discovery for services with no fallback.
The 200-node test could materially overestimate savings because production fan-in, service churn, or duplicate query patterns differ.
Incompatible or partially upgraded clients could silently retain blocking queries or fall back inconsistently.
A server or client regression could disrupt discovery, KV configuration, or locks across the entire fleet.
The measured 60% server CPU reduction could be offset by increased network traffic, client CPU, memory pressure, or Raft instability.
Use a staged rollout with a production-representative canary rather than an all-at-once enablement. Add immediate instrumentation and selectively reduce redundant blocking-query subscriptions if the canary does not achieve the required aggregate benefit.
Run a production-like staging benchmark using the actual service count, client versions, query fan-in, update churn, reconnect pattern, and representative failure scenarios; compare streaming with the current blocking queries and record server CPU, network bytes, client CPU/memory, freshness latency, errors, and reconnect amplification.
The proposal is supported only if streaming produces a sustained, material reduction in total server load without violating freshness or stability thresholds and with documented client/rollback compatibility; materially smaller savings, increased amplification, or correctness failures falsify the rollout assumption.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table receiving 25k inserts/s and periodic bulk deletes. Keep autovacuum enabled, but reduce its per-table cost throttle and vacuum cost limit, schedule manual VACUUMs during low-traffic periods, and monitor vacuum duration, dead tuples, bloat, transaction-ID age, and WAL/checkpoint impact.
A weekly VACUUM can complete before the next accumulation of dead tuples and transaction IDs.
The observed autovacuum workload can be spread over enough low-traffic time without exceeding operational I/O limits.
Bulk deletes do not create a rate of dead tuples that outpaces effective vacuuming.
The database has sufficient free space and WAL capacity for the resulting maintenance workload.
Autovacuum can be safely throttled per table in PostgreSQL 9.4 without materially increasing transaction-ID wraparound risk.
A weekly VACUUM on a multi-terabyte table may run for many hours or fail to complete before the next cycle, allowing severe bloat and transaction-ID wraparound pressure.
Disabling autovacuum removes the safety mechanism that responds to unexpectedly rapid delete activity or transaction-ID growth.
The manual vacuum may itself create the same I/O spikes, merely at a different time, and may overlap peak traffic if it runs longer than expected.
Unbounded dead-tuple growth can increase index size, cache pressure, query latency, and storage consumption.
A single fixed schedule does not adapt to varying delete rates, vacuum progress, or replication and storage constraints.
Tune autovacuum for events with an appropriate autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, retain emergency autovacuum behavior, and use a carefully monitored off-peak VACUUM ANALYZE as a supplement rather than disabling automatic vacuum.
Compare the timestamps and durations of recent autovacuum runs on events with pg_stat_all_tables.n_dead_tup, pg_stat_all_tables.last_autovacuum, and pg_stat_database.xact_commit, while reviewing PostgreSQL logs for vacuum duration and I/O saturation.
If vacuum runs routinely exceed a week or leave n_dead_tup and transaction age increasing, the weekly-disable proposal is falsified; if throttled vacuum consistently completes with low dead-tuple and bloat levels, the proposed schedule is also unlikely to provide a meaningful improvement.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but restrict promotion by replica region, verified replication state, and maximum acceptable lag; add reliable fencing and route applications through a dedicated database endpoint whose update is tested with existing connection pools. Do not claim Raft prevents split brain by itself, and validate acknowledged-write loss and end-to-end recovery time in network-partition game days before production automation.
A promoted West replica can serve writes within Rails timeout and latency budgets.
Orchestrator can identify the most up-to-date replica and safely verify binlog continuity.
Raft availability and quorum are independent of the failed database host or East network path.
Consul and Rails clients promptly replace pooled connections to the failed primary.
Recovered replicas can rejoin without incompatible binlogs, missing GTIDs, or topology corruption.
A partitioned but still writable old primary can form a dual-primary topology and diverge data.
Asynchronous failover can lose recently acknowledged East writes even if quorum approved the decision.
A West primary can cause connection, transaction, or pool timeout failures that exceed the one-minute objective.
Insufficient fencing or lag checks can promote a stale replica and then cause irreversible replication conflicts.
Consul propagation, stale resolver caches, or pooled connections may leave applications targeting the old primary after promotion.
Use guarded Orchestrator automation with an explicit candidate policy: prefer a healthy East replica, require verified lag/binlog eligibility, reserve West promotion for a declared disaster condition, fence the old primary, and update a stable database proxy or service endpoint. Semi-synchronous cross-region replication is a possible separate enhancement if the measured latency cost is acceptable.
Run one isolated game day that blocks all East-to-West database traffic, kills the East primary, and measure from failure injection to successful Rails reads and writes while recording failed or unacknowledged transactions, recovery duration, primary-host writability, and West-primary latency.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary remains independently writable, acknowledged writes are lost beyond the accepted bound, recovery exceeds 60 seconds, or normal Rails writes fail or materially breach latency/timeout limits through the promoted West replica.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Streaming is the preferred direction, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. Upgrade through normal Raft-compatible rolling procedures, then enable it for a small production canary and expand by controlled cohorts with CPU, network, freshness, error-rate, and reconnect metrics plus explicit rollback thresholds. Retain blocking-query fallback until representative clients have survived a server-loss or rolling-restart test.
All production clients support the relevant 1.10 streaming backend and can be upgraded or configured without incompatible agent versions.
Streaming preserves health-update ordering, completeness, authorization, and freshness semantics for every consumer.
The 200-node staging result is representative of production polling rates, update rates, query diversity, and reconnect behavior.
A tested rollback to blocking queries is possible before the rollout reaches most clients.
Clients will not synchronize reconnection attempts after a server, network, or deployment event.
A fleet-wide configuration change exposes version skew or unsupported-client failures across all 18,000 nodes simultaneously.
A correlated disconnect or deploy triggers a reconnect storm that recreates or exceeds current server load.
Semantic differences silently deliver stale or incomplete health state, causing failed dependency resolution without obvious client errors.
The 200-node benchmark understates production query diversity or update fan-out, so staging gains fail to materialize.
An untested rollback becomes impractical after broad adoption, turning a client defect into a cluster-wide discovery outage.

Enable streaming for one small, representative production cohort, then terminate and restore its connections while comparing server CPU, network traffic, update freshness/completeness, client errors, and reconnect concurrency against a blocking-query control cohort.
The proposal is supported if CPU and network remain materially lower without correctness errors or harmful reconnect amplification; stale or missing updates, sustained CPU/network regression, client failures, or a reconnect storm falsifies the fleet-wide rollout as currently proposed.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver path, but do not allow an arbitrary CI-passing PCRE to enter the inline request path or automatically block globally after a fixed 10-minute observation period. Require a strict evaluation-time/CPU budget, reject unsafe regex constructs, preserve an independently controlled kill switch and atomic rollback, and validate benign traffic volume and latency during the log period before enabling blocking.
The WAF engine enforces a hard per-rule evaluation timeout and can safely terminate pathological PCRE execution.
Quicksilver updates are versioned and can be rolled back consistently across all PoPs within minutes.
CI's benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives before global enforcement.
Log-mode evaluation has a bounded CPU and memory cost comparable to block-mode evaluation.
A global configuration update can be gated, audited, and reversed without waiting for the normal staged pipeline.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, degrade or halt all customer traffic because WAF evaluation is inline and proxies are already CPU-bound.
Ten minutes of match-volume observation may miss low-frequency false positives, false negatives, regional traffic differences, or application-specific behavior.
Automatic global blocking could deny legitimate requests across every customer immediately, with no safe mechanism to disable the rule quickly.
Configuration propagation or version skew could produce inconsistent enforcement across PoPs and make rollback unreliable.
The safety check may itself overload the request path if log mode materially increases latency or creates large match/event volumes.

Run each candidate PCRE against the production benign corpus and representative attack payloads using the production WAF engine, with a hard timeout, while measuring p99 evaluation latency and CPU time.
The proposal is falsified if any CI-passing rule exhibits superlinear execution, exceeds the proxy's defined per-request CPU/latency budget, or causes the corpus run to approach the timeout; otherwise this supports retaining the expedited path with the stated safeguards.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Do not treat Orchestrator Raft quorum as MySQL split-brain protection: it coordinates Orchestrator instances, not the old primary. Enable automated promotion only when the primary is reliably fenced or otherwise proven dead, and base promotion on a verified replica freshness signal; also test network partitions and recovery of the old primary, not only host kills.
An unreachable primary cannot continue serving writes.
Orchestrator can reliably identify the replica with the greatest applied position before promotion.
Application clients promptly and consistently honor service-discovery changes.
West can accept production write traffic at acceptable latency and capacity.
Recovered former primaries cannot rejoin as writable nodes.
A network partition can cause a replica to be promoted while the isolated primary continues accepting writes, creating concurrent writable primaries and divergence.
Asynchronous cross-region promotion can lose acknowledged transactions committed on the old primary but not yet replicated.
Incorrect lag or position comparison can promote a stale replica and make data loss substantially larger.
A West promotion can sharply increase write latency for East-only application servers and may exceed their timeout or capacity assumptions.

In staging, isolate the East primary from Orchestrator and the replica while leaving its application path writable, commit distinct transactions through both paths, and observe whether promotion occurs.
If Orchestrator promotes the replica while the isolated primary still commits writes, the design is unsafe; safety requires no promotion until the old primary is fenced or demonstrated incapable of writes.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep serializing `id` as a decimal string in the long term, but avoid a breaking type change across all existing v1 clients. Introduce a versioned response, or temporarily add an `id_string` field while preserving numeric `id`; let the web app adopt the safe representation immediately and announce a v1 deprecation deadline.
Most active iOS, Android, and partner clients update their generated SDKs or models before or shortly after the API change.
Existing generated SDKs treat the change from numeric to string as a breaking type change.
No service, proxy, cache, logging pipeline, or downstream system coerces the new string back through a JavaScript number.
The API can deploy a versioned response or backward-compatible alias within two weeks.
Strict v1 clients tolerate an additional response field if an alias strategy is used.
Released iOS models declaring Int64 may reject the quoted ID instead of decoding it.
Kotlin, Moshi, and generated partner SDK clients may fail to decode the changed type or produce null/default IDs.
A breaking v1 change strands users who do not update and approximately 40 partner integrations.
Regenerating SDKs and adding a changelog does not protect already deployed clients.
Any JavaScript consumer left on numeric `id` will continue displaying corrupted IDs.
Add a versioned response where `id` is a string and update OpenAPI for that version. If strict-client testing shows that an extra field is tolerated, retain numeric `id` temporarily and add `id_string`; deploy the web app against `id_string`, track adoption, and remove the legacy field only after a published migration deadline and compatibility checks.
Decode a v1 response containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the exact released iOS decoder and one representative generated partner SDK.
If either decoder reports a type mismatch, returns no model, or maps the ID to null/default rather than the exact value, the proposed breaking v1 rollout is unsafe.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but add a shadow period and require near-zero enforcement-decision equivalence before each service is deregistered from the legacy manager. Treat user-ID as a separately approved cutover with cross-region failure testing, conservative temporary headroom, and an immediate rollback switch; do not assume the grace period alone makes automatic allocation reduction safe.
Copying an allocation preserves the exact units, effective time, grace-period state, and regional consistency used for enforcement.
Both managers make identical enforcement decisions for the same usage history.
Allocation and usage timestamps and telemetry are accurate and comparable, including during replica failover.
Deregistering the legacy registration does not bypass required reporting or audit integrations.
Automatic quota reduction is paused or guarded during migration anomalies and has sufficient service-specific headroom.
An unobserved semantic or configuration mismatch can reject legitimate writes immediately when a service moves.
For user-ID, inconsistent enforcement across replicas can turn a quota decision into failed logins, account updates, or region-dependent behavior.
Weeks-long grace periods may still be unsafe for bursty services, delayed telemetry, or allocation changes near the reduction threshold.
Direct deregistration removes the legacy fallback before migration behavior is validated, making rollback and incident comparison harder.
Dashboards provide visibility but do not prove enforcement equivalence, completeness of reporting, or cross-region consistency.
Use a staged migration per wave: dual-report to the new manager in shadow mode, replay recent histories and compare decisions, add bounded headroom while monitoring, then switch enforcement behind a reversible flag. Validate user-ID with fault-injection and cross-region write tests before its cutover, and shut down the legacy system only after a bounded observation period and audit confirmation.
Replay each service's recent usage and allocation history through both managers in a non-enforcing environment, then run a cross-region write test at the quota boundary for user-ID; compare the resulting allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision divergence, stale or incomplete usage signal, or region-dependent allow/reject result falsifies the safety of direct registration and deregistration; consistent results support proceeding with gated cutovers.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not send an unqualified ID list directly to permanent deletion. First reconcile the product team’s list against an authoritative, typed inventory of legacy add-on installations, validate every ID with canaries and preflight checks, then soft-delete in batches and verify that other products remain intact. Use permanent deletion only after the rollback window and an explicit go/no-go approval, with reconciliation and customer-impact monitoring.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an add-on installation rather than a site or another object.
The deletion API reliably resolves IDs by object type and cannot interpret an installation ID as a site ID.
Permanent deletion is necessary before backend shutdown and complies with applicable retention requirements.
The ID list is complete, current, deduplicated, and derived from a trustworthy source.
A 2-second pause and on-call monitoring provide adequate protection against rate limits and cascading failures.
Because both sites and installations have identical 24-character ID formats, a single wrong or mistyped ID could permanently destroy an entire customer site and its other-product data.
There is no dry run, object-type validation, allowlist, or second source of truth to detect a malformed or overbroad product-team list.
Immediate permanent deletion eliminates the API’s 14-day recovery path, making endpoint mistakes or incorrect targeting unrecoverable except through slow, site-by-site backup restoration.
Partial processing can leave installations active when the backend shuts down, while retries or duplicate requests may produce unclear or destructive behavior if idempotency is not established.
The justification assumes data minimization requires erasure, but legacy customer data may instead need to remain restorable until a verified retention and shutdown process is complete.
Run a reversible migration: import a product-team-approved manifest containing expected site ID, installation ID, installation type, and list version; reconcile it against site-management records; reject unknown, ambiguous, duplicate, or non-legacy records; canary the workflow; then call mode=mark in batches of 30. Verify successful installation soft-deletion and the continued presence of unrelated products, retain an immutable audit log, and obtain explicit approval before purging only the reconciled installation IDs in a later, separately controlled run.
Inspect the deletion API contract and run a non-destructive canary or supported dry-run request using one known installation ID, one known site ID, and one deliberately invalid ID.
The proposal is safe only if the API exposes unambiguous object typing or a dry run and demonstrably rejects a site ID supplied as an installation target. If the generic ids parameter has no type discriminator, validation, or dry-run behavior, permanent batch deletion is unsafe.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not permanently delete directly from the supplied list. First inventory-check every ID and assert that it resolves specifically to an installed “Insight Legacy” add-on, recording its site and current state; abort on any mismatch. Then soft-delete the verified installations with `mode=mark`, verify that no other site objects changed, and permanently purge only after the 14-day recovery window and a final revalidation.
A non-destructive lookup or inventory API can determine each ID's object type and owning site.
The product team's list contains installation IDs rather than site or product IDs.
Soft-deleting an add-on installation does not delete unrelated site or product data.
The 14-day restore window fits before the backend shutdown.
The delete API returns enough metadata to detect wrong-object deletion.
A single mistaken or malformed 24-character ID could permanently delete an entire customer site.
The generic API provides no stated type restriction, so batch processing does not prevent cross-object deletion.
Immediate permanent deletion removes the practical recovery path and could prevent correction before backend shutdown.
Logging responses alone would not distinguish a successfully deleted site from a successfully deleted add-on.
Partial failures could leave installations behind or produce an unreliable decommissioning state.
Use a staged, type-validated removal: reconcile the supplied IDs against the authoritative add-in inventory, soft-delete and verify, wait for the restore window, then permanently delete from a revalidated manifest while producing a per-ID audit report.
Perform a non-destructive inventory lookup for every supplied ID and inspect its object type and owning site before any deletion call.
The proposal's direct permanent-delete approach is unsafe if any ID is absent, resolves to a site/product or another object type, or cannot be conclusively classified as the retired add-on installation.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the read-through cache direction, but add permission-event-driven invalidation, a short safety TTL, single-flight/coalescing for concurrent misses, and strict rules against caching timeouts or ambiguous errors. Gate rollout on measured end-to-end p95, not hit rate: with roughly 99 ms of non-permission latency and a 180 ms check, an 85% hit rate would produce about 126 ms if hit/miss requests were uniformly mixed, so the stated ~40 ms p95 is unsupported.
A 15-minute stale-allow window is acceptable for unshare, account deletion, and group-membership revocation.
permission-events contains sufficient information to identify and invalidate every affected authorization key.
Redis has enough capacity, isolation, and network headroom for the expected key cardinality and peak request rate.
The check API clearly distinguishes false from timeout/error, and the document service can safely fail closed.
Requests are sufficiently uniform for the replayed hit-rate distribution to predict production p95.
Users retain document access for up to 15 minutes after an unshare, account removal, or group-membership removal.
The uncached request tail may still push p95 above 120 ms; 85% hit rate alone does not support the claimed ~40 ms result.
Synchronized expirations create a miss storm capable of degrading both Redis and the permissions service.
Undefined error semantics can cause outages to be cached as denials or, if fail-open, create unauthorized access.
Popular documents or users can create Redis hot keys and uneven expiry traffic across the cluster.

Run a representative 24-hour trace replay through the proposed cache, using captured permissions-check latency and measured Redis operations, then report total end-to-end latency percentiles segmented by hit/miss rather than deriving p95 from hit rate.
The proposal is falsified if overall p95 remains above 120 ms or any freshness/error-safety test shows unauthorized allow decisions beyond the accepted bound; a p95 comfortably below 120 ms confirms the latency benefit but not revocation safety.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for durable job dispatch; AOF does not persist published Pub/Sub messages, and consumers provide neither acknowledgement nor replay. Use Redis Streams consumer groups on the existing Redis deployment, with per-type streams, pending-entry recovery, explicit acknowledgements after processing, retry/DLQ handling, and idempotent handlers; validate it under peak load before retiring RabbitMQ.
Losing a dispatched payment, email, indexing, or thumbnail job is acceptable.
Publishers can tolerate ambiguous delivery and do not require acknowledgement that a job was durably accepted.
Workers remain continuously connected and process each message before any connection interruption.
A worker-side retry wrapper can recover failures even when the message was never delivered or was lost during a disconnect.
Redis Pub/Sub throughput and connection behavior remain adequate at 300 jobs/s with all worker types subscribed.
Messages published while workers are disconnected or restarting are irretrievably lost, which is especially damaging for payment webhooks and fulfilment.
Redis may drop or disconnect slow consumers under load because Pub/Sub has no durable queue or backpressure.
Worker crashes before processing or acknowledgement lose jobs; the existing retry wrapper cannot retry messages it never receives.
The proposed design cannot reliably implement the existing five-attempt retry policy or DLQ because it has no durable failed-message record.
Duplicate or redelivery semantics are unspecified, so introducing Streams without idempotency could cause duplicate charges, emails, indexing, or fulfilment.
Use Redis Streams as the existing-service queue: publishers XADD to a stream per job type, workers read with consumer groups, reclaim stale pending entries after Kubernetes restarts, and XACK only after successful processing. Add bounded retries and a dead-letter stream plus idempotency keys; retain RabbitMQ until replay, failure-rate, recovery, and 300-jobs/s load tests pass.
With a subscriber connected, stop the subscriber, publish 100 test messages, restart it, and attempt to recover and acknowledge all 100 without republishing.
The restarted subscriber receives zero messages because Pub/Sub retains no backlog, falsifying the dispatch design for jobs requiring retries, DLQ, or recovery after routine worker redeployment.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep JSON-string serialization as the target representation, but do not silently change the existing v1 contract in a single release. Add a versioned or negotiated string-ID representation, update the OpenAPI spec and generated SDKs with an explicit compatibility/migration window, and change the web, iOS, and Android clients together. If the two-week deadline requires an immediate v1 change, publish a breaking-change notice, provide transitional parsing/dual-format support in clients, and verify every partner SDK path before rollout.
All relevant consumers can be updated or given a compatibility adapter before the numeric v1 representation is removed.
The iOS Swift Codable Int64 and Android Moshi Long models can be changed or configured to decode JSON strings.
Generated partner SDKs will be regenerated, released, and adopted without an extended period of mixed old and new clients.
The API can version or negotiate the ID representation without changing the meaning of the numeric value.
Only response ID fields are changed; request paths, pagination tokens, and other 64-bit fields are handled consistently.
Changing v1 from integer to string is a breaking wire-format change and can cause immediate decoding failures in existing iOS, Android, and partner clients.
Regenerating SDKs does not help integrations that pin an older SDK or have hand-written numeric-ID models.
A partial rollout can produce mixed representations, causing clients to reject responses or inconsistently compare IDs.
Unrelated integer/int64 fields may remain vulnerable to JavaScript precision loss or fail schema validation if the contract is changed incompletely.
A next-weekly release does not address users who delay mobile updates, so compatibility must be maintained for an extended period.
Introduce a new API version or content-negotiated representation that serializes IDs as strings, while retaining the existing numeric v1 representation during a documented migration period. Update first-party clients to support both forms, deprecate numeric v1 IDs, and remove the old representation only after usage telemetry shows compatibility. If a breaking v1 change is unavoidable, add transitional string decoding/serialization support to released clients and maintain the previous API behavior behind an explicit compatibility flag.
Run a minimal decoding test using the current iOS JSONDecoder with a JSON string value against a Swift Int64 property, and a Moshi request/response test using a JSON string against a Kotlin Long adapter.
If either default client decoder rejects the string or requires a custom adapter, the proposed unreviewed v1 change is incompatible with existing consumers and confirms that a staged/versioned rollout or client compatibility update is required.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Retain the streaming approach, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. First verify the exact Consul 1.10 client/server compatibility and upgrade order, then canary it on a bounded production segment with explicit rollback criteria before staged expansion; benchmark a production-representative workload because 200 nodes may not predict behavior across thousands of services.
The stated `use_streaming_backend` setting is supported by the exact Consul 1.10 build and has the required server-side support.
Agents, servers, and clients can be upgraded in a compatibility-preserving order, including during rollback.
Streaming preserves the consistency, freshness, and failure semantics required for every health subscription.
The observed CPU and network reduction at 200 nodes generalizes to the production service and node cardinality.
The cluster and client fleet have enough temporary capacity for rolling upgrades and canary monitoring.
A simultaneous fleet-wide switch could remove or degrade the sole discovery path for all services without a fallback.
An unsupported setting or incorrect mixed-version deployment could make streaming ineffective or cause client failures.
A 200-node test may miss scale-dependent CPU, memory, bandwidth, Raft, or connection effects.
Incorrect rollout or rollback sequencing could create incompatible server-agent combinations.
Streaming could return stale or incomplete health data unless consistency and reconnect behavior are explicitly tested.

Run a production-representative streaming canary or isolated load test spanning thousands of services and the expected concurrent client count, while measuring health-update correctness, server CPU, network bytes, and reconnect behavior.
The approach is supported if it materially reduces CPU and network while preserving timely and consistent health results; the proposal is falsified if reduction disappears at scale, resource use regresses, or correctness or failover behavior degrades.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Do not perform a three-month big-bang replacement. Build billing-core incrementally with characterization tests and golden invoice comparisons for all 37 plans, then migrate one bounded workflow at a time behind an adapter while retaining the legacy path for rollback. Use production shadowing and explicit reconciliation before switching invoice generation, tax, payments, and notifications.
The existing 37 plans and their historical edge cases can be faithfully represented by the proposed clean domain model.
Unit tests for billing-core will be sufficient despite proration, tax, payment, and notification behavior currently spanning five services.
All five services can switch atomically to the new package without requiring coordinated changes across the other teams.
Historical plan definitions and representative invoice scenarios are available and cover grandfathered pricing behavior.
A single cut-over can provide an acceptable rollback and reconciliation strategy.
Unknown proration and grandfathering rules will produce silently incorrect invoices when the old code is deleted.
A three-month branch will diverge from roughly 40 weekly main-branch changes, creating integration and deployment failures.
A cut-over affecting invoicing, tax, and payments can cause duplicate charges, missed invoices, or irreversible customer-billing damage.
Deleting the legacy implementation eliminates the fastest rollback path and makes diagnosis difficult when production behavior differs.
The 22% existing coverage leaves critical service-level interactions untested, so a model that passes unit tests may still break end-to-end billing.
Use a strangler migration: first freeze and characterize current behavior with golden invoices and contract tests, then introduce billing-core behind a compatibility adapter and migrate subscriptions and invoice calculation incrementally. Shadow invoices in production, compare outputs and side effects, migrate tax/payments/notifications only after parity, and remove legacy code only after a defined bake period.
Create a representative golden corpus containing current production or captured outputs for all 37 plans, including the 11 grandfathered plans, proration changes, cancellations, renewals, taxes, payment failures, and retries; run both implementations against identical inputs and compare invoice line items, totals, taxes, due dates, and side effects.
Any unexplained difference, missing scenario, or inability to replay historical inputs falsifies the claim that a single cut-over can preserve invoices and supports incremental migration instead.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Retain the existing-bit approach, but prohibit direct client control: translate the bit to RLP only at an approved gateway and add a separately armed router-side RLP feature flag. Release compatible gateway/router versions through build attestation, canary one server, validate telemetry and reconciliation, and rehearse gateway disablement, router disablement, and rollback before progressive production enablement.
No current or dormant client, gateway, external interface, or malformed producer can set the legacy bit.
All gateways and routers interpreting the order will be upgraded compatibly before any client can request RLP.
The new RLP router path is semantically distinct from, and safely replaces, every legacy Power Peg code path.
A rapid router-side kill switch and deterministic mixed-version rollback behavior can be implemented within the release window.
The four teams can agree on and document one versioned meaning for the repurposed bit.
One month of observed traffic does not establish that the bit is unused by dormant clients, third parties, historical jobs, malformed input, or unobserved environments.
Direct client activation on launch day can route orders to mixed or incompatible router builds, causing incorrect routing or order loss.
Removing Power Peg in the same release may change behavior for unexpected legacy producers and turns an apparently unused-bit change into a breaking protocol change.
Enabling all clients and servers together removes canary isolation and makes failures or rollback difficult to contain.
Without explicit RLP probes, reconciliation checks, and an immediate kill switch, silent misrouting may remain undetected.
Use the bit as an RLP request only through a controlled gateway, while routers require separate operational arming. Canary and progressively enable the capability rather than activating it fleet-wide on launch day.
Audit all client repositories, gateway configurations and source, external producer interfaces, historical jobs, and retained packet captures for any ability or observed occurrence to set the retired bit.
Any unauthorized producer capable of setting the bit, or any captured order with the bit set outside the approved gateway, falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires quarantine or normalization before RLP use.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the reserved-bit approach, but do not enable it on clients until every production router is running the RLP-aware build and the deployed versions have been independently verified. Use a staged rollout with canaries, server-level health checks, explicit rollback criteria, and a client kill switch; retain rollback compatibility until the new router fleet is proven stable. Document the bit's new protocol meaning and test behavior for mixed old/new clients and malformed or retried messages.
The current router's Power Peg path is harmless or can be made harmless when the bit is set; zero observed traffic does not establish how old binaries will behave once clients begin setting it.
All order-message producers, including gateways, simulators, retries, and external clients, can be identified and updated or prevented from setting the bit prematurely.
Every one of the eight routers can be upgraded and its exact build verified before client activation.
The RLP implementation has defined behavior for unsupported, duplicated, delayed, and retried orders, and rollback will not occur while RLP-setting clients remain active.
The exchange permits semantic reuse of a previously defined protocol bit without requiring a separate compatibility or governance review.
Clients setting the bit before all routers are upgraded could cause legacy routers to invoke the retired Power Peg algorithm, producing incorrect routing or order loss.
Manual deployment can leave servers on different builds; a later client rollout could expose some orders to incompatible behavior.
Removing the Power Peg implementation eliminates a straightforward rollback target, and rolling back while clients set the RLP bit could recreate the original danger.
A month of production traffic cannot prove the bit is unused by infrequent clients, archived gateways, maintenance tools, or future integrations.
Bit corruption, stale messages, retries, or an unrecognized bit state could accidentally select RLP or Power Peg behavior without a clear rejection/failsafe policy.
If the exchange permits the approximately one-month coordinated change, add an explicit RLP indicator or protocol/version field rather than redefining historical semantics. Otherwise, use the reserved bit only with a fully gated fleet rollout and a compatibility-preserving router release.
In staging, send one otherwise valid order to the currently deployed pre-RLP router with the header bit set, and compare its routing and resulting audit record with the same order using the bit clear.
If the old router invokes Power Peg, rejects the order, or produces any different routing outcome, client activation before complete fleet upgrade is unsafe and the proposal requires modification.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep Redis read-through caching, but add event-driven invalidation for permission-events, a bounded fallback TTL, and cross-pod request coalescing. Establish an explicit staleness policy for revocations, and do not claim a ~40 ms p95 without replaying end-to-end latency: at an 85% hit rate, p95 necessarily falls within the miss path.
A 15-minute stale grant is acceptable for sharing changes, account removal, and group-membership removal.
permission-events can map every relevant change to all affected authz keys, including group-based changes.
The permissions-service result is safely cacheable and does not vary materially within the TTL.
Redis and Redis connections have sufficient capacity for the key cardinality, miss stampedes, and existing session workloads.
Concurrent misses for the same key can be suppressed across all 12 pods.
Users retain document access for up to 15 minutes after revocation, which may be unacceptable for terminated accounts or sensitive documents.
Expiration and cold starts can create a permissions-service stampede; one request per replica is not enough protection for high-volume keys.
Redis eviction or failure can collapse the hit rate and overload the permissions service at peak load.
Kafka lag, gaps, or unrecognized group-membership changes would leave revoked access cached.
The proposed performance claim is not credible from hit rate alone: with 15% misses, p95 is determined by uncached requests, whose permissions call alone is reported at approximately 180 ms p95.
Use the same Redis cache but consume permission-events to delete affected keys, retain a shorter TTL as a repair mechanism, add distributed singleflight, and monitor Kafka consumer lag and cache freshness. If revocations must be near-immediate, use a versioned, reconciled authorization projection rather than TTL-only invalidation.
Replay the existing 24-hour request log with recorded end-to-end duration split into cache-hit and miss paths, applying the proposed 15-minute keyed cache and measuring the resulting uncorrelated request p95 without request coalescing.
A p95 near 40 ms would support the latency target; a p95 above 120 ms—expected when at least 15% of requests take the approximately 180 ms miss path—falsifies the proposal's central performance estimate.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Replace permanent deletion with a server-enforced, installation-scoped workflow that first performs an auditable dry run and validates every ID as an authorized, eligible Insight Legacy installation. Prefer mark mode with a verified shutdown deadline and rollback window; process small idempotent batches with per-ID results and reconciliation, and use permanent deletion only after confirming cascade behavior and recovery readiness.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an Insight Legacy installation rather than a site or another object.
Permanent mode deletes only the intended installation and does not cascade into sites, content, products, backups, or other add-ons.
The deletion API enforces tenant authorization and installation eligibility server-side.
Permanent deletion before backend shutdown is required for compliance or technical reasons.
The API and batch job provide idempotency and reliable per-ID results for partial failures.
A single misclassified site ID could cause irreversible loss of customer data.
Unintended deletion cascades could destroy related site content, products, backups, or add-ons.
Logging full responses may expose sensitive data while still lacking an immutable input manifest or per-ID audit trail.
Blind batch retries can repeat successful deletions or leave the operation partially reconciled.
Permanent mode provides no rollback if backend dependencies remain or shutdown timing changes.
Use an explicitly installation-scoped endpoint or bulk job that retrieves metadata, rejects unknown IDs, site IDs, ineligible tenants, and unauthorized records, then performs a dry run followed by small batches in mark mode. Reconcile activation and backend-call status before considering any later permanent cleanup.
Using a non-mutating lookup or type-check API, resolve every ID in an immutable copy of the product team's manifest and require object type, product eligibility, site ownership, and tenant authorization to match the deletion criteria.
The approach is safe only if every ID resolves to an authorized, eligible Insight Legacy installation and none resolves to a site, unknown object, or unrelated record; any mismatch falsifies the current permanent-delete proposal.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Retain the Redis read-through cache, but consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected authorization keys; do not rely solely on a 15-minute TTL for revocations or account/group removal. Also validate the latency claim with a production-shaped load test: an 85% hit rate still places the p95 request on the slow miss path, so the cache must exceed roughly 95% hit rate to bring p95 below 120 ms without a faster miss path.
Permission events contain enough identifiers to invalidate every affected `userId/docId/action` key, including indirect group and account changes.
The permissions service's Kafka publication is durable, ordered sufficiently, and has bounded end-to-end delivery latency.
A bounded stale-grant window is acceptable to the security owner; otherwise positive grants cannot safely be cached for 15 minutes.
The permissions decision depends only on the proposed user, document, and action inputs.
Peak key cardinality and Redis request volume fit the existing cluster's capacity.
Unshared documents, removed accounts, or removed group memberships could remain authorized for up to 15 minutes.
At 85% hits, 15% of requests are misses, so p95 is still a permissions-service miss and may remain above the 120 ms budget.
Malformed, incomplete, delayed, or replayed invalidation events could leave revoked grants cached until TTL expiry.
A high-cardinality workload could impose substantial memory and command pressure on the session Redis cluster.
Use Redis caching with event-driven invalidation, a short bounded TTL, and denial on authorization-service errors; require a measured hit rate above 95% before treating the p95 objective as met.
Replay representative production traffic through the proposed Redis cache at the measured 85% hit rate and measure end-to-end p95, including the actual permissions-service miss latency.
If p95 remains near the cache-miss path rather than falling to about 40 ms, the stated latency benefit is falsified; if revoking permissions can remain cached for 15 minutes under the event stream, the safety design is also falsified.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform a direct type alteration and rename on the 900M-row table in the pre-deploy job. Use an expand/contract rollout: add a new nullable or defaulted column, deploy dual-write/backfill code, backfill in bounded batches with rate limiting and replica-lag checks, validate reconciliation, then switch reads and only later remove the legacy column. Explicitly define the storage scale and currency-exponent rules, and verify capacity and rounding behavior before migration.
The existing integer values are all exactly representable under the new chosen scale and no business rounding or overflow behavior is being changed.
The pre-deploy migration can obtain an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and complete a full-table rewrite within the release window.
All application, reporting, and operational SQL can switch atomically from orders.amount to orders.amount_minor.
There is sufficient free disk, WAL capacity, and I/O headroom for rewriting roughly 410 GB of data and indexes.
The three reporting jobs tolerate a schema transition or can be deployed compatibly with the application.
ALTER COLUMN TYPE will rewrite the entire orders table and rebuild dependent indexes, causing a prolonged ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, latency spikes, transaction queuing, and likely missed checkout SLO.
The migration runs before old pods are replaced, so renaming amount to amount_minor can immediately break the currently running application and reporting jobs.
The transaction is atomic but is not instantaneous or safely rollbackable operationally; a rollback after a long rewrite can itself take substantial time and generate heavy WAL.
Streaming replicas may fall far behind, and the primary plus WAL/disk requirements could exhaust capacity or delay cutover.
NUMERIC(19,4) alone does not specify whether values are cents, three-decimal minor units, or a common scaled representation; incorrect interpretation can cause financial misstatement.
Use an online expand/contract migration with dual reads/writes and batched backfill, or retain the existing integer representation while introducing an explicit currency and scale/exponent abstraction. Validate the representation and maximum-value requirements before selecting BIGINT or NUMERIC storage.
On a production-sized or representative clone, run the proposed ALTER under a session that records lock duration, duration, WAL generated, and replica lag, while measuring checkout latency.
If the rewrite exceeds the deployment/maintenance window, blocks normal writes for a material interval, exhausts disk/WAL headroom, or causes replica lag beyond the cutover threshold, the proposal is disproven for this environment.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. Start with a small, representative client canary while retaining blocking queries and a centrally managed rollback switch, then expand only after measuring CPU, inbound/outbound traffic, errors, discovery latency, index lag, and freshness against baseline under service churn. Verify the exact server/client compatibility and streaming configuration requirements before production deployment rather than relying only on the vendor recommendation and staging CPU result.
All relevant client versions can be upgraded or configured for streaming within six weeks.
Streaming preserves required discovery freshness, ordering, index behavior, and failure semantics in the production workload.
Client populations and their configuration can be centrally identified, segmented, and rolled back.
Production network capacity can absorb increased or bursty push fan-out without harming other traffic.
The staging benchmark's 60% CPU reduction is representative of production query and churn patterns.
A fleet-wide rollout could expose stale-discovery or failure-propagation defects before they are detected.
Unmeasured push fan-out could increase outbound bandwidth, latency, or packet loss and degrade the cluster.
A staging-only CPU comparison may conceal production differences in query rate, service churn, payload size, or client behavior.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:

All concurrent requests for a coupon necessarily pass through the same Node.js process.
The existing charge and update operation remains atomic under process or network failures.
Retries can be safely distinguished using the existing order identity.
A database-level change can be implemented and operated within this week's release constraints.
Two replicas can each acquire their own mutex and both redeem the same coupon.
A successful charge followed by a failed database update leaves the coupon apparently available for another redemption.
A client timeout can cause a retry to charge or redeem again unless the charge and redemption are idempotent.
Marking the coupon before charging can permanently consume it when payment fails.
The proposed test can pass while the production multi-replica failure remains unresolved.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:

Permanent mode deletes only the intended installation and does not cascade into sites, content, products, backups, or other add-ons.
The deletion API enforces tenant authorization and installation eligibility server-side.
Permanent deletion before backend shutdown is required for compliance or technical reasons.
The API and batch job provide idempotency and reliable per-ID results for partial failures.
A single misclassified site ID could cause irreversible loss of customer data.
Unintended deletion cascades could destroy related site content, products, backups, or add-ons.
Logging full responses may expose sensitive data while still lacking an immutable input manifest or per-ID audit trail.
Blind batch retries can repeat successful deletions or leave the operation partially reconciled.
Permanent mode provides no rollback if backend dependencies remain or shutdown timing changes.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not perform this as one transactional ALTER on the live 900M-row table. Introduce a new column through an online, staged migration with application-compatible dual writes, batched backfills, validation, and a brief final rename/swap coordinated with deployment; if amounts remain minor-unit integers, retain an integer/BIGINT representation and store the currency exponent separately rather than silently introducing four-decimal values.
Existing values must retain their current scale; converting 1234 cents directly to NUMERIC(19,4) yields 1234.0000, not 12.3400 KWD.
Current application and reporting SQL can tolerate changed column names and return types before all running pods are replaced.
The database storage and lock behavior is the same as PostgreSQL 15.
A maintenance window long enough to rewrite the table and roll back if necessary is actually available.
INTEGER-to-NUMERIC conversion will rewrite a roughly 410 GB table while holding a strong table lock, blocking reads and writes long enough to violate checkout SLO.
The pre-deploy migration renames the column before old pods are replaced, so active application versions referencing orders.amount can fail immediately.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes the value contract by allowing quarter-minor-unit precision rather than representing three-decimal currencies directly.
A long-running transaction increases replica lag, WAL/load impact, and rollback exposure; transactional atomicity does not make the rewrite online or bounded.
Prefer BIGINT minor units plus a currency code/exponent, which represents three-decimal currencies exactly without changing existing integer values. If a new database type is mandatory, add a new column, deploy backward-compatible dual writes, backfill in small committed batches, validate counts/checksums, and only then perform a short coordinated name swap.

A changed relfilenode plus rewrite/lock time materially above the deployment or SLO budget falsifies the claim that an atomic transaction makes this deploy safe.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:

Redis AOF persists and recovers messages published through Pub/Sub.
A worker crash or Kubernetes redeployment does not lose in-flight jobs.
Subscribers can recover missed messages from a durable backlog.
Redis Pub/Sub provides queue-like redelivery, acknowledgements, and DLQ semantics.
Existing worker retry wrappers can safely compensate for transport-level message loss.
Messages published while all subscribers of a type are disconnected are discarded, causing lost payments, emails, thumbnails, or indexing updates.
Worker crashes after receipt but before completion lose the job because Pub/Sub has no acknowledgement or redelivery.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:

A table rewrite, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, WAL generation, and index/storage growth can be tolerated at the chosen time.
All consumers—including old pods, background workers, exports, and ad hoc SQL—can tolerate a compatibility period with old and new amount fields.

Backfill existing rows in small batches outside a single long transaction, validate counts and sampled conversions, and retain amount until reporting, all application versions, and downstream consumers are confirmed compatible. In a disposable PostgreSQL transaction, rename orders.amount and run the exact SELECT used by the currently deployed application: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; SELECT amount FROM orders LIMIT 1; ROLLBACK;
The SELECT fails with column "amount" does not exist, proving that the proposed migration breaks currently running pods during the required pre-deploy/rolling-deploy window.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month big-bang cut-over with characterization tests followed by a strangler migration. Introduce stable billing interfaces and migrate plan cohorts or capabilities incrementally, using shadow calculations and invoice diffs as gates; retain a narrow compatibility layer for grandfathering until coverage is complete.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:

Quicksilver delivers a consistent rule version to all PoPs quickly enough for the stated deadline.

Ten minutes of log-mode telemetry arrives and is evaluated early enough to prevent harmful promotion.
The rule can be disabled globally quickly enough to bound a bad rollout.
A false-positive rule blocks legitimate traffic across all customers before detection and rollback complete.
A computationally expensive PCRE consumes enough proxy CPU to degrade unrelated HTTP and TLS processing.
Partial version skew or Quicksilver failure leaves some PoPs unprotected or in inconsistent enforcement states.
A low or delayed aggregate match signal is mistaken for evidence that the rule is safe.
The fixed 10-minute delay materially extends exposure to attacks already occurring at disclosure.
Use risk-tiered emergency promotion: immediately block globally only high-confidence, performance-bounded mitigations, while validating other rules on short distributed canaries with automated promotion, rollback, and minimum CPU/headroom protections.
Benchmark each candidate on the production PCRE engine using the CI corpus plus generated near-miss and worst-case regex inputs, reporting p99 evaluation latency and total CPU normalized to current peak proxy utilization.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Retain streaming, but verify and configure `use_streaming_backend` in the scope required by Consul 1.10—particularly whether it is a server-side setting rather than only a client setting—and perform a production canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Progressively expand only after validating client compatibility, streaming-session errors, CPU, network, latency, and Raft health across servers and representative failure scenarios.
The installed client versions and service integrations support Consul 1.10 streaming correctly.
`use_streaming_backend` is being enabled in the configuration scope that actually activates the feature.
A mixed-version rolling upgrade and selective enablement are supported during deployment.
Streaming reduces load at 18,000-node production scale, not only in the 200-node staging environment.
Consul can safely recreate streaming sessions after server failure or leader election.
Enabling the option only on clients may leave the server blocking-query backend active, wasting the rollout while creating unnecessary risk.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Retain automated failover, but explicitly fence or demote the old primary before promotion and make replica selection and promotion policy safe for cross-region failure. Gate the 30-second detector and service-discovery changes through an end-to-end Rails write test that proves recovery remains below one minute and records the achievable RPO.
Orchestrator can prevent or detect writes on an isolated old primary; Raft quorum alone does not fence MySQL.
Topology and replication metadata are sufficiently current to avoid promoting a stale or wrongly positioned replica.
Every relevant cluster has a viable recovery candidate and required replication/GTID state is retained.
Consul clients and Rails connection pools reliably converge on the promoted primary within 30 seconds.
A bounded RPO from asynchronous cross-region replication is acceptable.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and unrecoverable divergence after promotion.
Promoting the West replica can create a large 60 ms write path and does not cover loss of East application servers.
Pseudo-GTID improves identification but does not prove replica freshness or prevent acknowledged-write loss.
A 30-second detection threshold leaves little time for fencing, election, topology repair, discovery propagation, reconnects, and a verified write.
Automated recovery of all clusters increases blast radius because a false-positive or topology error can affect multiple databases.

In a non-production cluster, partition the primary from Orchestrator and the application while leaving its server process running, then trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write against the original primary.
This falsifies the current proposal if the original primary still accepts writes. A correct design must reject them, terminate/disable the server, or otherwise prevent them from conflicting with the promoted primary.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Add an explicit reconciliation and cutover protocol: pre-populate historical usage, disable automatic reductions until each service has established complete reporting with the new manager, and require warm-up plus health verification before deregistration. For user-ID, use conservative fixed allocations, cross-region enforcement testing, and an independently controlled rollback/kill switch; do not rely on the generic grace period as the sole safeguard.
Copying the current allocation also initializes enough historical usage data to prevent immediate automatic reduction.
Registration and deregistration cannot create an interval in which inconsistent quota decisions are enforced.
Usage-reporting completeness and freshness are comparable between the legacy and new systems.
The new manager's reduced allocation propagates consistently across all user-ID database regions.
Weeks of unchanged reported usage reliably predict future peak demand.
An automatic reduction below the user-ID database's real retained-data footprint could reject writes globally across regions, including account creation and login flows.
During migration, the service might report to one manager while enforcement or stale usage data is obtained from the other, producing inconsistent accept/reject decisions.
The claimed grace period may begin before sufficient observations are collected, allowing an unproven allocation reduction.
Allocation copies may omit reserved, archival, replication, compaction, or growth requirements that the legacy manager included.
Deregistering the legacy manager without a tested rollback path could leave the service with no effective quota enforcement or make rollback unsafe.
Migrate noncritical services through a shadow period with dual reporting and decision comparison, followed by atomic enforcement cutover. Keep automatic reductions disabled until parity and forecasting thresholds are proven, then enable them first for low-risk services and only later for user-ID under fixed safety floors and regional write-failure tests.
