In staging, run user-ID with identical storage and replicated writes while the new manager is set just below current observed usage but above the proposed operational floor; then toggle manager registration during a write and inspect all regional write outcomes.
The proposal is unsafe if any region rejects a normal write, decisions differ between managers or regions, or registration transition changes enforcement before reporting is reconciled.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but limit it initially to the main East-primary cluster and prefer a healthy East replica rather than any replica regardless of region. Before production, require verified stale-primary fencing, atomic service-discovery redirection, connection draining/retry, and measured end-to-end recovery below one minute. Define the 30-second threshold as detection time, not total recovery time, and document that asynchronous failover can lose acknowledged writes.
Orchestrator detects a failed primary within approximately 30 seconds even when it is hung, isolated, or only partially partitioned.
A healthy, sufficiently current East replica will exist and be eligible when recovery triggers.
The failed primary is fenced at the host, network, or database layer before the replacement becomes writable.
Orchestrator can reconfigure remaining replicas and update Consul, while all application instances promptly refresh and drain old connections.
The three-site Raft quorum is available, healthy, and fast enough to complete detection and recovery within the remaining time budget.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, causing split brain and divergent committed transactions.
A region-blind selector may promote the West replica, increasing write latency and potentially selecting a staller copy.
Service discovery may update centrally while application connection pools continue using the old endpoint, delaying or extending an outage.
Pseudo-GTID simplifies topology verification but does not make asynchronous acknowledged writes durable or prove replica ordering under every failure.
Applying recovery to all clusters creates correlated automation risk; one misconfiguration could cause simultaneous, uncoordinated promotions.

Run one isolated-network game day in which clients can still reach the old primary while the new primary can reach its replicas and Consul; trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write on the old primary immediately before and throughout promotion.
The design is confirmed only if the old primary is reliably fenced from accepting writes before promotion, no conflicting writable nodes exist, and the application reaches the new primary within 60 seconds; any successful old-primary write or missed deadline falsifies it.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the wire-format approach, but phase it: deploy RLP-capable routers while retaining the unreachable Power Peg branch, add automated per-server build/capability verification, and centrally gate client activation until all eight routers are confirmed ready. Remove Power Peg only in a later release after an agreed compatibility window and review of retry, replay, and failover behavior.
No current, dormant, archived, internal, or external client can set the retired bit.
RLP eligibility truly fits a single boolean and does not require separate client/router state.
A central activation gate can prevent RLP clients from reaching any unupgraded router.
The proposed bit owner will approve reuse and can change its documented meaning.
Power Peg removal does not affect parsing, persistence, metrics, replay, or rollback behavior when the bit is clear.
A missed client or integration setting the bit could invoke unexpected RLP behavior or an unsafe intermediate Power Peg path.
Client launch before fleet-wide router completion could send RLP orders to incompatible routers.
Manual deployment can leave one server on an unknown build, with no automated detection.
Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a straightforward rollback path and complicates mixed-version troubleshooting.
A month of production traffic may not cover dormant, rare, archived, test, or partner-specific bit-writing paths.

Run an automated bit-write audit across all current client binaries and repositories, including test tools, administrative utilities, archived integrations, and any gateway code capable of writing the header; then compare the result with the protocol owner’s reservation history.
Any discovered writer that may set the bit for Power Peg or any other meaning falsifies immediate semantic reuse; only an authoritative protocol-owner confirmation plus an exhaustive zero-writer inventory supports it.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
The string representation is the right long-term fix, but changing the existing v1 `id` field in place is a breaking contract change and cannot be made safe merely by regenerating SDKs. Within two weeks, deploy a lossless web-client decoder and add an additive `idString` field, then migrate clients and measure adoption before versioning the API and making the string field canonical.
Existing released iOS and Android apps can tolerate an additive response field without strict decoding failures.
Existing partner SDKs and integrations will not be broken by retaining the numeric `id` during migration.
A lossless JSON parser or BigInt-aware decoder can be integrated into the web app within two weeks.
The API can expose a new field consistently across all order serializers and generated SDKs.
There is an API owner who can enforce the deprecation and version transition.
Changing v1 `id` from number to string can cause runtime deserialization failures in Swift `Int64`, Kotlin/Moshi `Long`, and partner clients that require numeric JSON.
Regenerating SDKs does not update already deployed apps or partner-deployed SDK versions.
Approximately 40 integrations may fail or silently mishandle responses, creating support and operational incidents.
A one-release migration may leave users on unsafe clients for weeks or longer, so the stated two-week objective is not achieved.
The OpenAPI change may cause generated-code or validation breakage independently of runtime behavior.
Use a compatibility migration: immediately fix the web client with lossless parsing; add `idString` while preserving numeric `id`; update the OpenAPI spec and SDKs to expose both; require clients to adopt `idString`; then introduce a new API version where the canonical `id` is a string and retire the unsafe field on a published schedule.
Run an integration test that feeds `{"id":"1234567890123456789"}` into the current released iOS `Int64` Codable model, Android Moshi `Long` model, and one representative partner SDK deserializer.
If all three decode the quoted value correctly and preserve the exact ID, the immediate v1 break risk is lower; any exception, truncation, null, or numeric fallback confirms the compatibility hazard and requires the additive migration path.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Keep the Consul 1.10 and streaming direction, but do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling order, enable streaming for a small production-representative canary, define CPU/network/freshness/error thresholds, and expand only after observing a sustained benefit. Document and test client rollback and ensure mixed-version behavior is understood before broader deployment.
The 200-node staging result predicts production CPU, network, memory, and freshness behavior at fleet scale.
All deployed service-discovery clients and libraries support the Consul 1.10 streaming backend and the proposed configuration.
A supported mixed-version rolling upgrade preserves health, KV, and lock availability.
Streaming maintains required freshness, ordering, and authorization semantics.
The production rollout has enough time and operational capacity for canarying, monitoring, and rollback.
A fleet-wide flag change could create reconnect or watch storms, excessive client load, or stale discovery for services with no fallback.
The 200-node test could materially overestimate savings because production fan-in, service churn, or duplicate query patterns differ.
Incompatible or partially upgraded clients could silently retain blocking queries or fall back inconsistently.
A server or client regression could disrupt discovery, KV configuration, or locks across the entire fleet.
The measured 60% server CPU reduction could be offset by increased network traffic, client CPU, memory pressure, or Raft instability.
Use a staged rollout with a production-representative canary rather than an all-at-once enablement. Add immediate instrumentation and selectively reduce redundant blocking-query subscriptions if the canary does not achieve the required aggregate benefit.
Run a production-like staging benchmark using the actual service count, client versions, query fan-in, update churn, reconnect pattern, and representative failure scenarios; compare streaming with the current blocking queries and record server CPU, network bytes, client CPU/memory, freshness latency, errors, and reconnect amplification.
The proposal is supported only if streaming produces a sustained, material reduction in total server load without violating freshness or stability thresholds and with documented client/rollback compatibility; materially smaller savings, increased amplification, or correctness failures falsify the rollout assumption.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach, but do not ship it as described without a compatibility check across every client/gateway/parser, an explicit rollback control, and a per-server build/version verification after the manual deployment. Preserve the old Power Peg code until rollout is proven safe rather than deleting it in the same release; a month of zero observed bits does not prove that all readers treat it identically.
The bit is unused by every current and planned client, gateway, parser, diagnostic tool, and counterparty, not merely absent in observed traffic.
All relevant components can agree on the new meaning without a wire-format change and will not reject or ignore it.
The new RLP path is functionally, operationally, and performance-tested for eligible and ineligible orders.
The router can distinguish RLP eligibility consistently, including orders that lack the bit.
A documented kill switch can disable RLP without requiring a synchronized client and router redeployment.
A legacy or divergent implementation interprets the bit as Power Peg, causing unintended routing or inconsistent behavior.
Removing the old code eliminates the safest fallback and makes rollback dependent on a new build or another control.
Manual deployment leaves servers on mixed builds, producing nondeterministic participation and making incidents hard to attribute.
Launch-day client flag changes expose untested interactions at full volume, including latency, matching, liquidity, and risk-limit failures.
A configuration or eligibility mismatch causes some RLP-eligible orders to bypass RLP or some ineligible orders to enter it.

Perform a repository/protocol inventory and staging end-to-end test: search all parsers and routing branches for the bit, then send representative orders with it set and unset through each client/gateway version and verify identical non-RLP behavior except for the intended RLP selection.
Any additional semantic use, a component that ignores or rejects the bit, or changed behavior for ineligible/non-RLP orders falsifies the claimed compatibility and blocks the proposed release.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not send the untyped list directly to permanent deletion. Resolve every ID against an authoritative inventory, require it to be an active "Insight Legacy" add-on installation, reject site IDs and unknown or ambiguous records, and obtain a reviewed deletion manifest before execution. Then canary the process, use checkpoints and fail-closed stopping rules, and permanently delete only the validated manifest while recording request and response evidence.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies the intended add-on installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The product team's list is complete, current, and free of stale, duplicated, malformed, or incorrectly scoped IDs.
Permanent deletion removes the installation and its legacy data without cascading into unrelated products or site content.
The API returns enough metadata or errors to verify object type and successful deletion.
Completing validation and a controlled canary is possible before the backend shutdown.
A single site ID in the list could permanently destroy an entire customer site and all products on it.
IDs from the same 24-character format may be misclassified because no type validation is performed.
A stale or incorrect product-team manifest could irreversibly delete valid customer objects.
Unexpected API behavior or cascading deletion could affect unrelated product data.
Batching and weekend scheduling do not mitigate irreversible damage; on-call monitoring detects failures only after they occur.
Generate a canonical manifest by joining the product-team list to authoritative object metadata, including object type, site ID, add-on name/version, and status. Require 100% type and scope matches, explicitly assert that no site IDs or ambiguous records remain, and produce a signed count and hash for approval. Test a small representative sample, verify deletion and unaffected site data, then execute idempotently with per-ID results, checkpoints, an exact allowlist, and immediate halt on any mismatch.
Run a read-only preflight that resolves every supplied ID through the canonical inventory or object metadata API and asserts object_type = add-on installation, add-on = Insight Legacy, expected site association, and uniqueness; explicitly search for any resolved site object.
The direct permanent-delete approach is falsified if even one ID is missing, ambiguous, duplicated across object types, identifies a site, or identifies a different add-on. It is safe to proceed only if all records match the expected type and scope and the manifest count reconciles exactly.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep IDs as strings, but do not change the existing v1 schema in place. Introduce a versioned v2 contract with string IDs and an explicit migration/deprecation window for v1, while immediately updating the web client and testing or updating mobile and partner deserializers. Regenerating SDKs alone does not make a breaking response-schema change safe for already deployed clients or independently upgraded partner integrations.
All existing clients can be upgraded or patched before the API changes.
Swift's default Int64 Codable decoding and Moshi's default Long adapter can be configured to accept JSON strings.
Approximately 40 partner integrations control their SDK upgrade and application deployment schedules.
There is no independently deployed or cached client that must continue consuming v1 indefinitely.
The API gateway, analytics pipeline, and internal consumers will all tolerate the changed JSON field type.
Existing Swift and Kotlin models will generally fail to decode a JSON string into Int64 or Long with their default adapters.
Changing the OpenAPI field from integer/int64 to string is source-breaking for generated SDKs, potentially causing partner compilation failures.
Already deployed mobile and partner clients can break immediately after deployment because they cannot be upgraded atomically with the API.
A partial rollout may leave consumers decoding the same logical field as different types, causing outages, rejected orders, or support incidents.
The two-week deadline is unlikely to cover store review and staggered mobile adoption across the user base.
Add a string-typed field such as `id_string` while retaining the legacy numeric `id` during migration, and make it the sole identifier in a new versioned v2 endpoint. Update the web client to use the string field immediately; deprecate the numeric field only after usage data shows consumers have migrated. This preserves ID generation and gives clients an unambiguous, non-lossy contract without an uncoordinated breaking change.
Feed a response containing `"id": "1234567890123456789"` through the currently shipped Swift Codable model, Moshi Long model, and one representative generated partner SDK.
Any default decoder rejecting the string or returning a compile-time type mismatch falsifies the claim that the in-place v1 change is safe with existing clients; explicit adapters or regenerated string-typed models are required.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
An in-process mutex cannot serialize the 4-12 Kubernetes replicas, so concurrent requests routed to different pods can still both pass the check and redeem the coupon. Replace it with a Postgres-backed atomic redemption claim or unique redemption record, and make charging/retry handling idempotent so a client retry cannot create a second order charge.
All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process, which is false with multiple replicas.
The service is not horizontally scaled or restarted during the redemption window.
The charge operation can be safely retried or reconciled using an idempotency key.
Postgres uniqueness or conditional-update semantics are available for the coupon redemption operation.
The existing test exercises multiple application instances rather than only two calls in one process.
Two requests handled by different pods can both observe redeemedAt as null and both charge orders.
A process crash after charging but before updating redeemedAt leaves a charged order with an apparently unused coupon.
A timeout-driven retry can repeat the charge unless order/payment idempotency is enforced.
Naively deleting a mutex entry after release can allow a new mutex to be created while an earlier waiter still exists, breaking serialization within a process.
A database claim that occurs before a failed charge can permanently consume a coupon unless failures are explicitly released or reconciled.
Use a durable Postgres operation: atomically claim the coupon with an UPDATE ... WHERE redeemedAt IS NULL and a unique redemption identifier, or insert into a redemptions table with UNIQUE(coupon_id). Persist an order/payment idempotency key and state transitions so retries return the existing result; handle charge failure with an explicit recoverable state and reconciliation. Add a test that sends concurrent requests through separate service instances or directly validates the atomic database operation.
Run two concurrent redeem requests for one coupon while forcing them to different pods, for example by scaling the Deployment to at least two replicas and targeting separate pod IPs through separate test clients.
If both requests succeed or both reach the charge operation, the in-process mutex proposal is falsified; a correct database-backed claim should allow exactly one claim and return AlreadyUsed or the original idempotent result to the other request.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Retain the existing-bit approach, but prohibit direct client control: translate the bit to RLP only at an approved gateway and add a separately armed router-side RLP feature flag. Release compatible gateway/router versions through build attestation, canary one server, validate telemetry and reconciliation, and rehearse gateway disablement, router disablement, and rollback before progressive production enablement.
No current or dormant client, gateway, external interface, or malformed producer can set the legacy bit.
All gateways and routers interpreting the order will be upgraded compatibly before any client can request RLP.
The new RLP router path is semantically distinct from, and safely replaces, every legacy Power Peg code path.
A rapid router-side kill switch and deterministic mixed-version rollback behavior can be implemented within the release window.
The four teams can agree on and document one versioned meaning for the repurposed bit.
One month of observed traffic does not establish that the bit is unused by dormant clients, third parties, historical jobs, malformed input, or unobserved environments.
Direct client activation on launch day can route orders to mixed or incompatible router builds, causing incorrect routing or order loss.
Removing Power Peg in the same release may change behavior for unexpected legacy producers and turns an apparently unused-bit change into a breaking protocol change.
Enabling all clients and servers together removes canary isolation and makes failures or rollback difficult to contain.
Without explicit RLP probes, reconciliation checks, and an immediate kill switch, silent misrouting may remain undetected.
Use the bit as an RLP request only through a controlled gateway, while routers require separate operational arming. Canary and progressively enable the capability rather than activating it fleet-wide on launch day.
Audit all client repositories, gateway configurations and source, external producer interfaces, historical jobs, and retained packet captures for any ability or observed occurrence to set the retired bit.
Any unauthorized producer capable of setting the bit, or any captured order with the bit set outside the approved gateway, falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires quarantine or normalization before RLP use.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Add a shadow-and-compare phase before each cohort moves, using historical and live near-threshold traffic to verify usage semantics, allocation/grace behavior, and regional consistency. Keep a time-bounded legacy fallback with explicit rollback criteria, and initially disable automatic reductions or prove their parity before enabling them; dashboards alone are insufficient validation.
Legacy and new usage reports have identical units, scope, deduplication, and timestamp semantics.
Copying current allocations also preserves grace-period and delayed/missing-report behavior.
Services can switch registration and enforcement paths at runtime and safely recover from quota-manager outages.
Regional replication and failover enforce consistent quota decisions.
Automatic reductions cannot reject legitimate writes before the grace period provides safe rollback time.
User-ID writes begin failing in wave 3 because new quota decisions differ near allocation thresholds.
Semantic reporting differences create false quota exceedances or allow excess storage.
Replication lag or regional conflicts cause inconsistent write acceptance and account-data divergence.
An omitted service or lost connectivity leaves usage unmanaged while deregistered from the legacy manager.
Enabling automatic reductions during migration compounds allocation mismatches and removes the rollback safety margin.
Use compatibility-gated shadowing: normalize reports through a compatibility layer, compare decisions and allocations without enforcement, then migrate lower-risk services in cohorts before user-ID. Retain a controlled legacy fallback until parity, resilience, audit, and rollback exit criteria pass.
Replay historical and recent live user-ID usage, including near-threshold, delayed, missing, and out-of-order reports, through both managers in shadow mode and compare every allocation and enforcement decision by region.
Any material unexplained decision mismatch, false rejection, regional divergence, or difference in grace and missing-report behavior would falsify the proposed wave cutover as currently specified.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with an atomic database-backed claim using Postgres, such as a conditional update or a redemption ledger with a unique constraint on the coupon code. Add payment idempotency and explicit handling for charge failure, timeout, and crash recovery; the mutex alone only serializes requests handled by the same Node.js process.
A mutex map is shared by every request that can redeem a coupon; this is false with multiple Kubernetes replicas unless the deployment is a single process.
Requests for the same code can be routed to different pods, so a local lock cannot enforce the global invariant.
The coupon database update and the payment operation have compatible failure and retry semantics.
Concurrent requests use the same logical redemption identifier so payment-provider idempotency can prevent duplicate charges.
Two requests on different replicas can both read redeemedAt as null, both pass the mutex, and both redeem the coupon.
A process can crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt, allowing a later request to charge again.
A process can claim or mark the coupon before charging and then crash, leaving a permanently unusable coupon.
A process-local mutex can grow without bound or behave incorrectly if cleanup races with a waiter.
The concurrent test can pass in a single process while failing to cover the production multi-replica topology.
Use an indexed atomic transition in Postgres, for example updateMany({where:{code, redeemedAt:null}, data:{...}}) and accept the redemption only when exactly one row is updated. Add a redemption state/ledger and payment idempotency, with reconciliation for uncertain payment outcomes.
Run two separate Node.js processes, each with its own mutex map, and issue simultaneous redemptions for the same unused coupon against the shared database; additionally run the same test with one process and verify the database claim count.
If the two-process test allows both redemptions to succeed, the proposal is falsified; if one atomic database claim succeeds and the other returns no affected row, the replacement approach is confirmed.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the Redis read-through cache, but consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected authorization keys before or during their TTL; a 15-minute stale window is unsafe for unsharing and account/group removal. First verify that events identify all affected user/document pairs, including bulk membership changes, and measure revocation propagation latency against the endpoint's security requirements.
`permission-events` contains enough identifiers to invalidate every affected cache entry.
Permission revocation propagation allows a bounded staleness window shorter than 15 minutes.
Redis availability and eviction behavior will not make the permissions service unavailable.
A permissions write can emit multiple decisions or affect multiple documents and actions.
A recently unshared document can remain readable for up to 15 minutes.
An account or group-membership removal can leave multiple stale allow decisions.
Kafka consumer failure or lag silently extends revocation latency.
Unbounded or unindexed invalidation across `authz:*` keys can overload Redis.

Warm the cache for a test user/document, revoke access through the normal unshare or account-removal path, then immediately request the document while recording both cached decisions and direct `permissions-service.check` results.
If the cached result remains allowed after the authoritative service denies access beyond the accepted revocation window, the TTL-only proposal is unsafe.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator-based recovery, but restrict promotion to a verified, sufficiently caught-up East replica and require explicit fencing of the old primary before any new primary becomes writable. Define measurable detection, fencing, promotion, discovery-propagation, and Rails-reconnect deadlines; validate replica capacity and connection-retry safety under load. Use East-local semi-synchronous replication only if the agreed RPO requires stronger acknowledged-write durability, while retaining asynchronous West replication.
At least one East replica is reachable, sufficiently caught up, and has adequate CPU, memory, IOPS, and write capacity.
The old primary can be fenced reliably before the replacement is promoted or exposed for writes.
The three-site Raft deployment can reach quorum within the failover deadline; a three-site quorum does not guarantee availability if two sites fail.
Applications use a stable Consul-managed writable endpoint and safely reconnect or retry after topology changes.
The agreed RPO permits the replication lag and any acknowledged-write loss from asynchronous replication.
Promoting a West or otherwise stale replica can silently lose recently acknowledged writes.
Raft consensus does not fence the old primary, allowing split brain and divergent writes if it remains reachable.
Updating service discovery before promotion completes can direct applications to an unavailable or unsafe endpoint.
A 30-second detection threshold does not establish completion within the required 60-second end-to-end objective.
Non-idempotent retries during connection resets can duplicate application side effects, while insufficient replica capacity can cause write failures after promotion.
Use the proposed Orchestrator promotion, but make it an explicitly fenced East-local failover with a stable writable service, tested end-to-end recovery timing, and optional validated MySQL 5.7 semi-synchronous replication for stronger RPO.
Run one controlled East-primary failure and, from the old primary host, attempt a write while monitoring Orchestrator promotion and Consul endpoint changes.
If the old primary accepts writes before fencing, promotion is unsafe and the proposal is falsified; if the complete sequence exceeds the agreed 60-second deadline, the stated objective is also falsified.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain global log mode as an expedited detection lane, but require preflight regex-complexity and worst-case CPU benchmarks plus benign-regression testing before promotion. Promote to block through automated 1%, 10%, 50%, and 100% cohorts with latency, error, CPU, match-rate, and false-positive gates, and preserve an atomic, tested global rollback to the last known-good ruleset.
Candidate regexes cannot cause pathological CPU usage on production proxy hardware.
The CI payload and benign-request corpora represent production attacks and legitimate traffic.
Quicksilver can atomically roll back the ruleset on every machine within the required window.
A ten-minute global log interval provides enough traffic and representative PoP coverage for reliable promotion decisions.
The rule-management system supports automated cohort control and managed-rule rollback.
A catastrophic regex can overload proxies even in log mode because evaluation remains in the inline request path.
A false-positive rule can block legitimate customers globally before cohort-level safeguards detect it.
Ten minutes may omit low-volume PoPs, customers, payload variants, and benign edge cases.
Promotion or rollback performed manually may miss the one-hour objective.
An unsafe rule could become fleet-wide before aggregate match and error signals reveal the problem.
Use a narrowly scoped emergency mitigation immediately, deploy the production rule globally in log mode, and then promote it through minute-scale cohorts with automated safety gates. Require a known-good signed configuration, regex complexity limits, representative benign testing, and a tested one-click global rollback.
Benchmark each candidate regex on production proxy hardware using generated worst-case inputs plus the CI payload and benign corpora, while measuring request latency and CPU.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes material CPU saturation, latency inflation, or unacceptable error rates; otherwise the benchmark clears the most immediate catastrophic-regression risk, though production cohort gates are still required.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the wave structure and placing user-ID later, but do not deregister any service until the new system has shadow-evaluated real usage and demonstrated parity with the legacy decision for an agreed observation period. Start automatic reductions in non-enforcing or conservatively bounded mode, and add explicit completeness, cross-region, rollback, and emergency-bypass gates; dashboards alone are insufficient.
Copying the current allocation preserves the legacy system's units, scope, grace-period semantics, and enforcement behavior.
New-system usage reports are complete, timely, deduplicated, and consistent across regions before legacy enforcement is removed.
Automatic allocation reductions cannot produce a harmful false reduction or reduce resilience below required peaks during the grace period.
Each wave can be rolled back or temporarily bypassed without losing authoritative quota enforcement, especially for replicated user-ID writes.
A wave's services and policies are fully inventoried, with no legacy-only exceptions or split registrations.
A semantic mismatch or incorrect allocation translation could reject valid user-ID writes and impair login globally.
Stale, missing, duplicated, or regionally inconsistent reports could trigger enforcement or reduction against incorrect usage.
The proposal has no pre-enforcement comparison, so discrepancies are discovered while users are exposed rather than during shadow operation.
The observation that a grace period is long does not protect against a sharp usage increase, report outage, replication event, or misconfigured reduction policy.
Wave rollback may restore legacy registration only after data or policy diverges, leaving no safe immediate enforcement path.
Use shadow-first wave migration: register a cohort without making the new system authoritative, compare historical and live usage, effective allocations, grace-period transitions, and would-be write decisions against the legacy manager, and require predefined parity thresholds. Then enforce on a small cohort, retain tested rollback or bypass controls through the observation period, and enable automatic reduction only after telemetry completeness and reduction behavior are validated; migrate user-ID with conservative limits and cross-region failure testing.
Run the new quota engine in non-enforcing mode for one representative cohort, replay available historical reports, and compare its effective allocation, reduction schedule, and enforcement decisions with the legacy manager over a period covering grace-period transitions.
Any unexplained decision mismatch, missing/late report, cross-region discrepancy, or materially different reduction schedule falsifies copy-and-deregister as a safe default; exact agreement across representative cases supports proceeding with the modified gates.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Do not ship the process-local mutex as the correctness boundary. Replace it with a shared Postgres-backed atomic reservation or state machine, combined with an idempotency key for retries and an explicit policy for charge failures or process crashes. The mutex may be retained only as a same-process optimization, never as the protection against duplicate redemption.
All concurrent redemptions for a coupon happen to land in the same Node.js process, which conflicts with the 4-12 replica deployment.
The mutex remains held across the complete charge and persistence operation.
No process crash, eviction, or request termination can occur between charging the order and setting redeemedAt.
Map cleanup cannot remove a lock while another request is acquiring or using it.
The proposed test accurately represents production routing and concurrency rather than only invoking both calls from one process.
Two requests routed to different replicas can both pass the redeemedAt check and charge the coupon.
A crash after chargeOrder but before the database update can leave a charged order with an apparently redeemable coupon.
Retry traffic can create long mutex queues and increase latency or resource usage.
A mutex cleanup race can permit simultaneous critical sections even within one process.
A process-local test can pass while the actual distributed failure remains.
Use Postgres as the cross-replica coordination point: atomically claim the coupon with a conditional update or durable reservation record, enforce uniqueness for the coupon and idempotency key, then charge using an idempotent payment request and finalize or recover the reservation. Validate the added database operations and payment behavior against the 800 ms p99 requirement.
Run two simultaneous redeem requests for one coupon while forcing them to different application pods, and inspect the charge/provider results and final coupon row.
If both requests can pass the redeemedAt check and invoke chargeOrder, or if the final state permits a subsequent redemption, the proposed mutex is falsified in the deployed topology; a single-process test is insufficient.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the read-through cache, but do not use a 15-minute TTL without revocation handling: consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected keys, while retaining a short bounded TTL for missed or invalid events. Re-estimate the latency target using the actual miss distribution, add request coalescing and negative-cache safeguards, and roll out with explicit revocation-latency monitoring.
Permission events contain enough identifiers to invalidate every affected `userId/docId/action` key.
Kafka event delivery and processing complete within the maximum acceptable authorization-staleness window.
The replayed access-log hit rate is representative of production traffic and includes the same key/action distribution.
Redis capacity and eviction policies can accommodate the additional authorization keys without harming sessions.
A cache hit and a cache miss have predictable latency distributions under peak concurrency.
A 15-minute stale allow decision can grant access after an account, group membership, or document share is revoked, creating a serious confidentiality and compliance incident.
With only an 85% hit rate, approximately 15% of requests still miss; those misses are the slowest population, so p95 will generally remain near the 180 ms permissions-call latency rather than fall to about 40 ms.
A sudden cache expiry or deployment can cause a permissions-service thundering herd, increasing latency and potentially cascading into the permissions service.
Incorrect event-to-key mapping or delayed/consumed events can leave revoked access cached, especially for broad group or tenant changes.
Filling the shared Redis cluster may evict session data or degrade session traffic, converting an authorization optimization into an availability incident.
Use a versioned or explicitly event-invalidated authorization cache: populate on misses, invalidate synchronously as soon as possible from `permission-events`, and use a short TTL only as a safety net. If the event payload cannot support precise invalidation, reduce the TTL to the business-approved revocation window and require at least approximately 99% effective hit rate before relying on cache hits to improve p95.
Run a representative peak-load test or trace-based benchmark with 85% cache hits and 15% misses, where misses take 180 ms p95, then revoke a currently cached user and measure the time until access is denied.
The p95 will remain close to the miss latency near 180 ms rather than 40 ms if the proposed 85% hit rate is accurate; a revoked user will also remain able to access the document for up to 15 minutes, demonstrating both the performance estimate and security risk.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Keep the expedited, infrastructure-based rollout, but do not treat a 10-minute log-only period as sufficient safety validation. Require adversarial regex complexity and performance tests before publication, enforce signed/versioned atomic bundles and per-rule rollback, and use explicit CPU, latency, and false-positive thresholds before global blocking; add a narrowly scoped emergency containment rule when the final signature is not immediately safe.
Quicksilver can atomically publish a consistent, signed rule bundle to every machine and transition modes within the target hour.
The WAF evaluator supports rule-level log/block transitions and rollback without restarting proxies.
A rule passing the existing CI corpus has acceptable worst-case PCRE behavior on malformed and adversarial inputs.
Near-real-time match counts and request health metrics are available and trustworthy during the 10-minute window.
Log-mode evaluation has approximately the same CPU cost as block-mode evaluation.
Catastrophic regex backtracking can exhaust proxy CPU even while the rule is only logging, affecting all customer traffic.
A low match count can be caused by a faulty, narrowly scoped, or traffic-dependent rule and therefore does not establish safety.
A false positive discovered after the global block transition can affect every PoP simultaneously.
Inconsistent bundle versions or mode transitions can create temporary unprotected gaps or conflicting behavior.
A compromised release credential or control plane could inject a globally evaluated denial rule.
Use a hybrid release: deploy a narrowly scoped temporary deny policy immediately where appropriate, then publish the precise rule globally in log mode for 1–5 minutes with automated performance and false-positive gates, followed by rapid promotion and one-click per-rule rollback. This preserves sub-hour protection while reducing reliance on a single noisy observation window.
Replay the candidate rule and a representative/adversarial benign corpus through the actual WAF evaluator on a production-equivalent proxy, including encoded, truncated, and pathological inputs, while measuring CPU, p95/p99 latency, and evaluation count.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes superlinear evaluation, CPU saturation, or unacceptable proxy latency; also falsified if log-mode overhead is materially lower than block-mode overhead.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub as the durable dispatch mechanism or decommission RabbitMQ until equivalent delivery guarantees are demonstrated. Migrate incrementally to Celery on RabbitMQ with explicit acknowledgements, durable queues, retries, idempotency contracts, graceful worker termination, and end-to-end backlog/dead-letter monitoring; retain the existing path during each migration stage.
Redis Pub/Sub messages must survive subscriber disconnects and worker restarts, although Pub/Sub provides no such guarantee.
AOF persistence protects queued work, although Redis AOF does not persist Pub/Sub messages for disconnected subscribers.
An existing retry wrapper can provide delivery guarantees without a durable source of missed work.
All publishers and workers can tolerate message loss during the dual-path week or Redis failover.
The 300 msg/s throughput target is sufficient evidence of reliability and failure recovery, not merely capacity.
Payment or fulfilment messages published while a worker is restarting, disconnected, or being rolled out can be silently lost.
Redis node failure, failover, memory pressure, or eviction can cause dispatch loss or interrupt unrelated cache and rate-limit traffic.
Worker-side retries cannot recover a message that was never durably queued or received.
Running both paths without idempotency and reconciliation can create duplicate side effects when jobs are published or retried.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ removes the current durability and replay boundary before migration behavior is validated.
Adopt Celery incrementally on the existing RabbitMQ cluster, using durable or quorum queues, explicit acknowledgements, per-job-type retry policies, dead-letter handling, idempotency, graceful Kubernetes shutdown, and metrics for queue age, backlog, retries, and dead letters. Migrate one representative job type first and retain RabbitMQ until failure-injection and business-reconciliation tests pass.
Publish a representative payment job while its worker is offline, then restart Redis and the worker; also terminate the worker immediately after receipt but before acknowledgement. Compare published, received, acknowledged, and completed job IDs.
Any published job that is absent after subscriber downtime or an unacknowledged job that disappears during worker or Redis termination falsifies the required at-least-once guarantee; a correct design must redeliver it and produce no unexplained loss.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Keep the expedited global log-to-block model, but require a versioned atomic bundle, explicit benign-regression and PCRE complexity budgets, and automated promotion based on block volume, 5xx rate, latency, and CPU—not match volume alone. Preserve the previous bundle for immediate rollback, and define who can terminate or reverse the release; add a brief 1% block canary only if it still meets the one-hour objective.
A globally activated log-mode rule is propagated atomically and consistently within minutes.
Ten minutes of telemetry is timely and representative enough to expose false positives and operational regressions.
The CI suite includes benign requests in addition to attack payloads and runs before expedited activation.
Rule compilation and matching have enforced CPU, memory, and worst-case backtracking limits.
Block-mode changes can be rolled back globally within minutes without waiting for another configuration deployment.
A high-cost PCRE consumes substantial proxy CPU in log mode before match-count monitoring detects degradation.
A benign traffic pattern absent from CI causes a global false-positive outage when block mode begins.
Match volume alone can remain normal while latency, 5xx responses, or regional traffic distributions deteriorate.
A non-atomic Quicksilver update can produce mixed rule versions or activate block mode before every proxy has validated the bundle.
Telemetry delay or concurrent updates can cause unsafe promotion or rollback to an unintended bundle.
Use the proposed global log window as the emergency safety gate, but combine it with deterministic pre-activation limits and automated multi-signal promotion: global log for 5–10 minutes, immediate rollback on any safety threshold breach, then block at 1% and 100% if latency and traffic permit. This is safer than relying on a fixed ten-minute timer while remaining within the disclosure-hour target.
Replay a representative benign and adversarial request corpus through the candidate rule in log mode on a production-like proxy at measured peak request rate, comparing CPU and p99 latency with the rule disabled.
The design is viable only if worst-case evaluation stays within an agreed CPU and latency budget and no unbounded backtracking occurs; materially higher p99 latency, CPU saturation, or pathological evaluation time falsifies the claim that log mode is a safe universal first stage.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not send the untyped list directly to permanent deletion. Resolve every ID against an authoritative inventory, require it to be an active "Insight Legacy" add-on installation, reject site IDs and unknown or ambiguous records, and obtain a reviewed deletion manifest before execution. Then canary the process, use checkpoints and fail-closed stopping rules, and permanently delete only the validated manifest while recording request and response evidence.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies the intended add-on installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The product team's list is complete, current, and free of stale, duplicated, malformed, or incorrectly scoped IDs.
Permanent deletion removes the installation and its legacy data without cascading into unrelated products or site content.
The API returns enough metadata or errors to verify object type and successful deletion.
Completing validation and a controlled canary is possible before the backend shutdown.
A single site ID in the list could permanently destroy an entire customer site and all products on it.
IDs from the same 24-character format may be misclassified because no type validation is performed.
A stale or incorrect product-team manifest could irreversibly delete valid customer objects.
Unexpected API behavior or cascading deletion could affect unrelated product data.
Batching and weekend scheduling do not mitigate irreversible damage; on-call monitoring detects failures only after they occur.
Generate a canonical manifest by joining the product-team list to authoritative object metadata, including object type, site ID, add-on name/version, and status. Require 100% type and scope matches, explicitly assert that no site IDs or ambiguous records remain, and produce a signed count and hash for approval. Test a small representative sample, verify deletion and unaffected site data, then execute idempotently with per-ID results, checkpoints, an exact allowlist, and immediate halt on any mismatch.
Run a read-only preflight that resolves every supplied ID through the canonical inventory or object metadata API and asserts object_type = add-on installation, add-on = Insight Legacy, expected site association, and uniqueness; explicitly search for any resolved site object.
The direct permanent-delete approach is falsified if even one ID is missing, ambiguous, duplicated across object types, identifies a site, or identifies a different add-on. It is safe to proceed only if all records match the expected type and scope and the manifest count reconciles exactly.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the per-process mutex with a database-level atomic compare-and-set claim, such as `UPDATE coupons SET redeemed_at = now(), order_id = ... WHERE code = ? AND redeemed_at IS NULL RETURNING ...`, and reject when no row is returned. Perform this claim before charging, make charging retry-safe, and define compensation or reconciliation for failures after the claim; preserve the proposed concurrent test but exercise requests through separate application instances.
The coupon-service Deployment can have multiple active replicas, so an in-memory lock cannot provide cross-replica exclusion.
Postgres is the authoritative shared state accessible by every redemption request.
A coupon claim can be committed before payment without unacceptable latency or availability impact.
Payment operations can be made idempotent or correlated with the claimed order.
Two requests routed to different pods can acquire separate mutexes and both redeem the same coupon.
The proposed single-process concurrency test can pass while production remains vulnerable across the 4-12 replicas.
Claiming before charging introduces abandoned claims if the process crashes, requiring explicit recovery semantics.
Retrying `chargeOrder` can itself create duplicate charges unless payment idempotency is enforced.
Use an atomic database state transition guarded by `redeemed_at IS NULL`, ideally with a claim/status and order correlation, followed by an idempotent charge and compensating or reconciling failed claims.
Run the two-request redemption race through two separately deployed service instances backed by the same Postgres database, then query the coupon and orders.
If both instances report successful redemption, or two orders reference the coupon, the mutex proposal is disproven; a correct atomic claim should allow exactly one success regardless of routing.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Add an explicit migration safety gate for the user-ID service: keep its allocation fixed above observed peak usage plus reporting-lag and growth headroom, with alerts and a tested rollback path before enabling automatic reductions. Verify equivalent quota units and continuous reporting, and perform a staged cutover that cannot create a registration gap or prematurely enforce a reduced allocation.
Legacy and new quota systems use identical allocation and usage units.
Copying the current allocation preserves all existing quota protections.
Service reporting has bounded lag and remains continuous during manager handoff.
Allocation will not be reduced below actual user-ID database usage.
Usage can grow materially during the grace period or reporting delay.
Automatic reduction could lower the user-ID allocation below real distributed-database usage, causing login-related writes to be rejected across regions.
A gap or mismatch during deregistration and registration could leave usage unreported or enforce an incorrect quota.
Different accounting semantics could make the copied allocation smaller in the new system than in the legacy system.
Stale or lagging reports could trigger reductions based on usage that is no longer current.
An untested rollback could restore the legacy manager after writes have been rejected.

In staging, configure the user-ID service exactly as proposed and simulate reporting below allocation through one full grace period while actual usage remains near the pending reduced allocation; then attempt a database write.
If the allocation is reduced below actual usage and the write is rejected, the automatic-reduction design is unsafe as proposed; if the system maintains a safe floor and accepts the write, that specific risk is refuted.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Retain streaming as the preferred direction, but replace the single fleet-wide rollout with a gated canary across representative production services and client libraries. Establish compatibility, fallback, discovery-freshness, reconnect, and rollback gates before expanding, and verify that the original 60% staging reduction persists at production cardinality.
All relevant client libraries and server versions can interoperate safely during a staged Consul 1.10 upgrade.
The 200-node staging benchmark is representative of production query rates, payload sizes, churn, and reconnect behavior.
Streaming provides the freshness, ordering, filtering, and failure semantics required by existing service-discovery consumers.
Clients can fall back safely to blocking queries when streaming is unavailable or disabled.
The six-week schedule permits inventory, canarying, soak testing, and progressive deployment rather than a one-shot change.
A fleet-wide configuration or version change could simultaneously break discovery for services that have no fallback.
Streaming could produce stale or missing updates, causing incorrect service routing or outages that CPU reductions alone would not reveal.
A version skew or unsupported client integration could leave critical services without a working discovery mechanism.
Reconnect storms or higher-volume updates could offset streaming's CPU and network gains and threaten the cluster before the holiday peak.
The measured gain may not generalize beyond staging, leaving production capacity constraints unresolved.
Upgrade a compatible canary cohort, enable streaming only for bounded, representative services, and compare them with unchanged blocking-query services. Expand in controlled stages only after validating server CPU/network reduction, client resource cost, update freshness, error rate, reconnect behavior, and rollback under an induced streaming failure.
Select one or a few representative production services with high query volume, canary streaming on a small compatible agent cohort, and compare them with matched blocking-query services over a peak-like period, including a controlled agent restart.
The proposal is supported only if streaming materially reduces server CPU and network without increasing stale or missed updates, client errors, reconnect load, or discovery latency, and remains correct through restart and fallback. If the gain is negligible, semantics differ, or reconnects create damaging load, the proposal is falsified for this fleet.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the bit-repurposing approach, but deploy gateway/router support disabled with strict validation, a centralized allowlist and kill switch, and compatible binaries before launch. Prove legacy-bit non-emission across all supported clients rather than inferring it from one month of production traffic, then canary and incrementally enable RLP while verifying actual build IDs, effective configuration, routing results, errors, and latency.
No current or supported client can emit the Power Peg bit under any supported configuration or order path.
Gateway and router versions handling the repurposed bit can be fully deployed before clients begin setting it.
The router can centrally disable RLP and reject invalid flag combinations without affecting legacy traffic.
The bit is exposed and routable consistently through every relevant gateway and router version.
Client rollout can be coordinated so the bit is not set before server compatibility is confirmed.
A stale, archival, or rarely exercised client sets the bit and unintentionally activates RLP.
Partial gateway/router deployment produces inconsistent interpretation, dropped orders, or failed routing.
Immediate client activation skips canarying and removes any safe period for detecting compatibility defects.
Compatibility checks accept unknown flag combinations or fail open.
Operators cannot verify the binary and effective RLP configuration actually running on each host.

Inventory every supported client release, its source/configuration paths, and retained traffic captures, then test representative order submissions for any nonzero Power Peg value.
Any supported client or configuration found capable of setting the bit falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires explicit sender identification, migration blocking, or rollout segmentation before repurposing it.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for authoritative job dispatch: AOF does not retain Pub/Sub messages for later subscribers, so disconnects, worker redeployments, Redis restarts, or failover can silently lose payments and other jobs. Keep or harden RabbitMQ with supported quorum queues and migrate custom workers to Kombu or Celery; if a Redis migration remains desirable, evaluate Celery or Dramatiq with a durable transport such as Streams and isolated capacity rather than Pub/Sub.
A currently connected subscriber will receive every message before any process or Redis failure occurs.
AOF persistence can restore Pub/Sub messages for disconnected or restarted consumers; it cannot.
Worker-side retry handling compensates for messages that were never delivered.
Publishing the same job to both systems will be safely deduplicated across every job type.
Latency and raw throughput alone satisfy the delivery and recovery requirements.
Payment webhooks can disappear during the frequent worker redeployment window, preventing order payment and fulfilment without any producer-side error.
Redis restart or failover can terminate active subscriptions and lose in-flight messages; AOF replay does not recreate Pub/Sub delivery state.
The proposed dual run can process jobs twice, and many job types may lack sufficient cross-system idempotency.
Sharing Redis capacity with caching and rate limiting creates a correlated failure domain under load spikes.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ removes the only tested durable queue semantics before parity is established.
Incrementally standardize workers on RabbitMQ using Kombu or Celery, configure quorum queues and per-job-type retry/DLQ policies, and automate rolling upgrades. This preserves at-least-once delivery and backpressure while reducing custom operational code without introducing a new managed service.
Run two Redis CLI clients on the same test server: `SET retained value`, execute `PUBLISH jobs:test payload` before starting the subscriber, then start `SUBSCRIBE jobs:test`; afterward restart Redis and repeat while a subscriber is temporarily disconnected. Inspect whether the message arrives in either case and whether AOF contains any replayable message.
The proposal is falsified if the published job is not delivered after the later subscription or disconnect/reconnect/restart, even though the unrelated `SET` value survives AOF recovery.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator as the topology manager, but do not enable unconditional promotion of the most up-to-date replica across regions. Restrict automation to proven candidates, add explicit lag and reachability checks, enforce fencing of the old primary, and make East-local promotion the normal path with West promotion reserved for a tested East outage procedure. Validate the complete detection-to-write-recovery duration and data-loss behavior under continuous writes before declaring the one-minute objective met.
A candidate with the highest available replication position contains every acknowledged write required by the application.
Orchestrator can safely classify host failure without allowing the old primary to continue accepting writes after promotion.
East-only Rails clients can reach and tolerate a West primary through the discovery and connection-reconnection path.
Thirty seconds plus promotion, topology propagation, and application reconnection consistently fits inside the one-minute objective.
Pseudo-GTID and Orchestrator topology metadata provide reliable candidate ordering but sufficient promotion safety.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can permanently lose committed transactions, despite Raft consensus protecting the orchestration decision itself.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, creating split brain, divergent transactions, and potential corruption or unrecoverable conflicts.
Promoting a West replica may exceed the objective or degrade write latency and connection behavior for East-only application servers.
Consul updates or cached Rails connections may direct some applications to stale or changing endpoints during failover, causing failed or retried writes.
A Raft quorum outage can prevent automated promotion precisely when the primary is unavailable, leaving the manual runbook necessary.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, recorded writes while killing the East primary, then measure transaction success, whether any acknowledged write is absent from the promoted replica, old-primary writability, and time until all applications are writing to the new primary.
A complete pass requires zero acknowledged-write loss, inability of the old primary to accept writes, and end-to-end write recovery under 60 seconds. Any acknowledged-write loss, split-brain writes, or recovery above one minute falsifies the proposal as written.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
The mutex only serializes requests within one Node.js process, while the Deployment has 4-12 replicas, so it does not prevent cross-replica double redemption. Replace it with a database-level atomic claim (for example, updateMany on redeemedAt: null) and make chargeOrder idempotent for the same order/payment; if claiming precedes charging, add explicit failure, retry, and release/expiry handling. A single-process concurrency test is insufficient; test concurrent requests through separate service instances.
A process-local mutex can coordinate all redemption requests, despite requests being distributed across multiple replicas.
All concurrent requests for a coupon necessarily pass through the same Node.js process.
The existing charge and update operation remains atomic under process or network failures.
Retries can be safely distinguished using the existing order identity.
A database-level change can be implemented and operated within this week's release constraints.
Two replicas can each acquire their own mutex and both redeem the same coupon.
A successful charge followed by a failed database update leaves the coupon apparently available for another redemption.
A client timeout can cause a retry to charge or redeem again unless the charge and redemption are idempotent.
Marking the coupon before charging can permanently consume it when payment fails.
The proposed test can pass while the production multi-replica failure remains unresolved.

Run two concurrent redeem requests for one unused coupon against two service replicas sharing the production-equivalent database.
If both requests succeed or the coupon has two redemption records, the process-local mutex is proven ineffective; a correct implementation should allow exactly one success and produce one durable claim/redemption.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Replace immediate permanent deletion with authoritative preflight validation requiring each ID to resolve to the expected add-on installation and site, followed by small, reconciled soft-delete batches. After a short observation period, permanently purge only validated IDs; any mismatch, cascade effect, ambiguous response, or failed reconciliation must stop promotion to permanent deletion.
The deletion API reliably distinguishes add-on installation IDs from site IDs before mutating either object.
Permanent deletion cannot cascade to the site, site content, or other products.
The supplied list is complete, current, duplicate-free, and mapped to the correct expected sites.
The endpoint provides reliable per-ID status and safe retry semantics.
Permanent mode actually guarantees deletion before backend shutdown and satisfies the data-minimisation policy.
A wrong or stale site ID could irreversibly delete an entire site.
An ID could resolve to another object type in a shared or ambiguous ID namespace.
Hidden cascades could remove unrelated products or site data.
Batch-level logging may obscure partial failures or invalid IDs, leading to undetected omissions or repeated mutations.
The irreversible operation provides no recovery window before the retired backend becomes unavailable.
Join every supplied ID to an authoritative inventory containing object type, expected parent site, and deletion eligibility; reject all unresolved or mismatched entries. Process a canary and then small soft-delete batches with per-ID results, reconcile object state, monitor for cross-object effects, and permanently purge only the validated set after a short observation period that does not extend beyond backend availability.
Inspect the deletion API contract or run a no-op/preflight request for one known add-on ID and one site ID, checking whether it returns object type and parent site and refuses a site or mismatched-site deletion before mutation.
If the API cannot establish type and site scope or accepts deletion based solely on an opaque ID, the permanent batch job is unsafe; if it rejects both wrong-type and wrong-site targets and exposes per-ID eligibility, the core safety assumption is supported.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but do not promote an arbitrary or West-region replica based only on Raft quorum and 30-second unreachability. Restrict promotion to a prevalidated, sufficiently caught-up East replica where possible, require explicit fencing or STONITH of the old primary, and test the complete 30-second detection-to-write-path timing. Validate Consul integration and application reconnect behavior, and explicitly account for data loss inherent in asynchronous replication.
The old primary is reliably fenced or otherwise prevented from accepting writes after being declared unreachable.
A candidate replica's replication lag is within an explicitly approved data-loss bound at promotion time.
An East-region replica remains reachable and is preferred for a single-East-host failure; cross-region promotion is an intentional fallback.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum is not treated as a substitute for MySQL primary fencing.
Consul updates and Rails connection handling cause applications to route to the promoted primary within the required time.
An isolated but still-live old primary can continue accepting writes, causing split-brain and divergence.
Asynchronous replication can lose committed transactions even when the promoted replica has the highest observed position.
A transient East network fault can trigger an unnecessary promotion and outage or make West promotion unexpectedly slow.
A West promotion may exceed the one-minute objective because of 60 ms RTT, discovery propagation, and application reconnection.
Pseudo-GTIDs simplify identity and positioning but do not eliminate the need to verify replication state, lag, and write fencing.

Run a controlled network partition between the old East primary and Orchestrator while leaving it able to serve client connections, then verify whether it is fenced before the replica is promoted and whether any writes made on the old primary are lost or divergent.
If the old primary continues accepting writes, or the test produces acknowledged writes that are absent from the promoted replica, the proposed safety claims are falsified.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse direction only as a time-boxed compatibility measure, but make rollout two-phase: deploy the backward-compatible RLP-capable router to all eight servers, verify exact build identity and RLP readiness, then permit clients to set the bit through a centrally controlled admission gate. Do not remove Power Peg in the same release; retain it behind an explicit server-side deny/default-off control until the RLP path is proven and rollback safety is established.
No legitimate producer outside the inspected production traffic—including replay, recovery, administrative, test, archived, or failover clients—can set the bit.
No order can reach a stale or old router after clients begin setting the bit.
The gateway can centrally withhold RLP-bit traffic until every production server is verified RLP-capable.
RLP eligibility is implemented consistently by all clients, gateways, and routers.
The old router's Power Peg behavior cannot be activated by the new RLP traffic if mixed versions occur.
A stale router may receive the RLP bit and execute the retired Power Peg algorithm, misrouting orders across the entire 3M-order/day workload.
Rollback to a pre-RLP router while clients still set the bit may immediately create mixed-version behavior.
A month of traffic does not establish that archived, replayed, test, administrative, or failover producers never set the bit.
Manual deployment provides no reliable evidence that all eight servers run the intended build.
Simultaneously removing Power Peg and introducing RLP makes rollback and incident diagnosis substantially harder.
If the date cannot accommodate a versioned message change, isolate RLP traffic on a separate listener or transport with an RLP-capable router fleet, so legacy routers can never receive the RLP signal. If isolation is infeasible, retain a coordinated protocol-version change and seek a staged exchange launch rather than relying on bit semantics.
In a production-like staging test, run an unmodified pre-RLP router and send otherwise valid orders with the reused header bit set through the actual gateway-to-router path; also search every producer and replay/recovery code path for writes to the bit.
Any old-router path that accepts and acts on the set bit, or any non-RLP producer capable of setting it, falsifies the proposal's safety premise and requires a separate admission boundary or replacement approach.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Replace permanent deletion with a server-enforced, installation-scoped workflow that first performs an auditable dry run and validates every ID as an authorized, eligible Insight Legacy installation. Prefer mark mode with a verified shutdown deadline and rollback window; process small idempotent batches with per-ID results and reconciliation, and use permanent deletion only after confirming cascade behavior and recovery readiness.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an Insight Legacy installation rather than a site or another object.
Permanent mode deletes only the intended installation and does not cascade into sites, content, products, backups, or other add-ons.
The deletion API enforces tenant authorization and installation eligibility server-side.
Permanent deletion before backend shutdown is required for compliance or technical reasons.
The API and batch job provide idempotency and reliable per-ID results for partial failures.
A single misclassified site ID could cause irreversible loss of customer data.
Unintended deletion cascades could destroy related site content, products, backups, or add-ons.
Logging full responses may expose sensitive data while still lacking an immutable input manifest or per-ID audit trail.
Blind batch retries can repeat successful deletions or leave the operation partially reconciled.
Permanent mode provides no rollback if backend dependencies remain or shutdown timing changes.
Use an explicitly installation-scoped endpoint or bulk job that retrieves metadata, rejects unknown IDs, site IDs, ineligible tenants, and unauthorized records, then performs a dry run followed by small batches in mark mode. Reconcile activation and backend-call status before considering any later permanent cleanup.
Using a non-mutating lookup or type-check API, resolve every ID in an immutable copy of the product team's manifest and require object type, product eligibility, site ownership, and tenant authorization to match the deletion criteria.
The approach is safe only if every ID resolves to an authorized, eligible Insight Legacy installation and none resolves to a site, unknown object, or unrelated record; any mismatch falsifies the current permanent-delete proposal.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain the expedited path, but require versioned, signed configuration with local schema/resource validation, an automated global kill switch, and staged enforcement that still completes within one hour. Do not treat CI corpus success or ten minutes of low log volume as sufficient evidence of safety, because benign traffic may be absent or insufficiently represented and catastrophic PCRE backtracking remains possible.
Quicksilver can atomically distribute versioned WAF configuration to every proxy within the required latency.
Every proxy can reject invalid, incompatible, or computationally unsafe rules before activation.
The CI benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives.
Ten minutes of traffic across all PoPs provides statistically meaningful coverage.
A rule can be disabled and previous configuration restored automatically within minutes.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic at every edge simultaneously.
A PCRE pattern with pathological backtracking could saturate already CPU-bound proxies; log mode still executes the regex.
A malformed or incompatible configuration could cause proxy reload failures or inconsistent enforcement.
Low observed match volume could conceal false positives because attack types and benign traffic vary by customer and PoP.
A partial Quicksilver distribution or failed flip could leave the fleet exposed or produce an unreviewable mixed state.
Publish a signed, versioned rule bundle with a precomputed PCRE complexity/resource limit; validate and benchmark it on proxy builds, enable observation on a small representative canary for several minutes, then automatically progress through 1%, 10%, and 100% block enforcement within the one-hour objective. Continuously compare match rates, latency, CPU, errors, and representative benign traffic, with automatic rollback on any threshold breach.
Replay a production-representative benign request trace plus the CI payload corpus through the exact proxy/WAF build, measuring incremental p99 latency and CPU while enabling the proposed rule in log mode.
The proposal is falsified if any single rule exceeds the defined per-request CPU/latency budget, causes PCRE resource growth with input length, or matches representative benign traffic at a rate that would create material customer impact.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the shared Redis cache direction, but do not use a plain 15-minute TTL or claim p95 improvement from an 85% hit rate. Add event-driven invalidation with race protection, shorter TTLs for deny decisions, per-key single-flight, and explicit fail-closed behavior; measure end-to-end p95 by hit and miss before expanding the rollout. If testing still leaves the miss path above the request budget, move authorization decisions to an event-fed local read model.
A 15-minute stale authorization window is acceptable for grants and revocations, which is unlikely without an explicit security bound.
Redis and the permissions service can meet latency and availability requirements at projected cardinality and peak traffic.
The 85% and 78% replay figures use comparable request populations and denominators.
A permissions-service miss can complete within the remaining endpoint budget.
Feature-flagged rollout traffic is representative and dashboards will identify miss-path latency and errors.
Revoked access can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes because there is no invalidation consumer.
The 15% miss population may determine p95, so the asserted approximately 40 ms p95 is unsupported and could remain above 120 ms.
Concurrent misses can stampede the permissions service, especially during Redis outages or a cold cache.
