Caching all decisions for the same long TTL can delay legitimate access after share or other grant changes.
Redis failure behavior is unspecified and could accidentally fail open or create an uncontrolled permissions-service surge.
If the required effective hit rate cannot be demonstrated above 95% or the miss path cannot be made reliably sub-100 ms, use Kafka-fed authorization snapshots or read models in each pod, with Redis only as shared transport or storage where appropriate, plus safe cold-start and lag handling.
Replay the 24-hour access-log trace through a cache simulator with a 15-minute TTL, using measured cache-hit, permissions-service, Redis, and document-service latencies, and report end-to-end p95 split by hit and miss.
The proposal is falsified if the 85% hit-rate scenario still produces endpoint p95 above 120 ms, or if the miss-path service latency cannot fit within the remaining request budget.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month parallel rewrite and single cut-over with an incremental strangler migration. First build characterization and golden-invoice tests, then introduce billing-core behind compatibility adapters, migrate plan families and services in stages, and remove legacy code only after measured parity. This preserves rollback options and avoids accumulating three months of merge divergence.
The existing observable inputs, outputs, and state transitions are known well enough to reproduce all 37 plans exactly.
Undocumented proration, rounding, tax, timezone, and grandfathering rules can all be isolated inside billing-core rather than depending on service interactions.
The five services can adopt billing-core through stable compatibility boundaries and do not require a synchronized release.
A three-person team can maintain correct billing-core while continuously reconciling with approximately 40 weekly main-branch integrations.
Deleting the old implementation in one final PR is simpler and safer than removing it incrementally.
A clean domain model may omit legacy exceptions or shared-state side effects, changing real invoices despite unit-test parity.
A long-lived branch will conflict repeatedly with billing changes merged into main, making the final merge and validation substantially harder.
The final cut-over has excessive blast radius: a missed interaction or rounding discrepancy can affect all plans and five services simultaneously.
Without end-to-end characterization tests, the team may mistake reconstructed behavior for parity while preserving incorrect legacy behavior.
The three-month effort may end with dual implementations still present, negating the proposal's claimed maintenance savings.
Use an incremental strangler migration with a plan/policy catalog and differential golden-invoice tests. Characterize the 37 plans first, extract one representative plan family behind the current interfaces, then migrate ordinary and grandfathered cohorts one at a time. Add compatibility adapters temporarily, run shadow comparisons where feasible, and remove each legacy path after verified parity.
Choose the most complex grandfathered plan plus one ordinary proration plan, capture their existing service inputs and invoices across proration, rounding, timezone, and tax edge cases, and implement those cases in a small billing-core slice for differential testing.
Any output difference that requires service-level state, undocumented exceptions, or repeated manual branching would falsify the assumption that a clean core can be ported safely and support a single cut-over; exact parity would support the approach only for those tested cases.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but do not enable it for all health subscriptions in one rollout. First verify the exact 1.10 configuration scope and client compatibility, then canary representative cohorts, measure CPU, network, update correctness, and reconnect behavior under realistic load, and expand only against explicit thresholds. Retain a tested configuration rollback and use query/watch tuning as a complementary control.
The deployed client and server versions support the same streaming protocol and configuration semantics.
`use_streaming_backend` is set at the correct agent/server scope and actually causes production health reads to use streaming rather than merely enabling an unused feature.
The 200-node staging workload is representative of production subscription breadth, result sizes, churn, and holiday concurrency.
Streaming preserves watch ordering, completeness, and freshness during reconnects and leader changes.
The rollout can be stopped or reverted quickly enough to prevent a fleet-wide failure.
A mixed-version or mis-scoped rollout leaves blocking queries active or causes incompatible streaming behavior.
An all-at-once change can create a reconnect or subscription storm, increasing CPU, network, Raft pressure, and latency.
Incorrect streaming freshness or missed-event handling could leave services with stale dependency state or route traffic to unhealthy instances.
The staging CPU reduction may not scale linearly when every service subscribes simultaneously.
Because there is no discovery fallback, a streaming defect or partition could broadly disrupt service resolution.
Use a staged canary: begin with a bounded, diverse set of services and nodes, validate correctness and resource metrics during expected load, then expand by cohorts. Keep the existing blocking-query configuration available for immediate rollback, and add endpoint/watch coalescing or narrower subscriptions if streaming does not deliver the expected fleet-wide reduction.
Run the proposed 200-node staging configuration under a production-representative subscription mix and concurrent holiday-level load, while comparing effective configuration and measuring server CPU, network bytes, streaming versus blocking-query counts, and watch freshness or missed updates.
The proposal is falsified if clients do not actually use streaming, or if streaming causes material missed/stale updates, a reconnect storm, or higher server CPU/network than the current blocking-query baseline at representative load; a reproducible, scalable CPU reduction with correct updates supports expansion.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on the events table or rely on a weekly vacuum without measuring dead-tuple generation and vacuum completion time. Keep autovacuum enabled with events-specific vacuum cost pacing and tuned thresholds, coordinate controlled expiration deletes during low-traffic periods, and investigate partitioning if vacuum cannot keep pace. A regular VACUUM reuses space but does not return it to the operating system and may be inadequate against sustained delete and index-cleanup volume.
Dead-tuple creation and indexed-row deletion remain low enough for one weekly VACUUM to prevent unacceptable bloat.
The weekly VACUUM can complete before the next accumulation cycle without causing unacceptable I/O or latency.
The events workload is genuinely append-mostly rather than producing substantial delete volume or dead indexed rows.
Bulk deletes are bounded, off-peak, and do not recreate a large maintenance spike.
Storage latency, WAL, checkpoints, replication, and other maintenance are not contributing independently to the latency spikes.
Dead tuples and index bloat can accumulate for up to a week, increasing scan and write costs and potentially causing severe latency degradation.
Disabling autovacuum removes the feedback mechanism that responds when dead rows accumulate faster than expected.
A weekly VACUUM may be unable to finish within its window, leaving the table progressively less maintained.
Bulk deletes can generate substantial WAL and index I/O even when scheduled off-peak.
Grafana bloat monitoring alone may detect damage too late and does not measure vacuum lag, dead-tuple growth, or vacuum effectiveness.
Enable events-specific autovacuum with conservative vacuum_cost_delay and vacuum_cost_limit tuning, adjust per-table thresholds based on measured dead-tuple production, and schedule controlled expiration deletes during low traffic. Track dead tuples, vacuum duration, index growth, bloat, p99 latency, WAL/checkpoint activity, and device I/O wait; if vacuum cannot keep pace at approximately 25k inserts/s plus deletes, evaluate retention partitioning as the structural fix.
During one representative peak period, record the events table's dead-tuple estimate and index size at the start and end using SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid)), pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(relid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events'; repeat after the normal maintenance interval while reviewing vacuum logs.
The proposal is wrong if n_dead_tup and index size rise continuously, the scheduled VACUUM cannot complete before the next cycle, or resulting bloat/scan latency exceeds the agreed limit; stable or declining metrics would support the weekly schedule.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep Redis caching, but consume `permission-events` to invalidate affected cache keys rather than relying on a 15-minute TTL, retaining a short TTL only as a safety net. Define event ordering, lag, poison-message, and fail-open/fail-closed behavior, and validate the end-to-end p95 under production-like concurrency because an 85% hit rate cannot by itself reduce a bimodal latency distribution's p95 to 40 ms.
Every permission-changing write emits a correctly scoped event containing the affected user, document, and action.
Kafka event delivery is timely enough to meet the application's revocation requirements.
The permissions service's decision is deterministic for a user/document/action tuple until a relevant change event occurs.
Redis availability and capacity are sufficient for roughly 2,500 rps plus existing session traffic.
Caching both allow and deny decisions is security-compliant.
Unshared documents or access removed by the HR integration can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes, causing real data exposure.
At 85% cache hits, 15% of requests still incur the approximately 180 ms permissions call, so p95 may remain near the slow-path latency rather than fall to 40 ms.
Kafka consumer lag, partitions processed out of order, or missed invalidations could extend stale authorization beyond the intended window.
Redis eviction or cluster failure could sharply increase permissions-service load and latency at peak.
The log-replay hit rate may not represent live traffic, especially around sharing and account-removal events.
Use Redis as an event-coherently invalidated read-through cache: consume `permission-events`, delete all affected tuple keys, use a short TTL as a backstop, and publish cache-invalidated shadow metrics before broad rollout. If the resulting hit rate remains below the level needed for p95, pursue a permissions-service batch-check API when its ownership constraints permit or reconsider the endpoint's authorization architecture.
Run a production-like shadow benchmark using the measured hit/miss distribution and 180 ms miss latency, including the approximately 40 ms non-permissions request cost.
If the 15th-percentile request still lands on the 180 ms miss path or p95 remains near 200 ms rather than approximately 40 ms, the claimed latency improvement is falsified.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Keep automatic maintenance enabled and retune it per table: lower the vacuum trigger threshold/scale factor and increase the autovacuum cost delay to spread reads and writes over time. Schedule controlled off-peak vacuum capacity if necessary, continuously monitor dead-tuple growth and vacuum progress, and retain frequent autoanalyze; do not rely on a fixed weekly full-table vacuum for a 1.8 TB table.
The observed autovacuum IO can be smoothed by throttling without falling behind the deletion rate.
A full vacuum of events can complete within one low-traffic window and before the next deletion cycle.
Dead-tuple creation remains low enough that frequent maintenance can keep pace.
Weekly ANALYZE produces sufficiently fresh planner statistics for this workload.
The cron job will not remain running, be canceled, or overlap a subsequent run.
Disabling table autovacuum also disables autoanalyze, potentially causing stale statistics and poor query plans.
Dead tuples and table/index bloat may exceed safe bounds before the weekly vacuum, degrading scans and increasing write amplification.
At 25k inserts/s, even the default 20% scale-factor threshold can be reached in roughly 4.2 days, contradicting the claim of slow accumulation.
A vacuum lasting many hours may still create unacceptable IO or overlap the next scheduled run.
Maintenance delays can eventually force urgent anti-wraparound or manual vacuum activity with larger latency and duration spikes.
Retain autovacuum on events, lower `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` and `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`, and tune per-table autovacuum cost delay/limit to smooth IO while verifying that vacuum throughput exceeds dead-tuple production. Use a longer off-peak maintenance window and alerts based on dead tuples, bloat, and vacuum duration; keep autoanalyze independent and frequent.
Using existing logs and `pg_stat_all_tables` for `events`, measure a representative deletion cycle's dead-tuple growth, vacuum duration, and completion time relative to the proposed seven-day interval.
If vacuum cannot finish before the next cycle or dead tuples/bloat remain above the pre-agreed bound, the weekly schedule is falsified; stable low bloat and reliable completion would support the schedule's feasibility, though not its safety under autovacuum being disabled.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Keep the new billing-core direction, but replace the three-month, single-cutover migration with characterization, immutable/versioned domain contracts, and incremental adapter cutover per service or billing path. Establish shadow invoice comparisons and explicit rollback before deleting legacy code; do not delete it until parity evidence covers all 37 plans, grandfathering, proration, taxes, payments, and execution-order effects.
The current invoice behavior can be characterized accurately before the new model is frozen.
The proposed model can represent all historical proration and grandfathering exceptions without lossy abstractions.
Services can be migrated or shadowed independently behind compatibility adapters.
Invoice parity can be measured for identical inputs despite current mutable-context behavior.
The team can enforce billing changes, compatibility tests, and retirement tracking across frequent incoming PRs.
A clean model may silently change legacy rounding, proration, tax, payment, or state-order behavior, producing incorrect customer invoices.
A single final cutover creates a high-blast-radius release with inadequate rollback and incident containment.
Deleting legacy code immediately removes the reference implementation before edge cases are discovered.
Porting all plans and all services in parallel concentrates coordination risk and makes diagnosis of parity failures difficult.
Ongoing feature work may continue modifying the old path, causing the new implementation to become stale or forcing incompatible changes.
Create versioned, deterministic billing functions with immutable inputs and outputs, while retaining the legacy engine as a shadow oracle. Characterize representative and adversarial invoice scenarios first, migrate one bounded path at a time through adapters, compare outputs and side effects, and remove legacy code only after a defined parity and rollback gate. Represent simple plan terms in data, but preserve genuinely exceptional rules as explicit versioned strategies rather than forcing them into a universal abstraction.
Build a replay harness that runs the current billing path and billing-v2 on the same captured inputs for all 37 plans, especially the 11 grandfathered plans, covering upgrades, downgrades, cancellations, backdating, proration, taxes, and payment timing.
Any invoice difference attributable to rounding, amounts, line items, tax, payment allocation, or execution order falsifies the claim that a single cutover is safe; a completely clean replay would support proceeding, but still would not establish production cutover safety.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but place the user-ID service in a dedicated early canary with dual reporting and shadow enforcement, and do not deregister the legacy manager until multi-region validation and rollback are proven. Initially disable automatic reductions or set an explicit allocation floor for the user-ID service, then enable reductions only after monitoring shows accurate usage, expected headroom, and safe behavior under replication and failover. Keep the legacy manager available through the quarter until each service has completed an observation period and an independently tested rollback.
The new quota manager can accurately receive and attribute user-ID usage from every region without a reporting gap during handoff.
Allocation values and quota semantics are identical between the legacy and new managers, or any differences have been reconciled.
The user-ID database has enough write and authentication headroom for delayed, stale, or inconsistent usage data.
Automatic quota reduction can be delayed, overridden, or given a safe minimum allocation for at least the user-ID service.
A tested rollback can restore legacy enforcement without losing writes or creating divergent quota state.
Automatic reduction during the weeks-long grace period could still reject legitimate account writes when usage reporting is delayed or inaccurate, causing login or account-access failures.
Because the database replicates writes across regions, one region's stale or excessive usage report could trigger quota rejection in another region and produce global user-visible impact.
Registering the user-ID service in the new manager before shadow validation could make it subject to enforcement based on incomplete or differently interpreted telemetry.
Deregistering the legacy manager before proving rollback would remove the only known safe enforcement path and make recovery dependent on the new system's state.
A copied allocation may not account for migration traffic, failover, backlog, or growth, leaving insufficient capacity despite apparently matching configuration.
Migrate the user-ID service first under dual reporting and shadow evaluation, with reductions disabled and both managers receiving data. Compare decisions across regions, test quota rejection and recovery under simulated failover and stale telemetry, then perform a canary handoff with immediate rollback; migrate the remaining services in waves and enable reductions gradually only after verified headroom and stable telemetry.
In a staging replica of the user-ID database, verify whether the new manager supports a per-service hold on automatic allocation reduction; if it does, lower the simulated allocation below current usage and exercise writes and logins in each region.
If there is no reliable hold, override, or rollback mechanism, or if any reduced allocation causes legitimate writes or logins to be rejected in any region, the proposed unrestricted-reduction migration is unsafe.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform this as one transactional ALTER on the live 900M-row table. Introduce a new column through an online, staged migration with application-compatible dual writes, batched backfills, validation, and a brief final rename/swap coordinated with deployment; if amounts remain minor-unit integers, retain an integer/BIGINT representation and store the currency exponent separately rather than silently introducing four-decimal values.
Existing values must retain their current scale; converting 1234 cents directly to NUMERIC(19,4) yields 1234.0000, not 12.3400 KWD.
Current application and reporting SQL can tolerate changed column names and return types before all running pods are replaced.
The database storage and lock behavior is the same as PostgreSQL 15.
A maintenance window long enough to rewrite the table and roll back if necessary is actually available.
INTEGER-to-NUMERIC conversion will rewrite a roughly 410 GB table while holding a strong table lock, blocking reads and writes long enough to violate checkout SLO.
The pre-deploy migration renames the column before old pods are replaced, so active application versions referencing orders.amount can fail immediately.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes the value contract by allowing quarter-minor-unit precision rather than representing three-decimal currencies directly.
A long-running transaction increases replica lag, WAL/load impact, and rollback exposure; transactional atomicity does not make the rewrite online or bounded.
Prefer BIGINT minor units plus a currency code/exponent, which represents three-decimal currencies exactly without changing existing integer values. If a new database type is mandatory, add a new column, deploy backward-compatible dual writes, backfill in small committed batches, validate counts/checksums, and only then perform a short coordinated name swap.
On a production-sized staging clone, record pg_class.relfilenode for orders, run the proposed ALTER with lock and duration monitoring, and compare the relation file and maximum observed blocking time.
A changed relfilenode plus rewrite/lock time materially above the deployment or SLO budget falsifies the claim that an atomic transaction makes this deploy safe.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Streaming is the preferred direction, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. Upgrade through normal Raft-compatible rolling procedures, then enable it for a small production canary and expand by controlled cohorts with CPU, network, freshness, error-rate, and reconnect metrics plus explicit rollback thresholds. Retain blocking-query fallback until representative clients have survived a server-loss or rolling-restart test.
All production clients support the relevant 1.10 streaming backend and can be upgraded or configured without incompatible agent versions.
Streaming preserves health-update ordering, completeness, authorization, and freshness semantics for every consumer.
The 200-node staging result is representative of production polling rates, update rates, query diversity, and reconnect behavior.
A tested rollback to blocking queries is possible before the rollout reaches most clients.
Clients will not synchronize reconnection attempts after a server, network, or deployment event.
A fleet-wide configuration change exposes version skew or unsupported-client failures across all 18,000 nodes simultaneously.
A correlated disconnect or deploy triggers a reconnect storm that recreates or exceeds current server load.
Semantic differences silently deliver stale or incomplete health state, causing failed dependency resolution without obvious client errors.
The 200-node benchmark understates production query diversity or update fan-out, so staging gains fail to materialize.
An untested rollback becomes impractical after broad adoption, turning a client defect into a cluster-wide discovery outage.

Enable streaming for one small, representative production cohort, then terminate and restore its connections while comparing server CPU, network traffic, update freshness/completeness, client errors, and reconnect concurrency against a blocking-query control cohort.
The proposal is supported if CPU and network remain materially lower without correctness errors or harmful reconnect amplification; stale or missing updates, sustained CPU/network regression, client failures, or a reconnect storm falsifies the fleet-wide rollout as currently proposed.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the phased migration, but exempt the user-ID service from automatic quota reduction or configure a conservative floor based on measured peak usage, replication lag, and operational growth. Validate this behavior under write load before cutover, and retain legacy reporting or an equivalent rapid rollback path until the new system is proven stable.
The new quota system supports a per-service exemption, fixed floor, or equivalent override for automatic reduction.
Reported user-ID usage includes all distributed writes and is sufficiently current across regions.
Current allocations have enough headroom for normal peaks and cross-region replication lag.
An allocation reduction can be detected and reversed before production writes are rejected.
Automatic reduction below actual user-ID usage could cause login-related database writes to be rejected globally.
Regional reporting lag could make usage appear low, trigger reduction, and then expose the replicated database to quota-exceeded failures.
A single user-ID quota incident could prevent authentication or account updates for all users.
Deregistering from the legacy manager without a tested rollback may remove the recovery path needed during regional instability.
Migrate ordinary services in waves as proposed, but use a protected cutover for user-ID: maintain redundant reporting, disable or constrain reclaim for that service, test quota decisions with production-shaped load, and only then switch enforcement.
In a production-like test, drive user-ID usage to its current peak plus replication lag, allow the new system's grace period to elapse, and verify whether its allocation is reduced below actual usage and whether a subsequent cross-region write is rejected.
Any reduction below the protected usage floor, or any rejected write, falsifies the claim that enabling automatic reduction for user-ID is safe without an override.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Do not change the existing v1 wire type in place. Publish a versioned API that returns IDs as decimal JSON strings, keep v1 temporarily, and require lossless client parsing, regenerated SDK validation, and a communicated v1 deprecation date. This addresses the defect without breaking already deployed mobile versions or partner integrations during their update lag.
The proposal assumes changing an existing schema from integer to string is not a breaking change.
All strict or automatically generated v1 clients can tolerate a JSON string immediately.
Every partner uses regenerated SDKs rather than maintained custom clients.
Clients deserialize identifiers before any JavaScript Number conversion can occur.
The API has no version negotiation or compatibility mechanism capable of isolating the new representation.
Released iOS and Android versions expecting Int64 or Long may reject string values, causing order lookups and lists to fail.
Partner SDKs and generated code may continue parsing the old numeric schema until independently upgraded.
The two-week release deadline may be met while fixes remain absent from many self-updating clients.
A changelog entry cannot make an uncoordinated wire-format break backward compatible.
The new OpenAPI type may cause generators to emit String models, requiring broader client-code changes than ID formatting alone.
Add v2 endpoints with `id` encoded as a decimal JSON string and explicit examples/pattern, while preserving v1 responses temporarily. Update the deployed web client with lossless parsing, add mobile serializers that decode strings into Int64/Long, and publish tested SDK guidance plus a v1 deprecation timeline.
Run a contract test against one currently supported production v1 SDK or representative mobile model using the proposed string response.
If the existing client successfully decodes `"1234567890123456789"` without a release or configuration change, the immediate compatibility objection is weakened; a decode type error confirms the in-place change is unsafe.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep string serialization as the target representation, but do not change the existing v1 `id` field from number to string without a compatibility plan. Introduce the string representation through a new API version or an additive field such as `idString`, update the web client to consume it immediately, and deprecate numeric `id` only after mobile and partner migration thresholds are met.
Existing installed mobile applications can be forced to update before the response contract changes.
Swift Codable and Kotlin Moshi clients currently reject JSON strings when decoding `Int64` or `Long`.
Partner SDKs and integrations will not break when an integer field changes to a string.
API gateways, caches, and downstream systems preserve the distinction between numeric and string JSON values.
A two-week rollout can include consumer migration and backward-compatibility support.
The API change would cause decoding failures or incorrect behavior in existing iOS and Android applications.
The approximately 40 partner integrations could experience outages, failed requests, or corrupted identifiers.
Regenerating SDKs does not update already-deployed partner applications or independently implemented clients.
Changing a v1 field in place violates compatibility expectations and may permanently retain old application versions in app stores.
Publish the canonical string field in a new v2 contract while adding `idString` to v1 for an agreed deprecation window. Update first-party clients and SDKs to use the string field, monitor adoption, then remove or version the numeric field later; the Snowflake generation scheme itself remains unchanged.
Run an integration test that decodes a representative v1 response containing `"id":"1234567890123456789"` with the current Swift Codable and Kotlin Moshi models.
If both existing models decode the string successfully and all partner contract tests accept the type change, the stated backward-compatibility concern is reduced; any decoding exception or validation failure confirms that an immediate v1 break is unsafe.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform a single pre-deploy rename on this table. Use an expand/contract rollout: add the new scaled numeric column, deploy dual-write/backfill-compatible code, backfill in bounded online batches, switch reads, and only later remove or rename the old column. Choose NUMERIC(19,3), or explicitly document a four-unit scale, and verify migration duration, lock behavior, disk capacity, and application compatibility before release.
Existing INTEGER values are exact cent/minor-unit values and no lossy conversion is required.
The release can tolerate a substantial schema backfill and temporary additional storage.
Old application pods and any unupdated SQL consumers can continue accessing the original column during the migration.
PostgreSQL and the Django/database driver behavior for NUMERIC serialization has been tested end to end.
The reporting jobs can be switched atomically or are compatible with the expand/contract transition.
Changing INTEGER to NUMERIC on a roughly 900-million-row table is likely to rewrite the table and hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking night-time writes for far longer than a normal deployment window.
The migration runs before old pods are replaced, but the rename immediately removes the amount column those pods and potentially other consumers use, causing production read failures during the 25-minute rolling deployment.
A 410-GB indexed table plus rewrite/WAL and temporary objects may exhaust disk or overload streaming replicas, despite the migration role having no statement timeout.
NUMERIC(19,4) changes the storage and serialization contract and does not clearly match the required three-decimal minor-unit scale, creating financial and reporting compatibility risks.
Transactional DDL rollback does not make a long-running rewrite safe; lock acquisition, WAL, disk pressure, and replica impact can still block or disrupt checkout.
Use an online expand/contract migration: add a new NUMERIC(19,3) column without removing amount, deploy code that dual-writes and reads it, backfill existing rows in small indexed batches with rate and lock monitoring, validate totals, switch readers, and retire the old column in a later release.
On a production-sized staging clone, run the proposed ALTER under normal monitoring while an unchanged application pod executes a representative SELECT amount FROM orders query.
The ALTER holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock or exceeds the release window, and the unchanged pod fails with an undefined-column error after the rename; this directly falsifies the proposed rollout.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Retain the clean domain package, but replace the three-month big-bang cutover with staged, contract-tested migration. First capture current behavior, then migrate one representative rule family at a time through compatibility adapters and production shadow comparisons; delete legacy code only after all 37 plans and side effects have remained equivalent for a defined observation period.
All historical behavior can be represented by the proposed Plan, Subscription, Invoice, ProrationPolicy, and TaxRule model without service-specific exceptions.
Invoice equality is a sufficient equivalence criterion despite payments, tax calls, retries, notifications, and mutable context dependencies.
A three-person team can build, validate, coordinate merges, and cut over a 14k-LOC replacement while concurrent billing changes continue.
The five services can adopt the new package's API simultaneously without incompatible release or deployment requirements.
A clean rewrite can achieve parity before any new plan is added, despite only about 22% existing test coverage.
A missed proration, grandfathering, time-zone, or rounding behavior could produce incorrect customer invoices at cutover.
Side effects can duplicate or disappear even when generated invoice documents match.
Concurrent billing PRs will target code that is being replaced, increasing merge conflicts and making the final rollback boundary enormous.
Without characterization tests, the team may interpret legacy behavior incorrectly and codify it as a bug.
The old and new implementations will be maintained throughout the three-month period regardless of the stated goal to avoid two implementations.
Use a strangler migration around the same billing-core target: build immutable inputs and invoice golden tests, extract proration first behind an adapter, shadow invoices without external side effects, then migrate tax, payment, invoicing, subscriptions, and notifications incrementally. Preserve legacy adapters for exceptional plans and remove old paths only after parity and operational rollback criteria are met.
Time-box a model spike by encoding the three most irregular grandfathered plans, including their proration and tax cases, and compare their outputs against captured legacy invoices across start, upgrade, downgrade, cancellation, and mid-cycle changes.
If any legacy behavior cannot be expressed without service conditionals, ad hoc BillingContext flags, or manual special cases—or if matching outputs requires more than roughly one day of adaptation—the proposed clean model is not a general replacement and the big-bang plan should be rejected.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Retain wave migration, but enable automatic reduction only after establishing a safety floor for user-ID and validating usage-decision parity between managers. Migrate user-ID last, switch enforcement atomically where possible, and require tested rollback before deregistering any service from the legacy manager.
The new system can accurately receive current user-ID allocations and usage reports from every region.
The grace period is long enough to detect sustained underuse before reductions become harmful, rather than merely delaying reduction by a fixed number of weeks.
User-ID has enough allocation headroom for account-data growth, replication metadata, reporting lag, and peak demand.
Deregistering a service from the legacy manager also makes the new manager authoritative without conflicting enforcement.
Quota-manager outages and stale decisions will not block user-ID database writes.
Automatic reduction could lower user-ID allocation below live or near-term storage demand, causing rejected account writes and replicated login-related impact.
Stale or out-of-order usage data could trigger an incorrect reduction or produce inconsistent enforcement.
A cutover gap or dual-authority conflict could cause nondeterministic quota decisions.
A new-system outage could block user-ID writes if enforcement fails closed.
Operational dashboards could look correct while regional enforcement or replication behavior remains unsafe.
Use the proposed waves with a user-ID exception: configure a protected minimum allocation or temporarily disable automatic reduction for user-ID, while retaining it for other services. Before each cutover, shadow or compare usage and enforcement decisions, then atomically transfer authority with rollback tested under concurrent regional writes.
Query historical user-ID usage by region and compare maximum recent usage plus observed growth against its copied allocation through the full reduction grace period.
If even peak-plus-projected-growth usage approaches the copied allocation during the grace period, the claim that weeks of buffer make universal automatic reduction safe is falsified and user-ID requires a floor or exemption.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver rollout, but do not make global blocking conditional only on aggregate match volume. Require bounded PCRE evaluation (complexity limits and a per-rule CPU/time budget), production-like load validation, and an automated rollback based on proxy latency, error rate, and false-positive indicators. Use a short 1% blocking canary with monitoring before global blocking, and aggregate or sample log-mode matches rather than performing unbounded per-request logging; this can still complete within the one-hour objective.
The CI corpus and benign-request set provide sufficiently representative coverage for newly disclosed attacks.
Quicksilver propagation and rule activation are atomic and fail-safe across all proxies and regions.
The WAF engine can enforce per-rule evaluation limits and disable a rule without taking down the proxy.
There is sufficient CPU headroom to evaluate the new rule on every request during log mode.
A reliable, low-latency signal exists for distinguishing attack matches from false positives.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, increase request latency, or cause an outage even when it does not block requests.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic globally after only ten minutes of insufficiently targeted monitoring.
Attackers could deliberately generate high match volume, making log mode itself expensive or obscuring benign false positives.
Inconsistent Quicksilver updates could leave some machines blocking while others only log, complicating incident response.
CI payload coverage may miss the disclosed exploit variant, allowing the rule to be published without detecting the actual attack.

Run a production-like peak-load benchmark with the candidate rule enabled in log mode on the proxy, comparing CPU utilization, p95/p99 latency, request errors, and match-processing cost against the same workload without the rule.
The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation materially reduces available CPU or violates the proxy's latency/error SLOs, or if match volume causes unsafe logging overhead; negligible overhead and stable latency support proceeding with the expedited path.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
The mutex is only process-local, so with 4-12 Kubernetes replicas concurrent requests for the same coupon can enter the critical section independently and both pass the redeemedAt check. Replace it with an atomic database claim (conditional update or transaction) backed by a coupon redemption state and payment idempotency/reconciliation; keep the concurrency test, but run it across multiple application processes or replicas.
All redemption requests are routed through the same Node.js process, which is false for the stated HPA deployment unless the Service or traffic policy guarantees it.
The mutex remains held until the coupon update completes, including successful charge and database update.
The payment provider can safely handle retries, including requests whose prior result is unknown.
Coupon code and order association have database-enforced uniqueness.
Coupon state can represent pending or reserved redemption, not only redeemedAt.
Two replicas can both read an unredeemed coupon, both charge orders, and both update the coupon.
A process crash or pod termination after charging but before update leaves an externally paid order with a redeemable coupon.
A charge timeout may trigger a retry that charges again unless the payment request is idempotent.
The in-memory Map provides no correctness across restarts, pod eviction, or multiple Node.js workers.
A test using two concurrent calls in one process can pass while the production multi-replica race remains.
Use an atomic Postgres claim such as updateMany({ where: { code, status: "AVAILABLE", redeemedAt: null }, data: { status: "PENDING", orderId, reservedAt } }) and require exactly one affected row. Charge through a provider idempotency key derived from the order, then transition to REDEEMED; retries and reconciliation must first inspect the existing pending redemption and provider status. Add a unique constraint and expiration/recovery handling for abandoned reservations.
Run two redemption requests for the same unused coupon simultaneously through separate application processes or two Kubernetes replicas, using distinct orders, and record charge and database results.
If both requests succeed, the proposed process-local mutex is disproven; if exactly one claim succeeds, that validates the race fix only if the test also exercises a crash or timeout between charge and finalization.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain immediate global shadow deployment, but require hard rule evaluation budgets, payload-variant verification, representative canary enforcement, automated health/false-positive gates, and a tested global kill switch before promotion. Treat ten minutes as a minimum evidence window rather than an automatic promotion timer, and prioritize proven high-confidence signatures for blocking within minutes.
CI’s benign corpus represents production traffic and input encodings closely enough to prevent broad false positives.
Quicksilver can activate and later roll back rules globally within minutes with bounded version skew.
The ten-minute log period provides sufficiently complete, timely, representative match and latency telemetry.
New rules have bounded worst-case PCRE execution under concurrent peak load.
A coherent log-to-block transition and emergency rollback mechanism already exists or will be added.
A pathological PCRE or high-match-volume rule consumes proxy CPU and degrades TLS and HTTP service for every customer at that PoP.
The rule logs rather than blocks during the initial window, or blocks before all machines are ready, leaving material exposure to the disclosed attack.
Rare benign requests absent from CI are blocked after a superficially normal ten-minute match-volume result.
Quicksilver skew or a failed transition produces partial protection or inconsistent enforcement for longer than the objective permits.
The signature matches the test payload but misses common encodings, alternate syntaxes, or actual exploit variants.
Use a risk-tiered emergency pipeline: shadow deploy globally, enforce narrowly scoped high-confidence signatures immediately or after very short canaries, and delay uncertain or CPU-heavy rules until broader validation. Promote only after automated checks on attack matches, benign match deltas, evaluation time, proxy saturation, and rollout completeness, with automatic global rollback.
Run every eligible emergency rule in the existing CI harness against its payload variants, the benign corpus, and generated pathological inputs under representative peak concurrency, reporting incremental per-request evaluation time and worst-case completion time.
The design is falsified if any rule that would pass the current CI corpus exceeds the documented per-request CPU/time budget, can exhibit unbounded backtracking, or blocks any benign sample. Results showing bounded cost and zero benign matches would support the shadow-to-block mechanism, though production representativeness and rollout controls would still need validation.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain an expedited path, but require representative canary/shadow validation, regex execution-cost limits, benign-traffic false-positive thresholds, and an automatically enforced global rollback before blocking. Publish first in log mode with per-rule match/error/latency telemetry, then promote only after a defined observation window; make block activation and rollback atomic, versioned, and audited.
The CI corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives and catastrophic backtracking.
Log-mode evaluation has bounded CPU and latency impact despite running on every request.
Quicksilver propagation is strongly consistent enough to prevent machines from enforcing different rule versions during activation.
A ten-minute observation window is sufficient to expose false positives and performance degradation.
Operators can reliably identify and disable a bad rule globally within minutes.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic across all PoPs after only ten minutes of observation.
A pathological PCRE pattern could consume substantial proxy CPU, causing latency spikes, outages, or TLS/HTTP starvation even in log mode.
Incomplete, delayed, or partially failed configuration propagation could produce inconsistent enforcement and an unreliably reversible incident.
Low attack volume or an unrepresentative log sample could permit a harmful rule to be promoted prematurely.
The proposed path lacks an explicit emergency kill switch, automated rollback, version pinning, and promotion criteria.
Implement a risk-tiered fast lane: validate the rule against both attack and benign corpora, enforce static and runtime regex cost limits, shadow it on a small representative canary, then propagate globally in log mode with automated thresholds. Promote to block only after the canary and global observation pass, while providing a tested one-action global rollback.
Run the candidate rule in shadow mode on a representative production PoP while replaying the benign corpus and peak-shaped request load, comparing p99 latency, CPU, error rate, and benign matches against the same traffic without the rule.
Any material p99/CPU increase, request errors, or benign matches would falsify the claim that immediate global log-mode deployment is safe; negligible impact and zero benign matches would support proceeding to a controlled rollout.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table whose cleanup is demonstrably hours long. Instead, retain autovacuum, tune per-table trigger and cost-delay settings to smooth maintenance I/O, and investigate batching bulk deletes and reducing unnecessary index maintenance. Instrument and trial these changes before considering partitioning for longer-term retention redesign.
Dead-tuple production is low enough for one Sunday vacuum to keep pace with both inserts and expired-row deletes.
That vacuum can scan the entire table, clean indexes, and update statistics before Sunday traffic resumes.
No long-running transactions, prepared transactions, or other blockers will delay dead-row cleanup.
A full-table vacuum at 02:00 will not overlap bulk deletes or cause WAL, checkpoint, or storage-I/O saturation.
Bloat and transaction-age metrics remain safe despite monitoring only through Grafana graphs.
Dead tuples may accumulate rapidly enough for visibility, index, planner, or XID-wraparound problems to develop before or during weekly maintenance.
If vacuum exceeds the low-traffic window, its I/O will move into business hours and produce the same or larger latency spikes.
Long-running transactions can make the weekly vacuum ineffective and prevent vacuum-only data from being removable.
Bulk deletes may run concurrently with the scheduled vacuum, invalidating the assumption that 02:00 is consistently available.
A missed or failed cron invocation leaves the table without autovacuum fallback, creating an operational single point of failure.
Tune events-specific autovacuum thresholds and vacuum_cost_delay so cleanup is distributed predictably rather than eliminating it. Verify that the autovacuum worker can keep up with dead-tuple production; also reduce delete and index-maintenance work before evaluating partitioning as a structural solution.
During one representative business cycle, record pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze, autovacuum log start/finish times, XID age, and disk I/O; also time a manual VACUUM ANALYZE outside the proposed low-traffic window.
The probe falsifies the proposal if manual vacuum requires materially more than the available low-traffic window or leaves n_dead_tup and XID age trending upward between runs. It supports the premise only if ordinary autovacuum is consistently falling behind, the full vacuum reliably finishes in the window, and it is the dominant source of write-latency spikes.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Keep the batched deletion objective, but add authoritative ID/type and parent-site validation, deduplication, inventory reconciliation, and an independently verified completion report. Test a small canary cohort and rollback/backup restoration before expanding to permanent deletion; use idempotent retries and explicit handling of partial failures and rate limits.
The product-team list is complete, current, and contains only add-on installation IDs.
The deletion API exposes or can be joined to authoritative object type and site ownership data.
Permanent deletion is isolated to the retired add-on and does not cascade into other products or the site.
The API handles duplicate or repeated deletion requests safely and reports failures reliably enough for reconciliation.
A tested site-by-site backup restore can recover a wrongly deleted site before the backend shutdown.
A 24-character site ID or another object ID is permanently purged because the batch has no type verification.
The supplied list is stale or incomplete, leaving installations behind or causing unrelated deletions.
Undisclosed dependencies cause removal of shared data belonging to other products.
Timeouts, partial failures, pagination, or rate limits cause the job to report incomplete success.
Weekend execution delays detection until after business impact, with no tested recovery path.
Use a preflight-and-cohort process: resolve and type-check IDs, reconcile them against an authoritative installation inventory, test backup restoration and deletion scope, permanently delete a small canary cohort, verify affected sites and remaining objects, then expand with monitoring and reconciliation.
Run a non-destructive or isolated test that submits a known site ID and a known add-on installation ID to the deletion workflow, with a type-validation check before any permanent call; inspect the recorded object type, parent site, and deletion scope.
If the workflow cannot reliably distinguish the two IDs or shows that deleting an installation also removes the site or other-product data, the proposed permanent batch process is unsafe and must not run.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but do not enable automatic quota reduction for the user-ID service until a global peak-load test demonstrates that its allocation has sufficient headroom for the entire reduction and regional replication delay window. Make manager cutover explicit and reversible to avoid overlapping enforcement or an enforcement gap, and retain a protected allocation and tested rollback path for user-ID throughout migration.
Copied allocations include enough capacity for user-ID growth and traffic spikes.
Usage reports are accurate, timely, and consistent across regions.
Quota decisions propagate to every database replica before writes are evaluated.
Registration and deregistration cannot create dual authority or an enforcement gap.
The stated grace period includes all propagation, scheduling, and regional failover delays.
Automatic reduction could cause user-ID database writes to be rejected during normal or peak login traffic.
A stale or region-specific usage report could trigger an unsafe quota reduction.
Concurrent registration in both managers could produce conflicting enforcement decisions.
A gap during deregistration could leave user-ID writes without quota enforcement.
Insufficient regional consistency could allow the global allocation to be exceeded before enforcement converges.
Migrate noncritical services in waves, but place user-ID in shadow mode first and use a fixed, protected allocation for its initial cutover. Enable automatic reduction only after production-scale testing across regions establishes safe headroom, then increase usage or allocation alerts before each reduction.
Run a production-scale user-ID write test against the new system using current and forecast peak traffic, exercising all regional replicas with realistic propagation delay and one failover.
Any legitimate account create or update is rejected, any replica observes a different enforcement state, or projected usage approaches the copied allocation before the earliest possible reduction confirms the proposal is unsafe as written.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Replace Redis Pub/Sub with Redis Streams and consumer groups, or retain and operationalize RabbitMQ if durable delivery is required. Stage the change by job type, preserve acknowledgements, retries, idempotency, and dead-letter handling, and validate behavior during worker restarts and Redis failover before migration.
The proposal silently assumes Redis Pub/Sub subscribers are continuously connected and can tolerate messages being dropped during disconnects or restarts.
It assumes the existing worker retry wrapper can compensate for messages that were never delivered, which it cannot.
It assumes Pub/Sub's throughput advantage matters more than delivery guarantees for payment webhooks and fulfilment-triggering jobs.
It assumes running both paths for a week provides safe reconciliation, but no duplicate-side-effect or cutover strategy is specified.
Messages published while a worker is disconnected, restarting, or deploying are lost permanently, potentially losing payment updates or fulfilment triggers.
Multiple worker replicas subscribing to the same channel can produce unintended fan-out or duplicate processing, depending on subscription topology.
A Redis restart, failover, or AOF recovery event can cause unavailability and loss of in-flight dispatch state.
The worker retry wrapper may repeatedly execute side effects after failures, while still offering no recovery for undelivered jobs.
Dual-running RabbitMQ and Pub/Sub can generate duplicate business actions and make the eventual cutover unverifiable.
Use Redis Streams with consumer groups, explicit acknowledgements, pending-entry recovery, bounded retention, and an idempotent DLQ/retry process. If that still changes operational burden too much, improve and automate the existing RabbitMQ setup rather than adopting lossy Pub/Sub.
In a non-production test, subscribe one worker to a dedicated Redis Pub/Sub channel, publish a fixed sequence of uniquely identified jobs, kill and restart the subscriber during delivery, then count uniquely processed jobs after the subscriber reconnects.
Any published but unprocessed job after the worker restart falsifies the proposal's suitability for durable job dispatch; zero loss only under continuously connected, non-failing conditions would not establish production safety.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Keep the batch-job direction, but do not execute permanent deletion from an unqualified ID list. First perform a read-only inventory proving every ID is an active Insight Legacy installation, capture backups or export snapshots, use a canary and idempotent checkpoints, and reconcile results; pause timing and on-call monitoring alone are insufficient.
The product list is complete, current, and contains only add-on-installation IDs.
The API can permanently delete the installation without cascading to the site or other products.
HTTP success means the intended deletion is complete and the backend no longer serves legacy data.
A backup or other recovery mechanism is available before deletion, even though the proposal does not mention it.
The 30-ID batch and 2-second pause respect rate limits and do not create timeout or retry ambiguity.
A wrong ID permanently deletes a site or product, with recovery requiring site-by-site backup restoration.
A valid installation deletion may cascade or otherwise remove data belonging to other products.
Timeout, rate limiting, or partial failure can leave the job with an unknown deletion state; retries may repeat or obscure destructive actions.
The backend may be shut down before asynchronous deletion, residual references, or legacy jobs are actually removed.
Running permanently over a weekend provides no rollback window and does not protect against incorrect scope.
Use soft deletion for the validated legacy installations, reconcile them during the 14-day restore window, then permanently purge only the reconciled set. If the deadline makes that infeasible, retain permanent mode but add authoritative type/site validation, backup verification, canaries, explicit idempotency and failure handling, and post-deletion reconciliation.
Perform a read-only metadata lookup for every supplied ID, including object type, containing site/customer, product/add-on identity, and deletion eligibility; then test one canary in a non-production or disposable environment and inspect the affected site's object inventory.
The approach is falsified if any ID is not uniquely an active Insight Legacy installation, if the canary removes or changes any non-legacy object/data, or if a successful API response does not produce complete, queryable deletion before backend shutdown.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Do not enable unrestricted promotion of the West replica under asynchronous replication. Restrict automatic recovery to a fenced, recently verified East replica, enable semi-synchronous replication where supported, and explicitly integrate Orchestrator recovery with Consul plus stale-primary fencing. Permit West promotion only as an operator-approved, acknowledged-data-loss procedure; Raft consensus protects Orchestrator decisions but does not make asynchronous MySQL replication current or prevent a database split brain.
An East replica normally remains available when the East primary host fails, which is not stated.
Orchestrator is configured with a safe promotion candidate, fencing, recovery timeouts, and Consul hooks for every relevant cluster.
The application can route writes to a West-promoted primary over the existing network and tolerate approximately 60 ms plus additional connection latency.
Promoting an asynchronously replicated West node without losing acknowledged writes is acceptable, despite replication lag.
Consul updates and application client behavior will reliably converge within the one-minute objective.
West promotion can lose committed writes because asynchronous replication may not have received them; choosing the apparently most advanced replica does not eliminate this.
A network partition or stalled primary can leave the old primary accepting writes after promotion unless storage/network fencing is enforced; Orchestrator Raft quorum does not fence MySQL.
Promoting a West node while application servers remain in East may create connectivity, latency, DNS/Consul propagation, and write-availability failures.
Applying automated recovery to all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can trigger simultaneous or incorrect promotions.
A 30-second detection threshold does not guarantee recovery under one minute after detection, topology repair, Consul propagation, and application reconnection.
Use Orchestrator automation only for a pre-approved East-local replica, configure semi-synchronous replication for East replicas, fence the failed primary before promotion, and have Consul publish a versioned primary endpoint. Keep West as an explicitly operator-invoked disaster-recovery path with documented possible data loss.
During sustained writes to the East primary, record `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` on the West replica and execute a controlled primary failure followed by West promotion; compare acknowledged write IDs with rows present on the promoted replica.
If any acknowledged write is absent on the promoted West replica, or if East applications cannot route and commit writes to it within one minute, the proposed cross-region automated promotion fails the stated safety/availability objective.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not execute the direct type alteration and rename in the pre-deploy job. Replace it with a phased expand/dual-write/backfill/switch/contract rollout, using an explicitly defined three-decimal representation and a compatibility window; enable the new currencies only after reconciliation and replica-lag validation.
The existing integer values can be interpreted using a persisted, reliable currency code.
The required maximum precision is three decimal places, not four.
All old and new code, jobs, and queries can tolerate a staged schema transition.
The release environment can provide enough disk and WAL capacity for a new column and batched backfill.
There is a rollback path and operational monitoring for replication lag, lock waits, and data mismatches.
PostgreSQL may rewrite the 900M-row table and hold a strong lock during ALTER TABLE, blocking the 1,200 writes/s peak and likely violating checkout SLO.
The same-migration rename breaks pods, reporting jobs, exports, ETL, and any raw SQL still referencing orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) creates an undocumented four-decimal contract and does not solve how existing integers map to major or minor units for each currency.
A full historical conversion may misinterpret legacy amounts, corrupt totals, or produce inconsistent values across paths.
Generating substantial WAL and I/O can cause replica lag, storage pressure, and rollback difficulty before the new application is available.
Use an expand-and-contract migration: add a new fixed-scale representation (preferably BIGINT with a documented currency-specific scale, or NUMERIC(19,3) if the API stores major units), deploy dual reads/writes, backfill in rate-limited batches, reconcile totals, switch reports and checkout, then remove the old column after the compatibility window. This avoids an unbounded table rewrite in the release job and makes rollback possible.
On a representative staging clone, run the proposed ALTER with a short lock_timeout and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL generation, and replication lag.
If it cannot acquire the lock promptly or produces prolonged strong-lock blocking, substantial WAL, or unacceptable replica lag, the proposed one-migration approach is disproven for this release; even successful completion would still not remove its mixed-version rename risk.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator as the topology manager, but do not enable unconditional promotion of the most up-to-date replica across regions. Restrict automation to proven candidates, add explicit lag and reachability checks, enforce fencing of the old primary, and make East-local promotion the normal path with West promotion reserved for a tested East outage procedure. Validate the complete detection-to-write-recovery duration and data-loss behavior under continuous writes before declaring the one-minute objective met.
A candidate with the highest available replication position contains every acknowledged write required by the application.
Orchestrator can safely classify host failure without allowing the old primary to continue accepting writes after promotion.
East-only Rails clients can reach and tolerate a West primary through the discovery and connection-reconnection path.
Thirty seconds plus promotion, topology propagation, and application reconnection consistently fits inside the one-minute objective.
Pseudo-GTID and Orchestrator topology metadata provide reliable candidate ordering but sufficient promotion safety.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can permanently lose committed transactions, despite Raft consensus protecting the orchestration decision itself.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, creating split brain, divergent transactions, and potential corruption or unrecoverable conflicts.
Promoting a West replica may exceed the objective or degrade write latency and connection behavior for East-only application servers.
Consul updates or cached Rails connections may direct some applications to stale or changing endpoints during failover, causing failed or retried writes.
A Raft quorum outage can prevent automated promotion precisely when the primary is unavailable, leaving the manual runbook necessary.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, recorded writes while killing the East primary, then measure transaction success, whether any acknowledged write is absent from the promoted replica, old-primary writability, and time until all applications are writing to the new primary.
A complete pass requires zero acknowledged-write loss, inability of the old primary to accept writes, and end-to-end write recovery under 60 seconds. Any acknowledged-write loss, split-brain writes, or recovery above one minute falsifies the proposal as written.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not immediately permanently delete IDs from an unvalidated generic list. Reconcile and type-check every installation, test cascade behavior, migrate in reversible site cohorts, verify site and unrelated-product integrity, then permanently delete validated installations with retries, deadline tracking, and alerting.
The product team's list is complete, current, duplicate-free, and contains only add-on installation IDs.
The generic API internally identifies each object by type rather than treating any 24-character value as deletable.
Permanent installation deletion has no destructive side effects on sites or other products.
A successful HTTP response reliably represents deletion of every requested ID.
Batching, pausing, and on-call monitoring can complete the purge before backend shutdown.
A site or product ID in the list could cause irreversible deletion of the entire site or unrelated data.
Undocumented cascading could damage other products even when the listed ID is correctly typed.
Partial failures could be missed, leaving installations active during backend shutdown.
A stale or incorrect list could delete installations that should be retained or fail to remove all required ones.
The irreversible job could begin without a tested rollback path or evidence that other product data remains intact.
Use a phased migration: obtain typed metadata for every supplied ID, reconcile counts per site, and first use mark mode or a typed add-on removal operation on a small cohort. Verify that only the legacy installation is affected, then permanently delete that cohort; expand gradually while monitoring per-ID results, unrelated-product integrity, completion time, and errors. Reserve irreversible deletion for reconciled IDs and establish a final cutoff before month-end.
On a disposable site containing Insight Legacy plus unrelated products, record typed metadata for the site, product, and installation IDs; call DELETE with the installation ID in permanent mode, then query all three objects and their site data.
The probe supports the proposal only if the API confirms the input is an add-on installation, the installation is permanently removed, the site and unrelated product remain unchanged, and the response clearly reports per-ID success. Any site/product deletion, ambiguous typing, or unreliable outcome falsifies the proposed direct permanent-deletion approach.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not perform the direct ALTER-and-rename migration. Use an expand-and-contract rollout: add a compatible representation, deploy readers/writers and all three reports for backward compatibility, backfill and reconcile in bounded batches, then switch and remove the legacy field. Define the conversion explicitly—reinterpreting existing cents as four-decimal values would change their meaning unless values are multiplied appropriately.
Existing orders.amount values are interpreted as cents and can be converted to the target three-decimal representation without changing business totals.
The target representation is actually three decimal places; NUMERIC(19,4) silently introduces a fourth precision choice.
The ALTER can complete without blocking production traffic beyond the release and SLO constraints.
No consumers beyond the identified application code and three reporting jobs access orders.amount.
The migration and application rollback can be coordinated despite the 25-minute rolling deployment.
PostgreSQL can rewrite the roughly 900M-row table and hold an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes while the pre-deploy job runs.
The rename is visible before old pods are replaced, causing currently running code and any unupdated consumers to fail or read the wrong field.
A long rewrite can generate substantial WAL and I/O, cause streaming-replica lag, and exhaust disk or deployment capacity.
Treating existing cents as NUMERIC(19,4) without conversion could produce values 100 times larger than the intended amount.
The migration may exceed the release window; transactional DDL prevents partial schema changes but does not make the operation online.
Prefer an expand-and-contract migration, ideally retaining efficient integer minor units with explicit currency scale, or adding a NUMERIC target column without removing the old column. Deploy compatible dual-read/write code, backfill with bounded batches while handling concurrent updates, validate totals and nullability, migrate the three reports, and only then retire the legacy column. This avoids an unbounded blocking rewrite and provides a rollback window.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed ALTER under a representative write workload and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL volume, and statement behavior; also insert a legacy value such as 100 and verify the intended converted result.
If ALTER requires a full rewrite and blocks normal reads or writes materially beyond the deployment/SLO budget, the proposal is unsafe; if value 100 is not explicitly converted to the intended three-decimal amount, the proposed type change is semantically wrong.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reassignment direction, but do not enable clients at launch day until the new RLP path is characterized, security/correctness tested, and load-tested. Deploy an attested compatible build to all eight routers before setting the bit, then use a centrally controlled, gradual traffic cohort with a kill switch and explicit in-flight-order rollback semantics. Do not remove the legacy Power Peg implementation until compatibility and archival behavior have been verified.
No current or archived client, gateway, or protocol component can set or interpret the legacy bit.
The existing Power Peg behavior can be safely replaced by the required RLP behavior without changing the binary layout or message semantics.
All eight production routers can be verified as running the same compatible build before any client sets the bit.
Centralized traffic control and an immediately enforceable per-cohort kill switch are available.
Orders already in flight, retries, duplicates, rejects, and cancels have defined behavior when the flag is disabled.
A dormant or removed seven-year-old path may contain routing, security, performance, or rejection defects that only appear under production load.
Activating clients immediately while router deployment is mixed or incomplete can misroute orders, rejects, or fills.
Traffic-zero observations do not exclude archived clients, scheduled jobs, configuration-based writers, or future compatibility clients.
Removing Power Peg semantics in the same release eliminates rollback and auditability if RLP behavior is incorrect.
Without routing-quality, fill, reject, latency, and dislocation monitoring, a harmful change could be mistaken for a successful launch.

Perform a repository, gateway, client, configuration, and archived-protocol search for every writer, reader, and semantic definition of the legacy bit, then run a compatibility test comparing the old Power Peg path with the new RLP path.
Any additional writer/reader or non-equivalent routing behavior falsifies the claim that the bit is safely and unambiguously reusable; if none exists and the behavioral comparison passes, it supports the direction but still does not validate production rollout.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Keep the streaming direction, but replace the single fleet-wide rollout with a small representative canary followed by staged cohort expansion. Before expansion, verify semantic equivalence, freshness and ordering, reconnect/error behavior, fallback capacity, and end-to-end CPU, network, memory, Raft, and client resource impact; retain blocking-query fallback and define rollback thresholds.
All production client versions, libraries, platforms, and service implementations support Consul 1.10 streaming without changing dependency or health-data semantics.
The staging 200-node test represents production update rates, query patterns, reconnects, and failure behavior rather than only demonstrating a CPU reduction.
The five-server cluster has sufficient spare capacity for streaming, reconnects, and any temporary blocking-query fallback during rollback.
Streaming will not materially increase Raft commits, memory, network traffic, or client CPU in production.
A six-week canary and staged rollout can complete without rushing compatibility or operational validation.
A client-library or platform incompatibility could silently deliver stale, incomplete, or differently ordered health data after fleet-wide activation.
Reconnect storms could overload the five voting servers or increase Raft and network load even while server CPU falls.
Rolling back or falling back to blocking queries could create a traffic surge and service-discovery disruption.
The observed 60% staging CPU reduction may not hold under production update rates, concurrency, or network and memory costs.
A single rollout provides little isolation or opportunity to detect service-specific failures before affecting all services.
Use a phased migration: canary a small representative set, measure correctness and end-to-end resource impact under load, then expand by service or node cohort while retaining blocking-query support and explicit rollback thresholds.
Run one representative production-like load test in staging with both protocols, including health updates, client reconnects, and fallback, then compare semantic correctness and server, network, Raft, and client metrics.
The proposal is falsified if streaming changes health-data freshness, completeness, or ordering, increases errors or reconnect load, or fails to reduce end-to-end cost after accounting for network, memory, Raft, and client overhead; a clean result with sustained CPU savings supports staged expansion.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Retain Orchestrator automated recovery, but require reliable primary fencing, explicitly define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, and verify atomic Consul endpoint replacement with client reconnection. Do not enable this blindly for all clusters or claim Raft makes failover safe: Raft protects topology decisions, not MySQL writes or replication consistency.
A failed old primary is made read-only or reliably fenced before another replica is promoted, including during network partitions.
Applications resolve the writable endpoint through Consul and reconnect after its value changes without retaining independent connections to the old primary.
Orchestrator selects a candidate with acceptable replication lag, and detection, promotion, discovery propagation, and reconnection consistently complete within the remaining time after the 30-second threshold.
Some acknowledged writes may be lost under asynchronous replication, or the deployment will add a replication mechanism that provides the required durability.
The promoted replica and its dependent systems can handle production write traffic from East, including approximately 60 ms cross-region latency.
