A network partition can leave the old primary accepting writes while Orchestrator promotes another node, causing split brain and irreversible divergence.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft quorum does not establish that the candidate contains the latest committed write.
The 30-second detection threshold leaves only about 30 seconds for promotion, Consul propagation, connection draining, and application reconnection, making the under-one-minute objective fragile.
Selecting a West replica 'regardless of region' may unnecessarily move writes across 60 ms even when a sufficiently current East replica is available.
Blind enablement across clusters can promote unsafe candidates or update unsupported discovery integrations, and pseudo-GTID does not remove the need to validate binlog-position and replication semantics.
Use Orchestrator as the recovery coordinator, but add an explicit fencing mechanism for every possible primary, configure and test region-aware candidate eligibility against measured replica lag, and route clients through a Consul-managed logical primary endpoint that switches atomically and supports fast connection refresh. Validate an explicit RPO and use native MySQL 5.7 GTID where applicable rather than treating pseudo-GTID as a durability mechanism.
In staging, continuously write committed, uniquely numbered rows through the current primary; isolate that primary from Orchestrator and replicas while leaving it reachable by the application, trigger automated recovery, then continue writing to the old endpoint.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary still accepts committed writes after another node is promoted, or if recovery plus Consul/client convergence exceeds 60 seconds. It is supported only if fencing prevents old-primary writes and the measured convergence meets the objective.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Keep the Consul 1.10 and streaming direction, but do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling order, enable streaming for a small production-representative canary, define CPU/network/freshness/error thresholds, and expand only after observing a sustained benefit. Document and test client rollback and ensure mixed-version behavior is understood before broader deployment.
The 200-node staging result predicts production CPU, network, memory, and freshness behavior at fleet scale.
All deployed service-discovery clients and libraries support the Consul 1.10 streaming backend and the proposed configuration.
A supported mixed-version rolling upgrade preserves health, KV, and lock availability.
Streaming maintains required freshness, ordering, and authorization semantics.
The production rollout has enough time and operational capacity for canarying, monitoring, and rollback.
A fleet-wide flag change could create reconnect or watch storms, excessive client load, or stale discovery for services with no fallback.
The 200-node test could materially overestimate savings because production fan-in, service churn, or duplicate query patterns differ.
Incompatible or partially upgraded clients could silently retain blocking queries or fall back inconsistently.
A server or client regression could disrupt discovery, KV configuration, or locks across the entire fleet.
The measured 60% server CPU reduction could be offset by increased network traffic, client CPU, memory pressure, or Raft instability.
Use a staged rollout with a production-representative canary rather than an all-at-once enablement. Add immediate instrumentation and selectively reduce redundant blocking-query subscriptions if the canary does not achieve the required aggregate benefit.
Run a production-like staging benchmark using the actual service count, client versions, query fan-in, update churn, reconnect pattern, and representative failure scenarios; compare streaming with the current blocking queries and record server CPU, network bytes, client CPU/memory, freshness latency, errors, and reconnect amplification.
The proposal is supported only if streaming produces a sustained, material reduction in total server load without violating freshness or stability thresholds and with documented client/rollback compatibility; materially smaller savings, increased amplification, or correctness failures falsify the rollout assumption.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain expedited propagation, but replace the unconditional 10-minute global log window with a compressed, observable rollout: begin in log mode, promote through small canaries, and reach global block within the one-hour objective only if false-positive and latency thresholds remain healthy. Require per-rule automatic rollback, confirm propagation completeness, and enforce regex complexity, evaluation-time, and CPU-budget limits before activation.
Quicksilver propagation and activation are atomic enough that no machine remains indefinitely on the old rule version.
Match counts can be attributed to each rule and monitored with sufficiently low latency to trigger rollback.
A ten-minute observation period contains traffic representative enough to expose likely false positives.
Candidate PCREs cannot cause pathological backtracking or materially increase peak CPU.
Emergency blocking and rollback do not depend on another multi-day configuration release process.
A false positive could block legitimate customer traffic globally after the log window.
Aggregate match volume can conceal false positives confined to a particular PoP, tenant, endpoint, or low-traffic region.
A computationally expensive regex could exhaust proxy CPU and cause an edge-wide availability incident.
Delayed or partial propagation could leave some machines unprotected or produce inconsistent enforcement.
The CI payload corpus may validate attack recall without adequately testing benign production traffic.

Replay a representative, anonymized production request trace against the candidate rule in shadow mode and compare benign matches and evaluation cost with the current ruleset.
Any benign matches above the team's false-positive tolerance, or material p95/p99 latency or CPU regression, would falsify the safety of immediate global promotion; negligible differences would support the expedited path.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Retain the clean billing-core direction, but replace the three-month big-bang rewrite with incremental adoption behind compatibility-tested interfaces. First freeze current invoice behavior with characterization tests and production-derived fixtures, then migrate one bounded billing capability at a time while continuously comparing legacy and new results before deleting legacy code.
The team can obtain representative historical billing inputs and expected invoice outputs for all 37 plans.
Existing behavior can be characterized sufficiently despite low happy-path coverage and six years of implicit proration rules.
The five services can adopt a new package interface without coordinated release or compatibility hazards.
Invoice output equality is sufficient to detect behavioral regressions, including tax, payment, and notification side effects.
The team can maintain a dedicated integration branch and reconcile frequent upstream merges throughout the migration.
A single cut-over could change invoices for grandfathered plans or uncommon proration, tax, timing, and lifecycle combinations.
Deleting the old implementation after only unit tests would remove the effective behavioral oracle and rollback path.
A three-month branch exposed to roughly 40 merged PRs per week will encounter substantial integration conflicts and stale assumptions.
Shared mutable context may encode undocumented cross-service behavior that a clean domain model does not capture.
Coordinated changes across five services create deployment, ordering, data-migration, and partial-outage risks.
Use a strangler migration: establish golden-master characterization tests and an immutable billing-core API, introduce an adapter around the existing implementation, migrate calculations capability by capability, and shadow-compare proposed and legacy results on real or anonymized cases. Keep legacy code as a temporary fallback until production comparison and invoice-level reconciliation pass, then remove it incrementally.
Create the smallest representative golden corpus that covers all 37 plans, all 11 grandfathered plans, and known proration edge cases, then run the existing implementation and proposed billing-core model against identical inputs and compare complete invoice outputs and side-effect commands.
Any unexplained difference, inability to express a historical case without behavior-breaking special cases, or missing relevant case data would show that the proposed clean model and single-cut-over strategy are not safe as written.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Retain automated failover, but explicitly fence or demote the old primary before promotion and make replica selection and promotion policy safe for cross-region failure. Gate the 30-second detector and service-discovery changes through an end-to-end Rails write test that proves recovery remains below one minute and records the achievable RPO.
Orchestrator can prevent or detect writes on an isolated old primary; Raft quorum alone does not fence MySQL.
Topology and replication metadata are sufficiently current to avoid promoting a stale or wrongly positioned replica.
Every relevant cluster has a viable recovery candidate and required replication/GTID state is retained.
Consul clients and Rails connection pools reliably converge on the promoted primary within 30 seconds.
A bounded RPO from asynchronous cross-region replication is acceptable.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and unrecoverable divergence after promotion.
Promoting the West replica can create a large 60 ms write path and does not cover loss of East application servers.
Pseudo-GTID improves identification but does not prove replica freshness or prevent acknowledged-write loss.
A 30-second detection threshold leaves little time for fencing, election, topology repair, discovery propagation, reconnects, and a verified write.
Automated recovery of all clusters increases blast radius because a false-positive or topology error can affect multiple databases.

In a non-production cluster, partition the primary from Orchestrator and the application while leaving its server process running, then trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write against the original primary.
This falsifies the current proposal if the original primary still accepts writes. A correct design must reject them, terminate/disable the server, or otherwise prevent them from conflicting with the promoted primary.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Retain streaming, but do not enable it fleet-wide at once. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling sequence first, then canary clients through representative tiers while measuring server and client CPU/network, health-update latency, missed or duplicate events, and reconnect behavior; define rollback thresholds and complete the rollout before the peak.
The exact target 1.10 patch release supports `use_streaming_backend` for the deployed OS and architecture and is compatible with the current mixed client/server versions.
Every health subscriber can be moved without breaking older clients during a mixed-version period.
The 200-node staging workload and subscription mix meaningfully represent production fan-out and event-change rates.
Streaming preserves freshness, ordering, filtering, and delivery semantics required by every service.
Reduced Consul server load will not merely shift unacceptable CPU, network, or memory costs onto clients.
A fleet-wide client switch could exhaust or disconnect all discovery clients simultaneously, with no fallback available.
Incorrect version ordering or unsupported mixed-version combinations could cause subscription failures or stale discovery state.
Streaming behavior differences could cause missed updates, excessive reconnects, duplicate processing, or lock/KV-adjacent application failures.
A production workload materially different from staging could fail to reproduce the reported CPU reduction or could overload clients.
Without explicit rollback criteria, a partial rollout could leave heterogeneous behavior that is difficult to diagnose or reverse.
Use a production-representative canary: upgrade servers first with health and Raft continuity checks, enable streaming on a small isolated client cohort, compare against an unchanged cohort, and expand in measured stages rather than making one fleet-wide cutover.
Run one production-scale or faithfully replayed health-subscription load test with streaming disabled and enabled, measuring both server and client CPU/network, update latency, and delivery correctness.
The proposal is falsified if streaming does not produce a material aggregate load reduction, or if it causes stale/missed events, unacceptable update latency, reconnection storms, or client resource saturation.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not change the existing `amount` column in place or reinterpret it as a new scale. Add a nullable `BIGINT amount_1000` column, populate legacy writes through a narrowly scoped trigger during the rolling deployment, migrate writers atomically, and backfill in measured batches with report queries using a compatibility expression until complete. Keep the old column unchanged for this release.
The 900M-row, 410 GB table can tolerate the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and full-table rewrite caused by the type alteration within the deployment lock budget.
NUMERIC(19,4) is semantically compatible with the application's required three-decimal minor-unit scale and all existing integer values.
A night deployment has enough spare database, WAL, I/O, and replica capacity to absorb the rewrite without violating checkout latency or the 99.95% SLO.
All writers and reporting queries can tolerate the atomic column rename and the transition between old and new application versions.
No historical, import, retry, or reporting path relies on the existing column's integer type or name.
The type alteration can rewrite substantially the entire 900M-row table while holding a strong lock, causing an outage or deployment failure.
The rewrite and rename can generate heavy WAL, storage pressure, replica lag, and degraded checkout latency even at night.
NUMERIC(19,4) does not establish the required 1,000-scaled integer semantics; incorrect interpretation can produce financial reporting errors.
Updating model, serializers, and reports in one PR does not handle mixed old/new pods during the rolling deployment.
Transactional DDL guarantees atomicity only, not bounded lock duration, low resource usage, or safe rollback after operational impact.
Use the additive nullable `amount_1000 BIGINT` migration, trigger legacy writes as `amount * 1000`, deploy exact scaled writers, and perform an online batched backfill with tested compatibility reporting.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed type alteration and rename with a realistic `lock_timeout`, while measuring lock wait, duration, WAL volume, and replica lag.
If the operation cannot complete within the deployment lock budget or causes unacceptable latency, WAL pressure, or replica lag, it is falsified; PostgreSQL's normal type-alteration rewrite would confirm that the in-place migration is unsafe.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the reserved-bit approach, but do not enable it on clients until every production router is running the RLP-aware build and the deployed versions have been independently verified. Use a staged rollout with canaries, server-level health checks, explicit rollback criteria, and a client kill switch; retain rollback compatibility until the new router fleet is proven stable. Document the bit's new protocol meaning and test behavior for mixed old/new clients and malformed or retried messages.
The current router's Power Peg path is harmless or can be made harmless when the bit is set; zero observed traffic does not establish how old binaries will behave once clients begin setting it.
All order-message producers, including gateways, simulators, retries, and external clients, can be identified and updated or prevented from setting the bit prematurely.
Every one of the eight routers can be upgraded and its exact build verified before client activation.
The RLP implementation has defined behavior for unsupported, duplicated, delayed, and retried orders, and rollback will not occur while RLP-setting clients remain active.
The exchange permits semantic reuse of a previously defined protocol bit without requiring a separate compatibility or governance review.
Clients setting the bit before all routers are upgraded could cause legacy routers to invoke the retired Power Peg algorithm, producing incorrect routing or order loss.
Manual deployment can leave servers on different builds; a later client rollout could expose some orders to incompatible behavior.
Removing the Power Peg implementation eliminates a straightforward rollback target, and rolling back while clients set the RLP bit could recreate the original danger.
A month of production traffic cannot prove the bit is unused by infrequent clients, archived gateways, maintenance tools, or future integrations.
Bit corruption, stale messages, retries, or an unrecognized bit state could accidentally select RLP or Power Peg behavior without a clear rejection/failsafe policy.
If the exchange permits the approximately one-month coordinated change, add an explicit RLP indicator or protocol/version field rather than redefining historical semantics. Otherwise, use the reserved bit only with a fully gated fleet rollout and a compatibility-preserving router release.
In staging, send one otherwise valid order to the currently deployed pre-RLP router with the header bit set, and compare its routing and resulting audit record with the same order using the bit clear.
If the old router invokes Power Peg, rejects the order, or produces any different routing outcome, client activation before complete fleet upgrade is unsafe and the proposal requires modification.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep Redis caching, but consume `permission-events` to invalidate affected cache keys rather than relying on a 15-minute TTL, retaining a short TTL only as a safety net. Define event ordering, lag, poison-message, and fail-open/fail-closed behavior, and validate the end-to-end p95 under production-like concurrency because an 85% hit rate cannot by itself reduce a bimodal latency distribution's p95 to 40 ms.
Every permission-changing write emits a correctly scoped event containing the affected user, document, and action.
Kafka event delivery is timely enough to meet the application's revocation requirements.
The permissions service's decision is deterministic for a user/document/action tuple until a relevant change event occurs.
Redis availability and capacity are sufficient for roughly 2,500 rps plus existing session traffic.
Caching both allow and deny decisions is security-compliant.
Unshared documents or access removed by the HR integration can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes, causing real data exposure.
At 85% cache hits, 15% of requests still incur the approximately 180 ms permissions call, so p95 may remain near the slow-path latency rather than fall to 40 ms.
Kafka consumer lag, partitions processed out of order, or missed invalidations could extend stale authorization beyond the intended window.
Redis eviction or cluster failure could sharply increase permissions-service load and latency at peak.
The log-replay hit rate may not represent live traffic, especially around sharing and account-removal events.
Use Redis as an event-coherently invalidated read-through cache: consume `permission-events`, delete all affected tuple keys, use a short TTL as a backstop, and publish cache-invalidated shadow metrics before broad rollout. If the resulting hit rate remains below the level needed for p95, pursue a permissions-service batch-check API when its ownership constraints permit or reconsider the endpoint's authorization architecture.
Run a production-like shadow benchmark using the measured hit/miss distribution and 180 ms miss latency, including the approximately 40 ms non-permissions request cost.
If the 15th-percentile request still lands on the 180 ms miss path or p95 remains near 200 ms rather than approximately 40 ms, the claimed latency improvement is falsified.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not use unconditional permanent deletion. First resolve every supplied ID to its object type, reject any site or ambiguous ID, canary the behavior, and then use monitored, idempotent soft deletion; escalate residual records rather than risking a site-wide outage. Reconcile each batch against a pre-deletion inventory and explicitly plan what happens when the 14-day window expires at backend shutdown.
Every supplied ID is known to identify an add-on installation before deletion.
The API or another authoritative inventory can distinguish add-on installations from sites despite the identical ID format.
Permanent deletion of an installation cannot cascade to other site objects.
The API returns object-level outcomes suitable for reconciliation and safe retries.
Permanent deletion is required for the stated policy or deadline rather than merely desirable.
A product, site, or malformed ID could be permanently deleted, causing severe customer data loss.
Logging HTTP responses does not prove that the intended object type was deleted.
Partial failures and retries may produce inconsistent or unverified state across roughly 900 sites.
The batch size and two-second delay do not establish throughput or rate-limit safety before shutdown.
Scheduling over a weekend reduces observation rather than technical risk; on-call monitoring cannot prevent a fast destructive error.
Run a phased, type-safe removal: take an immutable input snapshot; use authoritative type lookup to prove every ID is an add-on installation; hard-fail the batch on any site, unknown, duplicate, or ambiguous ID; soft-delete a small canary and verify unrelated site objects remain intact; then process verified IDs in monitored, idempotent batches. Reconcile inventory and deletion results after each batch, and permanently purge only after safety is demonstrated or when policy requires it.
Before any destructive call, run a read-only inventory join for the complete supplied ID list and fail unless every ID uniquely maps to an add-on installation and zero IDs map to sites, products, or unknown object types.
A complete exact-type match with zero site, product, duplicate, unknown, or ambiguous records is required to proceed; any such record falsifies the proposal's core safety premise and triggers quarantine.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Do not deregister legacy enforcement or enable automatic quota reductions immediately after copying allocations. First shadow usage and decisions for every service, reconcile semantic discrepancies, and then cut over service by service with rollback thresholds; handle user-ID last through a dedicated replicated-write and regional-failover canary. Retire legacy only after a defined soak period and verified audit, telemetry, ownership, and rollback procedures.
Copying current allocations also captures overrides, exemptions, grace periods, manual adjustments, and service-specific rejection semantics.
Current usage and pending automatic reductions can be reconstructed accurately in the new manager.
The grace period reliably delays reductions long enough to validate behavior without user-visible enforcement.
The user-ID service can fail closed consistently across regions when quota state is unavailable.
Rollback remains safe after new-manager enforcement has affected replicated user-ID writes.
Incomplete historical usage reconstruction could immediately overgrant or falsely reject users.
Enabling automatic reductions without shadow comparison could mishandle sustained-underuse reductions and cause user-visible quota changes.
Semantic differences in overrides, exemptions, or grace-period handling could produce incorrect enforcement.
Deregistering legacy before parity is demonstrated removes the authoritative fallback and makes rollback incomplete.
Moving user-ID in a general wave without regional-failover testing could cause inconsistent accepts, rejects, or split-brain enforcement.
Use a shadow migration with legacy remaining authoritative, compare replicated usage and quota decisions against it, and progressively transfer enforcement through controlled canaries; place user-ID last with explicit failover and automated rollback tests.
Select one low-risk service and replay a full grace period of production-like usage through both managers, including an override, an exemption, and a sustained-underuse reduction, then diff every decision and final allocation.
Any missing usage, decision mismatch, or allocation discrepancy falsifies the claim that registration plus allocation copying is sufficient for safe cutover; exact parity supports proceeding only through shadow and gated rollout.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Do not activate the repurposed bit until every production router is verified on the new build; otherwise clients can unintentionally enable the still-compiled Power Peg path on an unupgraded server. Use a two-phase rollout: first deploy the RLP-capable, Power-Peg-disabled build to all eight servers with client activation gated separately, verify each server's build and behavior, then enable the bit no later than launch day.
No current or retained client, saved message, replay process, or internal producer can emit the retired bit.
All eight production routers will be upgraded and verified before any client starts setting the bit.
The new router safely rejects or ignores the bit until RLP activation is explicitly enabled.
Old and new binaries are never mixed in a deployment batch while clients are setting the bit.
The protocol owner has confirmed that semantic reuse of the retired bit is permitted.
During the manual rollout, an old router receiving a flagged order may execute Power Peg and misroute orders.
A deployment or version-reporting mistake on one server could affect RLP orders despite fleet-wide verification.
Unknown legacy or queued producers could unexpectedly activate the bit, making one month of observed traffic insufficient assurance.
A partially deployed fleet could produce inconsistent order behavior across otherwise identical RLP orders.
Stage deployment and activation separately: ship a release that removes Power Peg and supports RLP but keeps the bit gated by an operator-controlled runtime feature flag, upgrade and verify the entire fleet, and only then enable RLP and client-side bit emission.
Run the currently deployed production router build in a test environment with the header bit set to 1 and route-eligible test orders through it.
If the deployed build enters the retired Power Peg path rather than rejecting or safely ignoring the order, the proposed rollout is unsafe until all routers are upgraded and the bit remains disabled.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but run the new manager in shadow/dual-report mode and compare usage, allocations, grace-period boundaries, and rejection decisions before making it authoritative. Cut over services and regions incrementally behind an enforcement flag, with an explicit rollback procedure that freezes or synchronizes allocation state; enable automatic reduction only after parity, load, replication-lag, and failover testing. Do not deregister the legacy manager until a bounded observation period, telemetry/audit validation, and incident rollback procedures are complete.
Copying the current allocation is sufficient to preserve authorization state and does not lose pending reductions or grace-period metadata.
The grace period reliably delays automatic allocation changes without delaying quota enforcement or creating a large rejection window.
The new manager can make authoritative quota decisions synchronously for user-ID writes, including during replication lag and regional failover.
Legacy and new managers produce equivalent decisions for production usage, allocation reductions, and grace-period edge cases.
A rollback can preserve or reconstruct the last authoritative allocation state without inconsistent authorization.
Directly deregistering the legacy manager after copying allocations can reject legitimate user-ID database writes because of timing, semantic, or propagation differences.
Enabling automatic reduction universally can unexpectedly shrink allocations or trigger false rejections before parity and grace-period behavior are validated.
Cross-region failover could use stale or divergent quota state and block replicated writes or allow over-quota operations.
Fallback after the new manager has reclaimed allocations could make legacy and new authorization states inconsistent.
Usage and allocation dashboards alone may not provide decision-level auditability, discrepancy detection, or proof that rollback and incident procedures work.
Use a staged shadow-and-cutover design: mirror reports and allocations while legacy remains authoritative, establish discrepancy thresholds and an end date, then migrate low-risk services and user-ID by region behind a reversible enforcement flag. Preserve allocation state during rollback and retire legacy only after synchronous-write, concurrent-request, replication-lag, failover, telemetry, and operational-readiness tests pass.
Replay a production-representative history of usage and allocation changes through both managers, including grace-period boundaries and allocation reductions, and compare their synchronous allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision mismatch, especially a new-manager rejection where legacy allows a valid write or a reduction occurring before the intended grace-period boundary, falsifies the claimed safe direct cutover.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table receiving 25k inserts/s and periodic bulk deletes. Keep autovacuum enabled, but reduce its per-table cost throttle and vacuum cost limit, schedule manual VACUUMs during low-traffic periods, and monitor vacuum duration, dead tuples, bloat, transaction-ID age, and WAL/checkpoint impact.
A weekly VACUUM can complete before the next accumulation of dead tuples and transaction IDs.
The observed autovacuum workload can be spread over enough low-traffic time without exceeding operational I/O limits.
Bulk deletes do not create a rate of dead tuples that outpaces effective vacuuming.
The database has sufficient free space and WAL capacity for the resulting maintenance workload.
Autovacuum can be safely throttled per table in PostgreSQL 9.4 without materially increasing transaction-ID wraparound risk.
A weekly VACUUM on a multi-terabyte table may run for many hours or fail to complete before the next cycle, allowing severe bloat and transaction-ID wraparound pressure.
Disabling autovacuum removes the safety mechanism that responds to unexpectedly rapid delete activity or transaction-ID growth.
The manual vacuum may itself create the same I/O spikes, merely at a different time, and may overlap peak traffic if it runs longer than expected.
Unbounded dead-tuple growth can increase index size, cache pressure, query latency, and storage consumption.
A single fixed schedule does not adapt to varying delete rates, vacuum progress, or replication and storage constraints.
Tune autovacuum for events with an appropriate autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit, retain emergency autovacuum behavior, and use a carefully monitored off-peak VACUUM ANALYZE as a supplement rather than disabling automatic vacuum.
Compare the timestamps and durations of recent autovacuum runs on events with pg_stat_all_tables.n_dead_tup, pg_stat_all_tables.last_autovacuum, and pg_stat_database.xact_commit, while reviewing PostgreSQL logs for vacuum duration and I/O saturation.
If vacuum runs routinely exceed a week or leave n_dead_tup and transaction age increasing, the weekly-disable proposal is falsified; if throttled vacuum consistently completes with low dead-tuple and bloat levels, the proposed schedule is also unlikely to provide a meaningful improvement.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with a durable, atomic Postgres reservation using a conditional status update and a unique coupon redemption constraint. Reserve using a stable order/idempotency key before charging, then finalize or reconcile by order ID; do not hold a database lock during payment I/O.
All redemption requests for a coupon are routed to the same process instance.
No competing application instance, pod, or horizontally scaled replica exists.
Processes cannot restart or crash between reading and updating the coupon.
Coupon lookup and redemption are handled exclusively by this mutex-owning service.
The existing check-and-update cannot interleave with any other database writer.
Concurrent requests handled by different replicas can both observe an available coupon and attempt redemption, causing duplicate orders or charges.
A process crash can permanently lose the mutex state while leaving partially completed work.
Cleanup after lock release can create lifecycle and race bugs under high concurrency.
The solution does not define safe behavior for payment timeouts, retries, failures, or abandoned reservations.
The test only validates one process and therefore provides no evidence of cross-replica correctness.
Use an atomic Postgres state transition to reserve the coupon with an idempotency token and order ID, enforce one redemption per coupon_id with a unique constraint, and perform the charge outside the database transaction through an idempotent interface. Finalize or reconcile reservations by stable order ID.
Start two independent application instances against the same database and issue simultaneous redemption requests for the same coupon code, one to each instance.
If both instances can pass the availability check and create separate orders or charges, the proposal is falsified; a single-process concurrency test cannot rule this out.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but do not enable automatic quota reduction for the user-ID service until a global peak-load test demonstrates that its allocation has sufficient headroom for the entire reduction and regional replication delay window. Make manager cutover explicit and reversible to avoid overlapping enforcement or an enforcement gap, and retain a protected allocation and tested rollback path for user-ID throughout migration.
Copied allocations include enough capacity for user-ID growth and traffic spikes.
Usage reports are accurate, timely, and consistent across regions.
Quota decisions propagate to every database replica before writes are evaluated.
Registration and deregistration cannot create dual authority or an enforcement gap.
The stated grace period includes all propagation, scheduling, and regional failover delays.
Automatic reduction could cause user-ID database writes to be rejected during normal or peak login traffic.
A stale or region-specific usage report could trigger an unsafe quota reduction.
Concurrent registration in both managers could produce conflicting enforcement decisions.
A gap during deregistration could leave user-ID writes without quota enforcement.
Insufficient regional consistency could allow the global allocation to be exceeded before enforcement converges.
Migrate noncritical services in waves, but place user-ID in shadow mode first and use a fixed, protected allocation for its initial cutover. Enable automatic reduction only after production-scale testing across regions establishes safe headroom, then increase usage or allocation alerts before each reduction.
Run a production-scale user-ID write test against the new system using current and forecast peak traffic, exercising all regional replicas with realistic propagation delay and one failover.
Any legitimate account create or update is rejected, any replica observes a different enforcement state, or projected usage approaches the copied allocation before the earliest possible reduction confirms the proposal is unsafe as written.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the Redis cache direction, but do not ship a 15-minute TTL without consuming permission-events and invalidating affected entries; use a short TTL as a fallback only. Prove the latency target with a representative load test: an 85% hit rate leaves 15% of requests taking the uncached path, so the current ~340 ms miss latency is approximately the p95 and the claimed ~40 ms p95 is not credible unless misses are also made fast or the hit rate is substantially higher.
permission-events reliably identifies every user/document/action decision affected by a write, membership change, or account removal
Kafka event delivery and processing are fast enough to remove revoked decisions before the next request
The 85% replay hit rate applies to production traffic and to the relevant request/key distribution, not just a historical log window
Cache hits can safely serve authorization decisions for the entire interval between writes
Redis capacity, eviction policy, key cardinality, and hot-key behavior remain acceptable at peak load
A 15-minute stale-positive window can allow users to access documents after sharing, action, group-membership, or account revocation.
Group or HR invalidations may affect many users/documents; without a defined fan-out/indexing strategy, stale entries may persist or invalidation may be prohibitively expensive.
A cache stampede on popular or newly changed documents can send large synchronized bursts to the permissions service at 2,500 rps.
Redis eviction, cluster failures, or memory pressure can silently reduce hit rate and overload the permissions service.
The proposed rollout can meet dashboards showing a high aggregate hit rate while p95 remains above budget because the uncached requests are precisely the slow tail.
Use an event-driven authorization decision cache: consume permission-events, maintain an affected-key index or a user/document decision version, and delete or version-bump matching entries; retain a short TTL and request coalescing as safety nets. Validate the event schema and invalidation completeness for group and HR changes before enabling positive caching, then benchmark p95 using production-shaped key reuse and revocation traffic.
Replay a representative production access trace against a deployment with the proposed Redis read-through cache and a permissions-service stub whose uncached p95 is 180 ms; measure end-to-end p95 at 2,500 rps while logging hit and miss latencies.
With only 85% cache hits, approximately the top 15% of requests are misses, so end-to-end p95 should remain near the uncached path (roughly 300-340 ms), not fall to ~40 ms; this would falsify the stated performance claim.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Retain Orchestrator automated recovery, but require reliable primary fencing, explicitly define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, and verify atomic Consul endpoint replacement with client reconnection. Do not enable this blindly for all clusters or claim Raft makes failover safe: Raft protects topology decisions, not MySQL writes or replication consistency.
A failed old primary is made read-only or reliably fenced before another replica is promoted, including during network partitions.
Applications resolve the writable endpoint through Consul and reconnect after its value changes without retaining independent connections to the old primary.
Orchestrator selects a candidate with acceptable replication lag, and detection, promotion, discovery propagation, and reconnection consistently complete within the remaining time after the 30-second threshold.
Some acknowledged writes may be lost under asynchronous replication, or the deployment will add a replication mechanism that provides the required durability.
The promoted replica and its dependent systems can handle production write traffic from East, including approximately 60 ms cross-region latency.
A network partition can leave the old primary accepting writes while Orchestrator promotes another node, causing split brain and irreversible divergence.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft quorum does not establish that the candidate contains the latest committed write.
The 30-second detection threshold leaves only about 30 seconds for promotion, Consul propagation, connection draining, and application reconnection, making the under-one-minute objective fragile.
Selecting a West replica 'regardless of region' may unnecessarily move writes across 60 ms even when a sufficiently current East replica is available.
Blind enablement across clusters can promote unsafe candidates or update unsupported discovery integrations, and pseudo-GTID does not remove the need to validate binlog-position and replication semantics.
Use Orchestrator as the recovery coordinator, but add an explicit fencing mechanism for every possible primary, configure and test region-aware candidate eligibility against measured replica lag, and route clients through a Consul-managed logical primary endpoint that switches atomically and supports fast connection refresh. Validate an explicit RPO and use native MySQL 5.7 GTID where applicable rather than treating pseudo-GTID as a durability mechanism.
In staging, continuously write committed, uniquely numbered rows through the current primary; isolate that primary from Orchestrator and replicas while leaving it reachable by the application, trigger automated recovery, then continue writing to the old endpoint.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary still accepts committed writes after another node is promoted, or if recovery plus Consul/client convergence exceeds 60 seconds. It is supported only if fencing prevents old-primary writes and the measured convergence meets the objective.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Keep the expedited, infrastructure-based rollout, but do not treat a 10-minute log-only period as sufficient safety validation. Require adversarial regex complexity and performance tests before publication, enforce signed/versioned atomic bundles and per-rule rollback, and use explicit CPU, latency, and false-positive thresholds before global blocking; add a narrowly scoped emergency containment rule when the final signature is not immediately safe.
Quicksilver can atomically publish a consistent, signed rule bundle to every machine and transition modes within the target hour.
The WAF evaluator supports rule-level log/block transitions and rollback without restarting proxies.
A rule passing the existing CI corpus has acceptable worst-case PCRE behavior on malformed and adversarial inputs.
Near-real-time match counts and request health metrics are available and trustworthy during the 10-minute window.
Log-mode evaluation has approximately the same CPU cost as block-mode evaluation.
Catastrophic regex backtracking can exhaust proxy CPU even while the rule is only logging, affecting all customer traffic.
A low match count can be caused by a faulty, narrowly scoped, or traffic-dependent rule and therefore does not establish safety.
A false positive discovered after the global block transition can affect every PoP simultaneously.
Inconsistent bundle versions or mode transitions can create temporary unprotected gaps or conflicting behavior.
A compromised release credential or control plane could inject a globally evaluated denial rule.
Use a hybrid release: deploy a narrowly scoped temporary deny policy immediately where appropriate, then publish the precise rule globally in log mode for 1–5 minutes with automated performance and false-positive gates, followed by rapid promotion and one-click per-rule rollback. This preserves sub-hour protection while reducing reliance on a single noisy observation window.
Replay the candidate rule and a representative/adversarial benign corpus through the actual WAF evaluator on a production-equivalent proxy, including encoded, truncated, and pathological inputs, while measuring CPU, p95/p99 latency, and evaluation count.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes superlinear evaluation, CPU saturation, or unacceptable proxy latency; also falsified if log-mode overhead is materially lower than block-mode overhead.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum for this high-throughput, bulk-deleted table; instead retain anti-wraparound and routine maintenance while tuning autovacuum per-table cost limits/delays and vacuum during low-traffic windows. Schedule targeted VACUUM jobs only if measurement shows they can complete between delete cycles, and alert on dead-tuple growth, bloat, vacuum duration, and XID age.
Bulk deletes create substantially more dead tuples than weekly maintenance can safely reclaim.
A VACUUM of the 1.8 TB table can complete within the proposed weekly interval without competing with peak ingestion.
Disabling table autovacuum would not leave transaction-ID wraparound protection or other required maintenance to an uncontrolled emergency vacuum.
Weekly ANALYZE provides acceptable planner-statistics freshness.
The observed latency spikes are caused primarily by maintenance I/O rather than delete workload or storage behavior.
Dead tuples and bloat may grow continuously at the stated insert/delete rates, causing increasing write amplification and latency.
A weekly VACUUM may run for many hours or overlap peak traffic, reproducing or worsening the same I/O spikes.
The table may approach transaction-ID wraparound conditions, triggering an urgent, highly disruptive vacuum despite table-level autovacuum being disabled.
Statistics may become stale, producing poor plans for the ingestion or deletion workload.
Cron overlap or failure can leave vacuum jobs running indefinitely without throttling or resource controls.
Keep autovacuum enabled and configure per-table vacuum cost throttling appropriate to the event workload, with lower cost during the nightly low-traffic period. Investigate partitioning or batching deletes if supported by the workload, and use measured, bounded VACUUM maintenance during off-peak hours rather than a weekly full-table job.
Take two snapshots one hour apart during normal operation and compare the table's dead tuples, bloat-related file size, and vacuum activity, while also recording the table's transaction-ID age.
Rapidly increasing dead-tuple or relation-size growth, a long/incomplete vacuum runtime, or an XID age trending toward the wraparound-safety threshold would falsify the claim that weekly VACUUM is sufficient.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Add explicit primary fencing before promotion and a Consul state machine that publishes the endpoint only after the promoted MySQL instance is writable and replication topology is stable. Restrict routine failover to deterministically prioritized East replicas, keep West as disaster recovery, and measure detection, promotion, and client reconnection convergence separately. Test acknowledged-write loss, transient stalls, stale replicas, manual topology changes, and connection-pool behavior rather than testing only host kills.
A supported fencing mechanism can revoke the failed primary's write capability before promotion.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum does not fence MySQL or prevent a surviving isolated primary from accepting writes.
Replica lag is low enough that selecting the most up-to-date replica does not lose acknowledged transactions.
Consul can atomically or sequentially gate endpoint publication on verified MySQL writability.
Applications and connection pools converge on a changed Consul endpoint without repeatedly retaining stale connections.
An isolated primary may continue accepting writes after replica promotion, causing split brain and divergent data.
Asynchronous failover may silently lose acknowledged writes present only on the failed primary.
Service discovery may route clients before the promoted server is writable or fully reconfigured.
Selecting a West replica for an East failure introduces cross-region latency and exposes the normal path to remote replication lag.
Enabling automation for all clusters without region-specific candidate priorities and conflict controls could promote unsafe or geographically distant replicas.
Use fenced, Orchestrator-driven East-local failover with deterministic candidate priorities, reserve West for regional disaster recovery, and publish the Consul endpoint through an explicit post-promotion writability state machine.
In staging, isolate one primary from Orchestrator and all replicas while continuing to execute successful local writes, then permit automated promotion and query both database identities for new writes.
The proposal is unsafe if the replica can be promoted while the isolated primary still accepts writes; safety requires the old primary to be reliably fenced before promotion.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not use unconditional permanent deletion. First resolve every supplied ID to its object type, reject any site or ambiguous ID, canary the behavior, and then use monitored, idempotent soft deletion; escalate residual records rather than risking a site-wide outage. Reconcile each batch against a pre-deletion inventory and explicitly plan what happens when the 14-day window expires at backend shutdown.
Every supplied ID is known to identify an add-on installation before deletion.
The API or another authoritative inventory can distinguish add-on installations from sites despite the identical ID format.
Permanent deletion of an installation cannot cascade to other site objects.
The API returns object-level outcomes suitable for reconciliation and safe retries.
Permanent deletion is required for the stated policy or deadline rather than merely desirable.
A product, site, or malformed ID could be permanently deleted, causing severe customer data loss.
Logging HTTP responses does not prove that the intended object type was deleted.
Partial failures and retries may produce inconsistent or unverified state across roughly 900 sites.
The batch size and two-second delay do not establish throughput or rate-limit safety before shutdown.
Scheduling over a weekend reduces observation rather than technical risk; on-call monitoring cannot prevent a fast destructive error.
Run a phased, type-safe removal: take an immutable input snapshot; use authoritative type lookup to prove every ID is an add-on installation; hard-fail the batch on any site, unknown, duplicate, or ambiguous ID; soft-delete a small canary and verify unrelated site objects remain intact; then process verified IDs in monitored, idempotent batches. Reconcile inventory and deletion results after each batch, and permanently purge only after safety is demonstrated or when policy requires it.
Before any destructive call, run a read-only inventory join for the complete supplied ID list and fail unless every ID uniquely maps to an add-on installation and zero IDs map to sites, products, or unknown object types.
A complete exact-type match with zero site, product, duplicate, unknown, or ambiguous records is required to proceed; any such record falsifies the proposal's core safety premise and triggers quarantine.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Do not treat Orchestrator Raft quorum as MySQL split-brain protection: it coordinates Orchestrator instances, not the old primary. Enable automated promotion only when the primary is reliably fenced or otherwise proven dead, and base promotion on a verified replica freshness signal; also test network partitions and recovery of the old primary, not only host kills.
An unreachable primary cannot continue serving writes.
Orchestrator can reliably identify the replica with the greatest applied position before promotion.
Application clients promptly and consistently honor service-discovery changes.
West can accept production write traffic at acceptable latency and capacity.
Recovered former primaries cannot rejoin as writable nodes.
A network partition can cause a replica to be promoted while the isolated primary continues accepting writes, creating concurrent writable primaries and divergence.
Asynchronous cross-region promotion can lose acknowledged transactions committed on the old primary but not yet replicated.
Incorrect lag or position comparison can promote a stale replica and make data loss substantially larger.
A West promotion can sharply increase write latency for East-only application servers and may exceed their timeout or capacity assumptions.

In staging, isolate the East primary from Orchestrator and the replica while leaving its application path writable, commit distinct transactions through both paths, and observe whether promotion occurs.
If Orchestrator promotes the replica while the isolated primary still commits writes, the design is unsafe; safety requires no promotion until the old primary is fenced or demonstrated incapable of writes.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Add a shadow-and-compare phase before each cohort moves, using historical and live near-threshold traffic to verify usage semantics, allocation/grace behavior, and regional consistency. Keep a time-bounded legacy fallback with explicit rollback criteria, and initially disable automatic reductions or prove their parity before enabling them; dashboards alone are insufficient validation.
Legacy and new usage reports have identical units, scope, deduplication, and timestamp semantics.
Copying current allocations also preserves grace-period and delayed/missing-report behavior.
Services can switch registration and enforcement paths at runtime and safely recover from quota-manager outages.
Regional replication and failover enforce consistent quota decisions.
Automatic reductions cannot reject legitimate writes before the grace period provides safe rollback time.
User-ID writes begin failing in wave 3 because new quota decisions differ near allocation thresholds.
Semantic reporting differences create false quota exceedances or allow excess storage.
Replication lag or regional conflicts cause inconsistent write acceptance and account-data divergence.
An omitted service or lost connectivity leaves usage unmanaged while deregistered from the legacy manager.
Enabling automatic reductions during migration compounds allocation mismatches and removes the rollback safety margin.
Use compatibility-gated shadowing: normalize reports through a compatibility layer, compare decisions and allocations without enforcement, then migrate lower-risk services in cohorts before user-ID. Retain a controlled legacy fallback until parity, resilience, audit, and rollback exit criteria pass.
Replay historical and recent live user-ID usage, including near-threshold, delayed, missing, and out-of-order reports, through both managers in shadow mode and compare every allocation and enforcement decision by region.
Any material unexplained decision mismatch, false rejection, regional divergence, or difference in grace and missing-report behavior would falsify the proposed wave cutover as currently specified.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but initially disable automatic quota reductions or add a per-service reduction freeze while validating parity and rollback behavior. Migrate the user-ID service only after testing replicated writes, reporting lag, and enforcement at the allocation boundary; retain legacy registration and a tested rollback path until each wave is proven stable.
The new manager can copy allocations without changing quota semantics or effective capacity.
Both managers can remain registered during migration, or equivalent shadow enforcement and rollback are available.
Reported usage is sufficiently complete, timely, and comparable across regions and services.
Automatic reductions cannot cause a service's legitimate burst usage to exceed its allocation.
Deregistering from the legacy manager does not remove an independent enforcement path or monitoring dependency.
Automatic reductions may reject writes for the user-ID service, including login/account operations, violating the no-user-visible-impact requirement.
Usage-reporting lag or regional replication inconsistency could make the new manager undercount usage and permit writes beyond the intended quota, or overcount and reject valid writes.
Migrating the user-ID database's enforcement path without a tested rollback could interrupt authentication globally.
A copied allocation may not represent current effective limits, causing an immediate quota breach during cutover.
Deregistration before parity is established could eliminate the only known-good enforcement or usage signal.
Use a staged shadow migration: dual-register services, mirror and compare usage and enforcement decisions while preserving legacy behavior, keep allocations frozen and reductions disabled, then canary enforcement and rollback before making the new manager authoritative. Handle user-ID separately with multi-region write-failure and authentication tests.
Inspect the new quota system's configuration/API and run a non-production simulation for one canary service whose reported usage stays below allocation, followed by a burst that reaches the current allocation.
If the allocation is reduced during the grace period or the burst is rejected because of the reduction, the proposed 'no user-visible impact' assumption is falsified; if reductions can be disabled and enforcement is unchanged, the mitigation is viable.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the per-process mutex with a database-level atomic compare-and-set claim, such as `UPDATE coupons SET redeemed_at = now(), order_id = ... WHERE code = ? AND redeemed_at IS NULL RETURNING ...`, and reject when no row is returned. Perform this claim before charging, make charging retry-safe, and define compensation or reconciliation for failures after the claim; preserve the proposed concurrent test but exercise requests through separate application instances.
The coupon-service Deployment can have multiple active replicas, so an in-memory lock cannot provide cross-replica exclusion.
Postgres is the authoritative shared state accessible by every redemption request.
A coupon claim can be committed before payment without unacceptable latency or availability impact.
Payment operations can be made idempotent or correlated with the claimed order.
Two requests routed to different pods can acquire separate mutexes and both redeem the same coupon.
The proposed single-process concurrency test can pass while production remains vulnerable across the 4-12 replicas.
Claiming before charging introduces abandoned claims if the process crashes, requiring explicit recovery semantics.
Retrying `chargeOrder` can itself create duplicate charges unless payment idempotency is enforced.
Use an atomic database state transition guarded by `redeemed_at IS NULL`, ideally with a claim/status and order correlation, followed by an idempotent charge and compensating or reconciling failed claims.
Run the two-request redemption race through two separately deployed service instances backed by the same Postgres database, then query the coupon and orders.
If both instances report successful redemption, or two orders reference the coupon, the mutex proposal is disproven; a correct atomic claim should allow exactly one success regardless of routing.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep string serialization as the target representation, but do not make an uncoordinated type change in existing v1 responses. Add a versioned or explicitly negotiated string-ID representation, update the web client and mobile models first, and provide a compatibility/deprecation period for partner SDKs before removing the numeric representation.
Existing deployed clients can tolerate receiving a JSON string where their model expects an integer.
The web frontend is updated in the same deployment and explicitly parses or renders the string form.
Partner integrations will update their deployed SDKs before the server changes.
The API can support a negotiated or versioned response during migration.
Changing the OpenAPI type will not cause generated SDKs to silently break source or runtime compatibility.
The existing Swift Codable Int64 model will typically fail decoding when the JSON value changes from a number to a string.
The existing Kotlin/Moshi Long adapter may reject a string, causing mobile request or response failures.
The roughly 40 partner integrations and their already-deployed SDKs can break immediately when v1 changes.
A regenerated SDK does not update integrations that are already deployed, so weekly SDK publication does not provide migration coverage.
Web components that perform numeric comparisons, sorting, or formatting may produce incorrect behavior even after avoiding JavaScript precision loss.
Introduce a new API version or negotiated representation that returns IDs as strings, migrate consumers incrementally, and retain the existing numeric v1 representation until usage has been audited and a deprecation deadline has passed.
Decode a response containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the currently released Swift model and Kotlin/Moshi model.
If either current model throws a type-mismatch or parsing exception, the proposed v1 cutover is incompatible with the deployed client population and requires a migration or versioned representation.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain immediate Quicksilver propagation, but do not make a global block decision solely from a 10-minute log window. Require explicit false-positive and performance gates, use a very short global or representative canary in log mode, and define an automatic rollback/kill switch based on error rate, latency, CPU, and match-volume anomalies. Ramp blocking across PoPs or traffic percentages within the hour, with an emergency mechanism independent of the normal rollout pipeline.
CI payload coverage predicts production behavior for a newly disclosed attack.
The new regex cannot cause pathological backtracking or excessive evaluation cost on attacker-controlled input.
Quicksilver propagation is sufficiently fast and atomic across all PoPs to meet the one-hour objective.
A 10-minute log interval provides statistically and operationally meaningful visibility into false positives and match volume.
The WAF has reliable real-time telemetry and a tested mechanism to disable or roll back a bad rule.
A catastrophic or merely expensive regex could consume the proxy CPU shared with TLS and HTTP handling, causing latency, timeouts, or outages across customer traffic.
The rule may block legitimate requests that were absent from the benign CI corpus, creating a global availability or business-impact incident.
A low or misleading match volume can be caused by logging failures, sampling, traffic-shape differences, or an incomplete attack signature, leading to premature blocking.
A globally propagated bad rule cannot be recalled quickly enough, and a 10-minute observation window may be too short to observe rare benign traffic.
Simultaneous deployment of many rules may create aggregate CPU or evaluation-budget overruns even when each rule passes isolated tests.

Replay the rule against a representative production request corpus, including benign traffic and adversarial regex inputs, at projected peak concurrency, and compare proxy CPU utilization and request latency with the rule disabled.
The proposal is falsified if the rule causes unacceptable CPU growth, latency, timeouts, or evaluation-budget exhaustion under realistic traffic; otherwise this validates only the performance prerequisite, not the safety of global blocking.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Representing Snowflake IDs as strings is the correct long-term fix, but changing every existing v1 response in the next release is not safely compatible with already deployed clients. Introduce a versioned or explicitly negotiated string-ID representation, update the web/mobile clients and generated SDKs to accept it, and retain numeric v1 responses only for a bounded migration period with a documented deprecation path.
Existing Swift Codable and Kotlin/Moshi clients reject a JSON string when decoding an Int64/Long field.
Regenerated partner SDKs will not be deployed atomically with the API change.
The API can support a new endpoint version or content-negotiated representation within two weeks.
Clients can be updated to use the new representation before the server stops emitting numeric IDs.
Current iOS and Android versions may fail order retrieval or list decoding rather than merely displaying an incorrect ID.
Older web clients will continue to parse numeric IDs through JavaScript's Number type until they switch representations.
Partner integrations generated from the changed OpenAPI schema may experience source-level or runtime breaking changes.
Changing the v1 contract without a migration window can cause widespread order lookup and reconciliation failures.
Add a new major API version, or a negotiated response mode, in which IDs are strings; update first-party clients and SDKs to consume that mode, then deprecate numeric v1 IDs after usage has migrated. Do not silently change the wire type under the same v1 contract.
Decode a fixture containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the currently released Swift Codable model and an unmodified Moshi Long adapter.
If either client rejects the string or requires a custom adapter, the proposed same-contract rollout is incompatible and must be modified; if both transparently accept it, compatibility risk is lower but partner SDK behavior still needs verification.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Keep the new billing-core direction, but replace the three-month branch and single cut-over with incremental migration: first capture characterization tests and invoice outputs for all 37 plans, then introduce billing-core behind a compatibility boundary and migrate one plan/service slice at a time. Run shadow calculations and reconcile old versus new results in production before switching writes, and use a staged rollout with rollback rather than deleting the legacy path at the end. Merge continuously with main to avoid accumulating incompatible changes.
A representative corpus of existing invoices and proration/tax/payment edge cases can be obtained for parity testing.
The five services can be migrated behind an adapter or feature flag without changing externally observable billing behavior.
Three engineers can maintain continuous integration with the main branch while implementing the migration.
The legacy implementation can remain available temporarily as a rollback and comparison path.
Invoice generation, not just plan definitions, is sufficiently covered to detect behavioral regressions.
A long-lived branch will conflict with roughly 40 weekly main-branch PRs and may become impossible to integrate safely.
A big-bang cut-over can produce incorrect invoices for grandfathered plans or evolved proration, tax, payment, and notification interactions.
Deleting the old implementation eliminates the rollback path and the ability to reconcile production discrepancies.
Low existing test coverage leaves hidden billing behavior undiscovered despite unit tests for the new model.
The shared mutable BillingContext creates coupling that may make a clean package boundary impossible without coordinated service changes.
Use a strangler migration: establish golden-master invoice fixtures, extract billing-core behind an adapter, migrate read-only or low-risk paths first, shadow-compare every invoice without charging customers, then switch cohorts of plans incrementally while retaining the legacy calculator as a temporary fallback. Remove old code only after production parity and rollback criteria are met.
Build a golden-master harness that runs the current production billing path for all 37 plans across representative subscription, upgrade, downgrade, cancellation, tax, payment-failure, and proration scenarios, then compare exact invoice line items, totals, taxes, payment instructions, and notifications with billing-core.
Any unexplained difference in legacy invoices, especially for the 11 grandfathered plans or proration edge cases, falsifies the claim that a single cut-over can safely preserve behavior and requires staged migration or expanded compatibility work.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep the wave-based direction, but add a shadow/validation phase that compares legacy and new usage and quota decisions before each enforcement cutover. Migrate user-ID with an explicitly tested, reversible write-admission procedure, and initially disable automatic reduction for it or prove that grace-period and reporting guarantees are safe. Confirm that allocation copies include all overrides and policies, and remove legacy only after a dependency check and bounded rollback window.
The new system can receive complete, consistent, and timely usage reports from every region before it becomes authoritative.
Switching a service's registration also switches the enforcement path atomically, or the proposal provides an equivalent mechanism preventing split or stale decisions.
Allocation copies preserve all service-specific overrides, reservations, exemptions, and policy settings.
The automatic-reduction grace period is safe under delayed reporting, outages, seasonal usage, and regional replication lag.
A reversible user-ID enforcement cutover can be performed without causing inconsistent replicated writes or user-visible login failures.
If registration changes before reporting is validated, the new manager may enforce from stale or zero usage and reject valid writes or reduce allocations prematurely.
User-ID quota enforcement errors can block database writes during login and account operations, and regional replication may produce inconsistent cross-region outcomes.
A copied allocation may differ from the effective legacy allocation, immediately tightening or loosening user-ID storage admission.
Enabling automatic reductions for user-ID during telemetry gaps or abnormal low-usage periods could cause genuine capacity denials.
Deregistering services too early may leave operational consumers dependent on the legacy manager, while shutting it down without a tested rollback could eliminate recovery options.
Use shadow-and-validate migration: run the new manager in observation-only mode using the same usage reports, compare its projected decisions with legacy behavior, then perform independently reversible enforcement cutovers. For user-ID, use a dedicated readiness gate, regional canary or controlled validation, conservative allocation floors, and tested fail-open/fail-closed and rollback behavior before enabling reductions.
Replay a representative production history of user-ID usage, allocation changes, reporting delays, and regional lag through the proposed registration/cutover and automatic-reduction sequence, then compare the new manager's admission decisions with the legacy manager's actual decisions.
Any valid write rejected by the new manager, materially different effective allocations, or a reduction caused by delayed or incomplete reports would falsify the safety of the proposed cutover; exact agreement across the tested period would support it but not cover the production rollback path.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep decimal strings as the canonical representation, but do not change all v1 responses without establishing backward compatibility. Prefer a new API version, or prove that every v1 consumer accepts strings and update web/mobile/SDK decoders before release. Explicitly handle ID fields in requests, URLs, pagination, errors, and all serializers, and add cross-client tests.
All v1 consumers can tolerate a JSON string in the id field within the release window.
The change is applied consistently to every response and request representation of an order ID.
Clients and generated SDKs will not coerce decimal strings through JavaScript Number.
Clients send IDs back as strings and URL-safe values without passing through an unsafe numeric representation.
No legacy numeric-ID endpoint or compatibility path is required during migration.
Older mobile or partner clients may reject string IDs, causing outages or failed orders.
An unupdated endpoint, error payload, or pagination payload may still emit numeric IDs and reintroduce precision loss.
SDK regeneration may produce JavaScript clients that parse or coerce IDs as Number despite the OpenAPI string type.
Clients may continue sending corrupted numeric IDs in requests or URLs after receiving string IDs.
An in-place v1 contract change can break consumers immediately, with no version boundary for rollback or migration.
Introduce a new API version that makes decimal strings canonical while retaining the existing numeric-ID version temporarily, then migrate first-party clients, SDK templates, and high-traffic partners with a documented deprecation plan.
Run a contract inventory and compatibility test: enumerate every v1 response/request field carrying an order ID, then execute representative requests against the web app, iOS/Android decoders, generated partner SDKs, and at least one legacy consumer.
If any field remains numeric, any client rejects or coerces strings, or any legacy consumer cannot be updated during the two-week window, the proposed in-place v1 change is unsafe; those results falsify its compatibility assumptions.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain immediate Quicksilver propagation, but permit global promotion to block only for rules meeting hard false-positive and regex-performance gates. Route other rules through short distributed canaries, require live match-rate and latency telemetry, and provide an automatically exercised global rollback before the 10-minute timer expires.
A passing CI corpus meaningfully predicts production false-positive safety.
Quicksilver delivers a consistent rule version to all PoPs quickly enough for the stated deadline.
The added regex work fits within peak proxy CPU headroom without pathological backtracking.
Ten minutes of log-mode telemetry arrives and is evaluated early enough to prevent harmful promotion.
The rule can be disabled globally quickly enough to bound a bad rollout.
A false-positive rule blocks legitimate traffic across all customers before detection and rollback complete.
A computationally expensive PCRE consumes enough proxy CPU to degrade unrelated HTTP and TLS processing.
Partial version skew or Quicksilver failure leaves some PoPs unprotected or in inconsistent enforcement states.
A low or delayed aggregate match signal is mistaken for evidence that the rule is safe.
The fixed 10-minute delay materially extends exposure to attacks already occurring at disclosure.
Use risk-tiered emergency promotion: immediately block globally only high-confidence, performance-bounded mitigations, while validating other rules on short distributed canaries with automated promotion, rollback, and minimum CPU/headroom protections.
Benchmark each candidate on the production PCRE engine using the CI corpus plus generated near-miss and worst-case regex inputs, reporting p99 evaluation latency and total CPU normalized to current peak proxy utilization.
Any rule that violates the defined per-request CPU/time budget, or whose aggregate load could exhaust measured peak headroom, falsifies the claim that immediate global rollout is safe; consistently bounded execution confirms only the performance assumption, not false-positive safety.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the wire-format approach, but phase it: deploy RLP-capable routers while retaining the unreachable Power Peg branch, add automated per-server build/capability verification, and centrally gate client activation until all eight routers are confirmed ready. Remove Power Peg only in a later release after an agreed compatibility window and review of retry, replay, and failover behavior.
No current, dormant, archived, internal, or external client can set the retired bit.
RLP eligibility truly fits a single boolean and does not require separate client/router state.
A central activation gate can prevent RLP clients from reaching any unupgraded router.
The proposed bit owner will approve reuse and can change its documented meaning.
Power Peg removal does not affect parsing, persistence, metrics, replay, or rollback behavior when the bit is clear.
A missed client or integration setting the bit could invoke unexpected RLP behavior or an unsafe intermediate Power Peg path.
Client launch before fleet-wide router completion could send RLP orders to incompatible routers.
Manual deployment can leave one server on an unknown build, with no automated detection.
