Removing Power Peg in the same release eliminates a straightforward rollback path and complicates mixed-version troubleshooting.
A month of production traffic may not cover dormant, rare, archived, test, or partner-specific bit-writing paths.

Run an automated bit-write audit across all current client binaries and repositories, including test tools, administrative utilities, archived integrations, and any gateway code capable of writing the header; then compare the result with the protocol owner’s reservation history.
Any discovered writer that may set the bit for Power Peg or any other meaning falsifies immediate semantic reuse; only an authoritative protocol-owner confirmation plus an exhaustive zero-writer inventory supports it.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not execute permanent deletion until every supplied ID is independently confirmed to be an Insight Legacy add-on installation associated with the intended site. Add authoritative type and ownership validation, a dry-run inventory, a small canary batch, bounded retries, and post-batch reconciliation before processing the full list.
The product-team list is complete and contains no site IDs or unrelated add-on IDs.
The job can obtain authoritative object type and site ownership before deletion.
Permanent deletion of an installation cannot cascade into other products or site data.
The API provides reliable per-ID results and safely handles retries.
A canary and recovery procedure can be completed before full execution.
A mixed or malformed list could permanently delete customer sites and their other products because both object types share the same ID format.
An incorrect validation or site mapping could cause irreversible cross-tenant deletion.
Transient failures could leave installations undeleted before backend shutdown.
Undetected partial failures could produce an inaccurate completion report.
Permanent deletion cannot use the stated 14-day restore window, so errors require site-by-site backup restoration.
Use a type-constrained workflow: generate and review an inventory, validate every ID as the intended Insight Legacy installation, canary a small batch and verify site integrity, then process the remainder in auditable batches. Prefer a product-specific uninstall or reversible soft deletion where available, reserving permanent deletion for independently verified installations.
In a non-production environment, call the exact endpoint with one known add-on installation ID and one known site ID, inspecting whether object type is validated and whether unrelated data is affected.
If the endpoint cannot distinguish or enforce object type before deletion, or either ID can cause deletion of the other object type, direct permanent batch deletion is unsafe.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for durable job dispatch; AOF does not persist published Pub/Sub messages, and consumers provide neither acknowledgement nor replay. Use Redis Streams consumer groups on the existing Redis deployment, with per-type streams, pending-entry recovery, explicit acknowledgements after processing, retry/DLQ handling, and idempotent handlers; validate it under peak load before retiring RabbitMQ.
Losing a dispatched payment, email, indexing, or thumbnail job is acceptable.
Publishers can tolerate ambiguous delivery and do not require acknowledgement that a job was durably accepted.
Workers remain continuously connected and process each message before any connection interruption.
A worker-side retry wrapper can recover failures even when the message was never delivered or was lost during a disconnect.
Redis Pub/Sub throughput and connection behavior remain adequate at 300 jobs/s with all worker types subscribed.
Messages published while workers are disconnected or restarting are irretrievably lost, which is especially damaging for payment webhooks and fulfilment.
Redis may drop or disconnect slow consumers under load because Pub/Sub has no durable queue or backpressure.
Worker crashes before processing or acknowledgement lose jobs; the existing retry wrapper cannot retry messages it never receives.
The proposed design cannot reliably implement the existing five-attempt retry policy or DLQ because it has no durable failed-message record.
Duplicate or redelivery semantics are unspecified, so introducing Streams without idempotency could cause duplicate charges, emails, indexing, or fulfilment.
Use Redis Streams as the existing-service queue: publishers XADD to a stream per job type, workers read with consumer groups, reclaim stale pending entries after Kubernetes restarts, and XACK only after successful processing. Add bounded retries and a dead-letter stream plus idempotency keys; retain RabbitMQ until replay, failure-rate, recovery, and 300-jobs/s load tests pass.
With a subscriber connected, stop the subscriber, publish 100 test messages, restart it, and attempt to recover and acknowledge all 100 without republishing.
The restarted subscriber receives zero messages because Pub/Sub retains no backlog, falsifying the dispatch design for jobs requiring retries, DLQ, or recovery after routine worker redeployment.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum solely on the assumption that append-mostly data makes dead tuples accumulate slowly; retain it as a safety mechanism or use carefully bounded table-specific autovacuum settings. Replace bulk retention deletes with incremental, rate-limited batches that complete before the next cycle, and replay peak ingestion plus deletion in staging while measuring vacuum duration, dead tuples, WAL, checkpoints, and I/O before relying on a weekly manual vacuum.
The weekly vacuum can finish within the low-traffic window without materially affecting ingestion.
Retention deletes are small enough that their resulting dead tuples and index work remain manageable.
Dead tuples and index bloat accumulate slowly enough that waiting seven days is safe.
Grafana already exposes actionable bloat and vacuum-duration metrics with alert thresholds.
Traffic at Sunday 02:00 leaves enough I/O and CPU headroom for maintenance.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe dead-tuple and index-bloat growth if a manual vacuum fails, is canceled, or does not finish.
A multi-hour vacuum of a very large events table can still create a maintenance I/O spike despite running off-peak.
Off-peak bulk deletes still generate WAL, index churn, and subsequent vacuum work; scheduling them off-peak does not remove their cost.
The schedule may not keep up with peak ingestion or recurring retention volume, causing unbounded maintenance lag.
A bloat-only dashboard may not reveal checkpoint pressure, index-write cost, or vacuum cancellation promptly.

In production-like staging, run one peak-insert retention cycle with autovacuum disabled and the Sunday manual-vacuum settings, sampling pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_user_tables, checkpoint/WAL statistics, index sizes, and I/O from before the bulk delete until VACUUM completes.
The proposal is falsified if the vacuum exceeds the available window, dead tuples or index size grow materially between runs, ingestion latency rises during maintenance, or WAL/checkpoint/I/O pressure shows that off-peak execution merely shifts the original spike.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the Redis read-through cache, but consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected authorization keys before or during their TTL; a 15-minute stale window is unsafe for unsharing and account/group removal. First verify that events identify all affected user/document pairs, including bulk membership changes, and measure revocation propagation latency against the endpoint's security requirements.
`permission-events` contains enough identifiers to invalidate every affected cache entry.
Permission revocation propagation allows a bounded staleness window shorter than 15 minutes.
Redis availability and eviction behavior will not make the permissions service unavailable.
A permissions write can emit multiple decisions or affect multiple documents and actions.
A recently unshared document can remain readable for up to 15 minutes.
An account or group-membership removal can leave multiple stale allow decisions.
Kafka consumer failure or lag silently extends revocation latency.
Unbounded or unindexed invalidation across `authz:*` keys can overload Redis.

Warm the cache for a test user/document, revoke access through the normal unshare or account-removal path, then immediately request the document while recording both cached decisions and direct `permissions-service.check` results.
If the cached result remains allowed after the authoritative service denies access beyond the accepted revocation window, the TTL-only proposal is unsafe.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Retain streaming, but do not enable it fleet-wide at once. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling sequence first, then canary clients through representative tiers while measuring server and client CPU/network, health-update latency, missed or duplicate events, and reconnect behavior; define rollback thresholds and complete the rollout before the peak.
The exact target 1.10 patch release supports `use_streaming_backend` for the deployed OS and architecture and is compatible with the current mixed client/server versions.
Every health subscriber can be moved without breaking older clients during a mixed-version period.
The 200-node staging workload and subscription mix meaningfully represent production fan-out and event-change rates.
Streaming preserves freshness, ordering, filtering, and delivery semantics required by every service.
Reduced Consul server load will not merely shift unacceptable CPU, network, or memory costs onto clients.
A fleet-wide client switch could exhaust or disconnect all discovery clients simultaneously, with no fallback available.
Incorrect version ordering or unsupported mixed-version combinations could cause subscription failures or stale discovery state.
Streaming behavior differences could cause missed updates, excessive reconnects, duplicate processing, or lock/KV-adjacent application failures.
A production workload materially different from staging could fail to reproduce the reported CPU reduction or could overload clients.
Without explicit rollback criteria, a partial rollout could leave heterogeneous behavior that is difficult to diagnose or reverse.
Use a production-representative canary: upgrade servers first with health and Raft continuity checks, enable streaming on a small isolated client cohort, compare against an unchanged cohort, and expand in measured stages rather than making one fleet-wide cutover.
Run one production-scale or faithfully replayed health-subscription load test with streaming disabled and enabled, measuring both server and client CPU/network, update latency, and delivery correctness.
The proposal is falsified if streaming does not produce a material aggregate load reduction, or if it causes stale/missed events, unacceptable update latency, reconnection storms, or client resource saturation.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Do not enable streaming for all services in one rollout. First run a representative production-like benchmark comparing streaming with the current blocking-query path, including index churn, result sizes, client resource usage, reconnect behavior, and correctness/freshness checks; then deploy to a small observable canary with explicit rollback thresholds. Expand by cohort only after stable operation through normal traffic, leader changes, partitions, and reconnects, while testing cheap blocking-query tunings as a control.
All client versions and discovery endpoints support Consul 1.10 streaming with unchanged required semantics.
The 200-node staging environment and observed 60% CPU reduction predict production server, network, and client savings.
Streaming preserves consistency, indexing, freshness, and blocking-read behavior for callers.
Clients and the network can handle the resulting long-lived connection and push-fanout load without reconnect or resync storms.
A deterministic rollback to the existing blocking-query path remains available.
A fleet-wide rollout could break incompatible clients or alter discovery freshness and consistency behavior.
Synchronized reconnects or resyncs could increase CPU, network traffic, and latency rather than reduce them.
Client-side CPU, memory, or connection exhaustion could damage availability even if server CPU improves.
A staging benchmark may not represent production service counts, index churn, result sizes, or failure conditions.
Without cohort thresholds and rollback criteria, a regression could affect all services before it is detected.
Use a benchmark-gated canary rollout: establish baseline metrics, enable streaming for a deterministic small cohort, compare against the existing path and blocking-query tuning, and expand only after correctness, freshness, resource, and failure-scenario thresholds pass.
Run a representative staging load test with current clients versus streaming clients, using production-like service counts, index churn, result sizes, and forced reconnects, while validating discovery outputs and recording server/client CPU, network, memory, connection count, latency, and freshness.
Streaming is supported and materially reduces total CPU and network use without increased client resource usage, reconnect amplification, errors, latency, or differences in required discovery results; otherwise the proposal is not validated.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Do not change the existing v1 `id` wire type globally. Add a canonical string field such as `id_string`, update the OpenAPI definition and web client to use it, and migrate SDKs and partners before introducing a versioned representation where `id` itself is a string. Retain the numeric field for a defined compatibility window.
All deployed v1 mobile and partner clients can tolerate `id` changing from JSON number to JSON string.
Existing clients do not perform numeric type checks, arithmetic, sorting, or framework-specific deserialization requiring `id` to be a number.
Partner SDKs and server serializers can be regenerated or updated before consumers migrate.
The v1 contract is not used by clients that cannot be updated within the compatibility period.
Older mobile clients may reject or deserialize the string incorrectly, causing order lookup, display, or persistence failures.
Partner integrations may break immediately despite regenerated SDKs because deployed SDK versions remain unchanged.
Code that compares, sorts, parses, or performs arithmetic on `id` as a JavaScript number will remain vulnerable or fail after the type change.
Changing the OpenAPI type without validating all serializers and generated artifacts can create contract drift.
Calling the release backward compatible would cause irreversible client breakage during a two-week migration window.
Use an additive `id_string` field in v1, update the contract and affected clients to consume it, retain numeric `id` temporarily, then introduce a versioned contract that makes the string canonical.
Run an integration test using the latest deployed mobile or partner v1 client against an order response whose `id` is a JSON string, including an ID above JavaScript's safe-integer range.
If the client rejects the response, reports a type error, or produces an incorrect identifier, the global v1 type change is proven incompatible; only an additive field or new version is safe.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not submit an untyped ID list to a generic permanent-delete endpoint. Resolve every ID to its authoritative object type and customer scope, quarantine unknown or ambiguous entries, and execute only verified Insight Legacy installations in audited batches; use soft deletion where operationally feasible, or require an approved backup and reconciliation plan before permanent deletion.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an Insight Legacy installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The authoritative lookup is complete, current, and covers exactly the intended ~900 installations.
Permanent deletion is truly necessary before backend shutdown; permanent mode does not create a better safety outcome than mark mode plus timely reconciliation.
Removing an installation cannot cascade into other products, site content, or shared integration data.
Logging every response provides neither idempotency, rollback, nor recovery for an incorrectly purged object.
A site ID is permanently deleted, potentially taking unrelated customer data with it.
The endpoint accepts IDs without type validation, and the same 24-character format encourages an object-type confusion failure.
A stale or erroneous product-team manifest can be treated as authoritative and cause irreversible deletion.
The job may mark successful HTTP responses as complete without verifying that the correct installations disappeared.
Running over a weekend reduces staffing, not deletion risk; permanent errors are not recoverable through the 14-day API window.
Build a manifest-enforced job: join every input ID to authoritative metadata proving type, product, and intended customer/site; produce a preflight mismatch report; require approval; delete only that allowlist in small idempotent batches; reconcile results; and retain immutable evidence. Use mark mode with a final permanent-purge checkpoint unless shutdown timing or audit requirements prove immediate purging unavoidable.
Inspect the DELETE API contract and run a non-mutating type-resolution check across the supplied IDs, specifically checking whether any resolve as sites, other object types, missing objects, or multiple object types.
Any non-installation, missing/unclassifiable ID, or absence of an authoritative type field would prove that passing the raw list to mode=permanent is unsafe.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not perform the type change and rename in the pre-deploy migration. Use an expand/backfill/contract rollout: add a nullable NUMERIC column without rewriting the table, backfill in small batches, deploy code that dual-writes and reads compatibly, validate counts and totals, then retire the old column in a later release after rollback and replication checks. Separately confirm the intended scale and representation for three-decimal currencies before selecting NUMERIC(19,4).
The pre-deploy migration completes while old application pods and reporting jobs continue serving reads and writes.
The table rewrite and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock duration are compatible with the 99.95% checkout SLO and Tuesday release deadline.
A NUMERIC(19,4) value has the intended business representation for currencies with three-decimal minor units.
No external consumers depend on the orders.amount column name beyond the three known reporting jobs.
The deployment can tolerate a schema transition in which both amount and amount_minor exist.
On a roughly 900M-row, 410-GB indexed table, changing INTEGER to NUMERIC will require a full table rewrite and prolonged ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locking, blocking checkout traffic and likely causing an SLO violation.
Because migrations run before old pods are replaced, renaming amount to amount_minor immediately breaks the currently running application and any unupdated reporting queries.
A failed or rolled-back rewrite may consume substantial database resources and create replication lag, while statement_timeout does not protect the migration because the migration role has none.
The migration is unlikely to fit the next-Tuesday release window without an extended outage or emergency operational intervention.
Using scale 4 without a documented currency and API contract can produce incorrect arithmetic or silently incompatible serializer/reporting behavior.
Add a nullable NUMERIC column, backfill in bounded batches with operational throttling, deploy backward-compatible code that writes both representations and reads the new one with a fallback, validate row counts and financial totals, and only then remove or rename the legacy column in a later contract migration.
Run the proposed ALTER against a production-sized restore or an equivalent PostgreSQL 15 dataset while measuring lock acquisition, rewrite duration, transaction termination, and old application queries.
If the ALTER holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for materially longer than the deployment/maintenance window, blocks checkout writes, or causes old amount queries to fail after the rename, the proposed rollout is unsafe and must be replaced.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Keep the batch-job direction, but do not execute permanent deletion from an unqualified ID list. First perform a read-only inventory proving every ID is an active Insight Legacy installation, capture backups or export snapshots, use a canary and idempotent checkpoints, and reconcile results; pause timing and on-call monitoring alone are insufficient.
The product list is complete, current, and contains only add-on-installation IDs.
The API can permanently delete the installation without cascading to the site or other products.
HTTP success means the intended deletion is complete and the backend no longer serves legacy data.
A backup or other recovery mechanism is available before deletion, even though the proposal does not mention it.
The 30-ID batch and 2-second pause respect rate limits and do not create timeout or retry ambiguity.
A wrong ID permanently deletes a site or product, with recovery requiring site-by-site backup restoration.
A valid installation deletion may cascade or otherwise remove data belonging to other products.
Timeout, rate limiting, or partial failure can leave the job with an unknown deletion state; retries may repeat or obscure destructive actions.
The backend may be shut down before asynchronous deletion, residual references, or legacy jobs are actually removed.
Running permanently over a weekend provides no rollback window and does not protect against incorrect scope.
Use soft deletion for the validated legacy installations, reconcile them during the 14-day restore window, then permanently purge only the reconciled set. If the deadline makes that infeasible, retain permanent mode but add authoritative type/site validation, backup verification, canaries, explicit idempotency and failure handling, and post-deletion reconciliation.
Perform a read-only metadata lookup for every supplied ID, including object type, containing site/customer, product/add-on identity, and deletion eligibility; then test one canary in a non-production or disposable environment and inspect the affected site's object inventory.
The approach is falsified if any ID is not uniquely an active Insight Legacy installation, if the canary removes or changes any non-legacy object/data, or if a successful API response does not produce complete, queryable deletion before backend shutdown.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Retain automated failover, but explicitly fence or demote the old primary before promotion and make replica selection and promotion policy safe for cross-region failure. Gate the 30-second detector and service-discovery changes through an end-to-end Rails write test that proves recovery remains below one minute and records the achievable RPO.
Orchestrator can prevent or detect writes on an isolated old primary; Raft quorum alone does not fence MySQL.
Topology and replication metadata are sufficiently current to avoid promoting a stale or wrongly positioned replica.
Every relevant cluster has a viable recovery candidate and required replication/GTID state is retained.
Consul clients and Rails connection pools reliably converge on the promoted primary within 30 seconds.
A bounded RPO from asynchronous cross-region replication is acceptable.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and unrecoverable divergence after promotion.
Promoting the West replica can create a large 60 ms write path and does not cover loss of East application servers.
Pseudo-GTID improves identification but does not prove replica freshness or prevent acknowledged-write loss.
A 30-second detection threshold leaves little time for fencing, election, topology repair, discovery propagation, reconnects, and a verified write.
Automated recovery of all clusters increases blast radius because a false-positive or topology error can affect multiple databases.

In a non-production cluster, partition the primary from Orchestrator and the application while leaving its server process running, then trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write against the original primary.
This falsifies the current proposal if the original primary still accepts writes. A correct design must reject them, terminate/disable the server, or otherwise prevent them from conflicting with the promoted primary.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for jobs; it is a transient broadcast mechanism, not durable dispatch. Standardize RabbitMQ with infrastructure-as-code and automated recovery first, or incrementally adopt Redis Streams for delay-tolerant work only if measured operational savings justify a second transport.
Critical jobs may be lost when no subscriber is connected.
A worker retry wrapper can compensate for broker-level message loss.
Redis AOF protects published Pub/Sub messages.
Submilligram latency and high throughput imply reliable job delivery.
A one-week dual run demonstrates adequate production behavior.
Redis Pub/Sub has no queue, acknowledgment, backlog, or consumer-group recovery, so messages published during restarts or disconnections disappear permanently.
Payment and fulfilment events could be lost while webhooks, emails, or indexing tasks run, causing missing or delayed business transactions.
Existing retry/DLQ infrastructure will not activate because the worker never received the message.
At peak or during rolling deployments, the three or more worker replicas will receive copies rather than share load, multiplying side effects.
Running RabbitMQ and Redis paths without a safe cutover and replay strategy creates an unrecoverable migration gap.
Retain RabbitMQ as the durable transport because the system already relies on its acknowledgments, retries, and DLQ. Reduce burden through topology-as-code, automated upgrades, shared publisher/worker libraries, and failover tests. If Redis consolidation is strategically necessary, evaluate Redis Streams with consumer groups, explicit pending-entry recovery, bounded retention, and idempotent handlers for nonpayment workloads before considering wider adoption.
With no Redis subscriber active, publish a uniquely identified test job, start a subscriber, and verify whether it receives and acknowledges the job; repeat during subscriber shutdown.
The proposal is falsified if the subscriber receives nothing after connecting, as Redis Pub/Sub does not retain messages. It would only be supported if an external durable mechanism independently retained and replayed every missing job.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Retain the billing-core domain-model direction, but replace the three-month big-bang cutover with incremental, cohort-based migration. First freeze current behavior with characterization and golden-master tests derived from production invoice scenarios, then shadow-compare billing-core outputs before moving small plan cohorts, keeping the old path available for rollback throughout migration.
All invoice-relevant legacy behavior can be captured from production scenarios and encoded as executable tests.
No plan-specific behavior is hidden outside the five services or depends on unrecorded operational data.
The long-lived branch can remain compatible with roughly 40 weekly main-branch merges touching billing code.
A one-time cutover can be exhaustively tested and safely rolled back.
The three engineers can maintain feature parity and migration infrastructure simultaneously.
Unknown proration, grandfathering, tax, payment, or notification edge cases could produce incorrect invoices after cutover.
The branch will accumulate severe integration drift and merge conflicts over approximately three months.
Deleting the old implementation at cutover removes the practical rollback path and makes diagnosis expensive.
Low test coverage and concentrated domain knowledge make a large rewrite likely to omit undocumented six-year-old rules.
Late discovery of parity failures could force an emergency extension of the old system, eliminating the claimed maintenance benefit.
Use a strangler migration around billing-core: establish production-derived compatibility fixtures, implement one plan or service boundary at a time, run shadow calculations against live inputs, compare complete invoice artifacts and side effects, and migrate cohorts gradually while retaining a tested rollback route.
Build a one-off replay harness that generates invoices for a representative production-derived corpus covering all 37 plans, especially the 11 grandfathered plans, across proration, tax, payment-failure, and notification scenarios, and compare the current implementation with the billing-core model.
Any unexplained difference in line items, totals, taxes, proration, invoice identity, or resulting side effects falsifies the claim that a single final cutover is sufficiently controlled; exact parity supports incremental migration but not the big-bang rollout.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the read-through cache, but do not use a 15-minute TTL without revocation handling: consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected keys, while retaining a short bounded TTL for missed or invalid events. Re-estimate the latency target using the actual miss distribution, add request coalescing and negative-cache safeguards, and roll out with explicit revocation-latency monitoring.
Permission events contain enough identifiers to invalidate every affected `userId/docId/action` key.
Kafka event delivery and processing complete within the maximum acceptable authorization-staleness window.
The replayed access-log hit rate is representative of production traffic and includes the same key/action distribution.
Redis capacity and eviction policies can accommodate the additional authorization keys without harming sessions.
A cache hit and a cache miss have predictable latency distributions under peak concurrency.
A 15-minute stale allow decision can grant access after an account, group membership, or document share is revoked, creating a serious confidentiality and compliance incident.
With only an 85% hit rate, approximately 15% of requests still miss; those misses are the slowest population, so p95 will generally remain near the 180 ms permissions-call latency rather than fall to about 40 ms.
A sudden cache expiry or deployment can cause a permissions-service thundering herd, increasing latency and potentially cascading into the permissions service.
Incorrect event-to-key mapping or delayed/consumed events can leave revoked access cached, especially for broad group or tenant changes.
Filling the shared Redis cluster may evict session data or degrade session traffic, converting an authorization optimization into an availability incident.
Use a versioned or explicitly event-invalidated authorization cache: populate on misses, invalidate synchronously as soon as possible from `permission-events`, and use a short TTL only as a safety net. If the event payload cannot support precise invalidation, reduce the TTL to the business-approved revocation window and require at least approximately 99% effective hit rate before relying on cache hits to improve p95.
Run a representative peak-load test or trace-based benchmark with 85% cache hits and 15% misses, where misses take 180 ms p95, then revoke a currently cached user and measure the time until access is denied.
The p95 will remain close to the miss latency near 180 ms rather than 40 ms if the proposed 85% hit rate is accurate; a revoked user will also remain able to access the document for up to 15 minutes, demonstrating both the performance estimate and security risk.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Do not fully disable autovacuum or rely on a fixed weekly schedule for a 1.8 TB table with bulk deletes. Keep it enabled as a safety net, tune autovacuum thresholds and cost limits for `events`, and explicitly trigger or schedule a strongly throttled vacuum after bulk deletes; retain a bounded off-peak manual vacuum if weekly maintenance is still needed.
Dead-tuple production and vacuum throughput are stable enough for Sunday's window to be predictable.
The bulk deletes are small and are not themselves a major source of write-latency spikes.
A low-traffic window exists that is long enough for a throttled vacuum to finish.
Disabling normal autovacuum cannot cause PostgreSQL's anti-wraparound autovacuum to run later.
Weekly ANALYZE is frequent enough to prevent materially stale statistics.
Autovacuum already runs for many hours; a weekly cron vacuum could overlap business hours and reproduce or prolong the latency problem.
Large delete batches may create enough dead tuples to exceed safe thresholds before Sunday.
Without autovacuum, vacuum backlog or transaction-age emergencies receive no normal cleanup and may trigger disruptive anti-wraparound work.
Default vacuum cost settings may still generate unacceptable I/O even during the cron window.
Statistics can become stale between weekly runs, causing poor query plans.
Use continuous, throttled targeted autovacuum with appropriately low scale-factor/threshold values and conservative cost limits, then trigger a throttled vacuum soon after each bulk delete. This adapts to actual churn while spreading I/O; monitor dead tuples, vacuum backlog, database age, and latency before considering additional off-peak runs.
Compare existing autovacuum log start/finish timestamps and dead-tuple counts around one bulk-delete cycle; calculate the observed vacuum rate and extrapolate cleanup duration for the week's accumulated dead tuples.
If projected cleanup time exceeds the available 02:00-to-business-hours window, or bulk deletes can generate more dead tuples than that window can process, the weekly-only proposal is falsified.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but run the new manager in shadow/dual-report mode and compare usage, allocations, grace-period boundaries, and rejection decisions before making it authoritative. Cut over services and regions incrementally behind an enforcement flag, with an explicit rollback procedure that freezes or synchronizes allocation state; enable automatic reduction only after parity, load, replication-lag, and failover testing. Do not deregister the legacy manager until a bounded observation period, telemetry/audit validation, and incident rollback procedures are complete.
Copying the current allocation is sufficient to preserve authorization state and does not lose pending reductions or grace-period metadata.
The grace period reliably delays automatic allocation changes without delaying quota enforcement or creating a large rejection window.
The new manager can make authoritative quota decisions synchronously for user-ID writes, including during replication lag and regional failover.
Legacy and new managers produce equivalent decisions for production usage, allocation reductions, and grace-period edge cases.
A rollback can preserve or reconstruct the last authoritative allocation state without inconsistent authorization.
Directly deregistering the legacy manager after copying allocations can reject legitimate user-ID database writes because of timing, semantic, or propagation differences.
Enabling automatic reduction universally can unexpectedly shrink allocations or trigger false rejections before parity and grace-period behavior are validated.
Cross-region failover could use stale or divergent quota state and block replicated writes or allow over-quota operations.
Fallback after the new manager has reclaimed allocations could make legacy and new authorization states inconsistent.
Usage and allocation dashboards alone may not provide decision-level auditability, discrepancy detection, or proof that rollback and incident procedures work.
Use a staged shadow-and-cutover design: mirror reports and allocations while legacy remains authoritative, establish discrepancy thresholds and an end date, then migrate low-risk services and user-ID by region behind a reversible enforcement flag. Preserve allocation state during rollback and retire legacy only after synchronous-write, concurrent-request, replication-lag, failover, telemetry, and operational-readiness tests pass.
Replay a production-representative history of usage and allocation changes through both managers, including grace-period boundaries and allocation reductions, and compare their synchronous allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision mismatch, especially a new-manager rejection where legacy allows a valid write or a reduction occurring before the intended grace-period boundary, falsifies the claimed safe direct cutover.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Retain immediate global shadow deployment, but require hard rule evaluation budgets, payload-variant verification, representative canary enforcement, automated health/false-positive gates, and a tested global kill switch before promotion. Treat ten minutes as a minimum evidence window rather than an automatic promotion timer, and prioritize proven high-confidence signatures for blocking within minutes.
CI’s benign corpus represents production traffic and input encodings closely enough to prevent broad false positives.
Quicksilver can activate and later roll back rules globally within minutes with bounded version skew.
The ten-minute log period provides sufficiently complete, timely, representative match and latency telemetry.
New rules have bounded worst-case PCRE execution under concurrent peak load.
A coherent log-to-block transition and emergency rollback mechanism already exists or will be added.
A pathological PCRE or high-match-volume rule consumes proxy CPU and degrades TLS and HTTP service for every customer at that PoP.
The rule logs rather than blocks during the initial window, or blocks before all machines are ready, leaving material exposure to the disclosed attack.
Rare benign requests absent from CI are blocked after a superficially normal ten-minute match-volume result.
Quicksilver skew or a failed transition produces partial protection or inconsistent enforcement for longer than the objective permits.
The signature matches the test payload but misses common encodings, alternate syntaxes, or actual exploit variants.
Use a risk-tiered emergency pipeline: shadow deploy globally, enforce narrowly scoped high-confidence signatures immediately or after very short canaries, and delay uncertain or CPU-heavy rules until broader validation. Promote only after automated checks on attack matches, benign match deltas, evaluation time, proxy saturation, and rollout completeness, with automatic global rollback.
Run every eligible emergency rule in the existing CI harness against its payload variants, the benign corpus, and generated pathological inputs under representative peak concurrency, reporting incremental per-request evaluation time and worst-case completion time.
The design is falsified if any rule that would pass the current CI corpus exceeds the documented per-request CPU/time budget, can exhibit unbounded backtracking, or blocks any benign sample. Results showing bounded cost and zero benign matches would support the shadow-to-block mechanism, though production representativeness and rollout controls would still need validation.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Retain immediate Quicksilver propagation, but permit global promotion to block only for rules meeting hard false-positive and regex-performance gates. Route other rules through short distributed canaries, require live match-rate and latency telemetry, and provide an automatically exercised global rollback before the 10-minute timer expires.
A passing CI corpus meaningfully predicts production false-positive safety.
Quicksilver delivers a consistent rule version to all PoPs quickly enough for the stated deadline.
The added regex work fits within peak proxy CPU headroom without pathological backtracking.
Ten minutes of log-mode telemetry arrives and is evaluated early enough to prevent harmful promotion.
The rule can be disabled globally quickly enough to bound a bad rollout.
A false-positive rule blocks legitimate traffic across all customers before detection and rollback complete.
A computationally expensive PCRE consumes enough proxy CPU to degrade unrelated HTTP and TLS processing.
Partial version skew or Quicksilver failure leaves some PoPs unprotected or in inconsistent enforcement states.
A low or delayed aggregate match signal is mistaken for evidence that the rule is safe.
The fixed 10-minute delay materially extends exposure to attacks already occurring at disclosure.
Use risk-tiered emergency promotion: immediately block globally only high-confidence, performance-bounded mitigations, while validating other rules on short distributed canaries with automated promotion, rollback, and minimum CPU/headroom protections.
Benchmark each candidate on the production PCRE engine using the CI corpus plus generated near-miss and worst-case regex inputs, reporting p99 evaluation latency and total CPU normalized to current peak proxy utilization.
Any rule that violates the defined per-request CPU/time budget, or whose aggregate load could exhaust measured peak headroom, falsifies the claim that immediate global rollout is safe; consistently bounded execution confirms only the performance assumption, not false-positive safety.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep Redis read-through caching, but do not rely solely on 15-minute expiration: consume permission-events to invalidate or refresh affected entries, and cap the risk of stale access with security-approved shorter TTLs. Before rollout, demonstrate the complete GET latency distribution under production-like key skew; an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests still miss, so the p95 will generally remain on the slow path unless misses are below 5% or the remaining call path is independently below budget.
A 15-minute stale-authorization window is acceptable for grants, shares, unshares, and account/group removal.
The logged 85% hit rate translates into at least 95% of requests completing under 120 ms; hit rate alone does not establish this.
permission-events is not needed for correctness because expiration is considered sufficient revocation handling.
Redis can serve the additional read traffic without material latency, hot-key contention, or cascading failure.
userId, docId, and action uniquely and safely identify the authorization decision, including all relevant group-membership context.
A revoked user can retain document access for up to 15 minutes, with especially serious exposure after HR-driven account or group removal.
The latency claim appears arithmetically inconsistent: with 15% misses, the overall p95 is likely still a permissions-service miss, not a 40 ms cache hit.
Cold starts, TTL synchronization, or hot documents can produce concurrent misses and overload permissions-service.
A Redis incident can eliminate the optimization or cause broad request failures unless cache-failure behavior is explicitly fail-closed.
Dashboards may show improved averages while the 120 ms p95 objective remains unmet.
Use event-driven invalidation and optionally a small per-pod L1 cache backed by Redis. Kafka events should remove or refresh entries affected by share, unshare, account, and group-membership changes; short TTLs remain a backstop, not the primary revocation mechanism. Prefetch or targeted warming may also be required to raise the effective cache-hit fraction above 95%.
Replay a representative 24-hour trace against a staging document service and Redis using the proposed key and TTL, then report the full GET p50/p95/p99 split by hit, miss, and permissions-service latency.
The proposal's estimate is supported only if end-to-end p95 is at or below 120 ms with production-like key skew and concurrent misses. If the 15% miss population remains above 120 ms, the 40 ms p95 claim is falsified regardless of the 85% aggregate hit rate.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but limit it initially to the main East-primary cluster and prefer a healthy East replica rather than any replica regardless of region. Before production, require verified stale-primary fencing, atomic service-discovery redirection, connection draining/retry, and measured end-to-end recovery below one minute. Define the 30-second threshold as detection time, not total recovery time, and document that asynchronous failover can lose acknowledged writes.
Orchestrator detects a failed primary within approximately 30 seconds even when it is hung, isolated, or only partially partitioned.
A healthy, sufficiently current East replica will exist and be eligible when recovery triggers.
The failed primary is fenced at the host, network, or database layer before the replacement becomes writable.
Orchestrator can reconfigure remaining replicas and update Consul, while all application instances promptly refresh and drain old connections.
The three-site Raft quorum is available, healthy, and fast enough to complete detection and recovery within the remaining time budget.
A network partition can leave the old primary writable, causing split brain and divergent committed transactions.
A region-blind selector may promote the West replica, increasing write latency and potentially selecting a staller copy.
Service discovery may update centrally while application connection pools continue using the old endpoint, delaying or extending an outage.
Pseudo-GTID simplifies topology verification but does not make asynchronous acknowledged writes durable or prove replica ordering under every failure.
Applying recovery to all clusters creates correlated automation risk; one misconfiguration could cause simultaneous, uncoordinated promotions.

Run one isolated-network game day in which clients can still reach the old primary while the new primary can reach its replicas and Consul; trigger automatic recovery and attempt a write on the old primary immediately before and throughout promotion.
The design is confirmed only if the old primary is reliably fenced from accepting writes before promotion, no conflicting writable nodes exist, and the application reaches the new primary within 60 seconds; any successful old-primary write or missed deadline falsifies it.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Retain the streaming approach, but do not enable it fleet-wide in one rollout. First verify the exact Consul 1.10 client/server compatibility and upgrade order, then canary it on a bounded production segment with explicit rollback criteria before staged expansion; benchmark a production-representative workload because 200 nodes may not predict behavior across thousands of services.
The stated `use_streaming_backend` setting is supported by the exact Consul 1.10 build and has the required server-side support.
Agents, servers, and clients can be upgraded in a compatibility-preserving order, including during rollback.
Streaming preserves the consistency, freshness, and failure semantics required for every health subscription.
The observed CPU and network reduction at 200 nodes generalizes to the production service and node cardinality.
The cluster and client fleet have enough temporary capacity for rolling upgrades and canary monitoring.
A simultaneous fleet-wide switch could remove or degrade the sole discovery path for all services without a fallback.
An unsupported setting or incorrect mixed-version deployment could make streaming ineffective or cause client failures.
A 200-node test may miss scale-dependent CPU, memory, bandwidth, Raft, or connection effects.
Incorrect rollout or rollback sequencing could create incompatible server-agent combinations.
Streaming could return stale or incomplete health data unless consistency and reconnect behavior are explicitly tested.

Run a production-representative streaming canary or isolated load test spanning thousands of services and the expected concurrent client count, while measuring health-update correctness, server CPU, network bytes, and reconnect behavior.
The approach is supported if it materially reduces CPU and network while preserving timely and consistent health results; the proposal is falsified if reduction disappears at scale, resource use regresses, or correctness or failover behavior degrades.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not change the existing `amount` column in place or reinterpret it as a new scale. Add a nullable `BIGINT amount_1000` column, populate legacy writes through a narrowly scoped trigger during the rolling deployment, migrate writers atomically, and backfill in measured batches with report queries using a compatibility expression until complete. Keep the old column unchanged for this release.
The 900M-row, 410 GB table can tolerate the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and full-table rewrite caused by the type alteration within the deployment lock budget.
NUMERIC(19,4) is semantically compatible with the application's required three-decimal minor-unit scale and all existing integer values.
A night deployment has enough spare database, WAL, I/O, and replica capacity to absorb the rewrite without violating checkout latency or the 99.95% SLO.
All writers and reporting queries can tolerate the atomic column rename and the transition between old and new application versions.
No historical, import, retry, or reporting path relies on the existing column's integer type or name.
The type alteration can rewrite substantially the entire 900M-row table while holding a strong lock, causing an outage or deployment failure.
The rewrite and rename can generate heavy WAL, storage pressure, replica lag, and degraded checkout latency even at night.
NUMERIC(19,4) does not establish the required 1,000-scaled integer semantics; incorrect interpretation can produce financial reporting errors.
Updating model, serializers, and reports in one PR does not handle mixed old/new pods during the rolling deployment.
Transactional DDL guarantees atomicity only, not bounded lock duration, low resource usage, or safe rollback after operational impact.
Use the additive nullable `amount_1000 BIGINT` migration, trigger legacy writes as `amount * 1000`, deploy exact scaled writers, and perform an online batched backfill with tested compatibility reporting.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed type alteration and rename with a realistic `lock_timeout`, while measuring lock wait, duration, WAL volume, and replica lag.
If the operation cannot complete within the deployment lock budget or causes unacceptable latency, WAL pressure, or replica lag, it is falsified; PostgreSQL's normal type-alteration rewrite would confirm that the in-place migration is unsafe.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the bit-reassignment direction, but do not enable clients at launch day until the new RLP path is characterized, security/correctness tested, and load-tested. Deploy an attested compatible build to all eight routers before setting the bit, then use a centrally controlled, gradual traffic cohort with a kill switch and explicit in-flight-order rollback semantics. Do not remove the legacy Power Peg implementation until compatibility and archival behavior have been verified.
No current or archived client, gateway, or protocol component can set or interpret the legacy bit.
The existing Power Peg behavior can be safely replaced by the required RLP behavior without changing the binary layout or message semantics.
All eight production routers can be verified as running the same compatible build before any client sets the bit.
Centralized traffic control and an immediately enforceable per-cohort kill switch are available.
Orders already in flight, retries, duplicates, rejects, and cancels have defined behavior when the flag is disabled.
A dormant or removed seven-year-old path may contain routing, security, performance, or rejection defects that only appear under production load.
Activating clients immediately while router deployment is mixed or incomplete can misroute orders, rejects, or fills.
Traffic-zero observations do not exclude archived clients, scheduled jobs, configuration-based writers, or future compatibility clients.
Removing Power Peg semantics in the same release eliminates rollback and auditability if RLP behavior is incorrect.
Without routing-quality, fill, reject, latency, and dislocation monitoring, a harmful change could be mistaken for a successful launch.

Perform a repository, gateway, client, configuration, and archived-protocol search for every writer, reader, and semantic definition of the legacy bit, then run a compatibility test comparing the old Power Peg path with the new RLP path.
Any additional writer/reader or non-equivalent routing behavior falsifies the claim that the bit is safely and unambiguously reusable; if none exists and the behavioral comparison passes, it supports the direction but still does not validate production rollout.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not submit an untyped ID list to a generic permanent-delete endpoint. Resolve every ID to its authoritative object type and customer scope, quarantine unknown or ambiguous entries, and execute only verified Insight Legacy installations in audited batches; use soft deletion where operationally feasible, or require an approved backup and reconciliation plan before permanent deletion.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an Insight Legacy installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The authoritative lookup is complete, current, and covers exactly the intended ~900 installations.
Permanent deletion is truly necessary before backend shutdown; permanent mode does not create a better safety outcome than mark mode plus timely reconciliation.
Removing an installation cannot cascade into other products, site content, or shared integration data.
Logging every response provides neither idempotency, rollback, nor recovery for an incorrectly purged object.
A site ID is permanently deleted, potentially taking unrelated customer data with it.
The endpoint accepts IDs without type validation, and the same 24-character format encourages an object-type confusion failure.
A stale or erroneous product-team manifest can be treated as authoritative and cause irreversible deletion.
The job may mark successful HTTP responses as complete without verifying that the correct installations disappeared.
Running over a weekend reduces staffing, not deletion risk; permanent errors are not recoverable through the 14-day API window.
Build a manifest-enforced job: join every input ID to authoritative metadata proving type, product, and intended customer/site; produce a preflight mismatch report; require approval; delete only that allowlist in small idempotent batches; reconcile results; and retain immutable evidence. Use mark mode with a final permanent-purge checkpoint unless shutdown timing or audit requirements prove immediate purging unavoidable.
Inspect the DELETE API contract and run a non-mutating type-resolution check across the supplied IDs, specifically checking whether any resolve as sites, other object types, missing objects, or multiple object types.
Any non-installation, missing/unclassifiable ID, or absence of an authoritative type field would prove that passing the raw list to mode=permanent is unsafe.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Retain the Redis read-through cache, but do not deploy the current 15-minute TTL-only design. First prove production-like p95; an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests are misses, so the p95 request is likely still paying the roughly 180 ms permissions-service call, making the claimed 40 ms p95 implausible. Add event-driven invalidation with bounded lag, and require a demonstrated hit rate and end-to-end p95 below 120 ms before broad rollout.
The 85% hit rate from log replay applies to production traffic and to identical key and action distributions.
A cache hit is sufficiently cheap that the overall p95—not merely average latency—falls below 120 ms.
Permission events identify all affected user/document/action entries, including HR account and group-membership changes.
Revoked access may remain cached for up to 15 minutes without violating security requirements.
Redis failure is handled fail-closed and does not silently bypass authorization.
With 15% misses, p95 remains a cache miss and can exceed the 120 ms budget, especially under peak load.
Stale grants, shared-document permissions, and HR-driven revocations can remain valid for 15 minutes.
A malformed or incomplete event-to-cache mapping can leave security-sensitive entries uncleared.
Per-user/document keys may create high Redis memory cardinality and eviction pressure at 2,500 rps.
The log-replay estimate may be biased by replay timing, request coalescing, or a different production workload.
Use the same cache only as one layer, but add Kafka-based invalidation and, if replay confirms that the attainable hit rate is below roughly 95%, build an asynchronously maintained authorization projection with synchronous fail-closed fallback. Local singleflight can reduce duplicate misses, but it cannot remove the tail caused by independent misses.
Replay a production-representative 24-hour trace through the exact cache-key and cache-miss implementation, preserving request timing and measuring the full GET /documents/:id latency distribution with Redis enabled.
If p95 remains above 120 ms, or if the measured hit rate is materially below the replayed 85%, the proposal's latency claim is falsified. Separately, replay a grant followed by a revoke and verify cache visibility; any grant remaining usable for 15 minutes confirms the invalidation risk.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Do not approve the stated p95 claim or 15-minute unrevoked TTL. Add Kafka-driven invalidation or an authorization snapshot, shorter bounded TTLs, singleflight/miss protection, and fail-closed Redis behavior; also validate end-to-end p95, because an 85% hit rate means at least 15% of requests still incur the roughly 180 ms permissions call.
A 15-minute delay in propagating user, account, or group revocation is acceptable.
The 85% hit rate is representative of the entire production workload, including cold documents and rare users.
A permissions-service miss takes long enough that 15% uncached requests place endpoint p95 above 120 ms.
userId, docId, and action uniquely identify a decision, with no tenant or policy-version dimension omitted.
Redis can safely be treated as authorization state and Redis failures do not trigger fail-open behavior.
A removed HR user or revoked document share remains authorized for up to 15 minutes because permission-events are ignored.
Cache stampedes during TTL expiry or cold keys can overload the permissions service and increase its p95.
The claimed roughly 40 ms endpoint p95 is incompatible with 15% misses when those misses already average about 180 ms before other work.
Fail-open handling for Redis faults would bypass authorization during an infrastructure incident.
Key collisions or omitted tenant/policy context could return another principal's authorization decision.
Retain read-through Redis caching, but consume permission-events to invalidate or update all affected keys, use a short TTL only as a recovery bound, and add request coalescing plus origin load shedding. If replay confirms that event-consistent caching cannot exceed 95% hit rate, build a continuously updated authorization snapshot with Redis and local L1 caches while retaining an explicit rebuild and rollback path.
Replay 24 hours of representative access logs through a 15-minute read-through cache model and separately measure the resulting document-request latency using measured Redis-hit and permissions-miss distributions.
Falsifies the proposal if at least 5% of requests miss the cache and the simulated or replayed endpoint p95 remains above 120 ms; the supplied 85% hit rate and approximately 180 ms miss dependency already predict this failure.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Replace immediate permanent deletion with authoritative preflight validation requiring each ID to resolve to the expected add-on installation and site, followed by small, reconciled soft-delete batches. After a short observation period, permanently purge only validated IDs; any mismatch, cascade effect, ambiguous response, or failed reconciliation must stop promotion to permanent deletion.
The deletion API reliably distinguishes add-on installation IDs from site IDs before mutating either object.
Permanent deletion cannot cascade to the site, site content, or other products.
The supplied list is complete, current, duplicate-free, and mapped to the correct expected sites.
The endpoint provides reliable per-ID status and safe retry semantics.
Permanent mode actually guarantees deletion before backend shutdown and satisfies the data-minimisation policy.
A wrong or stale site ID could irreversibly delete an entire site.
An ID could resolve to another object type in a shared or ambiguous ID namespace.
Hidden cascades could remove unrelated products or site data.
Batch-level logging may obscure partial failures or invalid IDs, leading to undetected omissions or repeated mutations.
The irreversible operation provides no recovery window before the retired backend becomes unavailable.
Join every supplied ID to an authoritative inventory containing object type, expected parent site, and deletion eligibility; reject all unresolved or mismatched entries. Process a canary and then small soft-delete batches with per-ID results, reconcile object state, monitor for cross-object effects, and permanently purge only the validated set after a short observation period that does not extend beyond backend availability.
Inspect the deletion API contract or run a no-op/preflight request for one known add-on ID and one site ID, checking whether it returns object type and parent site and refuses a site or mismatched-site deletion before mutation.
If the API cannot establish type and site scope or accepts deletion based solely on an opaque ID, the permanent batch job is unsafe; if it rejects both wrong-type and wrong-site targets and exposes per-ID eligibility, the core safety assumption is supported.

required_observation: Manual deploys without verification make partial deployment likely
review_text:
Keep the header-bit approach, but do not make an unverified global client-side launch the release mechanism. Add explicit compatibility tests, reject or safely quarantine any legacy Power Peg path before RLP enablement, deploy an identical verified artifact with post-deploy build/configuration checks, and use an allowlisted canary with monitoring and rollback before broad client activation.
No current or future non-RLP client, gateway, replay tool, retry path, or intermediary can set the bit.
The RLP specification permits the bit to carry order-level routing intent and does not require distinct semantics from Power Peg.
Every client that will set the bit can be released and coordinated with the router before launch, despite the unchanged wire layout.
Removing the old Power Peg implementation cannot invalidate persisted state, hidden configuration, or downstream assumptions.
The router can distinguish an RLP order from an invalid or unexpected legacy order and fail closed.
A month of zero observed bits is not proof that all traffic sources, historical messages, retries, or future integrations leave it unset.
A client or gateway may set the bit based on stale Power Peg documentation or a copied conditional, unexpectedly activating RLP.
The manual eight-server deployment can leave mixed binaries or configurations, producing inconsistent order behavior.
Deleting Power Peg in the same release creates a hazardous rollback if any legacy producer can still emit the bit.
Enabling all RLP-eligible clients simultaneously could expose router defects at the full ~3M-orders/day load before detection.
For RLP decisions that can be made from client/account identity or router policy, use a server-side allowlist and keep the bit unused until a formally versioned per-order contract is available. If the program explicitly requires per-order signaling, the proposed bit is preferable, but only with the safeguards above.
Run a repository-wide static and binary/protocol audit of every encoder, decoder, configuration default, retry/forwarding path, and client release artifact for assignments to the target header bit, followed by replay tests of legacy Power Peg configurations against the new router.
Any non-RLP path capable of setting the bit, any decoder that treats it as Power Peg, or any legacy configuration that remains effective falsifies safe direct reuse; otherwise it supports proceeding with canary rollout.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Keep the streaming direction, but do not enable it for all clients in one rollout. Upgrade servers first with a documented compatibility and rollback plan, then canary agents and services in production-like conditions, measuring CPU, network, query latency, stale-data behavior, lock/config correctness, and Raft load before expanding gradually. A 200-node staging test showing 60% CPU reduction is encouraging but not sufficient evidence for an 18,000-node, no-fallback cluster.
The current Consul version, client versions, and configuration are compatible with Consul 1.10 streaming.
The client library and service-discovery code support `use_streaming_backend = true` without changing consistency or failure semantics.
The 200-node staging test used representative health-subscription volume, payload sizes, churn, and network topology.
Consul 1.10 has no known streaming regressions affecting health data, KV, or distributed locks.
A tested rollback or failback procedure exists before the six-week deadline.
A fleet-wide client enablement could simultaneously overload or destabilize the five-server Raft cluster, leaving the entire service-discovery system without a fallback.
Streaming may reduce polling CPU while increasing persistent connection count, memory use, reconnect storms, or network load under node churn.
A client/server compatibility mismatch or streaming bug could serve stale or incomplete health results and disrupt dependency resolution.
The staging result may not transfer to thousands of services and 18,000 nodes, making the capacity benefit materially smaller than expected.
Upgrading directly to 1.10 could introduce unrelated regressions in KV configuration or locks, whose failure would affect more than discovery.

Run a production-shaped canary in staging using the expected number of health subscriptions, service churn, payload sizes, KV operations, and lock workloads; compare identical non-streaming and streaming runs while recording server CPU, network bytes, client latency, stale-result rate, and lock/config correctness.
The proposal is falsified if streaming fails to materially reduce CPU or network at representative scale, increases latency/error/stale-result rates, or changes KV or lock behavior; a substantial reduction with unchanged correctness supports gradual rollout.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Retain streaming, but do not enable it fleet-wide at once. Upgrade servers in a supported rolling sequence first, then canary clients through representative tiers while measuring server and client CPU/network, health-update latency, missed or duplicate events, and reconnect behavior; define rollback thresholds and complete the rollout before the peak.
The exact target 1.10 patch release supports `use_streaming_backend` for the deployed OS and architecture and is compatible with the current mixed client/server versions.
Every health subscriber can be moved without breaking older clients during a mixed-version period.
The 200-node staging workload and subscription mix meaningfully represent production fan-out and event-change rates.
Streaming preserves freshness, ordering, filtering, and delivery semantics required by every service.
Reduced Consul server load will not merely shift unacceptable CPU, network, or memory costs onto clients.
A fleet-wide client switch could exhaust or disconnect all discovery clients simultaneously, with no fallback available.
Incorrect version ordering or unsupported mixed-version combinations could cause subscription failures or stale discovery state.
Streaming behavior differences could cause missed updates, excessive reconnects, duplicate processing, or lock/KV-adjacent application failures.
A production workload materially different from staging could fail to reproduce the reported CPU reduction or could overload clients.
Without explicit rollback criteria, a partial rollout could leave heterogeneous behavior that is difficult to diagnose or reverse.
Use a production-representative canary: upgrade servers first with health and Raft continuity checks, enable streaming on a small isolated client cohort, compare against an unchanged cohort, and expand in measured stages rather than making one fleet-wide cutover.
Run one production-scale or faithfully replayed health-subscription load test with streaming disabled and enabled, measuring both server and client CPU/network, update latency, and delivery correctness.
The proposal is falsified if streaming does not produce a material aggregate load reduction, or if it causes stale/missed events, unacceptable update latency, reconnection storms, or client resource saturation.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but do not promote an arbitrary or West-region replica based only on Raft quorum and 30-second unreachability. Restrict promotion to a prevalidated, sufficiently caught-up East replica where possible, require explicit fencing or STONITH of the old primary, and test the complete 30-second detection-to-write-path timing. Validate Consul integration and application reconnect behavior, and explicitly account for data loss inherent in asynchronous replication.
The old primary is reliably fenced or otherwise prevented from accepting writes after being declared unreachable.
A candidate replica's replication lag is within an explicitly approved data-loss bound at promotion time.
An East-region replica remains reachable and is preferred for a single-East-host failure; cross-region promotion is an intentional fallback.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum is not treated as a substitute for MySQL primary fencing.
Consul updates and Rails connection handling cause applications to route to the promoted primary within the required time.
An isolated but still-live old primary can continue accepting writes, causing split-brain and divergence.
Asynchronous replication can lose committed transactions even when the promoted replica has the highest observed position.
A transient East network fault can trigger an unnecessary promotion and outage or make West promotion unexpectedly slow.
A West promotion may exceed the one-minute objective because of 60 ms RTT, discovery propagation, and application reconnection.
Pseudo-GTIDs simplify identity and positioning but do not eliminate the need to verify replication state, lag, and write fencing.

Run a controlled network partition between the old East primary and Orchestrator while leaving it able to serve client connections, then verify whether it is fenced before the replica is promoted and whether any writes made on the old primary are lost or divergent.
If the old primary continues accepting writes, or the test produces acknowledged writes that are absent from the promoted replica, the proposed safety claims are falsified.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with an atomic database-backed claim using Postgres, such as a conditional update or a redemption ledger with a unique constraint on the coupon code. Add payment idempotency and explicit handling for charge failure, timeout, and crash recovery; the mutex alone only serializes requests handled by the same Node.js process.
A mutex map is shared by every request that can redeem a coupon; this is false with multiple Kubernetes replicas unless the deployment is a single process.
Requests for the same code can be routed to different pods, so a local lock cannot enforce the global invariant.
The coupon database update and the payment operation have compatible failure and retry semantics.
Concurrent requests use the same logical redemption identifier so payment-provider idempotency can prevent duplicate charges.
Two requests on different replicas can both read redeemedAt as null, both pass the mutex, and both redeem the coupon.
A process can crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt, allowing a later request to charge again.
A process can claim or mark the coupon before charging and then crash, leaving a permanently unusable coupon.
A process-local mutex can grow without bound or behave incorrectly if cleanup races with a waiter.
The concurrent test can pass in a single process while failing to cover the production multi-replica topology.
Use an indexed atomic transition in Postgres, for example updateMany({where:{code, redeemedAt:null}, data:{...}}) and accept the redemption only when exactly one row is updated. Add a redemption state/ledger and payment idempotency, with reconciliation for uncertain payment outcomes.
Run two separate Node.js processes, each with its own mutex map, and issue simultaneous redemptions for the same unused coupon against the shared database; additionally run the same test with one process and verify the database claim count.
If the two-process test allows both redemptions to succeed, the proposal is falsified; if one atomic database claim succeeds and the other returns no affected row, the replacement approach is confirmed.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep string serialization as the target representation, but do not change the existing v1 `id` field from number to string without a compatibility plan. Introduce the string representation through a new API version or an additive field such as `idString`, update the web client to consume it immediately, and deprecate numeric `id` only after mobile and partner migration thresholds are met.
Existing installed mobile applications can be forced to update before the response contract changes.
Swift Codable and Kotlin Moshi clients currently reject JSON strings when decoding `Int64` or `Long`.
Partner SDKs and integrations will not break when an integer field changes to a string.
API gateways, caches, and downstream systems preserve the distinction between numeric and string JSON values.
A two-week rollout can include consumer migration and backward-compatibility support.
The API change would cause decoding failures or incorrect behavior in existing iOS and Android applications.
The approximately 40 partner integrations could experience outages, failed requests, or corrupted identifiers.
Regenerating SDKs does not update already-deployed partner applications or independently implemented clients.
Changing a v1 field in place violates compatibility expectations and may permanently retain old application versions in app stores.
Publish the canonical string field in a new v2 contract while adding `idString` to v1 for an agreed deprecation window. Update first-party clients and SDKs to use the string field, monitor adoption, then remove or version the numeric field later; the Snowflake generation scheme itself remains unchanged.
Run an integration test that decodes a representative v1 response containing `"id":"1234567890123456789"` with the current Swift Codable and Kotlin Moshi models.
If both existing models decode the string successfully and all partner contract tests accept the type change, the stated backward-compatibility concern is reduced; any decoding exception or validation failure confirms that an immediate v1 break is unsafe.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but replace the fleet-wide rollout with a compatibility gate followed by a production canary and measured expansion. Before broad deployment, verify exact version support, preserve health-query semantics, exercise reconnects and rolling restarts, and define automatic stop/rollback thresholds for errors, stale results, CPU, and network load.
The exact production server and client versions support streaming and `use_streaming_backend` as proposed, without silently falling back to blocking queries.
The staging workload is representative enough for the reported 60% CPU reduction to hold in production.
Streaming preserves the required freshness, filtering, consistency, and reconnect behavior for every service.
All clients can be upgraded and configured compatibly within six weeks.
