One month of captured traffic is sufficient evidence that no dormant or intermittent producer sets the bit.
RLP-capable routers preserve identical behavior for orders with the bit unset.
All eight production routers will be verified as running the RLP-capable build before any client sets the bit.
Deployment and rollback can be coordinated despite the manual per-server process.
A client enabling the bit before all routers are upgraded would make an old router execute the retired Power Peg path.
A partial deployment or unnoticed build mismatch could create inconsistent routing behavior across production servers.
A rollback to an old router while clients still set the bit would reactivate Power Peg.
Traffic sampling may miss a dormant, rare, or out-of-band producer of the bit.

Run one fleet-wide script over the eight production hosts that prints each host's router binary hash or embedded build ID and compares it with the RLP release artifact.
Any server reporting a different or legacy build falsifies the safety of enabling the client bit at launch; all eight matching establishes the required rollout prerequisite.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Keep the billing-core/clean-model direction, but reject the three-month single cut-over. First build a representative historical invoice corpus and characterize existing behavior, then introduce immutable inputs and service-specific adapters with incremental migrations and dual-run comparisons. Preserve the old implementation until equivalence and rollback criteria are demonstrated for all 37 plans and cross-service effects.
Historical invoice inputs and provider responses are sufficient to deterministically reproduce current outputs.
The five services can be migrated independently without changing business semantics during the transition.
The new model can represent all grandfathering, proration, tax, rounding, and billing-cycle variations without lossy mappings.
Other teams can tolerate or be isolated from a long-lived billing-v2 branch and eventual integration conflict.
Unit tests for billing-core can establish real invoice equivalence rather than merely validate the new model.
A single cut-over can change invoices for grandfathered plans, rounding, proration, tax, or payment sequencing, causing financial and contractual damage.
Deleting the old implementation removes the reference oracle needed to detect semantic regressions.
A shared mutable BillingContext may have service-specific mutation and interpretation behavior that a clean model silently normalizes.
A long branch will conflict with approximately 40 weekly PRs and force risky late integration.
A nominally unified core may still be interpreted differently by each service, preserving duplication while creating migration complexity.
Create billing-core as a versioned, pure domain boundary, but migrate rule families incrementally. Add characterization/golden tests from historical invoices, adapt legacy context into immutable typed inputs, migrate one service or rule family at a time, and use shadow or dual-run comparisons before switching behavior. Retain the old path behind a controlled flag until all 37 plans pass production-like equivalence tests.
Build a small replay harness over a representative set of stored historical invoices and provider responses, running the current production path and billing-core candidates and comparing normalized invoice line items, totals, tax, and proration outputs.
If the current path cannot be replayed deterministically, or if any representative historical case lacks enough information to reproduce the invoice, the proposed single cut-over and its claimed equivalence cannot be validated; the missing behavior must be characterized before migration.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not perform the direct ALTER-and-rename migration. Use an expand-and-contract rollout: add a compatible representation, deploy readers/writers and all three reports for backward compatibility, backfill and reconcile in bounded batches, then switch and remove the legacy field. Define the conversion explicitly—reinterpreting existing cents as four-decimal values would change their meaning unless values are multiplied appropriately.
Existing orders.amount values are interpreted as cents and can be converted to the target three-decimal representation without changing business totals.
The target representation is actually three decimal places; NUMERIC(19,4) silently introduces a fourth precision choice.
The ALTER can complete without blocking production traffic beyond the release and SLO constraints.
No consumers beyond the identified application code and three reporting jobs access orders.amount.
The migration and application rollback can be coordinated despite the 25-minute rolling deployment.
PostgreSQL can rewrite the roughly 900M-row table and hold an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes while the pre-deploy job runs.
The rename is visible before old pods are replaced, causing currently running code and any unupdated consumers to fail or read the wrong field.
A long rewrite can generate substantial WAL and I/O, cause streaming-replica lag, and exhaust disk or deployment capacity.
Treating existing cents as NUMERIC(19,4) without conversion could produce values 100 times larger than the intended amount.
The migration may exceed the release window; transactional DDL prevents partial schema changes but does not make the operation online.
Prefer an expand-and-contract migration, ideally retaining efficient integer minor units with explicit currency scale, or adding a NUMERIC target column without removing the old column. Deploy compatible dual-read/write code, backfill with bounded batches while handling concurrent updates, validate totals and nullability, migrate the three reports, and only then retire the legacy column. This avoids an unbounded blocking rewrite and provides a rollback window.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed ALTER under a representative write workload and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL volume, and statement behavior; also insert a legacy value such as 100 and verify the intended converted result.
If ALTER requires a full rewrite and blocks normal reads or writes materially beyond the deployment/SLO budget, the proposal is unsafe; if value 100 is not explicitly converted to the intended three-decimal amount, the proposed type change is semantically wrong.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Keep the expedited, infrastructure-based rollout, but do not treat a 10-minute log-only period as sufficient safety validation. Require adversarial regex complexity and performance tests before publication, enforce signed/versioned atomic bundles and per-rule rollback, and use explicit CPU, latency, and false-positive thresholds before global blocking; add a narrowly scoped emergency containment rule when the final signature is not immediately safe.
Quicksilver can atomically publish a consistent, signed rule bundle to every machine and transition modes within the target hour.
The WAF evaluator supports rule-level log/block transitions and rollback without restarting proxies.
A rule passing the existing CI corpus has acceptable worst-case PCRE behavior on malformed and adversarial inputs.
Near-real-time match counts and request health metrics are available and trustworthy during the 10-minute window.
Log-mode evaluation has approximately the same CPU cost as block-mode evaluation.
Catastrophic regex backtracking can exhaust proxy CPU even while the rule is only logging, affecting all customer traffic.
A low match count can be caused by a faulty, narrowly scoped, or traffic-dependent rule and therefore does not establish safety.
A false positive discovered after the global block transition can affect every PoP simultaneously.
Inconsistent bundle versions or mode transitions can create temporary unprotected gaps or conflicting behavior.
A compromised release credential or control plane could inject a globally evaluated denial rule.
Use a hybrid release: deploy a narrowly scoped temporary deny policy immediately where appropriate, then publish the precise rule globally in log mode for 1–5 minutes with automated performance and false-positive gates, followed by rapid promotion and one-click per-rule rollback. This preserves sub-hour protection while reducing reliance on a single noisy observation window.
Replay the candidate rule and a representative/adversarial benign corpus through the actual WAF evaluator on a production-equivalent proxy, including encoded, truncated, and pathological inputs, while measuring CPU, p95/p99 latency, and evaluation count.
The proposal is falsified if any input causes superlinear evaluation, CPU saturation, or unacceptable proxy latency; also falsified if log-mode overhead is materially lower than block-mode overhead.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Retain the existing-bit approach, but prohibit direct client control: translate the bit to RLP only at an approved gateway and add a separately armed router-side RLP feature flag. Release compatible gateway/router versions through build attestation, canary one server, validate telemetry and reconciliation, and rehearse gateway disablement, router disablement, and rollback before progressive production enablement.
No current or dormant client, gateway, external interface, or malformed producer can set the legacy bit.
All gateways and routers interpreting the order will be upgraded compatibly before any client can request RLP.
The new RLP router path is semantically distinct from, and safely replaces, every legacy Power Peg code path.
A rapid router-side kill switch and deterministic mixed-version rollback behavior can be implemented within the release window.
The four teams can agree on and document one versioned meaning for the repurposed bit.
One month of observed traffic does not establish that the bit is unused by dormant clients, third parties, historical jobs, malformed input, or unobserved environments.
Direct client activation on launch day can route orders to mixed or incompatible router builds, causing incorrect routing or order loss.
Removing Power Peg in the same release may change behavior for unexpected legacy producers and turns an apparently unused-bit change into a breaking protocol change.
Enabling all clients and servers together removes canary isolation and makes failures or rollback difficult to contain.
Without explicit RLP probes, reconciliation checks, and an immediate kill switch, silent misrouting may remain undetected.
Use the bit as an RLP request only through a controlled gateway, while routers require separate operational arming. Canary and progressively enable the capability rather than activating it fleet-wide on launch day.
Audit all client repositories, gateway configurations and source, external producer interfaces, historical jobs, and retained packet captures for any ability or observed occurrence to set the retired bit.
Any unauthorized producer capable of setting the bit, or any captured order with the bit set outside the approved gateway, falsifies the claim that it is provably unused and requires quarantine or normalization before RLP use.

required_observation: Global instant push removes blast-radius protection (no canary)
review_text:
Retain immediate global shadow deployment, but require hard rule evaluation budgets, payload-variant verification, representative canary enforcement, automated health/false-positive gates, and a tested global kill switch before promotion. Treat ten minutes as a minimum evidence window rather than an automatic promotion timer, and prioritize proven high-confidence signatures for blocking within minutes.
CI’s benign corpus represents production traffic and input encodings closely enough to prevent broad false positives.
Quicksilver can activate and later roll back rules globally within minutes with bounded version skew.
The ten-minute log period provides sufficiently complete, timely, representative match and latency telemetry.
New rules have bounded worst-case PCRE execution under concurrent peak load.
A coherent log-to-block transition and emergency rollback mechanism already exists or will be added.
A pathological PCRE or high-match-volume rule consumes proxy CPU and degrades TLS and HTTP service for every customer at that PoP.
The rule logs rather than blocks during the initial window, or blocks before all machines are ready, leaving material exposure to the disclosed attack.
Rare benign requests absent from CI are blocked after a superficially normal ten-minute match-volume result.
Quicksilver skew or a failed transition produces partial protection or inconsistent enforcement for longer than the objective permits.
The signature matches the test payload but misses common encodings, alternate syntaxes, or actual exploit variants.
Use a risk-tiered emergency pipeline: shadow deploy globally, enforce narrowly scoped high-confidence signatures immediately or after very short canaries, and delay uncertain or CPU-heavy rules until broader validation. Promote only after automated checks on attack matches, benign match deltas, evaluation time, proxy saturation, and rollout completeness, with automatic global rollback.
Run every eligible emergency rule in the existing CI harness against its payload variants, the benign corpus, and generated pathological inputs under representative peak concurrency, reporting incremental per-request evaluation time and worst-case completion time.
The design is falsified if any rule that would pass the current CI corpus exceeds the documented per-request CPU/time budget, can exhibit unbounded backtracking, or blocks any benign sample. Results showing bounded cost and zero benign matches would support the shadow-to-block mechanism, though production representativeness and rollout controls would still need validation.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the in-process async mutex with an indexed atomic Postgres claim, such as an UPDATE guarded by redeemedAt IS NULL or an insert into a redemptions table with a unique coupon identifier, and require exactly one successful claimant before charging. Persist CLAIMED/SUCCESS/FAILED state and use a stable payment idempotency key derived from the coupon and order; a same-process concurrency test does not validate correctness across replicas or retries.
All redemption requests are handled by one process, with no multiple Kubernetes replicas, rolling deployments, or horizontal autoscaling.
The mutex is held across the complete check/update/payment sequence and cannot be interrupted by process termination.
Payment timeouts and retries can be safely handled without releasing the coupon before the provider's outcome is known.
The application can durably record and reconcile claim state.
The coupon code uniquely identifies the coupon and can be protected by a database uniqueness constraint.
Two requests routed to different replicas can both observe the coupon as unused and redeem or charge it twice.
A process crash or pod eviction drops the mutex, allowing another request to proceed while the first payment may still complete.
A timeout or crash after payment but before redeemedAt is written can cause duplicate charges on retry.
The proposed concurrent test can pass while production routing exposes none of these races.
Map cleanup and lock release logic can introduce additional races or leak entries under contention.
Use an atomic database state transition to claim the coupon, backed by a unique coupon redemption record, then call chargeOrder with a stable coupon/order idempotency key and reconcile ambiguous or failed claims.
Inspect the production deployment and run two redemption requests through separate service replicas, or reproduce the flow with two application instances sharing the database while using distinct in-process mutex maps.
If two replicas can both reach the redemption path and both observe redeemedAt as null, the mutex-based proposal is falsified; only an atomic database claim should allow one request to proceed.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
The string representation is the right long-term fix, but changing the existing v1 `id` field in place is a breaking contract change and cannot be made safe merely by regenerating SDKs. Within two weeks, deploy a lossless web-client decoder and add an additive `idString` field, then migrate clients and measure adoption before versioning the API and making the string field canonical.
Existing released iOS and Android apps can tolerate an additive response field without strict decoding failures.
Existing partner SDKs and integrations will not be broken by retaining the numeric `id` during migration.
A lossless JSON parser or BigInt-aware decoder can be integrated into the web app within two weeks.
The API can expose a new field consistently across all order serializers and generated SDKs.
There is an API owner who can enforce the deprecation and version transition.
Changing v1 `id` from number to string can cause runtime deserialization failures in Swift `Int64`, Kotlin/Moshi `Long`, and partner clients that require numeric JSON.
Regenerating SDKs does not update already deployed apps or partner-deployed SDK versions.
Approximately 40 integrations may fail or silently mishandle responses, creating support and operational incidents.
A one-release migration may leave users on unsafe clients for weeks or longer, so the stated two-week objective is not achieved.
The OpenAPI change may cause generated-code or validation breakage independently of runtime behavior.
Use a compatibility migration: immediately fix the web client with lossless parsing; add `idString` while preserving numeric `id`; update the OpenAPI spec and SDKs to expose both; require clients to adopt `idString`; then introduce a new API version where the canonical `id` is a string and retire the unsafe field on a published schedule.
Run an integration test that feeds `{"id":"1234567890123456789"}` into the current released iOS `Int64` Codable model, Android Moshi `Long` model, and one representative partner SDK deserializer.
If all three decode the quoted value correctly and preserve the exact ID, the immediate v1 break risk is lower; any exception, truncation, null, or numeric fallback confirms the compatibility hazard and requires the additive migration path.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for job dispatch; it does not provide durable queuing, acknowledgements, retries, or dead-letter handling, and messages can be lost during subscriber disconnects or rolling deployments. Retain RabbitMQ and incrementally adopt a mature RabbitMQ-compatible Python task framework behind the current publishing interface, with feature flags, idempotency, graceful shutdown, DLQ ownership, and end-to-end metrics.
Losing a published job when no subscriber is connected is acceptable, which conflicts with durable at-least-once delivery.
A worker-side retry wrapper can compensate for broker or process failures without message loss or duplicate side effects.
Redis AOF persistence makes Pub/Sub messages recoverable, despite Pub/Sub not persisting or replaying messages.
The workload can tolerate duplicate processing from reconnects and rolling restarts.
Existing RabbitMQ routing, priority, acknowledgement, and DLQ semantics can be safely discarded rather than preserved.
Jobs published during subscriber outages, worker restarts, or deployment gaps are permanently lost.
There is no broker acknowledgement or visibility timeout, so worker crashes can cause silent job loss.
No native retry, dead-letter queue, replay, ownership, or backlog metrics exist for failed jobs.
Redis resource or persistence incidents can simultaneously affect dispatch and the existing cache workload.
The proposed week-long dual run does not establish at-least-once behavior, idempotency, or safe rollback before RabbitMQ is decommissioned.
Keep RabbitMQ and migrate incrementally to a mature Python task framework, preserving the current publishing contract and job-specific routing. Before each job type moves, validate idempotency, graceful worker shutdown, retry and DLQ behavior, and representative 300 jobs/s plus reconnect and rolling-restart tests.
Publish a uniquely identifiable message to a Redis Pub/Sub channel with no subscriber, then start a subscriber and inspect whether it receives the message; repeat while forcibly disconnecting the subscriber.
The message is absent after subscribing and may be lost during disconnect, confirming that Pub/Sub cannot satisfy durable at-least-once job delivery.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Keep the streaming direction, but do not enable it for all clients in one rollout. Upgrade servers first with a documented compatibility and rollback plan, then canary agents and services in production-like conditions, measuring CPU, network, query latency, stale-data behavior, lock/config correctness, and Raft load before expanding gradually. A 200-node staging test showing 60% CPU reduction is encouraging but not sufficient evidence for an 18,000-node, no-fallback cluster.
The current Consul version, client versions, and configuration are compatible with Consul 1.10 streaming.
The client library and service-discovery code support `use_streaming_backend = true` without changing consistency or failure semantics.
The 200-node staging test used representative health-subscription volume, payload sizes, churn, and network topology.
Consul 1.10 has no known streaming regressions affecting health data, KV, or distributed locks.
A tested rollback or failback procedure exists before the six-week deadline.
A fleet-wide client enablement could simultaneously overload or destabilize the five-server Raft cluster, leaving the entire service-discovery system without a fallback.
Streaming may reduce polling CPU while increasing persistent connection count, memory use, reconnect storms, or network load under node churn.
A client/server compatibility mismatch or streaming bug could serve stale or incomplete health results and disrupt dependency resolution.
The staging result may not transfer to thousands of services and 18,000 nodes, making the capacity benefit materially smaller than expected.
Upgrading directly to 1.10 could introduce unrelated regressions in KV configuration or locks, whose failure would affect more than discovery.

Run a production-shaped canary in staging using the expected number of health subscriptions, service churn, payload sizes, KV operations, and lock workloads; compare identical non-streaming and streaming runs while recording server CPU, network bytes, client latency, stale-result rate, and lock/config correctness.
The proposal is falsified if streaming fails to materially reduce CPU or network at representative scale, increases latency/error/stale-result rates, or changes KV or lock behavior; a substantial reduction with unchanged correctness supports gradual rollout.

required_observation: Gradual per-service rollout with a fast toggle back, scale load testing, isolation of workloads
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but do not enable it for all health subscriptions in one rollout. First verify the exact 1.10 configuration scope and client compatibility, then canary representative cohorts, measure CPU, network, update correctness, and reconnect behavior under realistic load, and expand only against explicit thresholds. Retain a tested configuration rollback and use query/watch tuning as a complementary control.
The deployed client and server versions support the same streaming protocol and configuration semantics.
`use_streaming_backend` is set at the correct agent/server scope and actually causes production health reads to use streaming rather than merely enabling an unused feature.
The 200-node staging workload is representative of production subscription breadth, result sizes, churn, and holiday concurrency.
Streaming preserves watch ordering, completeness, and freshness during reconnects and leader changes.
The rollout can be stopped or reverted quickly enough to prevent a fleet-wide failure.
A mixed-version or mis-scoped rollout leaves blocking queries active or causes incompatible streaming behavior.
An all-at-once change can create a reconnect or subscription storm, increasing CPU, network, Raft pressure, and latency.
Incorrect streaming freshness or missed-event handling could leave services with stale dependency state or route traffic to unhealthy instances.
The staging CPU reduction may not scale linearly when every service subscribes simultaneously.
Because there is no discovery fallback, a streaming defect or partition could broadly disrupt service resolution.
Use a staged canary: begin with a bounded, diverse set of services and nodes, validate correctness and resource metrics during expected load, then expand by cohorts. Keep the existing blocking-query configuration available for immediate rollback, and add endpoint/watch coalescing or narrower subscriptions if streaming does not deliver the expected fleet-wide reduction.
Run the proposed 200-node staging configuration under a production-representative subscription mix and concurrent holiday-level load, while comparing effective configuration and measuring server CPU, network bytes, streaming versus blocking-query counts, and watch freshness or missed updates.
The proposal is falsified if clients do not actually use streaming, or if streaming causes material missed/stale updates, a reconnect storm, or higher server CPU/network than the current blocking-query baseline at representative load; a reproducible, scalable CPU reduction with correct updates supports expansion.

required_observation: Tune autovacuum throttling instead, and/or partition and drop old partitions; monitor XID age
review_text:
Retain autovacuum on `events` and tune its per-table thresholds and I/O cost limits so vacuum work is gradual rather than bursty. Measure vacuum duration, dead-tuple growth, bloat, and wraparound distance before and after tuning, and batch the bulk deletes to limit dead-tuple production.
A complete `VACUUM ANALYZE` of the 1.8 TB table reliably finishes before the next weekly run and during low-impact hours.
Weekly vacuum keeps dead-tuple and bloat growth within safe operational limits at peak ingestion.
Plain `VACUUM` provides enough reusable space without increasing file size.
The bulk-delete schedule and volume are compatible with a fixed weekly maintenance window.
Autovacuum can safely be disabled without creating transaction-ID wraparound or visibility-map maintenance risk.
A fixed weekly job may overlap with the prior run, leaving only partial coverage and causing unbounded bloat.
Disabling autovacuum can allow transaction-ID wraparound emergencies and stale statistics or visibility maps.
Plain `VACUUM` does not return most ended-file space to the operating system, so filesystem-level bloat may remain.
Reading and rewriting a 1.8 TB table can create sustained I/O contention and degrade ingestion throughout the maintenance window.
The single maintenance job provides no adaptive response when delete volume, vacuum duration, or bloat changes.
Use per-table autovacuum tuning for `events`: raise the vacuum scale factor and thresholds, and set suitable per-table vacuum cost delay/cost-limit values to smooth I/O while preserving emergency vacuum capability. Validate the settings with production-like timing, monitor `pg_stat_all_tables`, `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` where applicable, relation size, dead tuples, and transaction-ID age, and reduce delete-bloat production through smaller delete batches.
On a production-sized copy, run `VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events` while sampling elapsed time, physical read/write rates, ingestion latency, relation size, and dead-tuple counts.
If the vacuum cannot complete within the proposed low-traffic window, materially increases relation size, or pushes write p99 above 500 ms, the weekly plain-vacuum design is falsified.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
An in-process mutex is insufficient because the Deployment has 4-12 replicas and retries can reach different pods; enforce the single-use invariant atomically in Postgres, for example with a conditional updateMany on redeemedAt and a durable pending/used state. Add a multi-replica concurrent test and explicitly handle charge failure, process crashes, and idempotent retries so a coupon cannot be charged twice or remain permanently claimed after a failure.
All redemption requests for a coupon may be routed to different application replicas.
The shared Postgres database is the authoritative consistency boundary.
The existing coupon update operation can be made atomic and conditional without relying on process-local state.
External payment/order charging is not itself safely idempotent under retries and process failures.
Two pods can both observe an unredeemed coupon and independently charge orders despite the local mutex.
Holding a mutex while awaiting charge increases wait time and can push p99 above the 800 ms requirement, especially when several retries arrive.
If charging succeeds but the coupon update fails or the process dies, a retry can charge again; the proposal does not address this existing failure window.
A cleanup-on-release Map can grow incorrectly or remove a mutex while another request still references it if cleanup is not carefully ownership-protected.
The proposed test with two calls in one process cannot detect the production cross-replica race.
Use a database-backed atomic state transition: claim the coupon with updateMany({ where: { code, redeemedAt: null }, data: { redeemedAt: now, orderId } }) and proceed only if count is 1, ideally with explicit pending/used/failed states and an idempotency key for the charge. Make the claim and order association durable and define recovery for crashes and payment failures; benchmark concurrent and retrying traffic through multiple replicas.
Run two simultaneous redemption requests for the same code against two application instances sharing the production-like Postgres database, with each instance using the proposed local mutex, and inspect redemption and charge records.
The proposal is falsified if both requests report success or two charges are created; a correct database-backed approach allows exactly one successful claim/charge and causes the other to return AlreadyUsed.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but replace the single fleet-wide rollout with a reversible canary and staged cohort expansion. First verify client compatibility, upgrade sequencing, event semantics, mass-reconnect behavior, Raft/BoltDB health, and rollback timing; monitor CPU, bandwidth, event lag, errors, elections, and disk growth between stages.
All production agents and dependent applications can be upgraded and configured without breaking health-query semantics.
The tested streaming configuration is supported with the selected server/client versions and upgrade order.
Streaming preserves the freshness and ordering guarantees required for discovery and dependency decisions.
Reconnect jitter, backoff, and buffering prevent mass client or server restarts from creating an overload event.
Production load will retain the staging CPU reduction rather than shifting cost to Raft, snapshots, or BoltDB.
A fleet-wide rollout exposes every service simultaneously to missed events, stale health state, or client failure, with no discovery fallback.
Mass reconnects after the configuration change could overload Consul even though steady-state staging CPU fell 60%.
An unsafe or incomplete server/client upgrade sequence could make rollback difficult or impossible within the six-week window.
A 200-node test may not reproduce event rates, network fan-in, Raft contention, or reconnect behavior at 18,000-node scale.
BoltDB growth, snapshot disruption, or increased Raft traffic could impair elections and availability despite lower polling CPU.
Use the same streaming solution through a low-risk canary, then progressively larger service cohorts with explicit hold points and a rehearsed rollback. Preserve short-term query tuning or temporary capacity headroom during validation rather than combining those changes with broad adoption, so their effects remain diagnosable.
On the existing 200-node staging deployment, simultaneously restart all streaming clients while forcing a Consul leader change, then track health-event loss, state convergence, client errors, CPU, network, Raft commit latency, and reconnect completion time.
The proposal is falsified if clients permanently miss or misorder health updates, fail to converge within the required freshness SLO, or cause CPU/Raft saturation or an unrecoverable reconnect storm. Clean convergence with sustained CPU and network reduction supports proceeding, but does not remove the need for staged production rollout.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Retain wave migration, but enable automatic reduction only after establishing a safety floor for user-ID and validating usage-decision parity between managers. Migrate user-ID last, switch enforcement atomically where possible, and require tested rollback before deregistering any service from the legacy manager.
The new system can accurately receive current user-ID allocations and usage reports from every region.
The grace period is long enough to detect sustained underuse before reductions become harmful, rather than merely delaying reduction by a fixed number of weeks.
User-ID has enough allocation headroom for account-data growth, replication metadata, reporting lag, and peak demand.
Deregistering a service from the legacy manager also makes the new manager authoritative without conflicting enforcement.
Quota-manager outages and stale decisions will not block user-ID database writes.
Automatic reduction could lower user-ID allocation below live or near-term storage demand, causing rejected account writes and replicated login-related impact.
Stale or out-of-order usage data could trigger an incorrect reduction or produce inconsistent enforcement.
A cutover gap or dual-authority conflict could cause nondeterministic quota decisions.
A new-system outage could block user-ID writes if enforcement fails closed.
Operational dashboards could look correct while regional enforcement or replication behavior remains unsafe.
Use the proposed waves with a user-ID exception: configure a protected minimum allocation or temporarily disable automatic reduction for user-ID, while retaining it for other services. Before each cutover, shadow or compare usage and enforcement decisions, then atomically transfer authority with rollback tested under concurrent regional writes.
Query historical user-ID usage by region and compare maximum recent usage plus observed growth against its copied allocation through the full reduction grace period.
If even peak-plus-projected-growth usage approaches the copied allocation during the grace period, the claim that weeks of buffer make universal automatic reduction safe is falsified and user-ID requires a floor or exemption.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Keep the batched deletion objective, but add authoritative ID/type and parent-site validation, deduplication, inventory reconciliation, and an independently verified completion report. Test a small canary cohort and rollback/backup restoration before expanding to permanent deletion; use idempotent retries and explicit handling of partial failures and rate limits.
The product-team list is complete, current, and contains only add-on installation IDs.
The deletion API exposes or can be joined to authoritative object type and site ownership data.
Permanent deletion is isolated to the retired add-on and does not cascade into other products or the site.
The API handles duplicate or repeated deletion requests safely and reports failures reliably enough for reconciliation.
A tested site-by-site backup restore can recover a wrongly deleted site before the backend shutdown.
A 24-character site ID or another object ID is permanently purged because the batch has no type verification.
The supplied list is stale or incomplete, leaving installations behind or causing unrelated deletions.
Undisclosed dependencies cause removal of shared data belonging to other products.
Timeouts, partial failures, pagination, or rate limits cause the job to report incomplete success.
Weekend execution delays detection until after business impact, with no tested recovery path.
Use a preflight-and-cohort process: resolve and type-check IDs, reconcile them against an authoritative installation inventory, test backup restoration and deletion scope, permanently delete a small canary cohort, verify affected sites and remaining objects, then expand with monitoring and reconciliation.
Run a non-destructive or isolated test that submits a known site ID and a known add-on installation ID to the deletion workflow, with a type-validation check before any permanent call; inspect the recorded object type, parent site, and deletion scope.
If the workflow cannot reliably distinguish the two IDs or shows that deleting an installation also removes the site or other-product data, the proposed permanent batch process is unsafe and must not run.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not submit an untyped ID list to a generic permanent-delete endpoint. Resolve every ID to its authoritative object type and customer scope, quarantine unknown or ambiguous entries, and execute only verified Insight Legacy installations in audited batches; use soft deletion where operationally feasible, or require an approved backup and reconciliation plan before permanent deletion.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an Insight Legacy installation rather than a site or another deletable object.
The authoritative lookup is complete, current, and covers exactly the intended ~900 installations.
Permanent deletion is truly necessary before backend shutdown; permanent mode does not create a better safety outcome than mark mode plus timely reconciliation.
Removing an installation cannot cascade into other products, site content, or shared integration data.
Logging every response provides neither idempotency, rollback, nor recovery for an incorrectly purged object.
A site ID is permanently deleted, potentially taking unrelated customer data with it.
The endpoint accepts IDs without type validation, and the same 24-character format encourages an object-type confusion failure.
A stale or erroneous product-team manifest can be treated as authoritative and cause irreversible deletion.
The job may mark successful HTTP responses as complete without verifying that the correct installations disappeared.
Running over a weekend reduces staffing, not deletion risk; permanent errors are not recoverable through the 14-day API window.
Build a manifest-enforced job: join every input ID to authoritative metadata proving type, product, and intended customer/site; produce a preflight mismatch report; require approval; delete only that allowlist in small idempotent batches; reconcile results; and retain immutable evidence. Use mark mode with a final permanent-purge checkpoint unless shutdown timing or audit requirements prove immediate purging unavoidable.
Inspect the DELETE API contract and run a non-mutating type-resolution check across the supplied IDs, specifically checking whether any resolve as sites, other object types, missing objects, or multiple object types.
Any non-installation, missing/unclassifiable ID, or absence of an authoritative type field would prove that passing the raw list to mode=permanent is unsafe.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub as the durable dispatch mechanism or decommission RabbitMQ until equivalent delivery guarantees are demonstrated. Migrate incrementally to Celery on RabbitMQ with explicit acknowledgements, durable queues, retries, idempotency contracts, graceful worker termination, and end-to-end backlog/dead-letter monitoring; retain the existing path during each migration stage.
Redis Pub/Sub messages must survive subscriber disconnects and worker restarts, although Pub/Sub provides no such guarantee.
AOF persistence protects queued work, although Redis AOF does not persist Pub/Sub messages for disconnected subscribers.
An existing retry wrapper can provide delivery guarantees without a durable source of missed work.
All publishers and workers can tolerate message loss during the dual-path week or Redis failover.
The 300 msg/s throughput target is sufficient evidence of reliability and failure recovery, not merely capacity.
Payment or fulfilment messages published while a worker is restarting, disconnected, or being rolled out can be silently lost.
Redis node failure, failover, memory pressure, or eviction can cause dispatch loss or interrupt unrelated cache and rate-limit traffic.
Worker-side retries cannot recover a message that was never durably queued or received.
Running both paths without idempotency and reconciliation can create duplicate side effects when jobs are published or retried.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ removes the current durability and replay boundary before migration behavior is validated.
Adopt Celery incrementally on the existing RabbitMQ cluster, using durable or quorum queues, explicit acknowledgements, per-job-type retry policies, dead-letter handling, idempotency, graceful Kubernetes shutdown, and metrics for queue age, backlog, retries, and dead letters. Migrate one representative job type first and retain RabbitMQ until failure-injection and business-reconciliation tests pass.
Publish a representative payment job while its worker is offline, then restart Redis and the worker; also terminate the worker immediately after receipt but before acknowledgement. Compare published, received, acknowledged, and completed job IDs.
Any published job that is absent after subscriber downtime or an unacknowledged job that disappears during worker or Redis termination falsifies the required at-least-once guarantee; a correct design must redeliver it and produce no unexplained loss.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but require explicit old-primary fencing, an approved promotion policy, pre-promotion topology/lag checks, and cluster-by-cluster canarying. Do not automatically select the most up-to-date replica regardless of region; use a designated preference and account for East application latency, replication lag, and a declared RPO.
A West promotion remains reachable from East application servers with acceptable latency and connection stability.
The old East primary can be conclusively fenced before the promoted replica accepts writes.
Orchestrator detection plus Raft election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and discovery convergence consistently complete within 60 seconds.
The chosen replica's replication lag and connection state provide a tolerable committed-write RPO.
Orchestrator 3.x, MySQL 5.7, and pseudo-GTID behave correctly through these failure and recovery transitions.
A network partition can trigger promotion without fencing the old primary, causing split brain and divergent writes.
Promoting a lagging West replica can lose committed transactions despite pseudo-GTID.
Automated reconfiguration can stall or partially complete, extending write unavailability or leaving inconsistent topology.
An unreachable West primary can make East applications fail or suffer unacceptable latency because service discovery alone does not ensure connectivity.
Applying automation to all clusters at once can create simultaneous elections, discovery churn, and an operator overload during the failure.

In a production-like staging environment, run one isolated end-to-end game day: continuously commit marked writes, hard-kill the East primary, record write errors and failure timing, and verify fencing, selected replica, data present, topology repair, and application recovery.
The proposal is supported only if there is a single authoritative primary, no unexplained lost acknowledged writes, all application writes recover within 60 seconds, replicas converge, and service discovery settles consistently; a split brain, unacceptable loss, or recovery beyond 60 seconds falsifies it.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Retain Redis caching, but add permission-events-driven invalidation or versioned entries and a short TTL fallback to bound revocation staleness. Also address cache stampedes and validate the latency model explicitly: an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests still take roughly the permissions-service path, so the 95th percentile cannot be assumed to become 40 ms unless misses are made much faster or occur in under 5% of requests.
A 15-minute stale-allow window is acceptable for unshare, account deletion, and group-membership changes.
The live workload will have enough locality to keep misses below the threshold needed for the p95 target, or misses can be served through a faster path.
Redis can sustain the projected key rate and memory footprint with acceptable tail latency and failover behavior.
Permission decisions can be safely cached by user, document, and action without additional context or hidden policy inputs.
The permissions-events stream can be consumed and mapped to affected cache entries or versions.
A revoked user may retain document access for up to 15 minutes, potentially including access following HR account removal.
At the reported 85% hit rate, the uncached 15% can still determine p95, leaving the 120 ms budget unmet.
Synchronized expiry or correlated revocations can produce a permissions-service stampede and cascading latency.
Redis failure or cluster hotspots may either block authorization or cause unsafe fallback behavior.
A log-replay hit rate may not represent live hit rate because real request locality, key cardinality, and decision churn may differ.
Use a Redis read-through cache with event-driven invalidation or permission-versioned entries, plus a short TTL safety net, stale-while-revalidate for stale entries where policy permits, and request coalescing for concurrent misses. Require measured miss rate and miss-path latency to demonstrate the p95 target before broad rollout.
Run a representative shadow-cache replay and calculate p95 from the measured cache-hit and cache-miss paths, while injecting a share-revocation event and measuring how long a previously cached allow remains usable.
The proposal is falsified if p95 remains above 120 ms at the observed hit rate, or if revocation remains accepted beyond the approved staleness window; results near 40 ms with sub-5% misses would support it.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
The in-process mutex cannot serialize requests across the 4–12 replicas, so concurrent retries routed to different pods can both redeem the coupon. Use a Postgres-backed atomic state transition or distributed lock, ideally with a unique redemption record and idempotent order charging; explicitly define compensation or retry behavior if charging fails after the coupon is claimed.
All redemption requests for a coupon may reach different application replicas.
Postgres is shared by every replica and is the authoritative consistency boundary.
A coupon may have only one successful redemption across the entire service.
Payment charging can be made idempotent or reconciled with the coupon state transition.
Two requests handled by different pods can both pass the check and charge orders.
The concurrency test can pass in one Node process while masking the production multi-replica failure.
Claiming before charging can consume the coupon when charging fails unless compensation or a pending state exists.
Holding a database transaction or lock across payment I/O may violate the checkout p99 target.
Replace the process-local mutex with a database-level compare-and-set or transaction. For example, atomically transition an eligible coupon to a unique pending redemption using `UPDATE ... WHERE redeemed_at IS NULL AND status = 'AVAILABLE'`; persist a unique order/redemption identifier, then make charging idempotent and finalize or compensate pending claims. A unique redemption ledger or constraint provides an additional correctness barrier.
In a test environment, deploy at least two replicas and send simultaneous same-code redemption requests with connections explicitly routed to different pods; repeat enough times to cover the observed 50–300 ms overlap.
If two requests can both reach chargeOrder and succeed, the proposal is disproven; a correct database-backed implementation should allow exactly one claim or redemption and reject the other.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator automated recovery, but make promotion region-aware and explicitly fence the failed primary before allowing writes; normally promote an East replica, reserving West promotion for an East-region failure. Define and test an RPO, replication-lag thresholds, application routing behavior, and recovery-time budget, and do not enable unattended recovery across all clusters until these checks pass. Raft protects the Orchestrator decision, not MySQL data durability or split-brain safety.
An East replica will normally be available and sufficiently caught up to serve the East application during a primary-host failure.
The failed primary can be reliably fenced or terminated before the replacement is made writable.
Consul integration and application retry/write behavior will route new connections to the promoted primary without unacceptable connection or DNS caching delays.
The acceptable RPO permits any asynchronous replication lag, including cross-region lag.
Orchestrator's recovery actions, topology updates, and promotion are safe for every cluster under the proposed automation.
Promoting a lagging asynchronous replica can lose acknowledged writes and create an unacceptable RPO; Raft does not make replication synchronous.
A network-partitioned old primary may continue accepting writes, causing split brain and divergence when connectivity returns.
Promoting a West replica may add roughly 60 ms or more to every write and may not satisfy the application's latency or availability requirements.
Unattended recovery for all clusters can amplify a topology error, bad promotion choice, or Consul integration failure into a broad outage.
The stated under-one-minute objective is not demonstrated: detection, promotion, fencing, Consul propagation, client reconnection, and application retries may exceed that budget.

During a controlled East-primary host failure, continuously issue uniquely identified committed writes, then promote the configured candidate and verify every acknowledged write ID is present before declaring recovery successful; also measure detection-to-write-readiness time.
Any missing acknowledged write falsifies safe automated promotion under the current asynchronous design; a recovery time over 60 seconds falsifies the stated objective.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep JSON-string serialization as the target representation, but do not silently change the existing v1 contract in a single release. Add a versioned or negotiated string-ID representation, update the OpenAPI spec and generated SDKs with an explicit compatibility/migration window, and change the web, iOS, and Android clients together. If the two-week deadline requires an immediate v1 change, publish a breaking-change notice, provide transitional parsing/dual-format support in clients, and verify every partner SDK path before rollout.
All relevant consumers can be updated or given a compatibility adapter before the numeric v1 representation is removed.
The iOS Swift Codable Int64 and Android Moshi Long models can be changed or configured to decode JSON strings.
Generated partner SDKs will be regenerated, released, and adopted without an extended period of mixed old and new clients.
The API can version or negotiate the ID representation without changing the meaning of the numeric value.
Only response ID fields are changed; request paths, pagination tokens, and other 64-bit fields are handled consistently.
Changing v1 from integer to string is a breaking wire-format change and can cause immediate decoding failures in existing iOS, Android, and partner clients.
Regenerating SDKs does not help integrations that pin an older SDK or have hand-written numeric-ID models.
A partial rollout can produce mixed representations, causing clients to reject responses or inconsistently compare IDs.
Unrelated integer/int64 fields may remain vulnerable to JavaScript precision loss or fail schema validation if the contract is changed incompletely.
A next-weekly release does not address users who delay mobile updates, so compatibility must be maintained for an extended period.
Introduce a new API version or content-negotiated representation that serializes IDs as strings, while retaining the existing numeric v1 representation during a documented migration period. Update first-party clients to support both forms, deprecate numeric v1 IDs, and remove the old representation only after usage telemetry shows compatibility. If a breaking v1 change is unavoidable, add transitional string decoding/serialization support to released clients and maintain the previous API behavior behind an explicit compatibility flag.
Run a minimal decoding test using the current iOS JSONDecoder with a JSON string value against a Swift Int64 property, and a Moshi request/response test using a JSON string against a Kotlin Long adapter.
If either default client decoder rejects the string or requires a custom adapter, the proposed unreviewed v1 change is incompatible with existing consumers and confirms that a staged/versioned rollout or client compatibility update is required.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum solely on the assumption that append-mostly data makes dead tuples accumulate slowly; retain it as a safety mechanism or use carefully bounded table-specific autovacuum settings. Replace bulk retention deletes with incremental, rate-limited batches that complete before the next cycle, and replay peak ingestion plus deletion in staging while measuring vacuum duration, dead tuples, WAL, checkpoints, and I/O before relying on a weekly manual vacuum.
The weekly vacuum can finish within the low-traffic window without materially affecting ingestion.
Retention deletes are small enough that their resulting dead tuples and index work remain manageable.
Dead tuples and index bloat accumulate slowly enough that waiting seven days is safe.
Grafana already exposes actionable bloat and vacuum-duration metrics with alert thresholds.
Traffic at Sunday 02:00 leaves enough I/O and CPU headroom for maintenance.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe dead-tuple and index-bloat growth if a manual vacuum fails, is canceled, or does not finish.
A multi-hour vacuum of a very large events table can still create a maintenance I/O spike despite running off-peak.
Off-peak bulk deletes still generate WAL, index churn, and subsequent vacuum work; scheduling them off-peak does not remove their cost.
The schedule may not keep up with peak ingestion or recurring retention volume, causing unbounded maintenance lag.
A bloat-only dashboard may not reveal checkpoint pressure, index-write cost, or vacuum cancellation promptly.

In production-like staging, run one peak-insert retention cycle with autovacuum disabled and the Sunday manual-vacuum settings, sampling pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_user_tables, checkpoint/WAL statistics, index sizes, and I/O from before the bulk delete until VACUUM completes.
The proposal is falsified if the vacuum exceeds the available window, dead tuples or index size grow materially between runs, ingestion latency rises during maintenance, or WAL/checkpoint/I/O pressure shows that off-peak execution merely shifts the original spike.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on the table and rely on a weekly manual vacuum. Keep autovacuum enabled with table-specific cost settings to smooth I/O, use rate-limited retention deletes, and investigate partitioning if routine vacuum still scans the full table. Validate the schedule against actual vacuum duration, dead-tuple growth, transaction horizons, and peak-load latency.
The table can accumulate dead tuples for an entire week without exceeding acceptable bloat or query-performance limits.
A weekly VACUUM can complete before the next traffic peak and without being blocked by old transactions or locks.
Traffic is consistently lowest at 02:00 Sunday and the workload tolerates a concentrated vacuum then.
The bulk deletion job does not create unacceptable WAL, lock, or index-I/O spikes.
Monitoring can detect missed cron runs, vacuum cancellation, dead-tuple growth, and bloat before damage occurs.
Disabling autovacuum can allow severe bloat to develop, producing longer and more damaging cleanup runs and degraded queries.
A weekly vacuum may overlap peak traffic or fail to finish, leaving dead tuples and index bloat accumulating.
Concentrating cleanup on Sunday can recreate write-latency and I/O spikes rather than spread maintenance across the day.
Long-running transactions or conflicting locks can prevent vacuum from reclaiming rows, regardless of the cron schedule.
A failed or delayed cron job has no automatic fallback cleanup, while a Grafana bloat alert may arrive after operational damage.
Use measured, table-specific autovacuum tuning, such as an appropriate vacuum cost limit and delay, combined with smaller rate-limited retention deletes and index validation. If vacuum must regularly scan the full 1.8 TB table or cannot complete safely, migrate to time-based partitions and drop expired partitions.
Over one complete retention cycle, record n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, vacuum duration, and p99 latency in pg_stat_user_tables and system I/O metrics.
If n_dead_tup grows substantially between scheduled runs, vacuum duration approaches or exceeds seven days, vacuum is canceled or blocked, or p99 latency rises during the weekly run, the weekly-manual-vacuum proposal is falsified.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep Redis read-through caching, but add event-driven invalidation for permission-events, a bounded fallback TTL, and cross-pod request coalescing. Establish an explicit staleness policy for revocations, and do not claim a ~40 ms p95 without replaying end-to-end latency: at an 85% hit rate, p95 necessarily falls within the miss path.
A 15-minute stale grant is acceptable for sharing changes, account removal, and group-membership removal.
permission-events can map every relevant change to all affected authz keys, including group-based changes.
The permissions-service result is safely cacheable and does not vary materially within the TTL.
Redis and Redis connections have sufficient capacity for the key cardinality, miss stampedes, and existing session workloads.
Concurrent misses for the same key can be suppressed across all 12 pods.
Users retain document access for up to 15 minutes after revocation, which may be unacceptable for terminated accounts or sensitive documents.
Expiration and cold starts can create a permissions-service stampede; one request per replica is not enough protection for high-volume keys.
Redis eviction or failure can collapse the hit rate and overload the permissions service at peak load.
Kafka lag, gaps, or unrecognized group-membership changes would leave revoked access cached.
The proposed performance claim is not credible from hit rate alone: with 15% misses, p95 is determined by uncached requests, whose permissions call alone is reported at approximately 180 ms p95.
Use the same Redis cache but consume permission-events to delete affected keys, retain a shorter TTL as a repair mechanism, add distributed singleflight, and monitor Kafka consumer lag and cache freshness. If revocations must be near-immediate, use a versioned, reconciled authorization projection rather than TTL-only invalidation.
Replay the existing 24-hour request log with recorded end-to-end duration split into cache-hit and miss paths, applying the proposed 15-minute keyed cache and measuring the resulting uncorrelated request p95 without request coalescing.
A p95 near 40 ms would support the latency target; a p95 above 120 ms—expected when at least 15% of requests take the approximately 180 ms miss path—falsifies the proposal's central performance estimate.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse approach, but do not ship it as described without a compatibility check across every client/gateway/parser, an explicit rollback control, and a per-server build/version verification after the manual deployment. Preserve the old Power Peg code until rollout is proven safe rather than deleting it in the same release; a month of zero observed bits does not prove that all readers treat it identically.
The bit is unused by every current and planned client, gateway, parser, diagnostic tool, and counterparty, not merely absent in observed traffic.
All relevant components can agree on the new meaning without a wire-format change and will not reject or ignore it.
The new RLP path is functionally, operationally, and performance-tested for eligible and ineligible orders.
The router can distinguish RLP eligibility consistently, including orders that lack the bit.
A documented kill switch can disable RLP without requiring a synchronized client and router redeployment.
A legacy or divergent implementation interprets the bit as Power Peg, causing unintended routing or inconsistent behavior.
Removing the old code eliminates the safest fallback and makes rollback dependent on a new build or another control.
Manual deployment leaves servers on mixed builds, producing nondeterministic participation and making incidents hard to attribute.
Launch-day client flag changes expose untested interactions at full volume, including latency, matching, liquidity, and risk-limit failures.
A configuration or eligibility mismatch causes some RLP-eligible orders to bypass RLP or some ineligible orders to enter it.

Perform a repository/protocol inventory and staging end-to-end test: search all parsers and routing branches for the bit, then send representative orders with it set and unset through each client/gateway version and verify identical non-RLP behavior except for the intended RLP selection.
Any additional semantic use, a component that ignores or rejects the bit, or changed behavior for ineligible/non-RLP orders falsifies the claimed compatibility and blocks the proposed release.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for job dispatch; it does not provide durable queuing, acknowledgements, retries, or dead-letter handling, and messages can be lost during subscriber disconnects or rolling deployments. Retain RabbitMQ and incrementally adopt a mature RabbitMQ-compatible Python task framework behind the current publishing interface, with feature flags, idempotency, graceful shutdown, DLQ ownership, and end-to-end metrics.
Losing a published job when no subscriber is connected is acceptable, which conflicts with durable at-least-once delivery.
A worker-side retry wrapper can compensate for broker or process failures without message loss or duplicate side effects.
Redis AOF persistence makes Pub/Sub messages recoverable, despite Pub/Sub not persisting or replaying messages.
The workload can tolerate duplicate processing from reconnects and rolling restarts.
Existing RabbitMQ routing, priority, acknowledgement, and DLQ semantics can be safely discarded rather than preserved.
Jobs published during subscriber outages, worker restarts, or deployment gaps are permanently lost.
There is no broker acknowledgement or visibility timeout, so worker crashes can cause silent job loss.
No native retry, dead-letter queue, replay, ownership, or backlog metrics exist for failed jobs.
Redis resource or persistence incidents can simultaneously affect dispatch and the existing cache workload.
The proposed week-long dual run does not establish at-least-once behavior, idempotency, or safe rollback before RabbitMQ is decommissioned.
Keep RabbitMQ and migrate incrementally to a mature Python task framework, preserving the current publishing contract and job-specific routing. Before each job type moves, validate idempotency, graceful worker shutdown, retry and DLQ behavior, and representative 300 jobs/s plus reconnect and rolling-restart tests.
Publish a uniquely identifiable message to a Redis Pub/Sub channel with no subscriber, then start a subscriber and inspect whether it receives the message; repeat while forcibly disconnecting the subscriber.
The message is absent after subscribing and may be lost during disconnect, confirming that Pub/Sub cannot satisfy durable at-least-once job delivery.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Add an explicit reconciliation and cutover protocol: pre-populate historical usage, disable automatic reductions until each service has established complete reporting with the new manager, and require warm-up plus health verification before deregistration. For user-ID, use conservative fixed allocations, cross-region enforcement testing, and an independently controlled rollback/kill switch; do not rely on the generic grace period as the sole safeguard.
Copying the current allocation also initializes enough historical usage data to prevent immediate automatic reduction.
Registration and deregistration cannot create an interval in which inconsistent quota decisions are enforced.
Usage-reporting completeness and freshness are comparable between the legacy and new systems.
The new manager's reduced allocation propagates consistently across all user-ID database regions.
Weeks of unchanged reported usage reliably predict future peak demand.
An automatic reduction below the user-ID database's real retained-data footprint could reject writes globally across regions, including account creation and login flows.
During migration, the service might report to one manager while enforcement or stale usage data is obtained from the other, producing inconsistent accept/reject decisions.
The claimed grace period may begin before sufficient observations are collected, allowing an unproven allocation reduction.
Allocation copies may omit reserved, archival, replication, compaction, or growth requirements that the legacy manager included.
Deregistering the legacy manager without a tested rollback path could leave the service with no effective quota enforcement or make rollback unsafe.
Migrate noncritical services through a shadow period with dual reporting and decision comparison, followed by atomic enforcement cutover. Keep automatic reductions disabled until parity and forecasting thresholds are proven, then enable them first for low-risk services and only later for user-ID under fixed safety floors and regional write-failure tests.
In staging, run user-ID with identical storage and replicated writes while the new manager is set just below current observed usage but above the proposed operational floor; then toggle manager registration during a write and inspect all regional write outcomes.
The proposal is unsafe if any region rejects a normal write, decisions differ between managers or regions, or registration transition changes enforcement before reporting is reconciled.

required_observation: Staging at 200 nodes does not represent production load/concurrency
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but replace the fleet-wide rollout with a compatibility gate followed by a production canary and measured expansion. Before broad deployment, verify exact version support, preserve health-query semantics, exercise reconnects and rolling restarts, and define automatic stop/rollback thresholds for errors, stale results, CPU, and network load.
The exact production server and client versions support streaming and `use_streaming_backend` as proposed, without silently falling back to blocking queries.
The staging workload is representative enough for the reported 60% CPU reduction to hold in production.
Streaming preserves the required freshness, filtering, consistency, and reconnect behavior for every service.
All clients can be upgraded and configured compatibly within six weeks.
Each client can safely transition and roll back while the cluster remains its only discovery path.
A broad rollout exposes every service simultaneously to missed subscriptions, stale or incomplete health data, or reconnect storms, with no discovery fallback.
A version/configuration mismatch could disable streaming or fail subscriptions, potentially increasing load through reconnect or fallback behavior.
The production mix of query filters, payload sizes, and service churn may erase the staging CPU and network savings.
Unexpected disconnect, leader-change, or rolling-upgrade behavior could reduce update freshness or temporarily exceed cluster capacity.
The untested upgrade and rollback sequence could consume the six-week window or create an unsafe prolonged mixed-version state.
Use a staged migration: validate exact compatibility and semantics in staging; enable streaming for a small, representative production cohort; monitor CPU, network, freshness, error rate, reconnects, and BoltDB/Raft health through leader changes and server restarts; then expand by service cohort with explicit rollback gates. Complement this with low-risk query scoping or request coalescing if profiling shows substantial redundant traffic.
In staging, run a representative mix of production clients and health queries against upgraded 1.10 servers with streaming enabled, including a forced client reconnect and server leader change, while comparing it with the current blocking-query baseline.
The proposal is falsified if streaming produces stale, incomplete, incorrectly filtered, or unavailable health results, causes material reconnect amplification, or fails to show a substantial CPU and network reduction after accounting for payload and churn differences.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Retain expedited propagation, but replace the unconditional 10-minute global log window with a compressed, observable rollout: begin in log mode, promote through small canaries, and reach global block within the one-hour objective only if false-positive and latency thresholds remain healthy. Require per-rule automatic rollback, confirm propagation completeness, and enforce regex complexity, evaluation-time, and CPU-budget limits before activation.
Quicksilver propagation and activation are atomic enough that no machine remains indefinitely on the old rule version.
Match counts can be attributed to each rule and monitored with sufficiently low latency to trigger rollback.
A ten-minute observation period contains traffic representative enough to expose likely false positives.
Candidate PCREs cannot cause pathological backtracking or materially increase peak CPU.
Emergency blocking and rollback do not depend on another multi-day configuration release process.
A false positive could block legitimate customer traffic globally after the log window.
Aggregate match volume can conceal false positives confined to a particular PoP, tenant, endpoint, or low-traffic region.
A computationally expensive regex could exhaust proxy CPU and cause an edge-wide availability incident.
Delayed or partial propagation could leave some machines unprotected or produce inconsistent enforcement.
The CI payload corpus may validate attack recall without adequately testing benign production traffic.

Replay a representative, anonymized production request trace against the candidate rule in shadow mode and compare benign matches and evaluation cost with the current ruleset.
Any benign matches above the team's false-positive tolerance, or material p95/p99 latency or CPU regression, would falsify the safety of immediate global promotion; negligible differences would support the expedited path.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not send an unqualified ID list directly to permanent deletion. First reconcile the product team’s list against an authoritative, typed inventory of legacy add-on installations, validate every ID with canaries and preflight checks, then soft-delete in batches and verify that other products remain intact. Use permanent deletion only after the rollback window and an explicit go/no-go approval, with reconciliation and customer-impact monitoring.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an add-on installation rather than a site or another object.
The deletion API reliably resolves IDs by object type and cannot interpret an installation ID as a site ID.
Permanent deletion is necessary before backend shutdown and complies with applicable retention requirements.
The ID list is complete, current, deduplicated, and derived from a trustworthy source.
A 2-second pause and on-call monitoring provide adequate protection against rate limits and cascading failures.
Because both sites and installations have identical 24-character ID formats, a single wrong or mistyped ID could permanently destroy an entire customer site and its other-product data.
There is no dry run, object-type validation, allowlist, or second source of truth to detect a malformed or overbroad product-team list.
Immediate permanent deletion eliminates the API’s 14-day recovery path, making endpoint mistakes or incorrect targeting unrecoverable except through slow, site-by-site backup restoration.
Partial processing can leave installations active when the backend shuts down, while retries or duplicate requests may produce unclear or destructive behavior if idempotency is not established.
The justification assumes data minimization requires erasure, but legacy customer data may instead need to remain restorable until a verified retention and shutdown process is complete.
Run a reversible migration: import a product-team-approved manifest containing expected site ID, installation ID, installation type, and list version; reconcile it against site-management records; reject unknown, ambiguous, duplicate, or non-legacy records; canary the workflow; then call mode=mark in batches of 30. Verify successful installation soft-deletion and the continued presence of unrelated products, retain an immutable audit log, and obtain explicit approval before purging only the reconciled installation IDs in a later, separately controlled run.
Inspect the deletion API contract and run a non-destructive canary or supported dry-run request using one known installation ID, one known site ID, and one deliberately invalid ID.
The proposal is safe only if the API exposes unambiguous object typing or a dry run and demonstrably rejects a site ID supplied as an installation target. If the generic ids parameter has no type discriminator, validation, or dry-run behavior, permanent batch deletion is unsafe.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not permanently delete an unvalidated list of type-ambiguous IDs. Resolve every ID against an authoritative inventory, require it to be an “Insight Legacy” installation, record the affected site and non-target objects, test a canary, and use soft deletion with a verified restore path before considering any later purge.
Every supplied ID identifies an add-on installation rather than a site or another product.
The deletion API returns enough metadata to validate the target before deletion.
Deleting the installation does not cascade into products or other site data.
Permanent deletion is authorized and necessary for compliance.
A complete site-level backup exists for every affected site.
A site ID mistakenly included in the list would permanently destroy the entire site, with recovery requiring backup-by-backup restoration.
A current or unrelated add-on ID could be purged because IDs share the same format.
Unexpected API behavior or cascading deletion could remove data belonging to other products.
Logging only responses provides no rollback, target attestation, or reliable reconciliation of what was deleted.
Waiting until the weekend may leave insufficient time to detect errors and use the 14-day restore window.
Run a preflight job that enriches each ID with object type, add-on name/version, site ID, and expected current state; reject the entire run on unknown, duplicate, site, or mismatched records. Then soft-delete a canary installation, verify the rest of that site and its other products remain intact, proceed in monitored batches, and reconcile results. Delay permanent deletion until retention requirements, authorization, backup coverage, and restoration procedures are explicitly confirmed.
Before running any deletion, resolve a small sample of the supplied IDs through the authoritative site-management inventory and compare each returned type and product identity with “Insight Legacy” add-on installation.
Any ID that resolves to a site, another add-on/product, an unknown object, or lacks authoritative type metadata proves the permanent-delete batch is unsafe as proposed.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Retain wave migration, but enable automatic reduction only after establishing a safety floor for user-ID and validating usage-decision parity between managers.
