Migrate user-ID last, switch enforcement atomically where possible, and require tested rollback before deregistering any service from the legacy manager.
The new system can accurately receive current user-ID allocations and usage reports from every region.
The grace period is long enough to detect sustained underuse before reductions become harmful, rather than merely delaying reduction by a fixed number of weeks.
User-ID has enough allocation headroom for account-data growth, replication metadata, reporting lag, and peak demand.
Deregistering a service from the legacy manager also makes the new manager authoritative without conflicting enforcement.
Quota-manager outages and stale decisions will not block user-ID database writes.
Automatic reduction could lower user-ID allocation below live or near-term storage demand, causing rejected account writes and replicated login-related impact.
Stale or out-of-order usage data could trigger an incorrect reduction or produce inconsistent enforcement.
A cutover gap or dual-authority conflict could cause nondeterministic quota decisions.
A new-system outage could block user-ID writes if enforcement fails closed.
Operational dashboards could look correct while regional enforcement or replication behavior remains unsafe.
Use the proposed waves with a user-ID exception: configure a protected minimum allocation or temporarily disable automatic reduction for user-ID, while retaining it for other services. Before each cutover, shadow or compare usage and enforcement decisions, then atomically transfer authority with rollback tested under concurrent regional writes.
Query historical user-ID usage by region and compare maximum recent usage plus observed growth against its copied allocation through the full reduction grace period.
If even peak-plus-projected-growth usage approaches the copied allocation during the grace period, the claim that weeks of buffer make universal automatic reduction safe is falsified and user-ID requires a floor or exemption.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Do not approve the stated p95 claim or 15-minute unrevoked TTL. Add Kafka-driven invalidation or an authorization snapshot, shorter bounded TTLs, singleflight/miss protection, and fail-closed Redis behavior; also validate end-to-end p95, because an 85% hit rate means at least 15% of requests still incur the roughly 180 ms permissions call.
A 15-minute delay in propagating user, account, or group revocation is acceptable.
The 85% hit rate is representative of the entire production workload, including cold documents and rare users.
A permissions-service miss takes long enough that 15% uncached requests place endpoint p95 above 120 ms.
userId, docId, and action uniquely identify a decision, with no tenant or policy-version dimension omitted.
Redis can safely be treated as authorization state and Redis failures do not trigger fail-open behavior.
A removed HR user or revoked document share remains authorized for up to 15 minutes because permission-events are ignored.
Cache stampedes during TTL expiry or cold keys can overload the permissions service and increase its p95.
The claimed roughly 40 ms endpoint p95 is incompatible with 15% misses when those misses already average about 180 ms before other work.
Fail-open handling for Redis faults would bypass authorization during an infrastructure incident.
Key collisions or omitted tenant/policy context could return another principal's authorization decision.
Retain read-through Redis caching, but consume permission-events to invalidate or update all affected keys, use a short TTL only as a recovery bound, and add request coalescing plus origin load shedding. If replay confirms that event-consistent caching cannot exceed 95% hit rate, build a continuously updated authorization snapshot with Redis and local L1 caches while retaining an explicit rebuild and rollback path.
Replay 24 hours of representative access logs through a 15-minute read-through cache model and separately measure the resulting document-request latency using measured Redis-hit and permissions-miss distributions.
Falsifies the proposal if at least 5% of requests miss the cache and the simulated or replayed endpoint p95 remains above 120 ms; the supplied 85% hit rate and approximately 180 ms miss dependency already predict this failure.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Do not enable unrestricted promotion of the West replica under asynchronous replication. Restrict automatic recovery to a fenced, recently verified East replica, enable semi-synchronous replication where supported, and explicitly integrate Orchestrator recovery with Consul plus stale-primary fencing. Permit West promotion only as an operator-approved, acknowledged-data-loss procedure; Raft consensus protects Orchestrator decisions but does not make asynchronous MySQL replication current or prevent a database split brain.
An East replica normally remains available when the East primary host fails, which is not stated.
Orchestrator is configured with a safe promotion candidate, fencing, recovery timeouts, and Consul hooks for every relevant cluster.
The application can route writes to a West-promoted primary over the existing network and tolerate approximately 60 ms plus additional connection latency.
Promoting an asynchronously replicated West node without losing acknowledged writes is acceptable, despite replication lag.
Consul updates and application client behavior will reliably converge within the one-minute objective.
West promotion can lose committed writes because asynchronous replication may not have received them; choosing the apparently most advanced replica does not eliminate this.
A network partition or stalled primary can leave the old primary accepting writes after promotion unless storage/network fencing is enforced; Orchestrator Raft quorum does not fence MySQL.
Promoting a West node while application servers remain in East may create connectivity, latency, DNS/Consul propagation, and write-availability failures.
Applying automated recovery to all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can trigger simultaneous or incorrect promotions.
A 30-second detection threshold does not guarantee recovery under one minute after detection, topology repair, Consul propagation, and application reconnection.
Use Orchestrator automation only for a pre-approved East-local replica, configure semi-synchronous replication for East replicas, fence the failed primary before promotion, and have Consul publish a versioned primary endpoint. Keep West as an explicitly operator-invoked disaster-recovery path with documented possible data loss.
During sustained writes to the East primary, record `SHOW SLAVE STATUS` on the West replica and execute a controlled primary failure followed by West promotion; compare acknowledged write IDs with rows present on the promoted replica.
If any acknowledged write is absent on the promoted West replica, or if East applications cannot route and commit writes to it within one minute, the proposed cross-region automated promotion fails the stated safety/availability objective.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Keep string serialization, but introduce it through a new API version or explicit content negotiation rather than changing every existing v1 response. Keep v1 available for legacy clients, migrate the web app immediately to the string-ID endpoint, publish a longer deprecation window for mobile and partner clients, and only regenerate SDKs after verifying backward compatibility and runtime decoding behavior.
Existing deployed clients are expected to tolerate an unannounced number-to-string response change.
Swift Codable and Moshi can be configured or are already configured to decode quoted Int64/Long values without source changes.
Approximately 40 partner integrations can upgrade their generated SDKs before the API response contract changes.
There is no separate v1 request-path or SDK type contract that would also require coordinated changes.
Clients can distinguish or negotiate a string-ID response before parsing it.
Stock Swift Codable decoding into Int64 rejects a JSON string, potentially causing order lookup and list failures in deployed iOS versions.
Moshi commonly rejects a quoted value for a Long property unless an adapter is configured, potentially crashing or failing Android responses.
Regenerating SDKs changes generated source types to String and can cause compile-time breakage for partner applications that cannot upgrade immediately.
Changing the v1 OpenAPI contract in place can invalidate existing generated documentation, mocks, tests, and integrations while providing no rollback path.
A two-week deployment window is too short for self-serve partners and store-update lag to adopt a breaking contract, extending the corruption problem or causing outages.
Add a string-ID representation under /v2 or an explicitly negotiated media type/header, retain the existing v1 representation during a negotiated deprecation period, and migrate first-party clients to it. At the same time, add compatibility tests and telemetry for response-format selection and decoding failures; do not alter ID generation.
Run one compatibility test matrix using the unchanged, currently deployed client versions and representative generated partner SDKs against a sample response containing "id":"1234567890123456789", decoding it as Swift Int64, Kotlin Moshi Long, generated OpenAPI int64/string SDK types, and JavaScript Number.
The proposal is falsified as a drop-in v1 change if any unchanged client fails decoding, changes the ID type, or produces an incorrect value; successful decoding alone does not address generated-source or partner rollout compatibility.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Replace the three-month branch and single cut-over with incremental strangler migration: first capture current behavior as characterization and golden-invoice tests, then introduce an immutable billing-core behind an adapter and migrate one plan cohort at a time. Run old and new calculators in shadow mode, establish invoice-level parity across all 37 plans, and retain rollback and legacy grandfathered-plan paths until production evidence is sufficient.
The current implementation's behavior is sufficiently documented or reproducible to serve as the compatibility specification.
All 37 plans can be represented by the proposed domain model without losing historical proration, tax, payment, or notification behavior.
A three-month branch can remain synchronized with roughly 40 weekly main-branch merges without excessive conflict and integration cost.
A comprehensive production invoice corpus can be obtained for replay and comparison.
Services can be migrated incrementally behind a stable adapter rather than requiring an atomic release.
Low happy-path coverage is likely to conceal proration and mutation-order edge cases, causing incorrect customer invoices or charges.
The long-lived branch will diverge from main, making merges unsafe and potentially discarding fixes introduced during the migration.
A single cut-over concentrates unknown failures across all plans and all five services, with limited ability to isolate or roll back individual cases.
Testing only billing-core will not detect integration differences in tax, payments, notifications, persistence, or service orchestration.
Deleting the implementation before parity evidence is available removes the only known behavior oracle and substantially increases incident and recovery risk.
Use a continuously integrated strangler migration. First build a shared adapter around the mutable BillingContext and add characterization tests plus historical invoice golden files. Then implement immutable domain types and dual-run both calculators in shadow mode without changing customer-facing results. Migrate current plans in small cohorts, followed by the 11 grandfathered plans, using feature flags, reconciliation dashboards, and per-cohort rollback; remove legacy code only after sustained invoice parity.
Create one replay test that runs a stratified sample of recent historical invoices covering all 37 plans through the proposed billing-core and compares normalized line items, taxes, totals, credits, and proration components against the persisted production results.
Any non-zero unexplained difference falsifies the claim that the new model can preserve existing invoices and shows that a single cut-over would be unsafe; zero differences across the sample would support, but not prove, migration readiness.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not perform a direct type change or rename on the 900M-row table. Add a nullable major-unit NUMERIC(19,3) column with expand/backfill/switch/contract, dual-write it, and gate reporting cutover on complete reconciliation. Preserve the existing integer column during rollout rather than changing its representation in place.
The existing amount values are integer minor units whose scale varies by currency, not major-unit numbers that can safely be stored as NUMERIC(19,4).
PostgreSQL can complete the ALTER with acceptable lock duration, replica lag, storage use, and rollback behavior on a 900M-row table.
All application versions and every reporting/export consumer can tolerate the renamed column and new numeric representation during deployment.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the intended wire and reporting format despite currencies using zero, two, or three minor-unit digits.
Historical three-decimal values' lost precision can be ignored or recovered from another source.
A table rewrite or long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock can breach the 99.95% availability SLO.
Renaming the column breaks mixed-version deployments and any consumer not included in the three query updates.
Leaving existing values numerically unchanged (for example, 1234 cents) while presenting them as major units produces orders that are 100 times too large.
Changing all integer values into a fixed four-decimal representation corrupts currency semantics and can misstate historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values.
The migration may exhaust disk or delay replication, causing checkout and reporting outages.
Use the additive NUMERIC(19,3) major-unit migration described in the independent position, with currency-aware backfill, rate limiting, dual-write compatibility, reconciliation, and a separately gated reporting cutover.
Run a read-only semantic check joining a representative sample of orders to currency metadata: compare the stored integer amount with the expected major-unit value (for example, integer 1234 cents for a two-decimal currency should become 12.34, not 1234).
If the proposed ALTER leaves existing values numerically unchanged, as its stated approach does, it confirms that the column is not a correct major-unit representation; additionally, a production-like migration dry run showing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock or rewrite exceeding the deployment/SLO window independently falsifies the deployment plan.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but restrict promotion by replica region, verified replication state, and maximum acceptable lag; add reliable fencing and route applications through a dedicated database endpoint whose update is tested with existing connection pools. Do not claim Raft prevents split brain by itself, and validate acknowledged-write loss and end-to-end recovery time in network-partition game days before production automation.
A promoted West replica can serve writes within Rails timeout and latency budgets.
Orchestrator can identify the most up-to-date replica and safely verify binlog continuity.
Raft availability and quorum are independent of the failed database host or East network path.
Consul and Rails clients promptly replace pooled connections to the failed primary.
Recovered replicas can rejoin without incompatible binlogs, missing GTIDs, or topology corruption.
A partitioned but still writable old primary can form a dual-primary topology and diverge data.
Asynchronous failover can lose recently acknowledged East writes even if quorum approved the decision.
A West primary can cause connection, transaction, or pool timeout failures that exceed the one-minute objective.
Insufficient fencing or lag checks can promote a stale replica and then cause irreversible replication conflicts.
Consul propagation, stale resolver caches, or pooled connections may leave applications targeting the old primary after promotion.
Use guarded Orchestrator automation with an explicit candidate policy: prefer a healthy East replica, require verified lag/binlog eligibility, reserve West promotion for a declared disaster condition, fence the old primary, and update a stable database proxy or service endpoint. Semi-synchronous cross-region replication is a possible separate enhancement if the measured latency cost is acceptable.
Run one isolated game day that blocks all East-to-West database traffic, kills the East primary, and measure from failure injection to successful Rails reads and writes while recording failed or unacknowledged transactions, recovery duration, primary-host writability, and West-primary latency.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary remains independently writable, acknowledged writes are lost beyond the accepted bound, recovery exceeds 60 seconds, or normal Rails writes fail or materially breach latency/timeout limits through the promoted West replica.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Retain Redis caching, but add permission-events-driven invalidation or versioned entries and a short TTL fallback to bound revocation staleness. Also address cache stampedes and validate the latency model explicitly: an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests still take roughly the permissions-service path, so the 95th percentile cannot be assumed to become 40 ms unless misses are made much faster or occur in under 5% of requests.
A 15-minute stale-allow window is acceptable for unshare, account deletion, and group-membership changes.
The live workload will have enough locality to keep misses below the threshold needed for the p95 target, or misses can be served through a faster path.
Redis can sustain the projected key rate and memory footprint with acceptable tail latency and failover behavior.
Permission decisions can be safely cached by user, document, and action without additional context or hidden policy inputs.
The permissions-events stream can be consumed and mapped to affected cache entries or versions.
A revoked user may retain document access for up to 15 minutes, potentially including access following HR account removal.
At the reported 85% hit rate, the uncached 15% can still determine p95, leaving the 120 ms budget unmet.
Synchronized expiry or correlated revocations can produce a permissions-service stampede and cascading latency.
Redis failure or cluster hotspots may either block authorization or cause unsafe fallback behavior.
A log-replay hit rate may not represent live hit rate because real request locality, key cardinality, and decision churn may differ.
Use a Redis read-through cache with event-driven invalidation or permission-versioned entries, plus a short TTL safety net, stale-while-revalidate for stale entries where policy permits, and request coalescing for concurrent misses. Require measured miss rate and miss-path latency to demonstrate the p95 target before broad rollout.
Run a representative shadow-cache replay and calculate p95 from the measured cache-hit and cache-miss paths, while injecting a share-revocation event and measuring how long a previously cached allow remains usable.
The proposal is falsified if p95 remains above 120 ms at the observed hit rate, or if revocation remains accepted beyond the approved staleness window; results near 40 ms with sub-5% misses would support it.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Add explicit primary fencing before promotion and a Consul state machine that publishes the endpoint only after the promoted MySQL instance is writable and replication topology is stable. Restrict routine failover to deterministically prioritized East replicas, keep West as disaster recovery, and measure detection, promotion, and client reconnection convergence separately. Test acknowledged-write loss, transient stalls, stale replicas, manual topology changes, and connection-pool behavior rather than testing only host kills.
A supported fencing mechanism can revoke the failed primary's write capability before promotion.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum does not fence MySQL or prevent a surviving isolated primary from accepting writes.
Replica lag is low enough that selecting the most up-to-date replica does not lose acknowledged transactions.
Consul can atomically or sequentially gate endpoint publication on verified MySQL writability.
Applications and connection pools converge on a changed Consul endpoint without repeatedly retaining stale connections.
An isolated primary may continue accepting writes after replica promotion, causing split brain and divergent data.
Asynchronous failover may silently lose acknowledged writes present only on the failed primary.
Service discovery may route clients before the promoted server is writable or fully reconfigured.
Selecting a West replica for an East failure introduces cross-region latency and exposes the normal path to remote replication lag.
Enabling automation for all clusters without region-specific candidate priorities and conflict controls could promote unsafe or geographically distant replicas.
Use fenced, Orchestrator-driven East-local failover with deterministic candidate priorities, reserve West for regional disaster recovery, and publish the Consul endpoint through an explicit post-promotion writability state machine.
In staging, isolate one primary from Orchestrator and all replicas while continuing to execute successful local writes, then permit automated promotion and query both database identities for new writes.
The proposal is unsafe if the replica can be promoted while the isolated primary still accepts writes; safety requires the old primary to be reliably fenced before promotion.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Keep amount as an integer count of minor units; KWD, BHD, and OMR fils fit naturally without changing the column type. Add or verify immutable currency-code storage, validate values against each currency's exponent, and update formatting/reporting logic to use that exponent. If range analysis requires BIGINT, plan a separately validated online schema change rather than combining it with this release.
The release process can update all code consumers atomically with the schema change.
No long-running transaction or old application instance will block or retain incompatible access during the ALTER TABLE.
The table and replicas have enough temporary space, WAL capacity, and lag tolerance for a full-table rewrite.
No unlisted reports, jobs, exports, or integrations directly reference orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the required storage contract rather than merely an integer minor-unit representation.
The pre-deploy migration renames amount before old pods are replaced, so checkout and other application requests can fail immediately.
Converting INTEGER to NUMERIC requires rewriting a roughly 900M-row table and can hold disruptive locks long enough to exceed the release window or violate the checkout SLO.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or disk space, and cause streaming-replica lag.
The three reporting jobs fail as soon as the rename commits unless they are separately gated or deployed first.
The NUMERIC(19,4) contract permits four-decimal fractional values even though the business field represents minor units, potentially allowing invalid data.
Retain orders.amount as an exact integer minor-unit amount and make currency-aware validation and presentation explicit. Store or join an immutable ISO currency code, map it to an exponent, and ensure serializers and reporting SQL format KWD, BHD, and OMR values with three decimal digits. This avoids schema locking, storage growth, semantic conversion, and rollout incompatibility; perform a range check before deciding whether an online BIGINT migration is ever needed.
At the intended deployment time, run the ALTER in a transaction with a short lock_timeout, then roll it back: BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4), RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; ROLLBACK;
A lock timeout or ALTER error while any normal application or reporting session is active falsifies the pre-deploy compatibility assumption and demonstrates that the migration cannot safely precede rolling replacement.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but run the new manager in shadow/dual-report mode and compare usage, allocations, grace-period boundaries, and rejection decisions before making it authoritative. Cut over services and regions incrementally behind an enforcement flag, with an explicit rollback procedure that freezes or synchronizes allocation state; enable automatic reduction only after parity, load, replication-lag, and failover testing. Do not deregister the legacy manager until a bounded observation period, telemetry/audit validation, and incident rollback procedures are complete.
Copying the current allocation is sufficient to preserve authorization state and does not lose pending reductions or grace-period metadata.
The grace period reliably delays automatic allocation changes without delaying quota enforcement or creating a large rejection window.
The new manager can make authoritative quota decisions synchronously for user-ID writes, including during replication lag and regional failover.
Legacy and new managers produce equivalent decisions for production usage, allocation reductions, and grace-period edge cases.
A rollback can preserve or reconstruct the last authoritative allocation state without inconsistent authorization.
Directly deregistering the legacy manager after copying allocations can reject legitimate user-ID database writes because of timing, semantic, or propagation differences.
Enabling automatic reduction universally can unexpectedly shrink allocations or trigger false rejections before parity and grace-period behavior are validated.
Cross-region failover could use stale or divergent quota state and block replicated writes or allow over-quota operations.
Fallback after the new manager has reclaimed allocations could make legacy and new authorization states inconsistent.
Usage and allocation dashboards alone may not provide decision-level auditability, discrepancy detection, or proof that rollback and incident procedures work.
Use a staged shadow-and-cutover design: mirror reports and allocations while legacy remains authoritative, establish discrepancy thresholds and an end date, then migrate low-risk services and user-ID by region behind a reversible enforcement flag. Preserve allocation state during rollback and retire legacy only after synchronous-write, concurrent-request, replication-lag, failover, telemetry, and operational-readiness tests pass.
Replay a production-representative history of usage and allocation changes through both managers, including grace-period boundaries and allocation reductions, and compare their synchronous allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision mismatch, especially a new-manager rejection where legacy allows a valid write or a reduction occurring before the intended grace-period boundary, falsifies the claimed safe direct cutover.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep wave-based migration and user-ID-last, but add shadow-mode decision comparison, explicit exit criteria per wave, and independently reversible cutover controls. Do not enable automatic quota reduction on the first authoritative cutovers: validate reporting completeness and grace-period behavior first, then enable it service by service; dashboards alone are not safety controls.
Copying an allocation preserves its effective value, unit, and reset/grace-period semantics in the new system.
Deregistering a service immediately redirects all usage reports and enforcement checks to only the new manager.
Usage reporting is complete and timely enough that automatic reduction cannot mistake missing telemetry for low usage.
The new manager's decisions are consistent across regions before user-ID begins relying on them.
Service owners can detect and reverse a bad cutover before user-ID writes are affected.
A missing or delayed report may be treated as low usage and trigger an inappropriate allocation reduction.
Deregistration can create an enforcement gap if old and new registrations do not update atomically.
Semantic differences in grace periods or allocation units can cause premature capacity reclamation.
User-ID replication may apply different quota decisions across regions.
A single quota mistake can reject account writes globally, making the wave difficult to reverse.
Usage/allocation dashboards may display apparently valid data while omitting stale, duplicated, or rejected reports.
Use a staged strangler design: run the new manager in shadow mode, compare every prospective accept/reject and allocation-reduction decision with the current authority, and promote one low-risk service at a time behind reversible flags. Keep user-ID shadowed through the final quarter and cut it over only after regional lag, failover, and partition tests; preserve a time-boxed rollback path before shutting down legacy.
Replay historical and synthetic low-usage, missing-report, stale-report, threshold-crossing, and grace-period-boundary events through both managers and compare accept/reject and allocation-reduction decisions.
The proposal is supported only if decisions match for all valid telemetry and the new system demonstrably fails safe—never reducing allocation or rejecting writes—during missing, stale, or divergent telemetry; any silent discrepancy or unsafe fallback falsifies readiness.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Do not use an in-process mutex as the correctness boundary. Implement a database-backed atomic claim using a conditional update such as `UPDATE coupons SET redemption_state='pending', order_id=... WHERE code=... AND redeemed_at IS NULL AND redemption_state='pending'`, requiring exactly one affected row; use a unique constraint on `orderId` and an idempotency key for retries, then finalize or compensate the claim around charging.
Each coupon is redeemed through only one Node.js process at a time, which is false with 4-12 replicas.
Concurrent requests for a code reach the same process, which a round-robin Service does not guarantee.
The charge provider offers idempotency keyed by coupon or order.
Coupon and order records can be committed independently from the external charge.
The existing Prisma schema permits an atomic conditional update or can be changed this week.
Requests routed to different pods hold different mutexes and can both pass the redeemedAt check.
Both requests can charge customers before either process persists redeemedAt.
A process crash after charging can leave a coupon pending and permanently prevent later redemption unless recovery exists.
Retries after a client timeout can duplicate the external charge unless the provider receives a stable idempotency key.
A process-local Map can grow or retain mutexes incorrectly if cleanup is not exception-safe.
Use Postgres as the serialization authority. Atomically transition an available coupon to a pending claim with a conditional update and verify `count === 1`; persist a stable idempotency/claim identifier, charge using that identifier, and then mark it redeemed. Add explicit handling for pending-claim recovery and unique constraints preventing one order from claiming multiple coupons. The proposed unit test should be supplemented with a multi-process integration test against one database.
Run two redeem requests for the same coupon concurrently against two independently started application instances sharing the same Postgres database, with a controllable charge mock, then assert that at most one charge occurs.
The current proposal is falsified if both instances succeed and invoke charge twice; the replacement is supported if exactly one atomic claim and one charge occur.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the wave migration, but add a shadow period and require near-zero enforcement-decision equivalence before each service is deregistered from the legacy manager. Treat user-ID as a separately approved cutover with cross-region failure testing, conservative temporary headroom, and an immediate rollback switch; do not assume the grace period alone makes automatic allocation reduction safe.
Copying an allocation preserves the exact units, effective time, grace-period state, and regional consistency used for enforcement.
Both managers make identical enforcement decisions for the same usage history.
Allocation and usage timestamps and telemetry are accurate and comparable, including during replica failover.
Deregistering the legacy registration does not bypass required reporting or audit integrations.
Automatic quota reduction is paused or guarded during migration anomalies and has sufficient service-specific headroom.
An unobserved semantic or configuration mismatch can reject legitimate writes immediately when a service moves.
For user-ID, inconsistent enforcement across replicas can turn a quota decision into failed logins, account updates, or region-dependent behavior.
Weeks-long grace periods may still be unsafe for bursty services, delayed telemetry, or allocation changes near the reduction threshold.
Direct deregistration removes the legacy fallback before migration behavior is validated, making rollback and incident comparison harder.
Dashboards provide visibility but do not prove enforcement equivalence, completeness of reporting, or cross-region consistency.
Use a staged migration per wave: dual-report to the new manager in shadow mode, replay recent histories and compare decisions, add bounded headroom while monitoring, then switch enforcement behind a reversible flag. Validate user-ID with fault-injection and cross-region write tests before its cutover, and shut down the legacy system only after a bounded observation period and audit confirmation.
Replay each service's recent usage and allocation history through both managers in a non-enforcing environment, then run a cross-region write test at the quota boundary for user-ID; compare the resulting allow/reject decisions.
Any material decision divergence, stale or incomplete usage signal, or region-dependent allow/reject result falsifies the safety of direct registration and deregistration; consistent results support proceeding with gated cutovers.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not migrate job dispatch to Redis Pub/Sub: it is an at-most-once, non-durable transport, so subscriber disconnects or worker restarts can silently lose jobs while AOF does not provide message replay. Use Redis Streams with consumer groups, explicit acknowledgements, pending-entry recovery, and a tested retention/retry/DLQ policy, while retaining RabbitMQ until failure and recovery tests pass. Avoid running both systems as active independent consumers for payment and fulfilment jobs unless duplicate side effects are prevented.
Every job must survive worker crashes, pod termination, Redis client reconnects, and transient network failures.
Job processing is at-least-once and handlers can be idempotent or use deduplication.
AOF persistence and the existing Redis topology provide sufficient durability and availability for dispatch.
Subscribers can independently discover and recover all messages missed while disconnected.
The operational team can monitor and maintain Redis Streams pending entries, trimming, retries, and dead-letter handling.
Pub/Sub messages are not retained, so a disconnected or restarted worker loses queued jobs with no acknowledgement or recovery mechanism.
The proposed worker retry wrapper cannot retry a message that was never delivered, and repeated deployments make this failure routine.
Duplicate or split processing during dual operation could repeat payment-provider, fulfilment, email, or indexing side effects.
AOF persistence does not convert Pub/Sub into a durable queue and may still lose data under Redis or storage failure.
A Redis outage would affect both dispatch and existing caching/rate-limiting workloads, increasing blast radius.
Use Redis Streams on the already-operated Redis deployment for durable dispatch, with one consumer group per job type or worker role, XADD publishing, XREADGROUP consumption, XACK after successful handling, and explicit recovery of pending entries. Configure replication, persistence, maxlen/retention, retry/DLQ handling, dead-letter visibility, and idempotent handlers; migrate traffic gradually without allowing RabbitMQ and Redis Streams to execute the same jobs concurrently.
In a disposable Redis instance, publish one message to a Pub/Sub channel, disconnect the subscriber, publish a second message, then reconnect and inspect what the subscriber receives; repeat the equivalent test with a Redis Stream consumer group.
If the disconnected subscriber misses the message after reconnect, or the Stream test cannot recover and acknowledge it after consumer termination, the Pub/Sub proposal is falsified; successful Stream recovery supports the replacement.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain immediate Quicksilver propagation, but do not make a global block decision solely from a 10-minute log window. Require explicit false-positive and performance gates, use a very short global or representative canary in log mode, and define an automatic rollback/kill switch based on error rate, latency, CPU, and match-volume anomalies. Ramp blocking across PoPs or traffic percentages within the hour, with an emergency mechanism independent of the normal rollout pipeline.
CI payload coverage predicts production behavior for a newly disclosed attack.
The new regex cannot cause pathological backtracking or excessive evaluation cost on attacker-controlled input.
Quicksilver propagation is sufficiently fast and atomic across all PoPs to meet the one-hour objective.
A 10-minute log interval provides statistically and operationally meaningful visibility into false positives and match volume.
The WAF has reliable real-time telemetry and a tested mechanism to disable or roll back a bad rule.
A catastrophic or merely expensive regex could consume the proxy CPU shared with TLS and HTTP handling, causing latency, timeouts, or outages across customer traffic.
The rule may block legitimate requests that were absent from the benign CI corpus, creating a global availability or business-impact incident.
A low or misleading match volume can be caused by logging failures, sampling, traffic-shape differences, or an incomplete attack signature, leading to premature blocking.
A globally propagated bad rule cannot be recalled quickly enough, and a 10-minute observation window may be too short to observe rare benign traffic.
Simultaneous deployment of many rules may create aggregate CPU or evaluation-budget overruns even when each rule passes isolated tests.

Replay the rule against a representative production request corpus, including benign traffic and adversarial regex inputs, at projected peak concurrency, and compare proxy CPU utilization and request latency with the rule disabled.
The proposal is falsified if the rule causes unacceptable CPU growth, latency, timeouts, or evaluation-budget exhaustion under realistic traffic; otherwise this validates only the performance prerequisite, not the safety of global blocking.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the header-bit approach, but do not make an unverified global client-side launch the release mechanism. Add explicit compatibility tests, reject or safely quarantine any legacy Power Peg path before RLP enablement, deploy an identical verified artifact with post-deploy build/configuration checks, and use an allowlisted canary with monitoring and rollback before broad client activation.
No current or future non-RLP client, gateway, replay tool, retry path, or intermediary can set the bit.
The RLP specification permits the bit to carry order-level routing intent and does not require distinct semantics from Power Peg.
Every client that will set the bit can be released and coordinated with the router before launch, despite the unchanged wire layout.
Removing the old Power Peg implementation cannot invalidate persisted state, hidden configuration, or downstream assumptions.
The router can distinguish an RLP order from an invalid or unexpected legacy order and fail closed.
A month of zero observed bits is not proof that all traffic sources, historical messages, retries, or future integrations leave it unset.
A client or gateway may set the bit based on stale Power Peg documentation or a copied conditional, unexpectedly activating RLP.
The manual eight-server deployment can leave mixed binaries or configurations, producing inconsistent order behavior.
Deleting Power Peg in the same release creates a hazardous rollback if any legacy producer can still emit the bit.
Enabling all RLP-eligible clients simultaneously could expose router defects at the full ~3M-orders/day load before detection.
For RLP decisions that can be made from client/account identity or router policy, use a server-side allowlist and keep the bit unused until a formally versioned per-order contract is available. If the program explicitly requires per-order signaling, the proposed bit is preferable, but only with the safeguards above.
Run a repository-wide static and binary/protocol audit of every encoder, decoder, configuration default, retry/forwarding path, and client release artifact for assignments to the target header bit, followed by replay tests of legacy Power Peg configurations against the new router.
Any non-RLP path capable of setting the bit, any decoder that treats it as Power Peg, or any legacy configuration that remains effective falsifies safe direct reuse; otherwise it supports proceeding with canary rollout.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Retain the billing-core domain-model direction, but replace the three-month big-bang cutover with incremental, cohort-based migration. First freeze current behavior with characterization and golden-master tests derived from production invoice scenarios, then shadow-compare billing-core outputs before moving small plan cohorts, keeping the old path available for rollback throughout migration.
All invoice-relevant legacy behavior can be captured from production scenarios and encoded as executable tests.
No plan-specific behavior is hidden outside the five services or depends on unrecorded operational data.
The long-lived branch can remain compatible with roughly 40 weekly main-branch merges touching billing code.
A one-time cutover can be exhaustively tested and safely rolled back.
The three engineers can maintain feature parity and migration infrastructure simultaneously.
Unknown proration, grandfathering, tax, payment, or notification edge cases could produce incorrect invoices after cutover.
The branch will accumulate severe integration drift and merge conflicts over approximately three months.
Deleting the old implementation at cutover removes the practical rollback path and makes diagnosis expensive.
Low test coverage and concentrated domain knowledge make a large rewrite likely to omit undocumented six-year-old rules.
Late discovery of parity failures could force an emergency extension of the old system, eliminating the claimed maintenance benefit.
Use a strangler migration around billing-core: establish production-derived compatibility fixtures, implement one plan or service boundary at a time, run shadow calculations against live inputs, compare complete invoice artifacts and side effects, and migrate cohorts gradually while retaining a tested rollback route.
Build a one-off replay harness that generates invoices for a representative production-derived corpus covering all 37 plans, especially the 11 grandfathered plans, across proration, tax, payment-failure, and notification scenarios, and compare the current implementation with the billing-core model.
Any unexplained difference in line items, totals, taxes, proration, invoice identity, or resulting side effects falsifies the claim that a single final cutover is sufficiently controlled; exact parity supports incremental migration but not the big-bang rollout.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain an expedited path, but require representative canary/shadow validation, regex execution-cost limits, benign-traffic false-positive thresholds, and an automatically enforced global rollback before blocking. Publish first in log mode with per-rule match/error/latency telemetry, then promote only after a defined observation window; make block activation and rollback atomic, versioned, and audited.
The CI corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives and catastrophic backtracking.
Log-mode evaluation has bounded CPU and latency impact despite running on every request.
Quicksilver propagation is strongly consistent enough to prevent machines from enforcing different rule versions during activation.
A ten-minute observation window is sufficient to expose false positives and performance degradation.
Operators can reliably identify and disable a bad rule globally within minutes.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic across all PoPs after only ten minutes of observation.
A pathological PCRE pattern could consume substantial proxy CPU, causing latency spikes, outages, or TLS/HTTP starvation even in log mode.
Incomplete, delayed, or partially failed configuration propagation could produce inconsistent enforcement and an unreliably reversible incident.
Low attack volume or an unrepresentative log sample could permit a harmful rule to be promoted prematurely.
The proposed path lacks an explicit emergency kill switch, automated rollback, version pinning, and promotion criteria.
Implement a risk-tiered fast lane: validate the rule against both attack and benign corpora, enforce static and runtime regex cost limits, shadow it on a small representative canary, then propagate globally in log mode with automated thresholds. Promote to block only after the canary and global observation pass, while providing a tested one-action global rollback.
Run the candidate rule in shadow mode on a representative production PoP while replaying the benign corpus and peak-shaped request load, comparing p99 latency, CPU, error rate, and benign matches against the same traffic without the rule.
Any material p99/CPU increase, request errors, or benign matches would falsify the claim that immediate global log-mode deployment is safe; negligible impact and zero benign matches would support proceeding to a controlled rollout.

required_observation: No characterisation tests of current behaviour before rewrite
review_text:
Keep the new billing-core direction, but replace the three-month, single-cutover migration with characterization, immutable/versioned domain contracts, and incremental adapter cutover per service or billing path. Establish shadow invoice comparisons and explicit rollback before deleting legacy code; do not delete it until parity evidence covers all 37 plans, grandfathering, proration, taxes, payments, and execution-order effects.
The current invoice behavior can be characterized accurately before the new model is frozen.
The proposed model can represent all historical proration and grandfathering exceptions without lossy abstractions.
Services can be migrated or shadowed independently behind compatibility adapters.
Invoice parity can be measured for identical inputs despite current mutable-context behavior.
The team can enforce billing changes, compatibility tests, and retirement tracking across frequent incoming PRs.
A clean model may silently change legacy rounding, proration, tax, payment, or state-order behavior, producing incorrect customer invoices.
A single final cutover creates a high-blast-radius release with inadequate rollback and incident containment.
Deleting legacy code immediately removes the reference implementation before edge cases are discovered.
Porting all plans and all services in parallel concentrates coordination risk and makes diagnosis of parity failures difficult.
Ongoing feature work may continue modifying the old path, causing the new implementation to become stale or forcing incompatible changes.
Create versioned, deterministic billing functions with immutable inputs and outputs, while retaining the legacy engine as a shadow oracle. Characterize representative and adversarial invoice scenarios first, migrate one bounded path at a time through adapters, compare outputs and side effects, and remove legacy code only after a defined parity and rollback gate. Represent simple plan terms in data, but preserve genuinely exceptional rules as explicit versioned strategies rather than forcing them into a universal abstraction.
Build a replay harness that runs the current billing path and billing-v2 on the same captured inputs for all 37 plans, especially the 11 grandfathered plans, covering upgrades, downgrades, cancellations, backdating, proration, taxes, and payment timing.
Any invoice difference attributable to rounding, amounts, line items, tax, payment allocation, or execution order falsifies the claim that a single cutover is safe; a completely clean replay would support proceeding, but still would not establish production cutover safety.

required_observation: Restrict automatic promotion to the same region / require explicit decision for cross-region
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but require explicit old-primary fencing, an approved promotion policy, pre-promotion topology/lag checks, and cluster-by-cluster canarying. Do not automatically select the most up-to-date replica regardless of region; use a designated preference and account for East application latency, replication lag, and a declared RPO.
A West promotion remains reachable from East application servers with acceptable latency and connection stability.
The old East primary can be conclusively fenced before the promoted replica accepts writes.
Orchestrator detection plus Raft election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and discovery convergence consistently complete within 60 seconds.
The chosen replica's replication lag and connection state provide a tolerable committed-write RPO.
Orchestrator 3.x, MySQL 5.7, and pseudo-GTID behave correctly through these failure and recovery transitions.
A network partition can trigger promotion without fencing the old primary, causing split brain and divergent writes.
Promoting a lagging West replica can lose committed transactions despite pseudo-GTID.
Automated reconfiguration can stall or partially complete, extending write unavailability or leaving inconsistent topology.
An unreachable West primary can make East applications fail or suffer unacceptable latency because service discovery alone does not ensure connectivity.
Applying automation to all clusters at once can create simultaneous elections, discovery churn, and an operator overload during the failure.

In a production-like staging environment, run one isolated end-to-end game day: continuously commit marked writes, hard-kill the East primary, record write errors and failure timing, and verify fencing, selected replica, data present, topology repair, and application recovery.
The proposal is supported only if there is a single authoritative primary, no unexplained lost acknowledged writes, all application writes recover within 60 seconds, replicas converge, and service discovery settles consistently; a split brain, unacceptable loss, or recovery beyond 60 seconds falsifies it.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not run this migration on the 410-GB table before deployment. Use an additive transition: add a nullable three-decimal-capable column or a separate canonical representation, deploy currency-aware dual writes, backfill in throttled primary-key batches, and switch reports only after reconciliation. Retire the legacy column later.
Every active report or application query is blocked throughout the ALTER, and the operational platform explicitly tolerates that outage.
Old application pods will not reference or write to the column named amount after the pre-deploy migration renames it.
A currency-specific conversion rule exists for historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values; preserving the stored integer does not itself normalize minor-unit scales.
NUMERIC(19,4) is intentionally compatible with all consumers and will not introduce a four-decimal minor-unit interpretation.
The PostgreSQL instance has enough free disk, WAL capacity, and maintenance time for a full-table rewrite.
INTEGER-to-NUMERIC conversion requires rewriting roughly 900M rows while holding an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes for hours or longer.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or filesystem capacity, and create replication lag or disk pressure.
Renaming amount before replacing old pods can cause immediate unknown-column failures during the 25-minute rolling deployment.
Atomic DDL only guarantees commit or rollback; it does not make an operation nonblocking, short, or operationally safe.
A nightly schedule does not mitigate a schema-level outage and conflicts with the 99.95% monthly checkout SLO; rollback would require another expensive rewrite or recovery process.
Add a nullable canonical column, preferably BIGINT in thousandths only if currency is explicitly available, or NUMERIC with a deliberate three-decimal scale. Avoid rewriting existing data: deploy compatible dual-write code first, then backfill small indexed batches with rate limits, lag monitoring, reconciliation, and completion criteria. Update reports after all rows and writers are verified, and remove the legacy column in a later release.
In one database session run BEGIN; SELECT amount FROM orders LIMIT 1. In a second session run SET lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); then ROLLBACK.
A lock_timeout error confirms that ordinary reads prevent the proposed migration from starting; if it unexpectedly succeeds, that only shows no lock contention at that instant and does not demonstrate that the 410-GB rewrite is operationally acceptable.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but require explicit old-primary fencing, an approved promotion policy, pre-promotion topology/lag checks, and cluster-by-cluster canarying. Do not automatically select the most up-to-date replica regardless of region; use a designated preference and account for East application latency, replication lag, and a declared RPO.
A West promotion remains reachable from East application servers with acceptable latency and connection stability.
The old East primary can be conclusively fenced before the promoted replica accepts writes.
Orchestrator detection plus Raft election, promotion, replica reconfiguration, and discovery convergence consistently complete within 60 seconds.
The chosen replica's replication lag and connection state provide a tolerable committed-write RPO.
Orchestrator 3.x, MySQL 5.7, and pseudo-GTID behave correctly through these failure and recovery transitions.
A network partition can trigger promotion without fencing the old primary, causing split brain and divergent writes.
Promoting a lagging West replica can lose committed transactions despite pseudo-GTID.
Automated reconfiguration can stall or partially complete, extending write unavailability or leaving inconsistent topology.
An unreachable West primary can make East applications fail or suffer unacceptable latency because service discovery alone does not ensure connectivity.
Applying automation to all clusters at once can create simultaneous elections, discovery churn, and an operator overload during the failure.

In a production-like staging environment, run one isolated end-to-end game day: continuously commit marked writes, hard-kill the East primary, record write errors and failure timing, and verify fencing, selected replica, data present, topology repair, and application recovery.
The proposal is supported only if there is a single authoritative primary, no unexplained lost acknowledged writes, all application writes recover within 60 seconds, replicas converge, and service discovery settles consistently; a split brain, unacceptable loss, or recovery beyond 60 seconds falsifies it.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Do not treat Orchestrator Raft quorum as MySQL split-brain protection: it coordinates Orchestrator instances, not the old primary. Enable automated promotion only when the primary is reliably fenced or otherwise proven dead, and base promotion on a verified replica freshness signal; also test network partitions and recovery of the old primary, not only host kills.
An unreachable primary cannot continue serving writes.
Orchestrator can reliably identify the replica with the greatest applied position before promotion.
Application clients promptly and consistently honor service-discovery changes.
West can accept production write traffic at acceptable latency and capacity.
Recovered former primaries cannot rejoin as writable nodes.
A network partition can cause a replica to be promoted while the isolated primary continues accepting writes, creating concurrent writable primaries and divergence.
Asynchronous cross-region promotion can lose acknowledged transactions committed on the old primary but not yet replicated.
Incorrect lag or position comparison can promote a stale replica and make data loss substantially larger.
A West promotion can sharply increase write latency for East-only application servers and may exceed their timeout or capacity assumptions.

In staging, isolate the East primary from Orchestrator and the replica while leaving its application path writable, commit distinct transactions through both paths, and observe whether promotion occurs.
If Orchestrator promotes the replica while the isolated primary still commits writes, the design is unsafe; safety requires no promotion until the old primary is fenced or demonstrated incapable of writes.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not permanently delete an unvalidated list of type-ambiguous IDs. Resolve every ID against an authoritative inventory, require it to be an “Insight Legacy” installation, record the affected site and non-target objects, test a canary, and use soft deletion with a verified restore path before considering any later purge.
Every supplied ID identifies an add-on installation rather than a site or another product.
The deletion API returns enough metadata to validate the target before deletion.
Deleting the installation does not cascade into products or other site data.
Permanent deletion is authorized and necessary for compliance.
A complete site-level backup exists for every affected site.
A site ID mistakenly included in the list would permanently destroy the entire site, with recovery requiring backup-by-backup restoration.
A current or unrelated add-on ID could be purged because IDs share the same format.
Unexpected API behavior or cascading deletion could remove data belonging to other products.
Logging only responses provides no rollback, target attestation, or reliable reconciliation of what was deleted.
Waiting until the weekend may leave insufficient time to detect errors and use the 14-day restore window.
Run a preflight job that enriches each ID with object type, add-on name/version, site ID, and expected current state; reject the entire run on unknown, duplicate, site, or mismatched records. Then soft-delete a canary installation, verify the rest of that site and its other products remain intact, proceed in monitored batches, and reconcile results. Delay permanent deletion until retention requirements, authorization, backup coverage, and restoration procedures are explicitly confirmed.
Before running any deletion, resolve a small sample of the supplied IDs through the authoritative site-management inventory and compare each returned type and product identity with “Insight Legacy” add-on installation.
Any ID that resolves to a site, another add-on/product, an unknown object, or lacks authoritative type metadata proves the permanent-delete batch is unsafe as proposed.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave-based migration, but initially disable automatic quota reductions or add a per-service reduction freeze while validating parity and rollback behavior. Migrate the user-ID service only after testing replicated writes, reporting lag, and enforcement at the allocation boundary; retain legacy registration and a tested rollback path until each wave is proven stable.
The new manager can copy allocations without changing quota semantics or effective capacity.
Both managers can remain registered during migration, or equivalent shadow enforcement and rollback are available.
Reported usage is sufficiently complete, timely, and comparable across regions and services.
Automatic reductions cannot cause a service's legitimate burst usage to exceed its allocation.
Deregistering from the legacy manager does not remove an independent enforcement path or monitoring dependency.
Automatic reductions may reject writes for the user-ID service, including login/account operations, violating the no-user-visible-impact requirement.
Usage-reporting lag or regional replication inconsistency could make the new manager undercount usage and permit writes beyond the intended quota, or overcount and reject valid writes.
Migrating the user-ID database's enforcement path without a tested rollback could interrupt authentication globally.
A copied allocation may not represent current effective limits, causing an immediate quota breach during cutover.
Deregistration before parity is established could eliminate the only known-good enforcement or usage signal.
Use a staged shadow migration: dual-register services, mirror and compare usage and enforcement decisions while preserving legacy behavior, keep allocations frozen and reductions disabled, then canary enforcement and rollback before making the new manager authoritative. Handle user-ID separately with multi-region write-failure and authentication tests.
Inspect the new quota system's configuration/API and run a non-production simulation for one canary service whose reported usage stays below allocation, followed by a burst that reaches the current allocation.
If the allocation is reduced during the grace period or the burst is rejected because of the reduction, the proposed 'no user-visible impact' assumption is falsified; if reductions can be disabled and enforcement is unchanged, the mitigation is viable.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Retain Redis read-through caching, but do not use a fixed 15-minute TTL as the sole revocation mechanism. Consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected user/document/action entries, with a freshness SLO and short fallback TTL; also use request coalescing, fail-closed behavior, and canary monitoring for both latency and unauthorized decisions.
Permission events identify every affected user, document, and authorization scope, or can be mapped to cache keys.
Kafka event delivery and consumer processing complete within the required authorization-freshness window.
The permissions service's write event is emitted for document sharing, unsharing, account removal, and group-membership changes.
A bounded stale-authorization window is acceptable only if it does not permit material access after revocation.
A user unshared with a document, removed from an account, or removed from a group could retain access for up to 15 minutes.
Incorrect or incomplete event-to-key invalidation could create persistent authorization bypasses across all document-service replicas.
A popular document or action could cause a permissions-service thundering herd when many entries expire simultaneously.
Redis failures or timeouts must not silently degrade to an allow decision.
The replay-derived hit rate may not translate to the stated p95 under production key distribution, event traffic, and cache contention.

Populate an allow cache entry for a test user/document/action, revoke access through the normal API or integration, then immediately issue the same request through the document service and record the decision.
If the request remains allowed until the 15-minute TTL expires, the proposed cache is unsafe as designed and event-driven invalidation or another freshness mechanism is required.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not fully disable autovacuum or rely on a fixed weekly schedule for a 1.8 TB table with bulk deletes. Keep it enabled as a safety net, tune autovacuum thresholds and cost limits for `events`, and explicitly trigger or schedule a strongly throttled vacuum after bulk deletes; retain a bounded off-peak manual vacuum if weekly maintenance is still needed.
Dead-tuple production and vacuum throughput are stable enough for Sunday's window to be predictable.
The bulk deletes are small and are not themselves a major source of write-latency spikes.
A low-traffic window exists that is long enough for a throttled vacuum to finish.
Disabling normal autovacuum cannot cause PostgreSQL's anti-wraparound autovacuum to run later.
Weekly ANALYZE is frequent enough to prevent materially stale statistics.
Autovacuum already runs for many hours; a weekly cron vacuum could overlap business hours and reproduce or prolong the latency problem.
Large delete batches may create enough dead tuples to exceed safe thresholds before Sunday.
Without autovacuum, vacuum backlog or transaction-age emergencies receive no normal cleanup and may trigger disruptive anti-wraparound work.
Default vacuum cost settings may still generate unacceptable I/O even during the cron window.
Statistics can become stale between weekly runs, causing poor query plans.
Use continuous, throttled targeted autovacuum with appropriately low scale-factor/threshold values and conservative cost limits, then trigger a throttled vacuum soon after each bulk delete. This adapts to actual churn while spreading I/O; monitor dead tuples, vacuum backlog, database age, and latency before considering additional off-peak runs.
Compare existing autovacuum log start/finish timestamps and dead-tuple counts around one bulk-delete cycle; calculate the observed vacuum rate and extrapolate cleanup duration for the week's accumulated dead tuples.
If projected cleanup time exceeds the available 02:00-to-business-hours window, or bulk deletes can generate more dead tuples than that window can process, the weekly-only proposal is falsified.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but restrict promotion by replica region, verified replication state, and maximum acceptable lag; add reliable fencing and route applications through a dedicated database endpoint whose update is tested with existing connection pools. Do not claim Raft prevents split brain by itself, and validate acknowledged-write loss and end-to-end recovery time in network-partition game days before production automation.
A promoted West replica can serve writes within Rails timeout and latency budgets.
Orchestrator can identify the most up-to-date replica and safely verify binlog continuity.
Raft availability and quorum are independent of the failed database host or East network path.
Consul and Rails clients promptly replace pooled connections to the failed primary.
Recovered replicas can rejoin without incompatible binlogs, missing GTIDs, or topology corruption.
A partitioned but still writable old primary can form a dual-primary topology and diverge data.
Asynchronous failover can lose recently acknowledged East writes even if quorum approved the decision.
A West primary can cause connection, transaction, or pool timeout failures that exceed the one-minute objective.
Insufficient fencing or lag checks can promote a stale replica and then cause irreversible replication conflicts.
Consul propagation, stale resolver caches, or pooled connections may leave applications targeting the old primary after promotion.
Use guarded Orchestrator automation with an explicit candidate policy: prefer a healthy East replica, require verified lag/binlog eligibility, reserve West promotion for a declared disaster condition, fence the old primary, and update a stable database proxy or service endpoint. Semi-synchronous cross-region replication is a possible separate enhancement if the measured latency cost is acceptable.
Run one isolated game day that blocks all East-to-West database traffic, kills the East primary, and measure from failure injection to successful Rails reads and writes while recording failed or unacknowledged transactions, recovery duration, primary-host writability, and West-primary latency.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary remains independently writable, acknowledged writes are lost beyond the accepted bound, recovery exceeds 60 seconds, or normal Rails writes fail or materially breach latency/timeout limits through the promoted West replica.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver path, but do not allow an arbitrary CI-passing PCRE to enter the inline request path or automatically block globally after a fixed 10-minute observation period. Require a strict evaluation-time/CPU budget, reject unsafe regex constructs, preserve an independently controlled kill switch and atomic rollback, and validate benign traffic volume and latency during the log period before enabling blocking.
The WAF engine enforces a hard per-rule evaluation timeout and can safely terminate pathological PCRE execution.
Quicksilver updates are versioned and can be rolled back consistently across all PoPs within minutes.
CI's benign-request corpus is representative enough to detect likely false positives before global enforcement.
Log-mode evaluation has a bounded CPU and memory cost comparable to block-mode evaluation.
A global configuration update can be gated, audited, and reversed without waiting for the normal staged pipeline.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, degrade or halt all customer traffic because WAF evaluation is inline and proxies are already CPU-bound.
Ten minutes of match-volume observation may miss low-frequency false positives, false negatives, regional traffic differences, or application-specific behavior.
Automatic global blocking could deny legitimate requests across every customer immediately, with no safe mechanism to disable the rule quickly.
Configuration propagation or version skew could produce inconsistent enforcement across PoPs and make rollback unreliable.
The safety check may itself overload the request path if log mode materially increases latency or creates large match/event volumes.

Run each candidate PCRE against the production benign corpus and representative attack payloads using the production WAF engine, with a hard timeout, while measuring p99 evaluation latency and CPU time.
The proposal is falsified if any CI-passing rule exhibits superlinear execution, exceeds the proxy's defined per-request CPU/latency budget, or causes the corpus run to approach the timeout; otherwise this supports retaining the expedited path with the stated safeguards.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Keep amount as an integer count of minor units; KWD, BHD, and OMR fils fit naturally without changing the column type. Add or verify immutable currency-code storage, validate values against each currency's exponent, and update formatting/reporting logic to use that exponent. If range analysis requires BIGINT, plan a separately validated online schema change rather than combining it with this release.
The release process can update all code consumers atomically with the schema change.
No long-running transaction or old application instance will block or retain incompatible access during the ALTER TABLE.
The table and replicas have enough temporary space, WAL capacity, and lag tolerance for a full-table rewrite.
No unlisted reports, jobs, exports, or integrations directly reference orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the required storage contract rather than merely an integer minor-unit representation.
The pre-deploy migration renames amount before old pods are replaced, so checkout and other application requests can fail immediately.
Converting INTEGER to NUMERIC requires rewriting a roughly 900M-row table and can hold disruptive locks long enough to exceed the release window or violate the checkout SLO.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or disk space, and cause streaming-replica lag.
The three reporting jobs fail as soon as the rename commits unless they are separately gated or deployed first.
The NUMERIC(19,4) contract permits four-decimal fractional values even though the business field represents minor units, potentially allowing invalid data.
Retain orders.amount as an exact integer minor-unit amount and make currency-aware validation and presentation explicit. Store or join an immutable ISO currency code, map it to an exponent, and ensure serializers and reporting SQL format KWD, BHD, and OMR values with three decimal digits. This avoids schema locking, storage growth, semantic conversion, and rollout incompatibility; perform a range check before deciding whether an online BIGINT migration is ever needed.
At the intended deployment time, run the ALTER in a transaction with a short lock_timeout, then roll it back: BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4), RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; ROLLBACK;
A lock timeout or ALTER error while any normal application or reporting session is active falsifies the pre-deploy compatibility assumption and demonstrates that the migration cannot safely precede rolling replacement.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with a database-enforced atomic claim, ideally a unique redemption ledger, and use explicit claimed/redeemed/failed states. Perform payment outside the database transaction with a stable provider idempotency key, and define recovery/reconciliation for crashes, timeouts, and failed charges.
All concurrent redemption requests reach the same application process, despite the stated 4-12 replicas.
The process remains alive while checking, charging, and recording redemption.
The payment provider is idempotent for retries and payment ambiguity.
Coupon code uniqueness and an appropriate database index already exist.
A coupon can be safely marked redeemed before payment completion.
Requests routed to different replicas can both observe the coupon as available and redeem it.
A process crash releases only the in-memory lock, providing no durable protection or recovery record.
Marking the coupon before charging can permanently consume it when payment fails.
Retries after a timeout can create duplicate external charges without payment idempotency.
A test using concurrent calls in one process cannot exercise the cross-replica race.
Use an indexed conditional update or unique ledger insert to claim the coupon atomically in Postgres, then charge externally using an order-scoped idempotency key and reconcile the claim to redeemed or released.
Run two separate application processes with independent mutex maps against the same database, synchronize simultaneous redemption requests for one coupon code, and assert that exactly one succeeds.
If both processes succeed, or if the database records duplicate successful redemptions/charges, the process-local mutex is proven insufficient.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Retain streaming, but replace the single all-services rollout with a staged production canary followed by measured expansion. Upgrade servers sequentially while preserving Raft quorum, then enable streaming on a bounded client cohort and monitor CPU, network, update latency, stale results, errors, and lock/KV behavior before proceeding; retain and test a documented rollback path throughout the six-week window.
Consul agents and servers can be upgraded to 1.10 in a supported order without breaking the five-server Raft quorum.
Clients at the selected canary scope support streaming and can revert cleanly to blocking queries.
The 200-node staging result remains representative of production subscription volume and update rates.
Streaming preserves health-update freshness and correctness under network interruption and server failure.
The cluster has enough six-week capacity for canarying, observation, rollback rehearsal, and final rollout.
A simultaneous fleet-wide upgrade or setting change could disrupt the sole discovery cluster and leave no fallback.
Streaming regressions could serve stale or missing health updates, causing incorrect routing at service scale.
Insufficient production canary capacity could allow CPU or network growth to overwhelm the cluster during the holiday peak.
A mixed or unsupported server/agent upgrade sequence could threaten quorum or client compatibility.
