Add a unique constraint and expiration/recovery handling for abandoned reservations.
Run two redemption requests for the same unused coupon simultaneously through separate application processes or two Kubernetes replicas, using distinct orders, and record charge and database results.
If both requests succeed, the proposed process-local mutex is disproven; if exactly one claim succeeds, that validates the race fix only if the test also exercises a crash or timeout between charge and finalization.

required_observation: Any server still on the old build interprets the bit with the old meaning (dead code reactivated)
review_text:
Use a phased rollout: deploy the RLP-capable router build to all eight servers while clients continue leaving the bit unset, verify the exact build identifier on every server, and only then enable the bit in clients. Automate or record that verification, and define rollback ordering so clients stop setting the bit before any router is rolled back.
Every producer capable of setting the header bit is controlled and can be updated or held back.
One month of captured traffic is sufficient evidence that no dormant or intermittent producer sets the bit.
RLP-capable routers preserve identical behavior for orders with the bit unset.
All eight production routers will be verified as running the RLP-capable build before any client sets the bit.
Deployment and rollback can be coordinated despite the manual per-server process.
A client enabling the bit before all routers are upgraded would make an old router execute the retired Power Peg path.
A partial deployment or unnoticed build mismatch could create inconsistent routing behavior across production servers.
A rollback to an old router while clients still set the bit would reactivate Power Peg.
Traffic sampling may miss a dormant, rare, or out-of-band producer of the bit.

Run one fleet-wide script over the eight production hosts that prints each host's router binary hash or embedded build ID and compares it with the RLP release artifact.
Any server reporting a different or legacy build falsifies the safety of enabling the client bit at launch; all eight matching establishes the required rollout prerequisite.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a high-churn table without measuring vacuum throughput against dead-tuple creation. Keep autovacuum enabled, use table-specific cost and concurrency limits to spread its I/O, and convert bulk deletes into bounded, rate-limited batches; schedule supplemental vacuum during low traffic only if measurements show it is needed. Verify the result using write p99, dead-tuple growth, and vacuum completion time.
Dead-tuple production remains low enough for one weekly vacuum to finish and for the table not to accumulate severe bloat between runs.
The weekly vacuum's read and write I/O will not create a larger spike even at 20% of peak traffic.
Autovacuum is not needed for transaction visibility or other operational behavior beyond the explicitly scheduled vacuum.
The bulk deletes are already bounded or otherwise do not create lock, WAL, or index-maintenance bursts.
Grafana bloat metrics are sufficiently fresh and accurate to detect a developing vacuum backlog.
Disabling autovacuum can let dead tuples and index bloat accumulate faster than the weekly job can remove them, eventually increasing scans, index size, storage use, and write amplification.
A manual weekly VACUUM can itself become a multi-hour I/O event, simply moving the latency spike to Sunday rather than eliminating it.
If the job fails, is canceled, or runs behind schedule, there is no automatic cleanup safety net.
A single VACUUM does not return disk space to the operating system; severe bloat may require VACUUM FULL or another disruptive rewrite.
The proposal does not address delete batching, so retention jobs may still cause foreground WAL, lock, and index I/O spikes.
Use table-specific autovacuum cost limits and concurrency, plus bounded rate-limited deletes. Add a monitored, low-traffic vacuum or reindex procedure only when measurements show that normal autovacuum cannot keep up.
Before changing settings, record `n_dead_tup`, `n_live_tup`, `last_autovacuum`, `autovacuum_count`, and total table/index size from `pg_stat_user_tables` and `pg_class` at several intervals, then run a controlled `VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events` while measuring duration, I/O, and write p99.
If dead-tuple growth is substantial and the vacuum requires many hours or materially raises p99 even at low traffic, weekly manual vacuum is unsafe. If vacuum completes well within the low-traffic window and dead-tuple growth remains bounded, the proposal's core schedule is plausible, but autovacuum smoothing and delete batching are still safer.

required_observation: New system may see zero/incorrect usage during migration (reporting path not switched or broken)
review_text:
Keep the wave-based direction, but add a shadow/validation phase that compares legacy and new usage and quota decisions before each enforcement cutover. Migrate user-ID with an explicitly tested, reversible write-admission procedure, and initially disable automatic reduction for it or prove that grace-period and reporting guarantees are safe. Confirm that allocation copies include all overrides and policies, and remove legacy only after a dependency check and bounded rollback window.
The new system can receive complete, consistent, and timely usage reports from every region before it becomes authoritative.
Switching a service's registration also switches the enforcement path atomically, or the proposal provides an equivalent mechanism preventing split or stale decisions.
Allocation copies preserve all service-specific overrides, reservations, exemptions, and policy settings.
The automatic-reduction grace period is safe under delayed reporting, outages, seasonal usage, and regional replication lag.
A reversible user-ID enforcement cutover can be performed without causing inconsistent replicated writes or user-visible login failures.
If registration changes before reporting is validated, the new manager may enforce from stale or zero usage and reject valid writes or reduce allocations prematurely.
User-ID quota enforcement errors can block database writes during login and account operations, and regional replication may produce inconsistent cross-region outcomes.
A copied allocation may differ from the effective legacy allocation, immediately tightening or loosening user-ID storage admission.
Enabling automatic reductions for user-ID during telemetry gaps or abnormal low-usage periods could cause genuine capacity denials.
Deregistering services too early may leave operational consumers dependent on the legacy manager, while shutting it down without a tested rollback could eliminate recovery options.
Use shadow-and-validate migration: run the new manager in observation-only mode using the same usage reports, compare its projected decisions with legacy behavior, then perform independently reversible enforcement cutovers. For user-ID, use a dedicated readiness gate, regional canary or controlled validation, conservative allocation floors, and tested fail-open/fail-closed and rollback behavior before enabling reductions.
Replay a representative production history of user-ID usage, allocation changes, reporting delays, and regional lag through the proposed registration/cutover and automatic-reduction sequence, then compare the new manager's admission decisions with the legacy manager's actual decisions.
Any valid write rejected by the new manager, materially different effective allocations, or a reduction caused by delayed or incomplete reports would falsify the safety of the proposed cutover; exact agreement across the tested period would support it but not cover the production rollback path.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not alter and rename the existing column in the 900M-row table. Use an expand migration adding a BIGINT minor-unit column plus an explicit per-order scale, deploy backward-compatible dual writes, backfill in throttled batches, validate, and only then cut over reads and reporting.
The existing INTEGER values and their units are suitable for direct conversion to NUMERIC(19,4), despite the required 2- or 3-decimal scale.
The application and all writers can tolerate the ALTER's lock and rewrite duration.
Old application versions, queued jobs, and reporting consumers will all use the renamed representation immediately.
The NUMERIC(19,4) precision and scale match every currency and future write without rounding or overflow.
No indexes, constraints, foreign keys, or deployment mechanisms make the type alteration substantially more disruptive.
PostgreSQL will generally rewrite the table for an INTEGER-to-NUMERIC type alteration, causing prolonged locks, bloat, replica lag, statement timeouts, and likely deployment failure at 900M rows.
NUMERIC(19,4) does not document whether values are cents, three-decimal minor units, or another scale, so existing orders can be silently misinterpreted.
The rename plus same-PR application changes can break old pods, queued writes, external integrations, or reports that still reference orders.amount.
Converting or rounding monetary values during the rewrite can corrupt financial totals if the legacy column is not already the intended exact unit.
Transactional DDL only provides atomicity; it does not make the rewrite online, bounded in duration, or safe for concurrent traffic.
Add a nullable BIGINT amount_minor column and an explicit immutable scale (for example, 2 or 3) with an online schema migration. Release dual-write code compatible with both schemas, backfill indexed rows in small throttled batches while monitoring lag, validate counts/totals/samples, then switch reads and reports before a later release considers retiring the legacy column.
On a production-sized disposable PostgreSQL clone, record pg_class.relfilenode for orders, run BEGIN; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; COMMIT;, and compare the relation file and elapsed lock/rewrite metrics.
A changed relation file and materially long ALTER duration confirm that the migration rewrites the large table rather than being a metadata-only online change, falsifying the proposal's safety premise.

required_observation: Writes accepted in East but not replicated are lost/diverged after promotion (async replication)
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator and Raft as the failover mechanism, but do not enable unqualified promotion of any replica across regions. Configure explicit candidate eligibility, split-brain/fencing protections, and Consul/application health-routing integration; define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, including writes during detection and promotion. Validate that East application hosts can reliably use a West primary and that recovery completes within the one-minute objective.
East application hosts have production-grade network connectivity and acceptable latency to a West MySQL primary.
Orchestrator is correctly integrated with the application's Consul-based primary discovery and can atomically publish the new endpoint.
The deployment has fencing or equivalent protection against an isolated old primary continuing to accept writes.
Promoting a cross-region asynchronous replica will lose no writes that the product requires to retain.
All clusters use compatible MySQL 5.7 binary logging, Pseudo-GTID, credentials, and replication settings for Orchestrator recovery.
A 30-second reachability threshold can trigger failover during a transient partition while the East primary continues accepting writes, creating divergent primaries and irreversible data loss.
Asynchronous cross-region replication permits committed East writes to be absent from the West replica at promotion time; selecting the most advanced replica does not eliminate this RPO.
Promoting a West replica without verified East-to-West database routing or adequate client/network behavior can cause an extended application outage rather than sub-minute recovery.
Orchestrator's topology update alone does not guarantee that every Rails connection pool, Consul consumer, and connection-establishment path will follow the new primary.
Enabling automated recovery for all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can cause simultaneous or unsafe failovers during a regional event.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, uniquely identifiable writes, kill the East primary, and measure from failure detection through successful application writes while checking the old primary, selected replica, Consul endpoint, and write continuity.
The proposal is falsified if writes accepted by the old primary are missing after promotion, the old primary remains writable, East clients cannot write to the promoted replica within the required interval, or Consul/application traffic does not converge to the new primary.

required_observation: A weekly vacuum on a 1.8 TB table may not complete; wraparound leads to forced shutdown / read-only
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on the events table or rely on a weekly vacuum without measuring dead-tuple generation and vacuum completion time. Keep autovacuum enabled with events-specific vacuum cost pacing and tuned thresholds, coordinate controlled expiration deletes during low-traffic periods, and investigate partitioning if vacuum cannot keep pace. A regular VACUUM reuses space but does not return it to the operating system and may be inadequate against sustained delete and index-cleanup volume.
Dead-tuple creation and indexed-row deletion remain low enough for one weekly VACUUM to prevent unacceptable bloat.
The weekly VACUUM can complete before the next accumulation cycle without causing unacceptable I/O or latency.
The events workload is genuinely append-mostly rather than producing substantial delete volume or dead indexed rows.
Bulk deletes are bounded, off-peak, and do not recreate a large maintenance spike.
Storage latency, WAL, checkpoints, replication, and other maintenance are not contributing independently to the latency spikes.
Dead tuples and index bloat can accumulate for up to a week, increasing scan and write costs and potentially causing severe latency degradation.
Disabling autovacuum removes the feedback mechanism that responds when dead rows accumulate faster than expected.
A weekly VACUUM may be unable to finish within its window, leaving the table progressively less maintained.
Bulk deletes can generate substantial WAL and index I/O even when scheduled off-peak.
Grafana bloat monitoring alone may detect damage too late and does not measure vacuum lag, dead-tuple growth, or vacuum effectiveness.
Enable events-specific autovacuum with conservative vacuum_cost_delay and vacuum_cost_limit tuning, adjust per-table thresholds based on measured dead-tuple production, and schedule controlled expiration deletes during low traffic. Track dead tuples, vacuum duration, index growth, bloat, p99 latency, WAL/checkpoint activity, and device I/O wait; if vacuum cannot keep pace at approximately 25k inserts/s plus deletes, evaluate retention partitioning as the structural fix.
During one representative peak period, record the events table's dead-tuple estimate and index size at the start and end using SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relid)), pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(relid)) FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'events'; repeat after the normal maintenance interval while reviewing vacuum logs.
The proposal is wrong if n_dead_tup and index size rise continuously, the scheduled VACUUM cannot complete before the next cycle, or resulting bloat/scan latency exceeds the agreed limit; stable or declining metrics would support the weekly schedule.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not migrate job dispatch to Redis Pub/Sub: it is an at-most-once, non-durable transport, so subscriber disconnects or worker restarts can silently lose jobs while AOF does not provide message replay. Use Redis Streams with consumer groups, explicit acknowledgements, pending-entry recovery, and a tested retention/retry/DLQ policy, while retaining RabbitMQ until failure and recovery tests pass. Avoid running both systems as active independent consumers for payment and fulfilment jobs unless duplicate side effects are prevented.
Every job must survive worker crashes, pod termination, Redis client reconnects, and transient network failures.
Job processing is at-least-once and handlers can be idempotent or use deduplication.
AOF persistence and the existing Redis topology provide sufficient durability and availability for dispatch.
Subscribers can independently discover and recover all messages missed while disconnected.
The operational team can monitor and maintain Redis Streams pending entries, trimming, retries, and dead-letter handling.
Pub/Sub messages are not retained, so a disconnected or restarted worker loses queued jobs with no acknowledgement or recovery mechanism.
The proposed worker retry wrapper cannot retry a message that was never delivered, and repeated deployments make this failure routine.
Duplicate or split processing during dual operation could repeat payment-provider, fulfilment, email, or indexing side effects.
AOF persistence does not convert Pub/Sub into a durable queue and may still lose data under Redis or storage failure.
A Redis outage would affect both dispatch and existing caching/rate-limiting workloads, increasing blast radius.
Use Redis Streams on the already-operated Redis deployment for durable dispatch, with one consumer group per job type or worker role, XADD publishing, XREADGROUP consumption, XACK after successful handling, and explicit recovery of pending entries. Configure replication, persistence, maxlen/retention, retry/DLQ handling, dead-letter visibility, and idempotent handlers; migrate traffic gradually without allowing RabbitMQ and Redis Streams to execute the same jobs concurrently.
In a disposable Redis instance, publish one message to a Pub/Sub channel, disconnect the subscriber, publish a second message, then reconnect and inspect what the subscriber receives; repeat the equivalent test with a Redis Stream consumer group.
If the disconnected subscriber misses the message after reconnect, or the Stream test cannot recover and acknowledge it after consumer termination, the Pub/Sub proposal is falsified; successful Stream recovery supports the replacement.

required_observation: Single critical cluster with no fallback: fleet-wide enablement maximises blast radius
review_text:
Keep streaming as the preferred direction, but replace the fleet-wide rollout with a compatibility gate followed by a production canary and measured expansion. Before broad deployment, verify exact version support, preserve health-query semantics, exercise reconnects and rolling restarts, and define automatic stop/rollback thresholds for errors, stale results, CPU, and network load.
The exact production server and client versions support streaming and `use_streaming_backend` as proposed, without silently falling back to blocking queries.
The staging workload is representative enough for the reported 60% CPU reduction to hold in production.
Streaming preserves the required freshness, filtering, consistency, and reconnect behavior for every service.
All clients can be upgraded and configured compatibly within six weeks.
Each client can safely transition and roll back while the cluster remains its only discovery path.
A broad rollout exposes every service simultaneously to missed subscriptions, stale or incomplete health data, or reconnect storms, with no discovery fallback.
A version/configuration mismatch could disable streaming or fail subscriptions, potentially increasing load through reconnect or fallback behavior.
The production mix of query filters, payload sizes, and service churn may erase the staging CPU and network savings.
Unexpected disconnect, leader-change, or rolling-upgrade behavior could reduce update freshness or temporarily exceed cluster capacity.
The untested upgrade and rollback sequence could consume the six-week window or create an unsafe prolonged mixed-version state.
Use a staged migration: validate exact compatibility and semantics in staging; enable streaming for a small, representative production cohort; monitor CPU, network, freshness, error rate, reconnects, and BoltDB/Raft health through leader changes and server restarts; then expand by service cohort with explicit rollback gates. Complement this with low-risk query scoping or request coalescing if profiling shows substantial redundant traffic.
In staging, run a representative mix of production clients and health queries against upgraded 1.10 servers with streaming enabled, including a forced client reconnect and server leader change, while comparing it with the current blocking-query baseline.
The proposal is falsified if streaming produces stale, incomplete, incorrectly filtered, or unavailable health results, causes material reconnect amplification, or fails to show a substantial CPU and network reduction after accounting for payload and churn differences.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Do not change the existing v1 `id` field from number to string in place. Add an authoritative `id_string` field immediately, have the web app consume it, and introduce a versioned contract where the primary `id` is a string; retain the numeric v1 field temporarily with equality validation and a deprecation plan. Regenerated SDKs alone do not protect already deployed mobile versions or partner integrations.
All active consumers can tolerate a breaking change from numeric to string IDs within the proposed release window.
Existing Swift Codable and Kotlin/Moshi configurations can decode the new quoted value without model or decoder changes.
No partner or mobile client relies on numeric equality, sorting, arithmetic, or generated numeric types for `id`.
The API can deploy a versioned or additive response contract within two weeks.
All response paths can emit both identifiers consistently and validate their equality.
Older clients may reject the quoted `id` or deserialize it incorrectly, breaking order retrieval across roughly 40 integrations.
The web application's other JSON ingestion paths may still use ordinary `JSON.parse`, `Number`, or `parseInt`, leaving corruption unresolved.
Changing OpenAPI and regenerating SDKs does not update already released mobile binaries or independently maintained partner clients.
A supposedly unchanged numeric value can still be corrupted by clients before migration, and quoted values may fail automatic mobile decoding.
A changelog entry does not provide a compatibility window or prevent accidental use of the wrong field during migration.
Use an additive migration: add and document a required, authoritative `id_string` in existing responses, switch the web app to it, validate that it matches the legacy numeric value at serialization boundaries, and publish a versioned response in which `id` is a JSON string. Inventory and migrate mobile and partner consumers before deprecating the legacy numeric field.
Run a contract/inventory check against current v1 consumers and response paths: identify every client or integration that reads `id`, then test one representative old mobile decoder and the web ingestion code against a response where `id` is quoted while `id_string` is present.
The proposal is falsified if any active released client rejects or misreads the quoted `id`, or if the web app still loses precision outside the updated path; otherwise the additive migration remains necessary for compatibility even if the string representation is technically supported.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not change the existing `amount` column in place or reinterpret it as a new scale. Add a nullable `BIGINT amount_1000` column, populate legacy writes through a narrowly scoped trigger during the rolling deployment, migrate writers atomically, and backfill in measured batches with report queries using a compatibility expression until complete. Keep the old column unchanged for this release.
The 900M-row, 410 GB table can tolerate the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and full-table rewrite caused by the type alteration within the deployment lock budget.
NUMERIC(19,4) is semantically compatible with the application's required three-decimal minor-unit scale and all existing integer values.
A night deployment has enough spare database, WAL, I/O, and replica capacity to absorb the rewrite without violating checkout latency or the 99.95% SLO.
All writers and reporting queries can tolerate the atomic column rename and the transition between old and new application versions.
No historical, import, retry, or reporting path relies on the existing column's integer type or name.
The type alteration can rewrite substantially the entire 900M-row table while holding a strong lock, causing an outage or deployment failure.
The rewrite and rename can generate heavy WAL, storage pressure, replica lag, and degraded checkout latency even at night.
NUMERIC(19,4) does not establish the required 1,000-scaled integer semantics; incorrect interpretation can produce financial reporting errors.
Updating model, serializers, and reports in one PR does not handle mixed old/new pods during the rolling deployment.
Transactional DDL guarantees atomicity only, not bounded lock duration, low resource usage, or safe rollback after operational impact.
Use the additive nullable `amount_1000 BIGINT` migration, trigger legacy writes as `amount * 1000`, deploy exact scaled writers, and perform an online batched backfill with tested compatibility reporting.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed type alteration and rename with a realistic `lock_timeout`, while measuring lock wait, duration, WAL volume, and replica lag.
If the operation cannot complete within the deployment lock budget or causes unacceptable latency, WAL pressure, or replica lag, it is falsified; PostgreSQL's normal type-alteration rewrite would confirm that the in-place migration is unsafe.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep automated Orchestrator recovery, but initially restrict it to the main East-primary cluster and prefer an East-local replica for host failures; reserve West promotion for confirmed East-region failure. Add reliable fencing so an isolated old primary cannot accept writes, and define the acceptable asynchronous RPO before enabling promotion regardless of region. Validate the complete detection-to-reconnect-and-write path, including ambiguous commits, under one minute; pseudo-GTID simplifies topology but does not establish freshness or prevent data loss.
Orchestrator can complete detection, candidate selection, promotion, and topology publication within the remaining 25 seconds after its 30-second trigger.
A Raft quorum will remain available throughout East database failures.
Orchestrator can reliably distinguish the freshest candidate, or the business explicitly accepts asynchronous replication loss.
The old primary can be fenced automatically at the host, network, or MySQL-access layer.
East application instances can reconnect to a West primary and tolerate roughly 60 ms database RTT.
A network partition can produce dual writable primaries because Orchestrator consensus does not itself fence the old database.
Asynchronous promotion can lose acknowledged transactions; Raft and pseudo-GTID do not prevent this.
Selecting a West replica for an East host failure shifts every write across regions and may exceed latency or throughput limits.
Enabling recovery for all clusters simultaneously creates a correlated automation blast radius.
Consul updates or Rails connection recovery may finish after promotion, or retries may duplicate non-idempotent writes.

In staging, partition the primary from Orchestrator while keeping a database client connected; after 35 seconds, attempt writes through both the old primary and the advertised replacement, while timing when a new write succeeds.
The proposal is falsified if the old primary accepts a conflicting write after replacement promotion, or if end-to-end writable recovery takes longer than 60 seconds. Success requires automatic fencing or refusal of old-primary writes, exactly one authoritative writer, and timely service rediscovery.

required_observation: Applications stay in East and would write cross-region with high latency
review_text:
Keep Orchestrator and Raft as the failover mechanism, but do not enable unqualified promotion of any replica across regions. Configure explicit candidate eligibility, split-brain/fencing protections, and Consul/application health-routing integration; define and test the accepted asynchronous-replication RPO, including writes during detection and promotion. Validate that East application hosts can reliably use a West primary and that recovery completes within the one-minute objective.
East application hosts have production-grade network connectivity and acceptable latency to a West MySQL primary.
Orchestrator is correctly integrated with the application's Consul-based primary discovery and can atomically publish the new endpoint.
The deployment has fencing or equivalent protection against an isolated old primary continuing to accept writes.
Promoting a cross-region asynchronous replica will lose no writes that the product requires to retain.
All clusters use compatible MySQL 5.7 binary logging, Pseudo-GTID, credentials, and replication settings for Orchestrator recovery.
A 30-second reachability threshold can trigger failover during a transient partition while the East primary continues accepting writes, creating divergent primaries and irreversible data loss.
Asynchronous cross-region replication permits committed East writes to be absent from the West replica at promotion time; selecting the most advanced replica does not eliminate this RPO.
Promoting a West replica without verified East-to-West database routing or adequate client/network behavior can cause an extended application outage rather than sub-minute recovery.
Orchestrator's topology update alone does not guarantee that every Rails connection pool, Consul consumer, and connection-establishment path will follow the new primary.
Enabling automated recovery for all clusters without per-cluster safeguards can cause simultaneous or unsafe failovers during a regional event.

Run a controlled game day with continuous, uniquely identifiable writes, kill the East primary, and measure from failure detection through successful application writes while checking the old primary, selected replica, Consul endpoint, and write continuity.
The proposal is falsified if writes accepted by the old primary are missing after promotion, the old primary remains writable, East clients cannot write to the promoted replica within the required interval, or Consul/application traffic does not converge to the new primary.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep string serialization, but introduce it through a new API version or explicit content negotiation rather than changing every existing v1 response. Keep v1 available for legacy clients, migrate the web app immediately to the string-ID endpoint, publish a longer deprecation window for mobile and partner clients, and only regenerate SDKs after verifying backward compatibility and runtime decoding behavior.
Existing deployed clients are expected to tolerate an unannounced number-to-string response change.
Swift Codable and Moshi can be configured or are already configured to decode quoted Int64/Long values without source changes.
Approximately 40 partner integrations can upgrade their generated SDKs before the API response contract changes.
There is no separate v1 request-path or SDK type contract that would also require coordinated changes.
Clients can distinguish or negotiate a string-ID response before parsing it.
Stock Swift Codable decoding into Int64 rejects a JSON string, potentially causing order lookup and list failures in deployed iOS versions.
Moshi commonly rejects a quoted value for a Long property unless an adapter is configured, potentially crashing or failing Android responses.
Regenerating SDKs changes generated source types to String and can cause compile-time breakage for partner applications that cannot upgrade immediately.
Changing the v1 OpenAPI contract in place can invalidate existing generated documentation, mocks, tests, and integrations while providing no rollback path.
A two-week deployment window is too short for self-serve partners and store-update lag to adopt a breaking contract, extending the corruption problem or causing outages.
Add a string-ID representation under /v2 or an explicitly negotiated media type/header, retain the existing v1 representation during a negotiated deprecation period, and migrate first-party clients to it. At the same time, add compatibility tests and telemetry for response-format selection and decoding failures; do not alter ID generation.
Run one compatibility test matrix using the unchanged, currently deployed client versions and representative generated partner SDKs against a sample response containing "id":"1234567890123456789", decoding it as Swift Int64, Kotlin Moshi Long, generated OpenAPI int64/string SDK types, and JavaScript Number.
The proposal is falsified as a drop-in v1 change if any unchanged client fails decoding, changes the ID type, or produces an incorrect value; successful decoding alone does not address generated-source or partner rollout compatibility.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not perform a direct type alteration and rename on the 900M-row table in the pre-deploy job. Use an expand/contract rollout: add a new nullable or defaulted column, deploy dual-write/backfill code, backfill in bounded batches with rate limiting and replica-lag checks, validate reconciliation, then switch reads and only later remove the legacy column. Explicitly define the storage scale and currency-exponent rules, and verify capacity and rounding behavior before migration.
The existing integer values are all exactly representable under the new chosen scale and no business rounding or overflow behavior is being changed.
The pre-deploy migration can obtain an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and complete a full-table rewrite within the release window.
All application, reporting, and operational SQL can switch atomically from orders.amount to orders.amount_minor.
There is sufficient free disk, WAL capacity, and I/O headroom for rewriting roughly 410 GB of data and indexes.
The three reporting jobs tolerate a schema transition or can be deployed compatibly with the application.
ALTER COLUMN TYPE will rewrite the entire orders table and rebuild dependent indexes, causing a prolonged ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, latency spikes, transaction queuing, and likely missed checkout SLO.
The migration runs before old pods are replaced, so renaming amount to amount_minor can immediately break the currently running application and reporting jobs.
The transaction is atomic but is not instantaneous or safely rollbackable operationally; a rollback after a long rewrite can itself take substantial time and generate heavy WAL.
Streaming replicas may fall far behind, and the primary plus WAL/disk requirements could exhaust capacity or delay cutover.
NUMERIC(19,4) alone does not specify whether values are cents, three-decimal minor units, or a common scaled representation; incorrect interpretation can cause financial misstatement.
Use an online expand/contract migration with dual reads/writes and batched backfill, or retain the existing integer representation while introducing an explicit currency and scale/exponent abstraction. Validate the representation and maximum-value requirements before selecting BIGINT or NUMERIC storage.
On a production-sized or representative clone, run the proposed ALTER under a session that records lock duration, duration, WAL generated, and replica lag, while measuring checkout latency.
If the rewrite exceeds the deployment/maintenance window, blocks normal writes for a material interval, exhausts disk/WAL headroom, or causes replica lag beyond the cutover threshold, the proposal is disproven for this environment.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep Redis read-through caching, but do not rely solely on 15-minute expiration: consume permission-events to invalidate or refresh affected entries, and cap the risk of stale access with security-approved shorter TTLs. Before rollout, demonstrate the complete GET latency distribution under production-like key skew; an 85% hit rate means 15% of requests still miss, so the p95 will generally remain on the slow path unless misses are below 5% or the remaining call path is independently below budget.
A 15-minute stale-authorization window is acceptable for grants, shares, unshares, and account/group removal.
The logged 85% hit rate translates into at least 95% of requests completing under 120 ms; hit rate alone does not establish this.
permission-events is not needed for correctness because expiration is considered sufficient revocation handling.
Redis can serve the additional read traffic without material latency, hot-key contention, or cascading failure.
userId, docId, and action uniquely and safely identify the authorization decision, including all relevant group-membership context.
A revoked user can retain document access for up to 15 minutes, with especially serious exposure after HR-driven account or group removal.
The latency claim appears arithmetically inconsistent: with 15% misses, the overall p95 is likely still a permissions-service miss, not a 40 ms cache hit.
Cold starts, TTL synchronization, or hot documents can produce concurrent misses and overload permissions-service.
A Redis incident can eliminate the optimization or cause broad request failures unless cache-failure behavior is explicitly fail-closed.
Dashboards may show improved averages while the 120 ms p95 objective remains unmet.
Use event-driven invalidation and optionally a small per-pod L1 cache backed by Redis. Kafka events should remove or refresh entries affected by share, unshare, account, and group-membership changes; short TTLs remain a backstop, not the primary revocation mechanism. Prefetch or targeted warming may also be required to raise the effective cache-hit fraction above 95%.
Replay a representative 24-hour trace against a staging document service and Redis using the proposed key and TTL, then report the full GET p50/p95/p99 split by hit, miss, and permissions-service latency.
The proposal's estimate is supported only if end-to-end p95 is at or below 120 ms with production-like key skew and concurrent misses. If the 15% miss population remains above 120 ms, the 40 ms p95 claim is falsified regardless of the 85% aggregate hit rate.

required_observation: AOF does not make Pub/Sub durable; use Streams with consumer groups or keep a durable broker
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for payment webhooks or other durable job dispatch; AOF persistence does not persist Pub/Sub messages. Replace it with a durable queue mechanism such as Redis Streams with consumer groups, or retain RabbitMQ while simplifying its operations. Before migration, load-test at 300 jobs/s with worker crashes, Redis restarts, pending-message recovery, idempotent handlers, retention, and memory limits.
Jobs may be lost when publishers, subscribers, or Redis restart or when a subscriber is disconnected.
AOF persistence protects queued jobs; it does not replay Redis Pub/Sub messages.
Redis Pub/Sub delivery semantics match the required work-queue and competing-consumer semantics; in fact, every subscriber in a channel receives each message.
The existing worker retry wrapper provides durable retry and recovery after process failure.
One week of dual-running provides sufficient evidence for production reliability and data consistency.
Payment webhooks and fulfilment-triggering jobs can disappear, causing unpaid or unfulfilled orders.
Multiple workers subscribed to the same channel can all execute the same job, creating duplicate payments, emails, indexing, or fulfilment unless handlers are fully idempotent.
Workers redeployed several times per day create recurring acknowledgement gaps and message loss.
A Redis outage or failover can interrupt dispatch and destroy in-flight Pub/Sub messages, despite Redis being used for caching and rate limiting.
The team may decommission RabbitMQ based on superficial latency/throughput results without testing crash recovery, ordering, backlog, or retention behavior.
Use Redis Streams with consumer groups and explicit acknowledgement, pending-entry recovery, bounded stream length/retention, and dead-letter handling. Validate its durability and capacity under realistic failure tests; otherwise retain RabbitMQ and reduce operational burden through worker-library/configuration improvements, autoscaling, and centralized retry/DLQ monitoring.
Publish several uniquely identifiable jobs through Redis Pub/Sub while a subscriber is connected, terminate the subscriber, restart Redis, and verify whether the jobs can be recovered and processed exactly once or effectively once.
Messages published during disconnection or before Redis restart are absent after subscribers reconnect, and multiple subscribers each receive the same message; this falsifies Pub/Sub as a durable replacement for the existing queue.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Do not execute permanent deletion against an unvalidated generic ID list: first resolve every ID through a typed inventory/detail API and require that it identifies the intended legacy add-on installation, not a site or product. Stage the operation using the reversible `mark` mode where feasible, add preflight, authorization, checkpointing, bounded retries, and an explicit stop/rollback procedure, then permanently delete only the verified set before the deadline. Log object identity and response status without exposing customer data, and reconcile the final result against the source inventory.
The product team's list contains only add-on installation IDs and has not been accidentally combined with site or product IDs.
The platform exposes a reliable way to inspect each ID's object type and associated site before deletion.
`mode=mark` is reversible for these installations and does not affect other objects on the site.
The deletion API is idempotent and batch failures can be safely retried without duplicate or cascading effects.
Permanent deletion is required by the data-minimisation policy before backend shutdown, rather than merely soft-deleting or disabling the add-on.
A single site ID in the list could permanently delete the entire site, including unrelated products and data, with recovery requiring per-site backup restoration.
A stale, malformed, or incorrectly scoped ID list could delete a valid customer object that is not the retired add-on.
Partial batch failure or unsafe retry behavior could leave installations behind or produce an unclear completion state before shutdown.
The proposal's claim that permanent mode satisfies data-minimisation policy is not established by the supplied facts and may unnecessarily destroy recoverable data.
Logging raw responses could expose customer or site data if responses contain sensitive fields.
Run a typed, preflighted migration: reconcile the supplied IDs against the legacy add-on installation inventory, soft-delete the verified installations, verify the resulting state, and permanently delete only after an explicit completion check. Use a dry-run or test-site execution first, with a manifest of expected object IDs and a kill switch that halts on type, count, or site mismatches.
Resolve a representative sample of the product team's IDs through the platform's site/object inventory or detail API and inspect each object's type, installation identity, and parent site.
Every sampled ID is confirmed as the intended `Insight Legacy` add-on installation and maps to the expected site; any site, product, unknown, or mismatched object falsifies the proposal as written.

required_observation: The API cannot distinguish a site ID from an add-on ID; validate object type before deleting
review_text:
Replace bulk permanent deletion with an add-on-specific uninstall or type-validated soft deletion. Build an audited manifest of expected installation types and site mappings, reject ambiguous IDs, canary a small batch, verify traffic and cross-product impact, and defer purge until the rollback window closes or verified snapshots exist.
Every supplied ID uniquely identifies an add-on installation and cannot resolve to a site.
The deletion API performs strict object-type validation even when given an arbitrary ID.
Permanent deletion is authorized and satisfies all retention and rollback requirements.
The list is complete, current, and mapped to the correct sites.
A 2-second pause and on-call monitoring provide adequate detection and recovery.
A site or mismatched object ID could be permanently and irreversibly deleted.
One bad batch could destroy up to 30 installations before errors are noticed.
Incorrect or stale mappings could remove other products' data.
Permanent deletion eliminates the required 14-day application-level rollback path.
Logging responses alone may not provide sufficient audit, idempotency, or per-ID reconciliation.
Use an add-on-specific uninstall that disables execution and scheduled jobs while preserving a 14-day restore window. If unavailable, resolve and classify all IDs, reject non-installations, canary soft deletion, verify absence of backend traffic and unrelated data changes, then permanently purge only after sign-off or independently verified snapshots.
Using a documented dry-run or non-destructive lookup, submit one known site ID and one known add-on installation ID to the exact deletion resolver and inspect the returned object types.
The proposal is falsified if the resolver accepts or classifies the known site ID as deletable; strict rejection of the site and correct identification of the installation would support safety controls, though the full manifest would still require review.

required_observation: Need canary + automatic rollback, regex CPU/complexity limits or a linear-time engine
review_text:
Keep the expedited Quicksilver rollout, but do not make global blocking conditional only on aggregate match volume. Require bounded PCRE evaluation (complexity limits and a per-rule CPU/time budget), production-like load validation, and an automated rollback based on proxy latency, error rate, and false-positive indicators. Use a short 1% blocking canary with monitoring before global blocking, and aggregate or sample log-mode matches rather than performing unbounded per-request logging; this can still complete within the one-hour objective.
The CI corpus and benign-request set provide sufficiently representative coverage for newly disclosed attacks.
Quicksilver propagation and rule activation are atomic and fail-safe across all proxies and regions.
The WAF engine can enforce per-rule evaluation limits and disable a rule without taking down the proxy.
There is sufficient CPU headroom to evaluate the new rule on every request during log mode.
A reliable, low-latency signal exists for distinguishing attack matches from false positives.
A catastrophic-backtracking or otherwise pathological regex could consume proxy CPU, increase request latency, or cause an outage even when it does not block requests.
A false-positive rule could block legitimate customer traffic globally after only ten minutes of insufficiently targeted monitoring.
Attackers could deliberately generate high match volume, making log mode itself expensive or obscuring benign false positives.
Inconsistent Quicksilver updates could leave some machines blocking while others only log, complicating incident response.
CI payload coverage may miss the disclosed exploit variant, allowing the rule to be published without detecting the actual attack.

Run a production-like peak-load benchmark with the candidate rule enabled in log mode on the proxy, comparing CPU utilization, p95/p99 latency, request errors, and match-processing cost against the same workload without the rule.
The proposal is falsified if log-mode evaluation materially reduces available CPU or violates the proxy's latency/error SLOs, or if match volume causes unsafe logging overhead; negligible overhead and stable latency support proceeding with the expedited path.

required_observation: Long-lived branch + single cut-over: no incremental rollout, comparison or rollback
review_text:
Retain the clean domain package, but replace the three-month big-bang cutover with staged, contract-tested migration. First capture current behavior, then migrate one representative rule family at a time through compatibility adapters and production shadow comparisons; delete legacy code only after all 37 plans and side effects have remained equivalent for a defined observation period.
All historical behavior can be represented by the proposed Plan, Subscription, Invoice, ProrationPolicy, and TaxRule model without service-specific exceptions.
Invoice equality is a sufficient equivalence criterion despite payments, tax calls, retries, notifications, and mutable context dependencies.
A three-person team can build, validate, coordinate merges, and cut over a 14k-LOC replacement while concurrent billing changes continue.
The five services can adopt the new package's API simultaneously without incompatible release or deployment requirements.
A clean rewrite can achieve parity before any new plan is added, despite only about 22% existing test coverage.
A missed proration, grandfathering, time-zone, or rounding behavior could produce incorrect customer invoices at cutover.
Side effects can duplicate or disappear even when generated invoice documents match.
Concurrent billing PRs will target code that is being replaced, increasing merge conflicts and making the final rollback boundary enormous.
Without characterization tests, the team may interpret legacy behavior incorrectly and codify it as a bug.
The old and new implementations will be maintained throughout the three-month period regardless of the stated goal to avoid two implementations.
Use a strangler migration around the same billing-core target: build immutable inputs and invoice golden tests, extract proration first behind an adapter, shadow invoices without external side effects, then migrate tax, payment, invoicing, subscriptions, and notifications incrementally. Preserve legacy adapters for exceptional plans and remove old paths only after parity and operational rollback criteria are met.
Time-box a model spike by encoding the three most irregular grandfathered plans, including their proration and tax cases, and compare their outputs against captured legacy invoices across start, upgrade, downgrade, cancellation, and mid-cycle changes.
If any legacy behavior cannot be expressed without service conditionals, ad hoc BillingContext flags, or manual special cases—or if matching outputs requires more than roughly one day of adaptation—the proposed clean model is not a general replacement and the big-bang plan should be rejected.

required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Keep the read-through cache direction, but add permission-event-driven invalidation, a short safety TTL, single-flight/coalescing for concurrent misses, and strict rules against caching timeouts or ambiguous errors. Gate rollout on measured end-to-end p95, not hit rate: with roughly 99 ms of non-permission latency and a 180 ms check, an 85% hit rate would produce about 126 ms if hit/miss requests were uniformly mixed, so the stated ~40 ms p95 is unsupported.
A 15-minute stale-allow window is acceptable for unshare, account deletion, and group-membership revocation.
permission-events contains sufficient information to identify and invalidate every affected authorization key.
Redis has enough capacity, isolation, and network headroom for the expected key cardinality and peak request rate.
The check API clearly distinguishes false from timeout/error, and the document service can safely fail closed.
Requests are sufficiently uniform for the replayed hit-rate distribution to predict production p95.
Users retain document access for up to 15 minutes after an unshare, account removal, or group-membership removal.
The uncached request tail may still push p95 above 120 ms; 85% hit rate alone does not support the claimed ~40 ms result.
Synchronized expirations create a miss storm capable of degrading both Redis and the permissions service.
Undefined error semantics can cause outages to be cached as denials or, if fail-open, create unauthorized access.
Popular documents or users can create Redis hot keys and uneven expiry traffic across the cluster.

Run a representative 24-hour trace replay through the proposed cache, using captured permissions-check latency and measured Redis operations, then report total end-to-end latency percentiles segmented by hit/miss rather than deriving p95 from hit rate.
The proposal is falsified if overall p95 remains above 120 ms or any freshness/error-safety test shows unauthorized allow decisions beyond the accepted bound; a p95 comfortably below 120 ms confirms the latency benefit but not revocation safety.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Keep amount as an integer count of minor units; KWD, BHD, and OMR fils fit naturally without changing the column type. Add or verify immutable currency-code storage, validate values against each currency's exponent, and update formatting/reporting logic to use that exponent. If range analysis requires BIGINT, plan a separately validated online schema change rather than combining it with this release.
The release process can update all code consumers atomically with the schema change.
No long-running transaction or old application instance will block or retain incompatible access during the ALTER TABLE.
The table and replicas have enough temporary space, WAL capacity, and lag tolerance for a full-table rewrite.
No unlisted reports, jobs, exports, or integrations directly reference orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) is the required storage contract rather than merely an integer minor-unit representation.
The pre-deploy migration renames amount before old pods are replaced, so checkout and other application requests can fail immediately.
Converting INTEGER to NUMERIC requires rewriting a roughly 900M-row table and can hold disruptive locks long enough to exceed the release window or violate the checkout SLO.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or disk space, and cause streaming-replica lag.
The three reporting jobs fail as soon as the rename commits unless they are separately gated or deployed first.
The NUMERIC(19,4) contract permits four-decimal fractional values even though the business field represents minor units, potentially allowing invalid data.
Retain orders.amount as an exact integer minor-unit amount and make currency-aware validation and presentation explicit. Store or join an immutable ISO currency code, map it to an exponent, and ensure serializers and reporting SQL format KWD, BHD, and OMR values with three decimal digits. This avoids schema locking, storage growth, semantic conversion, and rollout incompatibility; perform a range check before deciding whether an online BIGINT migration is ever needed.
At the intended deployment time, run the ALTER in a transaction with a short lock_timeout, then roll it back: BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4), RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; ROLLBACK;
A lock timeout or ALTER error while any normal application or reporting session is active falsifies the pre-deploy compatibility assumption and demonstrates that the migration cannot safely precede rolling replacement.

required_observation: Vacuum also prevents transaction ID wraparound (freezing), not just bloat
review_text:
Do not disable autovacuum on a 1.8 TB table receiving 25k inserts/s and bulk deletes. Keep it enabled for anti-wraparound protection, but raise its per-table trigger threshold and throttle its I/O cost; explicitly vacuum only during a bounded low-traffic window after confirming that the required work completes within that window. Monitor dead-tuple growth, vacuum duration, bloat, transaction age, and business-hour I/O before and after rollout.
A weekly VACUUM can scan and compact all pages made dead by the bulk deletes within the Sunday window.
The bulk-delete volume is small enough to maintain a bounded dead-tuple population.
Cron execution is monitored and will not be silently skipped, overlap, or terminate a vacuum on every run.
The table's transaction ID age will remain far from wraparound thresholds.
Most visible latency is caused by vacuum-generated I/O rather than delete WAL, checkpoint, or filesystem behavior.
Disabling table autovacuum also disables its anti-wraparound safety, creating a path to an emergency, prolonged vacuum and severe database impact.
A weekly vacuum may not complete on a 1.8 TB table, causing dead tuples and bloat to grow continuously between runs.
A failed cron invocation can leave the table without autovacuum indefinitely.
Overlapping manual VACUUM jobs can multiply storage-engine and WAL I/O.
Regular VACUUM reclaims dead space for reuse but does not return space to the operating system, so filesystem-level bloat may remain or worsen.
Use per-table autovacuum settings: keep `autovacuum_enabled=true`, increase `vacuum_threshold` and `vacuum_scale_factor` so routine vacuuming is not triggered too frequently, and use table-specific `vacuum_cost_delay`/`vacuum_cost_limit` values to reduce I/O bursts. Run a separately scheduled off-peak `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` only if measurements show one is needed, with a single-job lock, a strict completion deadline, alerting, and escalation that restarts autovacuum if the schedule fails.
Sample hourly during one week: `SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, age(datmin) FROM pg_stat_user_tables s JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=s.relid WHERE s.relname='events';`, and correlate the result with vacuum logs and disk I/O.
If dead tuples or transaction age continue rising throughout the week, a vacuum cannot complete within the low-traffic window, or vacuum-related I/O still overlaps business hours, the weekly-off-peak assumption is disproven.

required_observation: ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
review_text:
Do not perform the direct ALTER-and-rename migration. Use an expand-and-contract rollout: add a compatible representation, deploy readers/writers and all three reports for backward compatibility, backfill and reconcile in bounded batches, then switch and remove the legacy field. Define the conversion explicitly—reinterpreting existing cents as four-decimal values would change their meaning unless values are multiplied appropriately.
Existing orders.amount values are interpreted as cents and can be converted to the target three-decimal representation without changing business totals.
The target representation is actually three decimal places; NUMERIC(19,4) silently introduces a fourth precision choice.
The ALTER can complete without blocking production traffic beyond the release and SLO constraints.
No consumers beyond the identified application code and three reporting jobs access orders.amount.
The migration and application rollback can be coordinated despite the 25-minute rolling deployment.
PostgreSQL can rewrite the roughly 900M-row table and hold an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes while the pre-deploy job runs.
The rename is visible before old pods are replaced, causing currently running code and any unupdated consumers to fail or read the wrong field.
A long rewrite can generate substantial WAL and I/O, cause streaming-replica lag, and exhaust disk or deployment capacity.
Treating existing cents as NUMERIC(19,4) without conversion could produce values 100 times larger than the intended amount.
The migration may exceed the release window; transactional DDL prevents partial schema changes but does not make the operation online.
Prefer an expand-and-contract migration, ideally retaining efficient integer minor units with explicit currency scale, or adding a NUMERIC target column without removing the old column. Deploy compatible dual-read/write code, backfill with bounded batches while handling concurrent updates, validate totals and nullability, migrate the three reports, and only then retire the legacy column. This avoids an unbounded blocking rewrite and provides a rollback window.
On a production-sized clone, run the proposed ALTER under a representative write workload and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL volume, and statement behavior; also insert a legacy value such as 100 and verify the intended converted result.
If ALTER requires a full rewrite and blocks normal reads or writes materially beyond the deployment/SLO budget, the proposal is unsafe; if value 100 is not explicitly converted to the intended three-decimal amount, the proposed type change is semantically wrong.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Keep the expedited global log-to-block model, but require a versioned atomic bundle, explicit benign-regression and PCRE complexity budgets, and automated promotion based on block volume, 5xx rate, latency, and CPU—not match volume alone. Preserve the previous bundle for immediate rollback, and define who can terminate or reverse the release; add a brief 1% block canary only if it still meets the one-hour objective.
A globally activated log-mode rule is propagated atomically and consistently within minutes.
Ten minutes of telemetry is timely and representative enough to expose false positives and operational regressions.
The CI suite includes benign requests in addition to attack payloads and runs before expedited activation.
Rule compilation and matching have enforced CPU, memory, and worst-case backtracking limits.
Block-mode changes can be rolled back globally within minutes without waiting for another configuration deployment.
A high-cost PCRE consumes substantial proxy CPU in log mode before match-count monitoring detects degradation.
A benign traffic pattern absent from CI causes a global false-positive outage when block mode begins.
Match volume alone can remain normal while latency, 5xx responses, or regional traffic distributions deteriorate.
A non-atomic Quicksilver update can produce mixed rule versions or activate block mode before every proxy has validated the bundle.
Telemetry delay or concurrent updates can cause unsafe promotion or rollback to an unintended bundle.
Use the proposed global log window as the emergency safety gate, but combine it with deterministic pre-activation limits and automated multi-signal promotion: global log for 5–10 minutes, immediate rollback on any safety threshold breach, then block at 1% and 100% if latency and traffic permit. This is safer than relying on a fixed ten-minute timer while remaining within the disclosure-hour target.
Replay a representative benign and adversarial request corpus through the candidate rule in log mode on a production-like proxy at measured peak request rate, comparing CPU and p99 latency with the rule disabled.
The design is viable only if worst-case evaluation stays within an agreed CPU and latency budget and no unbounded backtracking occurs; materially higher p99 latency, CPU saturation, or pathological evaluation time falsifies the claim that log mode is a safe universal first stage.

required_observation: Use expand/contract: new column, dual-write, batched backfill, later drop
review_text:
Do not run this migration on the 410-GB table before deployment. Use an additive transition: add a nullable three-decimal-capable column or a separate canonical representation, deploy currency-aware dual writes, backfill in throttled primary-key batches, and switch reports only after reconciliation. Retire the legacy column later.
Every active report or application query is blocked throughout the ALTER, and the operational platform explicitly tolerates that outage.
Old application pods will not reference or write to the column named amount after the pre-deploy migration renames it.
A currency-specific conversion rule exists for historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values; preserving the stored integer does not itself normalize minor-unit scales.
NUMERIC(19,4) is intentionally compatible with all consumers and will not introduce a four-decimal minor-unit interpretation.
The PostgreSQL instance has enough free disk, WAL capacity, and maintenance time for a full-table rewrite.
INTEGER-to-NUMERIC conversion requires rewriting roughly 900M rows while holding an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes for hours or longer.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or filesystem capacity, and create replication lag or disk pressure.
Renaming amount before replacing old pods can cause immediate unknown-column failures during the 25-minute rolling deployment.
Atomic DDL only guarantees commit or rollback; it does not make an operation nonblocking, short, or operationally safe.
A nightly schedule does not mitigate a schema-level outage and conflicts with the 99.95% monthly checkout SLO; rollback would require another expensive rewrite or recovery process.
Add a nullable canonical column, preferably BIGINT in thousandths only if currency is explicitly available, or NUMERIC with a deliberate three-decimal scale. Avoid rewriting existing data: deploy compatible dual-write code first, then backfill small indexed batches with rate limits, lag monitoring, reconciliation, and completion criteria. Update reports after all rows and writers are verified, and remove the legacy column in a later release.
In one database session run BEGIN; SELECT amount FROM orders LIMIT 1. In a second session run SET lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); then ROLLBACK.
A lock_timeout error confirms that ordinary reads prevent the proposed migration from starting; if it unexpectedly succeeds, that only shows no lock contention at that instant and does not demonstrate that the 410-GB rewrite is operationally acceptable.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Do not repurpose the bit for a launch-critical release without an explicit protocol-version migration and rollback design. Prefer adding a versioned field through the coordinated release; if the deadline makes that impossible, use an out-of-band eligibility mechanism or keep the bit unused until every router and relevant gateway/client can be upgraded and verified atomically.
Every producer of orders to the router, including gateways, tools, replays, and external clients, has been exhaustively inventoried.
One month of traffic is representative and no legitimate message can set the bit during rollback or mixed-version operation.
The protocol owner can formally transfer the bit from Power Peg to RLP without compatibility or audit requirements.
RLP eligibility always fits a single bit and does not require independent acknowledgment or version negotiation.
No rollback, replica, delayed queue, or archived order can expose an RLP-flagged message to a router version that interprets it as Power Peg.
After clients start setting the bit, rolling back to the current router binary could make the allegedly retired Power Peg path reachable, potentially misrouting orders.
The eight manually deployed servers can temporarily run mixed versions; an RLP order reaching an old server could be mishandled.
The traffic sample can miss infrequent producers, historical/replayed messages, malformed input, or deployments outside the observed period.
Removing the old code in the same release increases regression risk and may eliminate a straightforward rollback target.
Without build attestation and post-deploy verification, operators cannot reliably prove that all servers contain the RLP-capable build.
Use a server-side configuration keyed by an existing stable property such as authenticated client/order class, so no wire semantic is reused, while retaining the unused bit as reserved. If per-order selection is mandatory, complete the coordinated schema/version change and stage clients only after all routers pass compatibility verification.
In a non-production environment, send one otherwise valid order with the header bit set to the currently deployed router build and observe whether it invokes the Power Peg path rather than rejecting or ignoring the bit.
If the current build ignores or rejects the bit, the stated rollback incompatibility is reduced; if it invokes Power Peg, the rollout and any rollback involving old binaries are unsafe.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not execute the direct type alteration and rename in the pre-deploy job. Replace it with a phased expand/dual-write/backfill/switch/contract rollout, using an explicitly defined three-decimal representation and a compatibility window; enable the new currencies only after reconciliation and replica-lag validation.
The existing integer values can be interpreted using a persisted, reliable currency code.
The required maximum precision is three decimal places, not four.
All old and new code, jobs, and queries can tolerate a staged schema transition.
The release environment can provide enough disk and WAL capacity for a new column and batched backfill.
There is a rollback path and operational monitoring for replication lag, lock waits, and data mismatches.
PostgreSQL may rewrite the 900M-row table and hold a strong lock during ALTER TABLE, blocking the 1,200 writes/s peak and likely violating checkout SLO.
The same-migration rename breaks pods, reporting jobs, exports, ETL, and any raw SQL still referencing orders.amount.
NUMERIC(19,4) creates an undocumented four-decimal contract and does not solve how existing integers map to major or minor units for each currency.
A full historical conversion may misinterpret legacy amounts, corrupt totals, or produce inconsistent values across paths.
Generating substantial WAL and I/O can cause replica lag, storage pressure, and rollback difficulty before the new application is available.
Use an expand-and-contract migration: add a new fixed-scale representation (preferably BIGINT with a documented currency-specific scale, or NUMERIC(19,3) if the API stores major units), deploy dual reads/writes, backfill in rate-limited batches, reconcile totals, switch reports and checkout, then remove the old column after the compatibility window. This avoids an unbounded table rewrite in the release job and makes rollback possible.
On a representative staging clone, run the proposed ALTER with a short lock_timeout and measure lock acquisition, duration, WAL generation, and replication lag.
If it cannot acquire the lock promptly or produces prolonged strong-lock blocking, substantial WAL, or unacceptable replica lag, the proposed one-migration approach is disproven for this release; even successful completion would still not remove its mixed-version rename risk.

required_observation: A network partition (not a host failure) can trigger promotion in the other region
review_text:
Retain automated Orchestrator recovery, but do not promote an arbitrary or West-region replica based only on Raft quorum and 30-second unreachability. Restrict promotion to a prevalidated, sufficiently caught-up East replica where possible, require explicit fencing or STONITH of the old primary, and test the complete 30-second detection-to-write-path timing. Validate Consul integration and application reconnect behavior, and explicitly account for data loss inherent in asynchronous replication.
The old primary is reliably fenced or otherwise prevented from accepting writes after being declared unreachable.
A candidate replica's replication lag is within an explicitly approved data-loss bound at promotion time.
An East-region replica remains reachable and is preferred for a single-East-host failure; cross-region promotion is an intentional fallback.
Orchestrator's Raft quorum is not treated as a substitute for MySQL primary fencing.
Consul updates and Rails connection handling cause applications to route to the promoted primary within the required time.
An isolated but still-live old primary can continue accepting writes, causing split-brain and divergence.
Asynchronous replication can lose committed transactions even when the promoted replica has the highest observed position.
A transient East network fault can trigger an unnecessary promotion and outage or make West promotion unexpectedly slow.
A West promotion may exceed the one-minute objective because of 60 ms RTT, discovery propagation, and application reconnection.
Pseudo-GTIDs simplify identity and positioning but do not eliminate the need to verify replication state, lag, and write fencing.

Run a controlled network partition between the old East primary and Orchestrator while leaving it able to serve client connections, then verify whether it is fenced before the replica is promoted and whether any writes made on the old primary are lost or divergent.
If the old primary continues accepting writes, or the test produces acknowledged writes that are absent from the promoted replica, the proposed safety claims are falsified.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for payment webhooks or other durable job dispatch; AOF persistence does not persist Pub/Sub messages. Replace it with a durable queue mechanism such as Redis Streams with consumer groups, or retain RabbitMQ while simplifying its operations. Before migration, load-test at 300 jobs/s with worker crashes, Redis restarts, pending-message recovery, idempotent handlers, retention, and memory limits.
Jobs may be lost when publishers, subscribers, or Redis restart or when a subscriber is disconnected.
AOF persistence protects queued jobs; it does not replay Redis Pub/Sub messages.
Redis Pub/Sub delivery semantics match the required work-queue and competing-consumer semantics; in fact, every subscriber in a channel receives each message.
The existing worker retry wrapper provides durable retry and recovery after process failure.
One week of dual-running provides sufficient evidence for production reliability and data consistency.
Payment webhooks and fulfilment-triggering jobs can disappear, causing unpaid or unfulfilled orders.
Multiple workers subscribed to the same channel can all execute the same job, creating duplicate payments, emails, indexing, or fulfilment unless handlers are fully idempotent.
Workers redeployed several times per day create recurring acknowledgement gaps and message loss.
A Redis outage or failover can interrupt dispatch and destroy in-flight Pub/Sub messages, despite Redis being used for caching and rate limiting.
The team may decommission RabbitMQ based on superficial latency/throughput results without testing crash recovery, ordering, backlog, or retention behavior.
Use Redis Streams with consumer groups and explicit acknowledgement, pending-entry recovery, bounded stream length/retention, and dead-letter handling. Validate its durability and capacity under realistic failure tests; otherwise retain RabbitMQ and reduce operational burden through worker-library/configuration improvements, autoscaling, and centralized retry/DLQ monitoring.
Publish several uniquely identifiable jobs through Redis Pub/Sub while a subscriber is connected, terminate the subscriber, restart Redis, and verify whether the jobs can be recovered and processed exactly once or effectively once.
Messages published during disconnection or before Redis restart are absent after subscribers reconnect, and multiple subscribers each receive the same message; this falsifies Pub/Sub as a durable replacement for the existing queue.

required_observation: Use a new field/bit or remove old code everywhere first; add deploy verification / kill switch
review_text:
Keep the bit-reuse direction, but do not enable clients based solely on one month of observed traffic. First audit every client and gateway path that writes or interprets the bit, deploy the new router build to all eight servers with artifact verification, and stage activation with shadow metrics, a kill switch, and explicit mixed-version testing before clients set the bit.
No current, archived, dormant, external, failover, replay, or recovery component sets or interprets the header bit.
All router nodes and relevant recovery processes will run the RLP-capable build before any client sets the bit.
Older routers preserve unknown header bits, so mixed-version operation is safe during staged deployment.
RLP eligibility and all required routing data already exist; a new message field is genuinely unnecessary.
RLP failure can be contained without exposing orders to divergent routing, duplicate execution, or loss of service.
A dormant or external client can set the retired bit and unintentionally activate RLP or incompatible semantics.
Manual deployment can leave servers on different builds, producing inconsistent routing with no prompt detection.
Early client activation can send RLP requests to unprepared routers, causing rejects, latency spikes, or incorrect order handling.
Removing the Power Peg code may eliminate latent behavior relied on by diagnostics, replay, or recovery tooling if the bit is not actually unreachable.
A new RLP failure path without tested fallback, rate limits, or a kill switch can harm order execution under adverse liquidity or latency conditions.

Perform a repository, binary-interface, configuration, and client inventory search for the exact header bit mask and legacy Power Peg flag across all client, gateway, replay, recovery, and external integration sources.
Any current or dormant component that sets, clears, or branches on the bit falsifies the 'provably unused' premise and blocks direct reuse without a compatibility plan; a complete audit finding no such use confirms that specific premise.

required_observation: Dry run / canary batch / verification of the ID list
review_text:
Do not permanently delete directly from the supplied list. First inventory-check every ID and assert that it resolves specifically to an installed “Insight Legacy” add-on, recording its site and current state; abort on any mismatch.
