required_observation: Invalidate from permission-events (or versioned keys); TTL only as backstop
review_text:
Retain Redis read-through caching, but do not use a fixed 15-minute TTL as the sole revocation mechanism. Consume `permission-events` and invalidate affected user/document/action entries, with a freshness SLO and short fallback TTL; also use request coalescing, fail-closed behavior, and canary monitoring for both latency and unauthorized decisions.
Permission events identify every affected user, document, and authorization scope, or can be mapped to cache keys.
Kafka event delivery and consumer processing complete within the required authorization-freshness window.
The permissions service's write event is emitted for document sharing, unsharing, account removal, and group-membership changes.
A bounded stale-authorization window is acceptable only if it does not permit material access after revocation.
A user unshared with a document, removed from an account, or removed from a group could retain access for up to 15 minutes.
Incorrect or incomplete event-to-key invalidation could create persistent authorization bypasses across all document-service replicas.
A popular document or action could cause a permissions-service thundering herd when many entries expire simultaneously.
Redis failures or timeouts must not silently degrade to an allow decision.
The replay-derived hit rate may not translate to the stated p95 under production key distribution, event traffic, and cache contention.

Populate an allow cache entry for a test user/document/action, revoke access through the normal API or integration, then immediately issue the same request through the document service and record the decision.
If the request remains allowed until the 15-minute TTL expires, the proposed cache is unsafe as designed and event-driven invalidation or another freshness mechanism is required.

required_observation: In-process mutex does not serialise across replicas
review_text:
Replace the in-process mutex with a database-enforced available/pending state machine and pass a stable idempotency key to chargeOrder. Atomically claim a coupon with a conditional update; only the request that changes state may charge, and retries must return the existing redemption result rather than charge again. Add a cross-process integration test, not only an in-memory concurrent-call test.
All redemption requests can be coordinated through the same Postgres database.
The in-process mutex would be shared by every request, which is false with four to twelve Deployment replicas.
The existing single-process test is representative of the client retry path.
chargeOrder can be coordinated by serializing execution, despite being an external side effect.
Postgres uniqueness or conditional updates can enforce one successful claimant.
Concurrent requests routed to different pods can both observe an unused coupon and both charge, continuing the financial loss.
A process crash after charging but before setting redeemedAt permanently permits another redemption.
A client retry after an ambiguous two-second timeout can charge twice even if the original process completed.
The Map and cleanup logic can leak mutex entries or leave incorrect state under exceptional concurrency.
The proposed test passes in one process while providing no protection for the actual production topology.
Add redemption status and a stable request/order idempotency key, then claim the coupon using an atomic conditional update such as UPDATE ... SET status='pending', redemption_id=?, order_id=? WHERE code=? AND status='available'. Execute the idempotent charge under that claim, finalize it conditionally, and have retries look up and resume or return the existing result. This coordinates all pods, makes ownership durable, and addresses post-charge timeout retries; rollout should be expedited with the smallest safe schema and service changes this week.
Run two concurrent redemption requests for one fresh coupon through two different pod instances, with the first call delayed between the read and charge, and inspect coupon state plus charge-provider idempotency records.
The proposal is wrong if both instances report successful claims or the provider receives two charge attempts for the same coupon/order; a shared database state machine should produce one claim and at most one provider charge.

required_observation: Rename breaks the old app version still serving during the rolling deploy
review_text:
Do not run this migration on the 410-GB table before deployment. Use an additive transition: add a nullable three-decimal-capable column or a separate canonical representation, deploy currency-aware dual writes, backfill in throttled primary-key batches, and switch reports only after reconciliation. Retire the legacy column later.
Every active report or application query is blocked throughout the ALTER, and the operational platform explicitly tolerates that outage.
Old application pods will not reference or write to the column named amount after the pre-deploy migration renames it.
A currency-specific conversion rule exists for historical KWD, BHD, and OMR values; preserving the stored integer does not itself normalize minor-unit scales.
NUMERIC(19,4) is intentionally compatible with all consumers and will not introduce a four-decimal minor-unit interpretation.
The PostgreSQL instance has enough free disk, WAL capacity, and maintenance time for a full-table rewrite.
INTEGER-to-NUMERIC conversion requires rewriting roughly 900M rows while holding an AccessExclusive lock, blocking reads and writes for hours or longer.
The rewrite can generate substantial WAL, consume temporary or filesystem capacity, and create replication lag or disk pressure.
Renaming amount before replacing old pods can cause immediate unknown-column failures during the 25-minute rolling deployment.
Atomic DDL only guarantees commit or rollback; it does not make an operation nonblocking, short, or operationally safe.
A nightly schedule does not mitigate a schema-level outage and conflicts with the 99.95% monthly checkout SLO; rollback would require another expensive rewrite or recovery process.
Add a nullable canonical column, preferably BIGINT in thousandths only if currency is explicitly available, or NUMERIC with a deliberate three-decimal scale. Avoid rewriting existing data: deploy compatible dual-write code first, then backfill small indexed batches with rate limits, lag monitoring, reconciliation, and completion criteria. Update reports after all rows and writers are verified, and remove the legacy column in a later release.
In one database session run BEGIN; SELECT amount FROM orders LIMIT 1. In a second session run SET lock_timeout = '100ms'; ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE NUMERIC(19,4); then ROLLBACK.
A lock_timeout error confirms that ordinary reads prevent the proposed migration from starting; if it unexpectedly succeeds, that only shows no lock contention at that instant and does not demonstrate that the 410-GB rewrite is operationally acceptable.

required_observation: Use an atomic DB operation (conditional UPDATE / unique constraint / row lock)
review_text:
Replace the process-local mutex with a database-enforced atomic claim, ideally a unique redemption ledger, and use explicit claimed/redeemed/failed states. Perform payment outside the database transaction with a stable provider idempotency key, and define recovery/reconciliation for crashes, timeouts, and failed charges.
All concurrent redemption requests reach the same application process, despite the stated 4-12 replicas.
The process remains alive while checking, charging, and recording redemption.
The payment provider is idempotent for retries and payment ambiguity.
Coupon code uniqueness and an appropriate database index already exist.
A coupon can be safely marked redeemed before payment completion.
Requests routed to different replicas can both observe the coupon as available and redeem it.
A process crash releases only the in-memory lock, providing no durable protection or recovery record.
Marking the coupon before charging can permanently consume it when payment fails.
Retries after a timeout can create duplicate external charges without payment idempotency.
A test using concurrent calls in one process cannot exercise the cross-replica race.
Use an indexed conditional update or unique ledger insert to claim the coupon atomically in Postgres, then charge externally using an order-scoped idempotency key and reconcile the claim to redeemed or released.
Run two separate application processes with independent mutex maps against the same database, synchronize simultaneous redemption requests for one coupon code, and assert that exactly one succeeds.
If both processes succeed, or if the database records duplicate successful redemptions/charges, the process-local mutex is proven insufficient.

required_observation: Revocations (unshare/offboarding) remain effective until TTL expiry
review_text:
Keep the shared Redis cache direction, but do not use a plain 15-minute TTL or claim p95 improvement from an 85% hit rate. Add event-driven invalidation with race protection, shorter TTLs for deny decisions, per-key single-flight, and explicit fail-closed behavior; measure end-to-end p95 by hit and miss before expanding the rollout. If testing still leaves the miss path above the request budget, move authorization decisions to an event-fed local read model.
A 15-minute stale authorization window is acceptable for grants and revocations, which is unlikely without an explicit security bound.
Redis and the permissions service can meet latency and availability requirements at projected cardinality and peak traffic.
The 85% and 78% replay figures use comparable request populations and denominators.
A permissions-service miss can complete within the remaining endpoint budget.
Feature-flagged rollout traffic is representative and dashboards will identify miss-path latency and errors.
Revoked access can remain authorized for up to 15 minutes because there is no invalidation consumer.
The 15% miss population may determine p95, so the asserted approximately 40 ms p95 is unsupported and could remain above 120 ms.
Concurrent misses can stampede the permissions service, especially during Redis outages or a cold cache.
Caching all decisions for the same long TTL can delay legitimate access after share or other grant changes.
Redis failure behavior is unspecified and could accidentally fail open or create an uncontrolled permissions-service surge.
If the required effective hit rate cannot be demonstrated above 95% or the miss path cannot be made reliably sub-100 ms, use Kafka-fed authorization snapshots or read models in each pod, with Redis only as shared transport or storage where appropriate, plus safe cold-start and lag handling.
Replay the 24-hour access-log trace through a cache simulator with a 15-minute TTL, using measured cache-hit, permissions-service, Redis, and document-service latencies, and report end-to-end p95 split by hit and miss.
The proposal is falsified if the 85% hit-rate scenario still produces endpoint p95 above 120 ms, or if the miss-path service latency cannot fit within the remaining request budget.

required_observation: Additive field (id_str) or new version with deprecation window
review_text:
Do not change the existing v1 `id` field from number to string in place. Add an authoritative `id_string` field immediately, have the web app consume it, and introduce a versioned contract where the primary `id` is a string; retain the numeric v1 field temporarily with equality validation and a deprecation plan. Regenerated SDKs alone do not protect already deployed mobile versions or partner integrations.
All active consumers can tolerate a breaking change from numeric to string IDs within the proposed release window.
Existing Swift Codable and Kotlin/Moshi configurations can decode the new quoted value without model or decoder changes.
No partner or mobile client relies on numeric equality, sorting, arithmetic, or generated numeric types for `id`.
The API can deploy a versioned or additive response contract within two weeks.
All response paths can emit both identifiers consistently and validate their equality.
Older clients may reject the quoted `id` or deserialize it incorrectly, breaking order retrieval across roughly 40 integrations.
The web application's other JSON ingestion paths may still use ordinary `JSON.parse`, `Number`, or `parseInt`, leaving corruption unresolved.
Changing OpenAPI and regenerating SDKs does not update already released mobile binaries or independently maintained partner clients.
A supposedly unchanged numeric value can still be corrupted by clients before migration, and quoted values may fail automatic mobile decoding.
A changelog entry does not provide a compatibility window or prevent accidental use of the wrong field during migration.
Use an additive migration: add and document a required, authoritative `id_string` in existing responses, switch the web app to it, validate that it matches the legacy numeric value at serialization boundaries, and publish a versioned response in which `id` is a JSON string. Inventory and migrate mobile and partner consumers before deprecating the legacy numeric field.
Run a contract/inventory check against current v1 consumers and response paths: identify every client or integration that reads `id`, then test one representative old mobile decoder and the web ingestion code against a response where `id` is quoted while `id_string` is present.
The proposal is falsified if any active released client rejects or misreads the quoted `id`, or if the web app still loses precision outside the updated path; otherwise the additive migration remains necessary for compatibility even if the string representation is technically supported.

required_observation: Disable/guard auto-reduction for critical services until reported usage is validated; alert on drops
review_text:
Keep the phased migration, but exempt the user-ID service from automatic quota reduction or configure a conservative floor based on measured peak usage, replication lag, and operational growth. Validate this behavior under write load before cutover, and retain legacy reporting or an equivalent rapid rollback path until the new system is proven stable.
The new quota system supports a per-service exemption, fixed floor, or equivalent override for automatic reduction.
Reported user-ID usage includes all distributed writes and is sufficiently current across regions.
Current allocations have enough headroom for normal peaks and cross-region replication lag.
An allocation reduction can be detected and reversed before production writes are rejected.
Automatic reduction below actual user-ID usage could cause login-related database writes to be rejected globally.
Regional reporting lag could make usage appear low, trigger reduction, and then expose the replicated database to quota-exceeded failures.
A single user-ID quota incident could prevent authentication or account updates for all users.
Deregistering from the legacy manager without a tested rollback may remove the recovery path needed during regional instability.
Migrate ordinary services in waves as proposed, but use a protected cutover for user-ID: maintain redundant reporting, disable or constrain reclaim for that service, test quota decisions with production-shaped load, and only then switch enforcement.
In a production-like test, drive user-ID usage to its current peak plus replication lag, allow the new system's grace period to elapse, and verify whether its allocation is reduced below actual usage and whether a subsequent cross-region write is rejected.
Any reduction below the protected usage floor, or any rejected write, falsifies the claim that enabling automatic reduction for user-ID is safe without an override.

required_observation: Existing typed clients (Int64/Long decoders, generated SDKs) break on a string
review_text:
Keep serializing `id` as a decimal string in the long term, but avoid a breaking type change across all existing v1 clients. Introduce a versioned response, or temporarily add an `id_string` field while preserving numeric `id`; let the web app adopt the safe representation immediately and announce a v1 deprecation deadline.
Most active iOS, Android, and partner clients update their generated SDKs or models before or shortly after the API change.
Existing generated SDKs treat the change from numeric to string as a breaking type change.
No service, proxy, cache, logging pipeline, or downstream system coerces the new string back through a JavaScript number.
The API can deploy a versioned response or backward-compatible alias within two weeks.
Strict v1 clients tolerate an additional response field if an alias strategy is used.
Released iOS models declaring Int64 may reject the quoted ID instead of decoding it.
Kotlin, Moshi, and generated partner SDK clients may fail to decode the changed type or produce null/default IDs.
A breaking v1 change strands users who do not update and approximately 40 partner integrations.
Regenerating SDKs and adding a changelog does not protect already deployed clients.
Any JavaScript consumer left on numeric `id` will continue displaying corrupted IDs.
Add a versioned response where `id` is a string and update OpenAPI for that version. If strict-client testing shows that an extra field is tolerated, retain numeric `id` temporarily and add `id_string`; deploy the web app against `id_string`, track adoption, and remove the legacy field only after a published migration deadline and compatibility checks.
Decode a v1 response containing "id":"1234567890123456789" with the exact released iOS decoder and one representative generated partner SDK.
If either decoder reports a type mismatch, returns no model, or maps the ID to null/default rather than the exact value, the proposed breaking v1 rollout is unsafe.

required_observation: Pub/Sub messages are lost when no subscriber is connected (deploys); no acks/redelivery
review_text:
Do not use Redis Pub/Sub for jobs: AFS/AOF persistence does not persist Pub/Sub messages for disconnected subscribers, and an in-worker retry wrapper cannot recover a message that was never delivered. Instead, simplify and harden RabbitMQ with a minimal topology, quorum queues for critical work, standardized idempotent handlers, graceful worker draining, and automated upgrades; consider Redis Streams only through a separately tested migration pilot.
That AOF makes Pub/Sub messages durable while subscribers are unavailable.
That job delivery is optional or can be reconstructed reliably from another source.
That every subscriber is continuously connected and processing each message exactly once.
That running RabbitMQ and Redis paths simultaneously will not cause duplicate side effects.
That sub-millisecond latency and high throughput imply the needed delivery semantics.
Payment, fulfillment, email, or indexing events can be silently lost during worker restarts, deployment, network partitions, or Redis failover.
A transiently healthy subscriber may acknowledge or attempt processing immediately before crashing, with no broker-side redelivery guarantee.
Dual-running paths can send the same job to both systems unless deduplication is proven, risking duplicate payment or fulfillment effects.
Treating Redis cache and rate-limit pressure as isolated becomes unsafe once job loss or restart pressure is coupled to those services.
Decommissioning RabbitMQ after a week would remove the only tested replay path for poison jobs, delayed retries, and DLQ investigation.
Reduce operational burden in place: standardize a small RabbitMQ queue/exchange topology, use quorum queues for critical durable jobs, implement explicit retry/DLQ streams or queues, require idempotency for all side effects, add graceful draining for frequent deployments, and automate node replacement and upgrades. This directly targets the reported toil without replacing at-least-once delivery with fire-and-forget messaging.
In a non-production Redis instance, subscribe to a test channel, publish 1,000 uniquely numbered payloads, terminate the subscriber before it can process them, restart it, and compare received IDs; also inspect Redis persistence and restart behavior.
The restarted subscriber receives zero or only a small number of the previously published messages, proving that AOF does not provide queued recovery and falsifying the durability assumption. Delivery while continuously subscribed would validate only transport performance, not failure safety.

required_observation: Log mode still executes the regex; a slow/backtracking rule hurts CPU globally
review_text:
Retain Quicksilver-based acceleration, but classify rules by confidence and deploy high-confidence signatures directly to block while broad rules use log mode and selected-PoP canaries. Before rollout, enforce regex complexity limits and per-rule CPU/latency budgets; automatically revert on proxy health, customer error-rate, or match-distribution thresholds, with a pretested global kill switch.
Passing the fixed CI corpus is strong enough to bound catastrophic false positives across production traffic.
All proxies have enough spare CPU to evaluate new log-mode rules during peak traffic without degrading TLS or HTTP processing.
Quicksilver provides sufficiently fast, atomic, version-consistent mode changes and global rollback.
Central match-volume telemetry is timely and complete enough to detect harmful rules within the ten-minute window.
A safe precompiled PCRE pattern or equivalent timeout mechanism can prevent catastrophic backtracking.
A globally blocked false positive could immediately disrupt traffic for many customers before the log-mode signal is detected.
A complex regex could cause pathological backtracking, raising request latency and exhausting CPU across edge proxies.
Delayed or partial Quicksilver propagation could leave some PoPs exposed or produce inconsistent enforcement.
Ten minutes of log mode leaves the newly disclosed attack unblocked during the observation period.
Aggregate match volume may conceal a severe false positive affecting a small customer or a concentrated real attack.
Use a risk-tiered expedited rollout: immediately block narrowly scoped, high-confidence exploit signatures, while logging broad rules and selectively canary-blocking them by PoP. Promote broad rules using production health and false-positive thresholds, rather than making a single global decision based only on aggregate match volume.
Run the exact candidate regexes through the production PCRE engine against a representative peak-traffic trace containing sampled benign requests and all CI attack payloads, comparing shadow evaluation with the rules disabled.
The proposal is falsified if even a small candidate set causes backtracking or exceeds the proxy's allocated CPU/p99 latency budget, or if observed benign matches indicate a plausible customer-wide false positive; acceptable overhead and expected-only attack matches support the rollout.

required_observation: Auto-reduction after grace period can cut a critical service below its real usage
review_text:
Keep wave-based migration and user-ID-last, but add shadow-mode decision comparison, explicit exit criteria per wave, and independently reversible cutover controls. Do not enable automatic quota reduction on the first authoritative cutovers: validate reporting completeness and grace-period behavior first, then enable it service by service; dashboards alone are not safety controls.
Copying an allocation preserves its effective value, unit, and reset/grace-period semantics in the new system.
Deregistering a service immediately redirects all usage reports and enforcement checks to only the new manager.
Usage reporting is complete and timely enough that automatic reduction cannot mistake missing telemetry for low usage.
The new manager's decisions are consistent across regions before user-ID begins relying on them.
Service owners can detect and reverse a bad cutover before user-ID writes are affected.
A missing or delayed report may be treated as low usage and trigger an inappropriate allocation reduction.
Deregistration can create an enforcement gap if old and new registrations do not update atomically.
Semantic differences in grace periods or allocation units can cause premature capacity reclamation.
User-ID replication may apply different quota decisions across regions.
A single quota mistake can reject account writes globally, making the wave difficult to reverse.
Usage/allocation dashboards may display apparently valid data while omitting stale, duplicated, or rejected reports.
Use a staged strangler design: run the new manager in shadow mode, compare every prospective accept/reject and allocation-reduction decision with the current authority, and promote one low-risk service at a time behind reversible flags. Keep user-ID shadowed through the final quarter and cut it over only after regional lag, failover, and partition tests; preserve a time-boxed rollback path before shutting down legacy.
Replay historical and synthetic low-usage, missing-report, stale-report, threshold-crossing, and grace-period-boundary events through both managers and compare accept/reject and allocation-reduction decisions.
The proposal is supported only if decisions match for all valid telemetry and the new system demonstrably fails safe—never reducing allocation or rejecting writes—during missing, stale, or divergent telemetry; any silent discrepancy or unsafe fallback falsifies readiness.

required_observation: Permanent mode removes the recovery window; use soft delete (mark) first
review_text:
Do not execute permanent deletions from an unvalidated ID list. Resolve every ID to an Insight Legacy installation, reject unknown or site IDs, canary the operation in a non-production environment, then use soft deletion in bounded batches with per-ID status, monitoring, and a tested rollback plan; permanently purge only after the restoration requirement is resolved and separately approved.
The product-team list is complete and contains no site IDs or unrelated object IDs.
The deletion endpoint does not validate object type or scope of the requested IDs.
Deleting an installation object does not cascade-delete the site or unrelated products.
Permanent deletion cannot be undone through the platform and only site-by-site backup restoration remains available.
Data-minimization policy does not require immediate physical erasure before the backend shutdown.
A single site ID or misclassified ID could permanently delete an entire customer site.
A systematic inventory or parsing error could cause irreversible, large-scale damage.
Unexpected cascades could remove unrelated products, directly violating the customer-data constraint.
Logging responses cannot distinguish a successfully deleted wrong object from a correct deletion.
The 14-day restoration window may be unusable after backend shutdown, leaving soft deletion operationally complex but permanent deletion with no recovery.
Build a preflight manifest that resolves each ID to its object type, counts installation/site/unknown matches, and fails closed on any unexpected result. Then mark a small representative cohort, verify affected sites and unrelated products, and proceed in bounded batches with resumability, explicit per-ID outcomes, and rollback. Use permanent deletion only as a later, independently authorized cleanup step after retention and recovery requirements are established.
Inspect the deletion API contract and run a non-destructive, authorized schema/type check using one known Insight Legacy installation ID and one known site ID, confirming whether the endpoint rejects wrong object types before deletion.
The proposal is falsified if the endpoint accepts arbitrary site and installation IDs without type validation, or if the preflight cannot reliably classify the supplied list; that demonstrates that batched permanent deletion lacks the required safety boundary.
